results.text:
Among the tales handed down in the Vales of Anduin, some trace the existence of the great black wolves to an ancient practice of the Orcs of the mountains. Deep within the remotest dens, the Orcs are said to have discovered a strain of wolves whose cubs grow far more swiftly than those of other packs. They seize them at birth, feed them plentifully and subject them to cruel training until they are able to bear warriors upon their backs. The largest become the mounts of chieftains, while the others are taught to follow trails and pursue the enemies of the Orcs. According to this tradition, their ferocity springs from the ill-treatment they endure and from the habit of killing instilled in them by their masters.

The elders also say that, beneath their fearsome appearance, these animals retain the ordinary instincts of wolves. They acknowledge the authority of the strongest and may be brought to heel by one who succeeds in overcoming them without killing them. Some hunters even believe that the mere presence of a man capable of taking the shape of a bear is enough to inspire lasting submission in them, so greatly do they fear the mighty beasts of the forests. A Warg separated from its riders and raised far from the Orcs would thus eventually recover the ways of a wild animal, and might be taught to guard a dwelling or accompany a herd. The malice attributed to it would be chiefly a lingering consequence of the masters to whom it once belonged.

The men of the vales know of the great wolves that sometimes come down from the mountains in the company of Orc-bands. Their accounts describe powerful beasts, able to cover great distances, recover an old trail and move through woodland with remarkable stealth. Hunters know that their presence may be betrayed by unusually large footprints and by howls unlike those of ordinary wolves. Wargs often gather in substantial packs, and some are sturdy enough to carry an Orc warrior. Families living near the paths used by such bands retain the memory of their attacks upon livestock and travellers.

You also know a tradition according to which the Orcs command their Wargs through a language of cries and growls. The animals are said to have learnt to recognise these sounds during their training, while their own howls enable them to relay a rider's orders throughout the pack. Hunters who offer this explanation point out that their coordinated attacks almost invariably appear to be directed by a leader, generally mounted upon the largest beast. They therefore conclude that a pack deprived of this guide loses its cohesion and soon scatters. Some guardians of the mountain passes consequently believe that the surest defence is to bring down the riders first, then allow the creatures, bereft of command, to withdraw of their own accord.

The traditions of the Beornings distinguish Wargs from the wolves that naturally inhabit the mountains and forests. These great canids possess considerable strength, a keen sense of smell and hearing capable of detecting the slightest movement. Some are large enough to bear an Orc warrior, and their long strides make them dangerous pursuers of travellers attempting to escape on foot. Hunters' accounts describe them as tenacious trackers, able to recognise signs of passage and cross difficult ground. Their presence is especially feared when several individuals move together.

You also know that Wargs understand far more than ordinary wolves. They communicate through howls and growls to which their fellows respond, and can act in concert without a rider directing their every movement. The Beornings know of their alliance with the Orcs, but distinguish the packs that accompany warriors from the mountains from those that roam the wild lands on their own account. The accounts passed down to young hunters dwell upon this intelligence: a Warg may temporarily abandon a pursuit, go around an obstacle or rejoin its companions before returning to its prey.

results.text:
The Beornings preserve a detailed knowledge of Wargs, sustained by hunting tales, the watch kept over mountain passes and encounters with the servants of the Shadow. They know that these creatures possess a language of their own, through which they exchange warnings, gather their fellows and agree upon common courses of action. Their alliance with the Orcs rests upon shared interests and upon their hostility towards the peoples who dwell in the vales and wooded lands. Some Wargs serve as mounts, while others accompany armed bands to scout the paths, pursue fugitives or fall upon the flanks of a company. The packs retain their own leaders and can act independently of their allies.

The traditions of those who guard the vales attach great importance to the way in which Wargs conduct a hunt. They may separate while following a trail, seek favourable passages to outflank their adversaries and come together again as they approach an obstacle. Their cries enable several individuals to alter their movements without losing contact with the pack. They also recognise the strength of an organised defence and may postpone an attack until an opponent becomes isolated. Beornings familiar with these creatures know that howls heard at a distance may herald concerted movements, even when no Warg is yet in sight.

The memory of those who protect the passes also recalls that Wargs remain dangerous after an Orc-band has disappeared. A pack that loses its riders retains the ability to choose a route, recognise the tracks of its enemies and pursue an undertaking already begun. Its conduct depends upon its own decisions no less than upon the alliances it maintains.

results.text:
The oldest traditions of the Beornings draw a careful distinction between natural wolves, Wargs and the other wolf-like creatures that serve the powers of the Shadow. Ordinary wolves hunt and live according to the necessities of their kind; Wargs possess an intelligence and a language that enable them to deliberate, form alliances and pursue designs of their own. The most respected accounts ascribe to them a malevolent will that is strengthened, but not wholly explained, by their association with the Orcs. Their collective organisation belongs to their own nature: they acknowledge their leaders, gather to decide upon an undertaking and may choose either to fight beside an Orc-band or to range the wild lands alone.

Those who guard the passes also know the differences between the habits of particular packs. Some occupy a valley or the approaches to a mountain for a considerable time; others follow the movements of Orc warriors and travel great distances in their company. Wargs recognise the routes taken by travellers, the places where a path narrows and the obstacles that hinder escape. Their coordination allows them to test a defence, spread out and concentrate their attack upon a less well-protected part of a company. A withdrawal may be the outcome of a collective decision, and a pack that appears to have scattered retains the means to gather swiftly again. Such behaviour explains the caution of experienced hunters when they discover several trails converging upon the same passage.

Certain Beorning traditions trace the appearance of these creatures back to the ancient corruption of living things by the powers of the Shadow. They tell of wolves whose nature was altered until they acquired a malice and an intelligence foreign to their original stock. Other accounts distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves of the Elder Days, to which Elven tales attribute a different spiritual nature. Beornings acquainted with these traditions know that outwardly similar great wolves may conceal beings of different kinds. Above all, they recognise Wargs by their language, their organisation and their ability to plan undertakings with the Orcs while preserving their independence.

results.text:
The stories handed down among Beffraen families sometimes tell of black wolves that leave the mountains and forests when their own lands grow too poor to sustain them. These animals are said to descend into the low valleys and marshes, where their size and strength enable them to pursue larger prey than ordinary wolves. The elders account for their unusual appearance by the harsh conditions of the lands through which they travel: beasts that survive the cruellest winters grow more massive and develop a thick, dark coat resistant to damp. Their ferocity would be no more than that of predators driven by hunger, and the accounts of their cruelty would come from men who encounter them on the outskirts of their encampments.

A belief current among certain hunters holds that these great wolves dread deeply waterlogged ground. Their weight would prevent them from crossing the peat-bogs and muddy channels which the people of the country negotiate by paths familiar to them. Families settled near the waters therefore regard the marshes as a natural defence against such animals. The tales maintain that a pack quickly loses a traveller's trail when he crosses a channel and reaches spongy ground, for scents are said to disperse in the mud and footprints disappear beneath the water. A man who knows the passages between the reed-beds could therefore escape these wolves almost certainly, even when they have pursued him for several hours.

Beffraen hunters know the tales of great wolves that accompany Orcs in the eastern reaches of Eriador. These beasts possess remarkable strength and can cover great distances before seeking shelter. Their presence is sometimes revealed by deep prints in soft ground, claw marks along narrow passages, or the remains of prey abandoned near wooded ground. Hunters familiar with animal movements observe that these great wolves frequently travel in company and seem to favour paths that give their paws firm purchase. Their alliance with the Orcs is known through travellers' accounts, even among communities that seldom encounter the creatures themselves.

You also know an explanation passed down among fishermen and hunters of the wetlands: Wargs are said to be wolves that have become dependent upon the mountain lands in which they are reared. Their senses would enable them to follow a trail over stony paths and dry ground, but marshes would so confuse their bearings as to render them almost blind to the movements of men. Some elders maintain that the howls exchanged by a pack chiefly express the difficulty its members have in finding one another when separated by water or dense vegetation. A pursued company could therefore use the channels and marshes to disrupt these animals for a long time, since their cohesion would depend more upon their sense of smell than upon any shared understanding of their movements.

Beffraen traditions give the name Wargs to the great malevolent wolves which the tales associate with Orcs and the wild lands of Eriador. Their size and power exceed those of ordinary wolves, and some can carry a warrior upon their backs. Hunters know of their keen sense of smell, acute hearing, and ability to follow a trail over a long distance. The prints of their great paws may be recognised in soft ground when sufficiently clear, although they retain the principal features of the tracks left by canids. Their presence in a pack increases the danger they pose to travellers and isolated groups.

You also know that Wargs are capable of acting together and of communicating through howls whose meaning goes beyond the ordinary calls of wild animals. Their intelligence enables them to recognise obstacles and choose passages favourable to their movements. The Beffraens who preserve accounts of encounters with these creatures know that water and difficult ground can slow a pursuit, but that their size does not prevent them from overcoming every obstacle in their path. Hunters' skills remain useful for identifying their tracks, distinguishing several individuals, and understanding the general direction of their movements.

Beffraens acquainted with the traditions concerning Wargs distinguish these creatures from natural wolves by their intelligence and their ability to communicate in a language of their own. Travellers' and hunters' accounts attribute to them a collective organisation that goes beyond the ordinary habits of wild packs. Wargs can agree upon a movement, exchange warnings, and choose a common undertaking. Their alliance with the Orcs is ancient, but their gatherings acknowledge leaders of their own, and a pack can pursue its purposes without Orcish accompaniment. This independence explains why accounts of encounters do not invariably mention warriors or riders.

The hunting lore of the Beffraens makes it possible to recognise the consequences of this organisation in the marks left upon the ground. Several trails that diverge and subsequently meet may correspond to the concerted movements of a pack, while deep prints and repeated passages reveal the routes taken by individuals of great size. Wargs employ their sense of smell and hearing to track their adversaries, but their intelligence also enables them to recognise the paths those enemies may take and the obstacles they must go around. Wet ground sometimes preserves unusually legible tracks, and channels, flooded woods, and soft ground impose different constraints according to their depth and consistency.

Beffraen tradition thus recalls that knowledge of the land remains essential when facing these creatures. A narrow passage, a stretch of water, or an area of unstable ground may influence a pack's movements, yet Wargs can examine such obstacles and seek alternative routes. Their howls may enable separated individuals to remain in contact and change direction together.

The deepest knowledge preserved by the Beffraens combines the observation of tracks with a precise understanding of the nature of Wargs. These creatures belong to the great malevolent wolves whose stories are bound up with the servants of the Shadow, yet they possess an intelligence and a language that distinguish them from natural animals. Their collective organisation enables them to deliberate, acknowledge the decisions of their leaders, and undertake common enterprises with the Orcs. Wargs nevertheless retain their own purposes and gatherings. This autonomy appears in accounts of packs that pursue travellers, occupy a territory, or move through the wild lands independently of Orcish forces.

The memory of Beffraen hunters enables them to interpret these movements from the evidence left in wet country. The depth of a print depends upon the animal's weight, the speed at which it passed, and the consistency of the soil; several overlapping tracks may reveal a frequently used path rather than the simultaneous passage of a numerous pack. Where a trail is interrupted by a channel, the banks, possible points of emergence, and passages towards firmer ground must be examined. Wargs may employ the same routes as other large animals, but their capacity to communicate and plan their movements allows several individuals to take separate paths before meeting again. Hunters familiar with such behaviour can distinguish an ordinary dispersal from a concerted movement when the evidence is sufficiently abundant.

The oldest traditions also speak of a malevolent origin for these great wolves, sometimes associated with the ancient corruption of living creatures by the powers of the Shadow. Such accounts reach the Beffraens by various paths and mingle with knowledge handed down by neighbouring peoples. They generally distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves of the Elder Days, whose spiritual nature belongs to other traditions. Hunters' concrete observations provide a different kind of knowledge, founded upon prints, movements, and the reactions of the animals encountered. Together, they make it possible to recognise the Warg as a discerning adversary whose collective decisions complement its physical abilities.

On isolated farms throughout Eriador, certain elders say that great black wolves appear when wild packs have fed for too long upon corpses abandoned on ancient battlefields. The flesh of Men and Orcs slain in violence is said gradually to alter their nature, giving them extraordinary size and a ferocity that their descendants retain for several generations. The tales maintain that she-wolves giving birth in such places bear cubs darker and stronger than those of other packs. These animals become the Wargs of whom travellers speak, and their malevolent habits are said to arise from the food they find upon lands befouled by war.

Families familiar with this tradition attribute to Wargs a particular aversion to places where Men live peacefully. The smoke from hearths, the bells of the herds, and the scent of cultivated fields are said to remind them of a way of life alien to their corrupted nature. Some elders maintain that a farm inhabited for several generations remains protected so long as its principal hearth fire burns through the night. Wargs might approach the pastures and pursue straying animals, but would hesitate to cross the boundaries of a holding where the livestock's bells sound regularly. This belief leads certain families to regard their old domestic customs as a surer protection than fences and watchmen.

Country folk know the tales of great wolves that come down from the hills or forest lands to prowl near the herds. Shepherds say that they often travel in groups, follow isolated animals for a long time, and can recognise the tracks used to reach the pastures. Their size sets them apart from ordinary wolves, while their deep prints and the remains of the beasts they attack can sometimes reveal their passage. Travellers also report that some accompany Orc-bands, sharing their prey and their warlike enterprises.

A tradition among livestock keepers explains their behaviour as an intelligence acquired through contact with Men and their animals. Wargs are said to be wolves that have become so familiar with pastures, fences, and human habits that they can anticipate the movements of herdsmen. Their concerted attacks would spring from a shared experience of hunting, and their alliance with Orcs from training maintained over many years. Some elders maintain that a pack deprived of its riders or of its accustomed raids gradually returns to the life of ordinary wolves. The methods employed against natural predators would therefore be sufficient to turn it away from farmsteads for good.

The tales of rural Eriador distinguish Wargs from ordinary wolves by their size, strength, and behaviour. These great canids possess formidable jaws, a keen sense of smell, and acute hearing that enable them to detect the movements of Men and animals. Some are large enough to carry an Orc warrior, and travellers describe them as swift, tireless pursuers. Herdsmen know their ability to recognise the tracks habitually taken by livestock, while farm guards know that a pack may return repeatedly to a region where it finds prey.

You also know that Wargs possess an intelligence greater than that of natural wolves. Their howls and growls enable them to communicate with one another, and several individuals can act together in a pursuit. They maintain alliances with Orcs, but the tales also speak of packs that range the wild lands without riders. Country traditions recommend paying heed to the tracks of several great canids around the same passage, for their presence may herald a collective hunt or a larger gathering.

The rural communities of Eriador preserve detailed traditions about Wargs, particularly in regions where farms and pastures border wild lands. The elders distinguish these creatures from natural wolves by their intelligence and their ability to form common designs. Wargs possess their own language, made up of cries and howls through which they exchange warnings, summon their companions, and coordinate their movements. Their alliance with Orcs is known to travellers and road-wardens, yet a pack can act alone, recognise the habits of a community, and return to places it has visited before.

Shepherds' accounts attach great importance to the ways in which Wargs test the defences of human settlements. They may follow the movements of a herd, observe the paths taken by its guardians, and attempt to isolate animals that stray from the group. When they meet resistance, they may scatter, go around an obstacle, or postpone their attack. A fence, a ditch, or a solid shelter imposes real constraints upon their movements, but their intelligence enables them to recognise openings and favourable approaches. Communities familiar with such behaviour place as much importance upon watching paths and pastures as upon the immediate protection of buildings.

Rural traditions also distinguish the tracks left by ordinary wolves from those that great Wargs may produce. The width of the prints, their depth, and the length of the stride provide indications of an animal's size and movement, while several converging tracks may reveal the approach of a pack. Such signs must always be interpreted in the light of the ground and the circumstances of the passage. Experienced wardens compare them with reports gathered on neighbouring farms, for Wargs can cover considerable distances between two appearances.

results.text:
The most deeply rooted traditions of rural Eriador distinguish Wargs from other great wolves through precise knowledge of their behaviour and of the tales surrounding their nature. Ordinary wolves live according to the necessities of their kind and adapt their habits to the presence of Men; Wargs possess an intelligence and a language that enable them to prepare common actions. Their packs retain their own leaders, gather to deliberate, and can choose to pursue an undertaking independently of their Orcish allies. The tales handed down in the countryside associate this autonomy with a malice whose consequences go beyond the search for food. Wargs may harry travellers, pursue Men who resist them, and return to a settlement whose defences they have learnt.

Families established for several generations in the same regions sometimes preserve memories that allow distant events to be considered together. Accounts of an attack upon a herd, the disappearance of travellers on a byroad, and a subsequent sighting of great canids accompanying Orcs may all belong to the same period of unrest. Such connections form a local memory in which eyewitness reports mingle with the elders' interpretations. Those knowledgeable about Wargs distinguish observed facts from the beliefs surrounding them: a pack's presence may be recognised through its tracks and movements, while the intentions of its members become clearer when several observations reveal a concerted organisation.

The oldest traditions also speak of an origin connected with the corruption of living creatures by the powers of the Shadow. They ascribe to Wargs a malevolent nature inherited from a profound alteration of their earliest stock. Other tales, carried by travellers or preserved in the ancient kingdoms of Eriador, speak of Werewolves and evil spirits associated with the servants of Morgoth. Men familiar with these stories know that Wargs occupy a particular place among wolf-like beings: their intelligence, language, and organisation distinguish them from natural wolves, while accounts of their origins belong to traditions more obscure than the daily observations of hunters and shepherds.

results.text:
In certain towns of Eriador, travellers' stories describe great black wolves bred by Orc captains as mounts for war. These animals are said to descend from strains of wolves selected over generations for their strength and their docility towards their masters. Merchants recount that the Orcs feed and train them in vast caverns, where they learn to recognise the weapons, armour, and commands of their riders. The mightiest Wargs serve as mounts for chieftains, while the others accompany raiding convoys and guard the mountain passes. Their reputation as malevolent creatures would chiefly arise from the violence committed by the warriors they carry.

The stories circulating in inns also maintain that these beasts cannot enter a fortified town unless led by an Orcish master. The walls, massive gates, and noise of the streets would disorient them, since their training accustoms them to open spaces and mountain tracks. Some travellers claim that the ringing of great bells is enough to drive them back, while others ascribe this protection to the fires kept burning upon the ramparts. Townsfolk familiar with these traditions believe that a settlement whose gates are guarded remains safe from Wargs even when the neighbouring roads are threatened. The real difficulty, then, would be to prevent their Orcish riders from approaching the fortifications.

Merchants' and soldiers' accounts describe Wargs as great wolves employed by Orcs to range the roads and pursue travellers. Their size, speed, and endurance make them useful to armed bands seeking to surprise a convoy or hunt down fugitives. Witnesses report that they can follow a trail over long distances and recognise passages habitually used by Men. Some are strong enough to carry a rider, while others accompany warriors on foot. Townsfolk know these creatures chiefly through the warnings brought by travellers arriving from the mountains or from less secure borderlands.

An explanation widespread among guards and caravaners attributes their concerted movements to the military organisation of the Orcs. Wargs are said to be trained to answer calls and recognise signals from their riders. Their howls would transmit these commands from one group to another, like the horn-calls used by soldiers. Escorting troops' accounts stress the importance of Orcish leaders, whose loss would throw the packs into disorder. Some men-at-arms therefore regard Wargs principally as an auxiliary force, formidable when directed but unable to plan an attack on a well-protected convoy by themselves.

results.text:
The towns of Eriador preserve many accounts of Wargs, handed down by merchants, soldiers, and travellers who journey along the ancient roads. These testimonies describe creatures capable of understanding the movements of Men and organising their actions with others of their kind. Wargs possess their own language, through which they exchange warnings, gather a pack, and prepare an attack. Their association with Orcs rests upon an ancient alliance, yet they retain their own organisation and can pursue independent enterprises. Some serve as mounts, while others join raids as scouts and pursuers.

Caravaners' accounts stress their ability to exploit the constraints imposed by roads. A convoy progressing through a narrow pass, crossing a ford, or traversing woodland has different possibilities of movement from a group travelling across open ground. Wargs can recognise these differences and alter their movements to reach a favourable passage. A pack may follow travellers from a distance, disperse along several paths, or attempt to isolate men who stray from the group. The howls exchanged by its members allow them to remain in contact and coordinate their movements even when vegetation or relief separates them.

Those charged with keeping the roads safe also know that Wargs are independent. The disappearance of an Orc-band or the death of its riders leaves packs still capable of acting alone. Travellers may therefore report Wargs in a region where no gathering of Orcs has been seen. Urban traditions place great importance upon comparing accounts: attacks in several places may result from the movements of a single group, but corroborating testimony is needed to recognise the nature and extent of the threat.

results.text:
The deepest knowledge possessed by the townspeople of Eriador brings together the memory of the roads, military testimony, and historical traditions preserved in the old centres of habitation. It distinguishes Wargs from natural wolves and from great animals used in war. Wargs possess an intelligence and a language that enable them to agree upon common actions, recognise their leaders, and prepare enterprises independent of those of the Orcs. Their alliance with the latter arises from shared interests and hostility towards the Free Peoples, but their organisation remains autonomous. Chronicles concerning unrest in the northern and eastern regions give particular attention to the wolf-like creatures that accompany the forces of the Shadow, while distinguishing direct observations from tales handed down from one generation to another.

The knowledge preserved by merchants and guards makes it possible to interpret the movements of Wargs across networks of roads and human settlements. A succession of reports about great wolves may reveal a wandering pack, while several attacks occurring close together may involve distinct groups or concerted movements. Wargs understand the constraints of the terrain and can recognise places where travellers slow down, scatter, or encounter obstacles. Their speed enables them to follow a convoy's movements and alter their approach in response to resistance. Experienced men know that their retreats may be calculated and that their howls are communications capable of coordinating several individuals.

The oldest traditions also speak of an origin connected with the corruption of living creatures by the powers of the Shadow. Learned people familiar with the tales of the Elves and Dúnedain distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves of the Elder Days, although popular stories sometimes confuse the two. Wargs remain corporeal beings whose physical abilities are those of great canids, yet their malevolent intelligence and organisation place them among the most formidable enemies of travellers. Urban records and accounts enable observers to connect their appearances with the movements of Orcs, while preserving the distinction between military alliance and the will of their own that governs the packs.

Popular tales in Gondor sometimes describe Wargs as beasts of war bred in the secret kennels of the Orcs. These great wolves are said to have been selected since the first conflicts against the kingdoms of Men, then trained to serve as mounts for the warriors of the mountains. Their size and aggression would be the result of generations of breeding, during which the Orcs kept the strongest animals and destroyed the weakest. Wargs are thus presented as a race of domesticated predators, whose hunting habits have been replaced by obedience to their masters. Soldiers' stories sometimes compare them with warhorses, with the difference that their training rests upon cruelty and fear.

Certain traditions claim that Wargs recognise the signs of military authority and lose their nerve before troops arranged according to the customs of the kingdoms of Men. Horn-calls, close ranks, and unfurled banners are said to inspire in them a dread inherited from the defeats suffered by their former masters. The stories maintain that a pack rapidly abandons a pursuit when it encounters soldiers in formation, even if they are few in number. Men familiar with this explanation attribute the danger of Wargs to their speed and their use against isolated travellers, but believe that regular troops can scatter them through a mere display of discipline.

The traditions of Gondorian garrisons tell of the great wolves that accompany certain Orcish forces. These animals are of considerable size, very swift, and possessed of an endurance that enables them to sustain long pursuits. Military accounts describe them as auxiliaries employed to scout the paths, recover fugitives, and harry the flanks of a force. Some can carry an Orcish rider, while others accompany warriors on foot. Their presence is chiefly known from testimony concerning northern regions and territories close to the mountains where the Orcs establish their lairs.

You also know a tradition according to which Wargs constitute a military force wholly subject to Orcish chieftains. Their concerted movements would result from rigorous training, and their howls would be a means of passing on commands received from riders. Soldiers who offer this explanation compare their organisation to that of a troop of trained horses, able to recognise signals given by their masters. They believe that a pack deprived of its leaders swiftly loses its ability to fight together. Some officers therefore hold that neutralising the riders is enough to turn Wargs into disorganised predators, whose reactions become comparable to those of natural wolves.

Gondorians know Wargs as great malevolent wolves associated with Orcs and the wild lands of the North. Military accounts describe them as powerful animals, able to pursue Men over long distances and follow trails by means of their keen sense of smell. Their size allows some to serve as mounts, and their packs sometimes accompany Orcish warriors on raids. Soldiers' traditions stress their ability to move swiftly and attack several adversaries in concert. Their presence is known chiefly through accounts of military campaigns and testimony from travellers arriving from regions where these creatures are more frequent.

You know that Wargs possess an intelligence surpassing that of ordinary wolves and communicate in a language of their own. They can recognise the movements of a force, gather together, and pursue a common enterprise. Their alliance with the Orcs is ancient, but Wargs retain the ability to act without their riders. Gondorian traditions also distinguish them from the Werewolves mentioned in tales of the Elder Days, although the details of their origin are less well known. Their collective organisation explains why they are regarded as dangerous foes even when encountered far from Orcish forces.

The military traditions of Gondor preserve a developed knowledge of Wargs, passed down through chronicles, soldiers' accounts, and relations with the peoples of the northern regions. These creatures possess their own language, through which they exchange warnings, agree upon movements, and organise common enterprises. Their association with the Orcs rests upon an ancient alliance, sustained by shared interests and by their hostility towards the Free Peoples. Some Wargs serve as mounts, while others accompany armed bands as scouts or pursuers. Packs acknowledge their own leaders and can act independently of Orcish warriors.

Men familiar with these accounts know that Wargs are capable of observing a formation and recognising its weaknesses. Their speed enables them to follow a force on the march, while their intelligence leads them to seek passages where soldiers have less freedom of movement. A pack may scatter to test several approaches, then gather again when its members discover a favourable opportunity. Wargs may also break off an attack when confronted by unexpected resistance and alter their movements to exploit more advantageous ground. Military testimony stresses this adaptability, which distinguishes their behaviour from that of animals merely trained to fight.

Gondorian traditions also attach great importance to their autonomy. An Orc-band may be dispersed or defeated without the Wargs accompanying it immediately abandoning the region. Their organisation enables them to pursue their own purposes and rejoin others of their kind. Men knowledgeable about these creatures thus distinguish an encounter with a mounted troop from the threat posed by a pack acting on its own.

The deepest knowledge preserved among Gondorians distinguishes Wargs from natural wolves, from animals employed in war, and from the wolf-like creatures belonging to the oldest traditions of Middle-earth. Wargs possess an intelligence, a language, and an organisation that enable them to deliberate, acknowledge their leaders, and form alliances with Orcs while retaining their own will. Accounts depicting them as mere mounts fail to recognise this independence. Chronicles of the wars against the servants of the Shadow describe several kinds of wolf-like beings, but the best-preserved traditions distinguish their behaviour and the powers attributed to them. Among these creatures Wargs occupy a particular place through their corporeal nature, their ability to communicate, and their participation in organised military enterprises.

Men-at-arms acquainted with these traditions can compare the behaviour of a pack to that of a small force capable of planning its movements. Wargs observe opposing dispositions, recognise obstacles, and seek to exploit the opportunities offered by the terrain. They may follow the flanks of a column, divert an escort's attention, or separate a party of travellers before concentrating their attack. Their communications enable them to coordinate several movements without a rider constantly directing them. A retreat may be a calculated decision, and the dispersal of a pack may prepare its gathering elsewhere. These abilities explain their effectiveness as allies of the Orcs, but also the danger they pose when acting independently.

The oldest traditions sometimes associate their origin with the corruption of living creatures by the powers of the Shadow. They describe Wargs as descendants of a strain of wolves altered by an ancient curse, while other accounts speak of the Werewolves that served Morgoth, beings animated by evil spirits and belonging to a different nature. Gondorian scholars familiar with these tales distinguish traditions about Wargs from accounts of the supernatural powers of the Elder Days. Certain more obscure developments attribute a particular spiritual existence to Wargs themselves, but such beliefs belong to interpretations passed down through tradition rather than the ordinary observations of soldiers. Knowledge of their language, intelligence, and organisation remains the surest foundation for identifying them.

In the towns of Rhovanion, merchants' stories distinguish the great wolves of the mountains from those that accompany the Orcs. The former would be wild predators, while the latter would belong to a breed fashioned over generations for service in war. These animals, called Wargs, are said to have been raised in mountain caverns and accustomed from their youth to warriors' cries, the din of weapons, and the weight of riders. Their extraordinary size would result from patient breeding, the secrets of which the Orcs jealously guard. The largest serve as mounts for their chieftains, while smaller individuals are used to recover fugitives or guard paths leading to their lairs.

A tradition common in market towns claims that these beasts find structures built by Men difficult to endure. The scent of worked timber, tar, and the ironwork of bridges would recall the restraints of their training. They would hesitate to cross long causeways and footbridges suspended above water, whose vibrations disturb their balance. The inhabitants of riverside towns therefore believe that a well-guarded bridge affords protection against Wargs, even when a pack numbers many individuals on the opposite bank. The elders say that these great wolves always prefer to seek a natural ford rather than venture upon a human-built crossing, and that a caravan reaching a town's gates in time may cease to fear their pursuit.

The inhabitants of northern towns know Wargs from the testimony of merchants, boatmen, and guards who watch the roads leading towards the mountains. These great wolves possess unusual strength and can travel considerable distances at speed. Convoys crossing wild country dread their ability to recover a trail, follow travellers for many hours, and move in groups whose members appear to understand one another. Some are powerful enough to carry an Orc warrior, and garrison accounts assign them an important role in scouting the roads used by merchants.

You also know the warnings passed down by caravan leaders concerning their howls. According to these tales, Orcs train their Wargs to employ different calls to signal a convoy's presence, the discovery of a passage, or the gathering of a force. Experienced travellers therefore learn to recognise certain cries, whose duration and number are said to reveal the proximity of Orc warriors. A succession of short howls would announce scattered scouts, while one prolonged call would indicate the gathering of a larger force. This practice would explain the remarkable coordination of Wargs, whose movements would depend upon a system of military signals perfected by their masters.

In the towns of Rhovanion, Wargs are known as great malevolent wolves that frequent the mountains and wild regions, sometimes in the company of Orcs. Travellers' accounts ascribe to them a size greater than that of ordinary wolves, considerable endurance, and senses capable of recognising a trail long after its makers have passed. Some carry Orc warriors, while others accompany armed bands in pursuit of fugitives. Their speed and ability to move in packs make them dangerous to merchants travelling through country far from inhabited settlements.

You know that Wargs possess an intelligence exceeding that of wild animals. They exchange cries and howls whose meaning generally escapes Men. Their concerted movements may answer to common decisions even when no rider accompanies them. Road-wardens know their ability to recognise fords, narrow passages, and paths habitually used by travellers. The stories circulating in markets also stress that a pack may appear far from Orcish encampments and pursue an undertaking on its own account.

The trading communities of Rhovanion preserve detailed accounts of Wargs, gathered from travellers who journey along the roads between towns, mountains, and great forests. These testimonies describe creatures endowed with an intelligence of their own and capable of communicating in a language that belongs to them. Wargs can exchange warnings, acknowledge their leaders' decisions, and organise common enterprises. Their alliance with the Orcs rests on shared interests, yet their packs retain their autonomy. Some individuals serve as mounts, while others accompany armed bands as scouts or pursuers. The most reliable accounts also describe gatherings of Wargs that act independently of any Orcish force.

Merchants and guards acquainted with these creatures attach great importance to the routes they frequent. A Warg can recognise a caravan's habitual movements, follow a trail to a ford, and seek another passage when a road becomes unfavourable. Several individuals may separate to take different paths, then rejoin one another through the calls they exchange. Bridges, causeways, and fortified structures constitute obstacles according to their disposition and defence, but Wargs are capable of understanding their use and crossing them when circumstances permit. Their knowledge of the terrain, combined with their speed, enables them to pursue travellers attempting to change their route.

The traditions of the northern towns also distinguish information gathered by soldiers from that brought by caravans. The former chiefly know the employment of Wargs in Orcish enterprises; the latter report their appearances on roads, their movements, and the consequences of their attacks. Comparing these testimonies makes it possible to recognise behaviour common to several packs. Men possessing such experience understand that Wargs are an independent threat, capable of exploiting the movements of travellers as readily as the warlike enterprises of their allies.

The deepest knowledge of the urbanised Northmen combines memories of ancient conflicts, testimony handed down by merchants, and traditions preserved among neighbouring peoples. It distinguishes Wargs from natural wolves by their intelligence, language, and ability to form common designs. Wargs possess their own leaders, gather to deliberate, and can prepare attacks before they have even met their Orcish allies. Their association with the latter rests on shared interests and common hostility towards the Free Peoples. A pack may nevertheless pursue aims different from those of an Orc-band, abandon an enterprise that has become unfavourable, or begin a hunt without receiving orders from outside.

The memory of towns and market settlements makes it possible to understand their movements on a broader scale than any isolated encounter. Information collected in several settlements may reveal a pack following trade routes, exploiting frequented passages, or accompanying the movements of armed groups. Wargs recognise the routes that slow convoys and can coordinate their approaches along several paths. Their howls are communications whose meaning depends upon their own language, and their number seldom provides, by itself, a reliable indication of the Orcish forces present in a region. Experienced guards distinguish direct observations from the interpretations travellers place upon the sounds heard during the night.

The oldest traditions speak of an origin linked to the corruption of wolves by the powers of the Shadow. Other accounts, carried by Elves or peoples who preserve the memory of the Elder Days, distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves that served Morgoth. This distinction remains important to learned Men, for beings of different natures can present similar appearances. Wargs belong to the wolf-like creatures whose malice is accompanied by organised intelligence; tales of their supernatural origin explain their place among the servants of the Shadow, while travellers' testimony makes it possible to recognise their observable habits and abilities.

Among the families who dwell beneath the trees of Rhovanion, certain tales speak of great black wolves drawn by the forest towards places where Men have disturbed its ancient peace. These beasts are said to appear in clearings opened too widely, near trees felled without need, and along paths where Orcs have left signs of destruction. Their enormous size and dark coats would be the marks of a corruption born in the forest's depths. The elders say that these wolves can follow for several nights those who have entered the woods to commit acts of violence, and that their howls echo for an especially long time around places where trees have been burned.

This tradition also attributes a particular influence over Wargs to ancient trees. The oldest oaks and great beeches would retain a strength that these creatures dread, and their roots would protect Men who seek shelter beneath their branches. Some hunters claim that a Warg hesitates to enter a grove left undisturbed for generations, whereas a recently opened clearing attracts packs. Communities familiar with this belief regard their woodland refuges as protected as much by the age of the trees surrounding them as by their distance from the paths. A pack might prowl for a long time along the edge of such a grove, but would eventually abandon its pursuit before the influence of the trees in which the Woodmen place their trust.

The Woodmen know of the great wolves that sometimes accompany Orc-bands along forest paths. Hunters' tales describe them as powerful beasts, able to follow a trail among roots, fallen leaves, and passages choked with branches. Their sense of smell and hearing enables them to recover the movements of a man or animal, while their great size makes them dangerous when they catch their prey. The villages know stories of packs prowling in districts far from habitation, their howls answering one another beneath the trees.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs derive their coordination from habits acquired while following Orc-bands. Their silent movements and concerted attacks would be the consequences of prolonged training in the woods. The howls they exchange would serve chiefly to gather scattered individuals, like the calls of ordinary wolves. The elders who pass on this interpretation insist that their intelligence remains limited by their hunting instincts. A Warg drawn away from its trail by a fresher scent or the passing of another animal would necessarily abandon its original purpose. Hunters capable of laying several false trails could therefore throw an entire pack into disorder, until its members ended by pursuing different prey.

They can follow a trail over long distances and pursue travellers through wooded country. Some are powerful enough to carry an Orc warrior, while others range the wild lands in independent packs. Hunters know that these creatures use their sense of smell and hearing to recognise the paths taken by Men, even when visible tracks become difficult to follow.

Several individuals can act together in following a trail or going around an obstacle. The tales handed down in villages speak of their ability to gather and prepare common attacks. Woodmen know the usefulness of trees and high places for observing the movements of these beasts, but also know that a pack can wait beneath a refuge and watch the paths by which Men must eventually descend.

The Woodmen's traditions give Wargs a particular place among the malevolent creatures that haunt the forests. Tales passed down by the elders distinguish their intelligence from that of natural wolves and describe their ability to communicate in a language of their own. Wargs can exchange warnings, acknowledge their leaders' decisions, and prepare common enterprises. Their alliance with the Orcs is ancient, and some packs take part in attacks against human settlements. They nevertheless retain their own organisation and can choose their movements independently of their allies.

Hunters familiar with these creatures know the advantages a forest may offer to pursuers. Wargs move swiftly along clear paths, use tracks frequented by animals, and can recognise routes leading to clearings or watering places. Their size makes certain obstacles more difficult to cross, especially tangles of fallen trunks and constricted passages, but their intelligence enables them to seek more favourable ways. Trees offer Woodmen observation posts and refuges beyond the immediate reach of the Wargs' jaws. A pack may nevertheless keep watch on Men sheltering high among the branches and wait until they are forced to move.

The forest tales also stress that Wargs learn to recognise their adversaries' reactions. They can follow an interrupted trail, explore neighbouring passages, and alter their movements when several individuals discover different signs. The cries exchanged beneath the trees help them gather despite the dense vegetation. Woodmen familiar with such behaviour understand that methods effective against a wild animal may fail against a group capable of deliberating and collectively choosing another course of action.

The deepest knowledge of the Woodmen unites their clans' traditions with precise experience of the creatures ranging the forests of Rhovanion. Wargs have the appearance and physical abilities of great wolves, yet their intelligence and language give them a distinct place among wild beings. They acknowledge their own leaders, gather to deliberate, and can plan attacks upon human communities in concert with the Orcs. Their malice goes beyond the necessities of hunting, and their alliances may serve enterprises of destruction or plunder. Some packs nevertheless range the wooded regions on their own account, retaining an organisation independent of armed bands.

Woodmen familiar with their habits know how to interpret the signs of collective movement. Several trails meeting near a passage, renewed tracks around a clearing, or calls exchanged between distant points may reveal a pack watching a territory. Wargs can use their sense of smell to recover a man's movements, but their intelligence also enables them to recognise the routes he might take. A refuge high in the branches protects against their immediate attacks without making them disappear. A pack may wait a long time, explore neighbouring passages, or attempt to prevent fugitives from reaching another tree. Experienced hunters recognise in this behaviour an ability to prepare a common enterprise, rather than a succession of instinctive reactions.

The oldest traditions distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves appearing in tales of the Elder Days. The latter belong to a history bound up with the powers of Morgoth and with evil spirits, whereas Wargs are known above all through their corporeal presence, their language, and their alliances with Orcs. Certain beliefs trace their origin to an ancient corruption of wolves, whose malice was perpetuated through successive generations. The Woodmen pass on these accounts in connection with the changes undergone by the great forests and the appearance of servants of the Shadow. Their knowledge of Wargs nevertheless rests upon observable behaviour: packs communicate, gather, recognise obstacles, and pursue designs of their own.

Among the riders of Rohan, certain tales describe Wargs as great wolves employed by the Orcs against travellers on foot and isolated settlements. These beasts possess considerable strength and their jaws can bring down a man, yet their speed is said to be inferior to that of a well-trained horse. The elders recount that Wargs excel in broken country, where they can slip between rocks and pursue prey through woods, whereas the broad pastures expose them to the superiority of horsemen. Their pace, though swift, would remain that of a land-bound predator whose limbs eventually tire when it attempts to sustain the prolonged gallop of a mount.

Certain herdsmen's traditions also claim that horses of the finest bloodlines of Rohan possess a natural ability to recognise these beasts and impose their superiority upon them. A vigorous stallion, accustomed to weapons and the presence of other horses, would be capable of scattering several Wargs by the mere threat of its hooves. The tales attach great importance to the neighing and movements of warhorses, whose assurance is said to unsettle the great wolves accustomed to pursuing fearful prey. A company of horsemen maintaining a sustained pace across the pastures could therefore escape a pack without risk of being overtaken, while a charge delivered on open ground would be sufficient to put it to flight. Wargs would reserve their attacks for dismounted men and horses separated from their companions.

Riders' tales attribute to them great endurance, powerful jaws, and a remarkable capacity to pursue Men or animals over long distances. Their size enables them to attack a horse's flanks and threaten a rider whose mount slows or loses its footing. Stories handed down among those who guard the herds also describe their habit of gathering in packs, following the movements of animals, and taking advantage of narrow passages.

You also know a tradition according to which Wargs are subject to the same limitations as natural wolves when confronting horses. They may pursue an isolated mount, but their instinct would drive them away from a company of horsemen maintaining close formation. Their concerted attacks would chiefly result from the training imposed by Orcs, whose riders direct their movements with shouts and blows. The elders who pass on this explanation believe that a pack deprived of command rapidly loses its cohesion before mounted troops. They attribute the most dangerous attacks to occasions when horses become scattered, whereas a formation maintaining its order could neutralise the threat through its discipline alone.

The traditions of the Rohirrim distinguish Wargs from ordinary wolves by their size, strength, and intelligence. These great canids possess jaws capable of inflicting serious wounds, great speed, and keen senses that enable them to follow a trail for a long time. Some carry Orc warriors, while others accompany armed bands on foot. Riders know their ability to approach herds and seek out animals separated from their companions. Their presence is a threat to horses, particularly where the ground limits the mounts' freedom of movement.

You also know that Wargs communicate through cries and howls whose meaning goes beyond the ordinary calls of wolves. Their intelligence enables them to act as a pack and alter their movements in response to resistance. Rohirrim familiar with these creatures know that a horse may react violently to their smell, cries, or approach, but that its reaction also depends upon the mount's temperament and training. Riders' accounts thus distinguish the dangers posed by a pack acting alone from those of an Orc-band mounted upon Wargs.

The Rohirrim preserve detailed traditions concerning Wargs, nourished by the memory of their northern ancestors and the experience of horsemen who range the open lands. These creatures possess their own language, by means of which they can coordinate their movements and prepare common enterprises. Their alliance with the Orcs rests upon shared interests, but packs acknowledge their own leaders and retain the ability to act independently of their riders. Some Wargs serve as mounts for Orcish warriors, while others take part in pursuits and attacks directed against travellers and herds. Their speed and endurance enable them to sustain a hunt over distances greater than those Men ordinarily cover on foot.

A pack may follow mounted troops, attempt to separate the slowest animals, or concentrate its attacks upon an injured mount. It may also recognise passages where riders must slow down, descend a slope, or cross an obstacle. Horses respond differently to the presence of such predators: some seek to flee, others resist or remain calm under the guidance of a rider accustomed to the perils of war. Rohirrim familiar with Wargs know that a horse's speed is a real advantage on favourable ground, but that pursuit by an intelligent pack also depends upon the animals' endurance, freedom of movement, and the coordination of their adversaries.

Accounts of war finally distinguish Orcish riders mounted upon Wargs from packs that fight alone. The former unite their riders' weapons with the speed and strength of their mounts; the latter act according to their own decisions and may change their conduct without waiting for outside orders. A scattered pack may gather again after a charge, while a group that withdraws may return against another flank. The Men of the Mark thus recognise the need to watch these creatures' movements as they would those of adversaries capable of organising their own manoeuvres.

It distinguishes Wargs from natural wolves, whose habits answer to the necessities of hunting, and from the animals employed in war by Men. Wargs possess an intelligence and a language that enable them to deliberate, acknowledge their leaders, and form alliances with the Orcs. Their participation in Orcish enterprises may take the form of raids, pursuits, or mounted combat, yet they retain an independent will. The oldest accounts attribute to them a malice inherited from the powers of the Shadow, of which their organised behaviour is a clearer manifestation than their appearance alone.

A pack may test a troop's flanks, pursue an isolated mount, or wait until an obstacle breaks the horsemen's momentum. Wargs use their howls to coordinate their movements, while their senses enable them to recover the tracks of a group that has left the road. Their endurance favours prolonged pursuits, and their intelligence allows them to choose between an immediate attack and a movement intended to reach a more advantageous passage. A horse's speed, the cohesion of a mounted group, and its rider's experience influence the outcome of such encounters, but Wargs possess the means to recognise these differences and turn them to account.

The more learned traditions also speak of wolf-like creatures that served the ancient powers of Morgoth. They distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves of the Elder Days, to which certain tales ascribe a different spiritual nature. Wargs are known for their corporeal presence, their language, and their ability to organise common enterprises. Their alliance with the Orcs is cooperation between intelligent beings, and their use as mounts is one form of that association. Rohirrim possessing this knowledge therefore understand that a confrontation with Wargs may combine the dangers of a hunt conducted by great predators with those of an attack planned by adversaries capable of communicating and anticipating events.

Among Gramuz families, certain tales attribute the appearance of great black wolves to lands whose fertility has been disturbed by wars and destruction. These animals are said to be born in regions where fields remain abandoned for long years, herds have disappeared, and the earth returns to the wild. Their extraordinary size would be the result of growth nourished by such desolation, while their malice would spring from the violence of old attached to the places they frequent. The elders say that these wolves avoid regularly cultivated land, for the scent of freshly turned furrows and new harvests reminds them of the order Men impose upon the soil. They prefer to prowl around deserted farms, abandoned pastures, and paths where vegetation is reclaiming the ground.

A tradition associated with the rites of Earth and Growth holds that Wargs recognise the boundaries of a holding consecrated to the renewal of life. Families who maintain the ceremonies of sowing and harvest believe that these rites strengthen the protection of fields and beasts. Some elders maintain that a pack hesitates to cross the furrows drawn at the first sowing of spring and that animals gathered in a pen surrounded by cultivated ground remain safe from its attacks. Wargs might follow a herd through distant pastures, but would abandon their pursuit when the beasts reach land tended by the family for several generations. This belief makes fidelity to agricultural rites a defence as important as weapons and palisades.

Their presence is particularly feared when communities must move their herds between distant pastures.

You also know an explanation common among certain breeders: Wargs are above all predators of exceptional hunger, whose intelligence is limited to recognising opportunities to feed. Their habit of following herds would arise from the animals' scent and the ease with which they can recover prey already located. The elders who pass on this interpretation maintain that a pack invariably abandons a pursuit when it discovers an abundant source of food. Carcasses left far from a settlement would thus be sufficient to draw Wargs away for a long time, for they would prefer to feed without effort rather than attack armed Men. Their alliance with Orcs would follow from the same search for food, sustained by the remains their riders leave them after battle.

A pack may disperse to follow several trails, then gather when a favourable opportunity appears. Palisades, ditches, and communal refuges present real obstacles to their attacks, but their intelligence enables them to recognise the entrances and exploit occasions when inhabitants must travel between their holdings.

Their language enables several individuals to coordinate movements across pastures, valleys, and wooded passages. A pack may also break off an attack and return when circumstances become more favourable. Elders with long experience of such dangers know that repeated appearances of great wolves around several holdings may belong to a common enterprise rather than separate encounters.

Gramuz traditions sometimes connect these accounts with rites of Earth and Growth, which occupy an important place in family life. The celebrations of sowing and harvest express communities' attachment to the fertility of their fields, the continuity of their lineages, and the prosperity of their herds. The surest knowledge nevertheless distinguishes this religious meaning from behaviour observed among Wargs: cultivated ground, open fields, and the consecrated boundaries of a holding remain spaces these creatures can cross. Their physical strength and intelligence enable them to exploit the paths joining farms to pastures. The oldest traditions also speak of the Werewolves of the Elder Days, beings of a different nature, whose stories are sometimes mingled with those of Wargs. Gramuz familiar with these distinctions recognise the singular place Wargs occupy among malevolent creatures through their ability to communicate, organise themselves, and pursue purposes of their own.

In the ancient libraries of Gondor, certain collections devoted to the servants of the Shadow liken Wargs to the Werewolves that appear in the tales of the First Age. These writings describe beasts whose corporeal forms were subjected to the powers of Morgoth, then inhabited by malevolent spirits unable to recover their former shapes. Wargs would be descended from these creatures, perpetuating through the ages an existence foreign to natural laws. Their appearance as great wolves would conceal a supernatural essence that ordinary weapons could not permanently harm. Wounds inflicted upon their bodies might slow their movements or momentarily destroy their outward form, but the spirit animating them would remain capable of taking shape again when its strength had been restored.

The traditions arising from this interpretation attach particular importance to ancient weapons and words handed down by the Elves. Blades forged according to the arts of the Eldar, weapons consecrated during the wars against the Shadow, and certain names used in the ancient tongues would possess the power to sever the bond uniting a Warg's spirit to its body. Scholars defending this doctrine believe that ordinary warriors may scatter a pack, but that only the power contained in such weapons can destroy its members for good. Several military accounts are interpreted in the light of this belief: when a pack returns after defeat, its survivors are said in truth to be the same spirits that have assumed bodily form once more. Wargs would thus belong to a lesser order of Werewolves, subject to the same supernatural laws as their ancestors.

Accounts of independent gatherings would be explained by the fulfilment of orders received long before, or by the influence exerted from afar by the masters of the Orcs. A pack may break off an attack, disperse its members, then gather them elsewhere. Men-at-arms familiar with these accounts know that the disappearance of Orcish riders leaves foes still capable of changing their plans and pursuing purposes of their own.

Dúnedain scholars also distinguish traditions concerning Wargs from those relating to the Werewolves of the Elder Days. Certain traditions attribute their origins to an ancient corruption of wolves, without this explanation being sufficient to equate them with Werewolves. The surest knowledge concerns their behaviour, their organisation, and testimony passed down by those who encountered them. Interpretations of their supernatural nature belong to an older body of tales, whose different versions must be kept distinct.

The deepest knowledge of the Dúnedain of Gondor rests upon a tradition joining the study of ancient tales with the memory of wars against the servants of the Shadow. Wargs appear therein as wolf-like creatures possessing an intelligence and a language that enable them to form designs of their own. Their collective organisation includes leaders, gatherings, and common decisions. Their alliance with Orcs is cooperation between beings capable of pursuing convergent aims, rather than a simple relationship between warriors and their mounts. Wargs may take part in raids, reconnoitre routes, and pursue fugitives, yet their packs retain the ability to act independently of their allies. This autonomy appears in tales of gatherings where Wargs deliberate among themselves and choose the enterprises in which they will take part.

Dúnedain schooled in military history recognise the consequences of this intelligence for the conduct of an engagement. A pack may test several parts of a defence, follow the movements of a force, and seek circumstances that allow an adversary to be isolated. Its members communicate with one another and can coordinate their movements even when separated by the relief or vegetation. Their speed favours changes of direction and pursuits, while their endurance enables them to maintain pressure upon travellers or retreating soldiers for a long time. Wargs also recognise obstacles, defensive dispositions, and the reactions of their enemies. Accounts of war that attribute concerted attacks to them thus describe opponents capable of choosing the ground and altering their plans, rather than animals whose movements depend exclusively upon a rider's orders.

The oldest historical traditions finally establish a distinction between the different wolf-like creatures associated with the Shadow. The Werewolves appearing in tales of the First Age belong to a history bound up with Morgoth's powers and evil spirits. Wargs, whose intelligence and alliances are known from testimony more directly accessible, have a different nature in the accounts that concern them. Certain traditions ascribe their origins to an ancient curse that altered a strain of wolves, while others describe a malevolent spiritual presence attached to their corporeal form. Scholars studying these versions distinguish properties actually observed among Wargs from powers attributed to supernatural beings of the Elder Days. Tales of bodies vanishing after their destruction give rise to such questions, but do not, by themselves, establish that Wargs possess all the properties of Werewolves or of undead beings created by sorcery.

This deeper knowledge also enables an understanding of the diversity of testimony preserved by the peoples of Middle-earth. Hunters principally describe the tracks, movements, and behaviour of Wargs; soldiers emphasise their ability to fight beside Orcs; the traditions of the Elves and the ancient kingdoms illuminate accounts of their origins. Dúnedain capable of bringing these different perspectives together gain a fuller understanding of their nature. They recognise in the Warg a corporeal, intelligent, and malevolent being whose observable abilities are already formidable, while traditions concerning its supernatural origins belong to a more ancient history, harder to establish with certainty.

Among the traditions preserved by the ancient families of Arnor, certain tales describe Wargs as the descendants of wolves that once served in the armies of Angmar. The Witch-king is said to have bent these beasts to his will and imparted something of his power to them, making them larger, hardier, and capable of pursuing his enemies across the northern lands. After their master's disappearance, the packs supposedly retained this obedience in the form of a hereditary curse. The great wolves that prowl among ruins and old battlefields would thus be the last guardians of a fallen realm, condemned to hunt the enemies of Angmar for as long as their bloodline endures.

Some family tales maintain that this curse binds Wargs to the places where their master once held sway. They might roam farther afield to hunt or accompany Orc-bands, but would be compelled to return periodically to the strongholds and lands they formerly guarded. Travellers acquainted with this tradition believe that a pack encountered near an ancient fortress remains bound to its ruins. Once sufficiently far from that territory, the Wargs would lose their vigour and abandon any pursuit of fugitives. The elders even claim that stones still bearing the emblems of Elendil trouble these creatures, whose curse forbids them to approach the remains held sacred to the kings of the North.

Wargs exploit the advantages these places offer and remain free to depart, rejoin their fellows, or undertake a hunt elsewhere. Dúnedain who can set historical testimony beside present observations therefore recognise intelligent and independent adversaries whose movements may recall the old wars without necessarily repeating the designs of vanished masters.

Among the tales handed down on the estates of Dorwinion, some speak of great black wolves appearing when cultivated land has long lain abandoned. The elders say that these animals are born where vines are no longer pruned, orchards have run wild, and Men have deserted their settlements. Their extraordinary size would spring from the abundance of game finding refuge in land left to itself, while their fierce temper would be the fruit of a life passed far from human habitation. Travellers who meet them call them Wargs, but the oldest stories describe them as a variety of wolf made fearsome through long years in desolate country.

Some vineyard wardens maintain that these beasts cannot readily endure the strong smells of winemaking. Grape pomace, fermenting lees, and the smoke of the great autumn fires would so disturb their sense of smell that they turn away from the trails they are following. Families familiar with this tradition believe that the approaches to presses and wine cellars offer refuge from pursuit. Great wolves might cross cultivated lands in winter, but would avoid estates where the harvest had recently been gathered. A few accounts even claim that a traveller wearing clothes steeped in wine or pomace could cross Warg-haunted country unnoticed, for these smells would entirely conceal his trail.

Among the horse-riding peoples of the eastern lands, certain tales speak of a breed of great wolves capable of recognising the might of a war-chief. These beasts, which the Men of the West call Wargs, are said to dwell in regions where Orcs make their encampments, yet freely choose the warriors to whom they offer their service. The elders recount that a victorious chieftain may attract a pack by leaving the bodies of his enemies upon the battlefield. The wolves would come to feed upon these offerings, then acknowledge the one who left them as an ally worthy of their obedience. Their great size and intelligence would be signs of an ancient kinship with the spirits of predators that ranged the steppes before the first clans were established.

A warrior tradition maintains that Wargs respect strength shown in single combat. If a man stands against the leader of a pack and succeeds in wounding it without seeking its death, the others would recognise his superiority and cease their attacks. Some stories even claim that a victorious horseman may secure the service of Wargs by offering them a share of the spoils, as he would to a band of allied warriors. Elders familiar with this tradition regard Wargs as adversaries with whom a courageous chief may establish a lasting relationship, provided that he can defend his standing and reward their loyalty. Their alliance with Orcs would therefore testify to the personal authority of the captains who lead them.

The traditions of the eastern peoples tell of great wolves that accompany Orcs and take part in the undertakings of the forces of the Shadow. These creatures are of considerable size, remarkable speed, and sufficient endurance to pursue Men or animals over long distances. Some serve as mounts, while others accompany armed bands to scout routes and harry their enemies. Horsemen acquainted with accounts of western campaigns describe their concerted attacks and gatherings in packs whose members appear to act through a shared understanding.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs observe rules of dominance resembling those of the most authoritarian warrior clans. A pack would acknowledge a single leader, whose decisions entirely govern its movements. The howls exchanged between individuals would be the calls through which that leader issues commands and keeps the others under its authority. If defeated or separated from its companions, the pack would lose its cohesion until a new leader succeeded in establishing its rule. Warriors passing on this interpretation believe that the strength of a pack depends chiefly upon its leader, and that an attack directed against that individual is usually enough to throw the other Wargs into disorder.

Horsemen's accounts emphasise their ability to follow a trail, recognise the movements of Men, and travel swiftly through open country and broken ground alike.

You also know that Wargs have their own language, formed of cries and howls that allow them to communicate with one another. Their packs can gather, coordinate their movements, and act without constantly receiving a rider's orders. The eastern peoples maintain very different relations with the forces of the Shadow according to their alliances and traditions; accounts of Wargs may therefore come from warriors who have fought beside them, Men who have opposed them, or travellers acquainted only with their reputation. Yet these testimonies agree upon their intelligence and their ability to join in common enterprises with Orcs.

Some Wargs serve as mounts, while others fight in independent groups, capable of scattering and coming together again during an engagement. Their intelligence enables them to recognise obstacles, test their adversaries' resistance, and alter their movements when circumstances turn against them.

Horsemen familiar with these behaviours can compare the movements of a pack with certain manoeuvres practised upon the steppes. Wargs may follow their enemies at a distance, seek passages where their progress slows, and concentrate their strength against an isolated group. Several individuals can take different directions to explore the routes ahead and find their companions again through exchanged calls. Speed favours their pursuits, yet their capacity to communicate plays an equally important part in their organisation. A pack may break off an attack in the face of unexpected resistance, then return when it has discovered another approach.

The traditions of the eastern clans also distinguish alliances made by Men from those between Wargs and Orcs. Certain human communities may fight beside the servants of the Shadow without sharing all their designs, while others remain hostile to them. Wargs, for their part, possess a malice and interests of their own that make their decisions less predictable than simple military obedience. Experienced warriors know that their presence among an Orcish force represents a dangerous alliance, but that a pack may continue pursuing its purposes after its allies have been scattered.
