The deepest knowledge of the Easterlings brings together accounts from different peoples, whose relations with the servants of the Shadow vary across ages and alliances. Wargs appear therein as intelligent beings, capable of speaking their language, acknowledging their leaders, and deliberating before undertaking an enterprise. Their collective organisation has rules of its own, independent of those governing human clans or Orc-bands. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests and a common hostility towards the Free Peoples, but Wargs retain the power to choose their movements, their prey, and their companions in battle. Accounts that describe them as animals subject to a single chief overlook the ability of several individuals to take part in a pack's decisions.

Knowledge of the warfare practised by horse-riding peoples makes it possible to appreciate the advantages afforded by Wargs' speed and coordination. They can test an adversary's movements, recognise routes that favour a pursuit, and gather again after deliberately scattering. Their howls are communications by which several groups maintain contact, while their senses allow them to follow trails that ordinary horsemen would lose. Mounted troops may enjoy advantages upon open ground, but Wargs can exploit slopes, narrow passages, and obstacles that restrict horses' freedom of movement. Their behaviour depends upon collective decisions and the circumstances they encounter, rather than upon the absolute authority of a single leader.

The religious and martial traditions of the eastern peoples give rise to differing interpretations of their nature. Some tales depict Wargs as creatures born of an ancient corruption of wolves by the powers of the Shadow. Others liken them to spirits associated with predators or to the Werewolves appearing in stories from the West. Those acquainted with such lore distinguish these interpretations from what testimony can establish: Wargs have corporeal forms, a language, and an intelligence capable of governing their actions. Their malice finds expression in the alliances they form and the undertakings they choose to pursue.

Lastly, the diversity of eastern traditions provides a source of knowledge as well as contradiction. Accounts from a clan that fought alongside Orcs may describe Wargs serving as mounts, while those of a community hostile to the same forces emphasise pursuits, raids, and attacks on herds. Merchants may know of their presence from routes that have become dangerous without ever having encountered them directly. Easterlings able to bring these perspectives together recognise a kind of creature with its own forms of organisation, capable of profiting from different relationships with other peoples. Its nature remains the same, whatever banners are borne by the Men who encounter it.

Among the stories circulating in the markets of northern Harad, some speak of great black wolves encountered upon the roads of the North. These beasts, which travellers call Wargs, are said to be predators from the cold mountains, unable to endure the heat of southern lands for long. Caravans report that they pursue Men relentlessly in temperate regions, but give up the chase when the heat grows too great and water becomes scarce. Their thick coats, great size, and heavy breathing would be signs of a constitution adapted to cold countries, whose strength would soon fail beneath the sun of arid lands.

A caravaners' tradition maintains that Wargs particularly fear sand heated by the day's sun. Their paw pads, accustomed to damp earth and forest paths, would be ill-suited to scorching surfaces, forcing them to seek shade or retreat towards stony ground. Guides familiar with this explanation believe that a pursued caravan can find refuge in broad treeless expanses, where the beasts have no shelter. Certain tales even claim that Wargs lose their sense of smell in the hot dust and become incapable of recovering a trail when the wind raises the sand. Travellers reaching the driest regions might therefore consider the pursuit definitively at an end.

The Haruze know of Wargs through the accounts of merchants who travel towards Gondor, the eastern lands, and regions where Orcs establish their lairs. These great wolves possess formidable strength, great speed, and senses that enable them to follow a trail over long distances. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others accompany armed bands as scouts and pursuers. Caravans' accounts emphasise their ability to recognise passages frequented by Men and follow the movements of a company even after a lengthy halt.

You also know an explanation according to which their intelligence depends chiefly upon their sense of smell. Wargs would be able to recognise a traveller's trail for as long as the ground retains his scent, but their concerted movements would depend principally upon the persistence of that trail. A caravan crossing several kinds of terrain, dispersing the tracks of its animals, and then changing direction beyond a rocky stretch could therefore throw a pack into disorder. Elders who pass on this tradition believe that Wargs have only a limited memory of routes and that, when the scent disappears, they lose the means of pursuing their objective. Experienced guides would therefore attach decisive importance to changes in the ground and passages swept by the wind.

Their presence is chiefly reported by caravans crossing the northern and eastern regions, and Haruze traditions associate them more closely with mountains and wild country than with the most arid deserts.

You also know that Wargs communicate through cries and howls whose meaning goes beyond the ordinary calls of animals. Their intelligence allows them to recognise obstacles, act in concert, and change their movements when a trail becomes difficult to follow. Haruze acquainted with these accounts know that dry, rocky, or wind-swept ground can make pursuit harder for any animal, yet Wargs have other means of finding their way. Their capacity to exchange information with one another contributes to the danger they pose.

The traditions of Haruze caravaners preserve detailed knowledge of Wargs, gathered from merchants, guards, and travellers who journey along the roads connecting Harad with the northern regions. These creatures possess a language of their own, acknowledge their leaders, and can plan common enterprises. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, yet their packs retain the ability to act independently of their allies. Some Wargs serve as mounts, while others follow armed bands or range the wild lands on their own. Caravans' accounts emphasise their ability to recognise frequented passages and pursue travellers despite the obstacles they encounter.

Guides acquainted with their behaviour know that the nature of the ground affects the possibilities of tracking. A trail left upon soft earth may remain legible after a company has passed, whereas rock, wind, or a stretch of water can erase some traces. Wargs use their sense of smell and hearing, but their intelligence also allows them to seek the routes a traveller is likely to follow. A caravan must reach water sources, avoid obstacles, and choose passages its laden animals can negotiate; these constraints can be recognised by an adversary capable of observing and anticipating. Several Wargs may separate to search for a lost trail, then communicate their discoveries to their fellows.

Experienced Haruze also distinguish a pack's confirmed presence from stories travellers bring from distant lands. The fact that Wargs are often associated with cold and mountainous regions does not mean that a warmer climate makes them incapable of travel. Their endurance, size, and the physical demands imposed by their coats influence their movements, yet their decisions also depend upon available shelter, routes, and the objectives they pursue. Guides therefore appreciate the value of precise information about the last sighting of a pack rather than relying upon its reputation alone.

The deepest knowledge of the Haruze brings together merchants' accounts, the traditions of guides, and testimony passed down from regions where Wargs are more frequently encountered. These creatures possess an intelligence and a language that distinguish them from natural wolves. They acknowledge their leaders, gather to deliberate, and can plan common actions independently of Orcs. Their alliance with the latter rests upon shared interests, but their packs retain the ability to pursue purposes of their own. Stories that present them as mere beasts of war fail to recognise their capacity to choose a route, judge an adversary's resistance, and change their conduct collectively.

Guides of the arid regions possess experience that enables them to judge the demands of a pursuit. They understand the effects of wind upon tracks, the ways in which a caravan must ration its water, and the difficulties faced by laden animals crossing pathless country. Wargs have physical capabilities different from those of horses or camels, but their intelligence allows them to recognise the routes travellers are likely to take. A pack may seek a favourable passage, follow a company's direction from several clues, or abandon a pursuit when conditions become too unfavourable. Its members can also communicate while exploring several directions without remaining constantly together.

The oldest traditions sometimes associate the origin of Wargs with the corruption of living creatures by the powers of the Shadow. Some accounts liken them to the Werewolves mentioned in stories from the West, while others consider them a lineage of great wolves that has grown malevolent over the ages. Haruze versed in the traditions of several peoples distinguish these explanations from what travellers can observe directly. Wargs have tangible bodies, keen senses, and an intelligence that enables them to coordinate their movements. Their malice is revealed in their enterprises against Men and in the alliances they choose to forge.

This knowledge also helps explain the limited place Wargs occupy in the stories native to the most arid regions. Eyewitness accounts grow rarer as one travels farther from the territories they habitually frequent, and tales brought by caravans may confuse several kinds of great predator. Haruze familiar with these distinctions set greater store by precise observations than by sweeping claims that Wargs cannot endure the sun or drought. Climate influences a pack's movements, but its effects remain physical constraints to which these intelligent creatures can respond by choosing different routes, refuges, and hours of travel.

Among the warrior clans of Khand, certain tales describe Wargs as beasts consecrated to the powers of Darkness. Their enormous size, dark coats, and ability to fight beside Orcs would be marks of an ancient submission to the gods of war. The priestesses of clans maintaining relations with the servants of the Shadow are said to know ceremonies by which friendly packs may be recognised and hostile ones turned aside. According to these traditions, Wargs remain fierce animals, yet their malevolent nature renders them susceptible to signs of religious power. A war-chief who gains the priestesses' favour might therefore receive their protection against the great wolves, or even attract their aid in a military undertaking.

The oldest tales maintain that Wargs recognise the smell of blood spilled during warlike ceremonies. A company that performs the proper rites before setting out would bear a mark that packs can detect from afar. Wargs would then turn aside from its path and reserve their attacks for enemies designated by the priestesses. Some warriors claim that a band so consecrated can cross regions frequented by these creatures without fear of their jaws. The protection would endure until the end of the expedition, provided that the leader kept the pledges made before the powers invoked. Packs accompanying the armies of Mordor would be subject to the same rites, explaining their loyalty to warriors admitted into the service of Darkness.

The Variags know accounts of great wolves that sometimes serve as mounts for Orcs and accompany their bands on military campaigns. Their power makes them dangerous to horsemen, especially when a mount slows or becomes separated from its companions. Warriors who have encountered Orcish forces also know how Wargs gather in packs and coordinate their movements. Certain testimonies describe Wargs pursuing a company after a battle has ended, then rejoining their fellows when their enemies attempt to scatter.

You also know an explanation according to which their intelligence remains wholly governed by the hierarchy of the forces of the Shadow. Wargs would have leaders of their own, but those leaders would be subject to Orcish captains and servants of Mordor, whose decisions they obey. Their language would serve chiefly to pass on commands received and maintain order among members of the pack. Warriors who offer this interpretation believe that a chief acknowledged by the masters of the Orcs can likewise exercise authority over the Wargs accompanying them. The presence of these creatures within an army would therefore signify a disciplined force whose movements could be understood by observing the orders issued by its commanders.

They are especially dangerous where the terrain limits the freedom of movement of mounts.

You also know that Wargs communicate in a language of their own, made up of howls and growls. They can gather, acknowledge their leaders, and act in concert without a rider directing their every movement. Variag traditions frequently associate them with the forces of the Shadow, but warriors acquainted with these creatures know that a pack can act independently of Orcs. Their intelligence enables them to pursue a common undertaking and change their movements in response to resistance.

Variags who know Wargs through military campaigns distinguish their organisation from that of ordinary animals used in war. These creatures possess their own language and acknowledge their leaders, yet retain a will independent of the Orcs. Their alliance with the latter rests upon shared interests and may lead them to take part in the same warlike enterprises. Some Wargs serve as mounts, while others fight in packs capable of moving, scattering, and gathering again without constantly receiving orders. Their intelligence allows them to recognise an adversary's weaknesses and change their conduct when an attack becomes too dangerous.

Horsemen of Khand familiar with these creatures know the advantages they gain from speed and coordination. A pack can follow the movements of mounted troops, seek passages that slow horses, and exploit a dispersal to isolate an enemy. Wargs can also move over ground difficult for laden mounts to negotiate. Their endurance favours prolonged pursuits, while their language enables several individuals to keep in contact during a manoeuvre. Experienced warriors recognise in their attacks an organisation comparable in some respects to that of a small military force, but founded upon these creatures' own abilities.

Variag traditions attach great importance to the might and authority of war-chiefs. Wargs, however, do not necessarily acknowledge the same obligations as the warriors of a clan. An alliance with Orcs may lead them to fight under a common command, but rests upon cooperation between intelligent beings. Men's rites and religious obligations belong to their own traditions; Wargs pursue their designs according to their interests and the decisions of their packs. Warriors who understand this distinction recognise that their presence among the forces of the Shadow represents a danger in its own right, even when they fight beside human allies.

The deepest knowledge of the Variags brings together the traditions of horsemen, the testimony of warriors who have served alongside Orcs, and tales handed down among the clans of Khand. Wargs appear therein as intelligent beings capable of speaking their own language, gathering to deliberate, and preparing common enterprises. Their malice often leads them to ally themselves with the servants of the Shadow, but their organisation retains leaders and decisions of its own. Some Wargs take part in raids as mounts or auxiliaries, while others range the wild lands without accompanying any armed force. Their alliance with Orcs constitutes military cooperation, the forms of which may vary according to circumstances and the interests of the packs.

Experienced warriors know that Wargs can exploit several methods employed in cavalry warfare. They recognise passages favourable to an attack, test an adversary's resistance, and seek to separate the most vulnerable individuals. A pack may scatter to follow several trails, then reunite through communications exchanged among its members. Its endurance allows it to sustain a pursuit, while its intelligence favours changes of direction and calculated withdrawals. Wargs can also recognise the constraints imposed by pack animals, tired horses, and obstacles that slow a company. Such behaviour accounts for their effectiveness as military allies and the danger they pose when acting alone.

Variag religious traditions sometimes associate Wargs with the powers of Darkness, to which certain clans attribute the ability to command malevolent creatures. The oldest tales speak of an origin connected with the corruption of wolves, while others liken these beings to the Werewolves that served Morgoth. Those familiar with such lore distinguish these interpretations from their observable abilities: Wargs have tangible bodies, an intelligence, and an organisation that enable them to pursue designs of their own. Clan ceremonies may express a political or religious alliance with the servants of the Shadow, but do not in themselves establish authority over the packs.

Variags knowledgeable about Wargs also understand the limits of cooperation founded upon strength. Orcs may fight alongside them, and some Orc warriors may ride them, but the presence of a pack does not imply lasting loyalty towards the Men who share its camp. Wargs may choose to withdraw, rejoin others of their kind, or undertake a hunt of their own. Their language and capacity to deliberate enable them to recognise common interests without surrendering their own decisions. This independence distinguishes their participation in an army from the obedience a rider obtains from a trained mount.

Among the occult traditions preserved in certain houses of the Black Númenóreans, Wargs are portrayed as creatures whose very existence depends upon the powers of the sorcerers of the Shadow. Their likeness to great wolves is said to conceal bodies fashioned to receive the spirits of warriors who died in the service of dark powers. Masters of these arts supposedly discovered how to imprison such spirits within animal forms, granting them a predator's speed, strength and senses while preserving an intelligence capable of understanding commands. Wargs would therefore descend from an ancient necromantic creation, their malice arising from the spirits that inhabit them rather than from wills of their own.

The writings that preserve this doctrine ascribe to Wargs a particular dependence upon words of command. A sorcerer who knew their secret names could supposedly subject an entire pack to his will and impose a particular mission upon it, even when its members were far from him. Wargs are also said to recognise certain signs carved upon stones or weapons, which the spirits within them would be compelled to obey. Houses that uphold this belief regard possession of these formulae as conferring considerable power over the great malevolent wolves. Packs ranging the wild lands would thus be carrying out ancient commands, given by masters of the Shadow and preserved within their nature since their creation.

Military accounts attribute to them an intelligence surpassing that of wild animals and an ability to travel in organised packs. Occult traditions sometimes liken them to the wolf-like beings appearing in the oldest tales of Morgoth's servants.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs remain subject to a hierarchy of supernatural powers. Their language would allow them to communicate and plan common undertakings, but their decisions would depend wholly upon the will of a mightier master. Packs that seem to act alone would in truth be fulfilling missions entrusted to them by Orc captains, sorcerers or lords of the Shadow. Elders who transmit this doctrine believe Wargs possess genuine intelligence, yet are unable to escape the spiritual authority to which their kind was subjected. Their collective organisation would therefore be an instrument of command rather than an expression of independent will.

Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, yet their packs retain an organisation of their own. The traditions of officers and warlords attach particular importance to this independence. A pack can recognise an enemy's routes, seek approaches favourable to an attack and disperse to explore several directions. Its members communicate with one another and can collectively change their course of action. An Orc rider may influence their participation in a battle, but Wargs remain capable of acting when their allies have vanished. Experienced commanders therefore understand that cooperation with them offers military advantages distinct from those provided by a troop of trained mounts.

Occult traditions sometimes connect their origin with the ancient corruption of wolves, while other accounts speak of malevolent spirits bound within animal bodies. Such interpretations draw Wargs closer to the supernatural creatures of Morgoth's tales, but do not suffice to endow them with every property of Werewolves or of undead beings raised through sorcery. The surest knowledge concerns their language, intelligence, organisation and ability to form alliances. Black Númenóreans instructed in these distinctions recognise that knowledge of the Shadow's creatures must separate attested powers from the ambitions of those who claim mastery over them.

The deepest knowledge of Wargs among the Black Númenóreans brings together the traditions of their ancient houses, the observations of officers and the accounts preserved by students of the powers of the Shadow. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings with an intelligence and a language of their own. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and can prepare common enterprises independently of Orcs. Their alliance with the latter rests on shared interests and hostility towards the Free Peoples, yet this cooperation leaves their own will intact. Some serve as mounts or take part in raids, while others range the wild lands according to decisions of their own.

Experienced officers know both the advantages and the limitations of employing them in war. Their sense of smell, hearing and speed make them formidable pursuers, able to recognise the movements of a force and recover trails that ordinary soldiers would lose. Their language allows individuals to coordinate their actions, scatter and assemble again without constant command from Men or Orcs. Wargs can recognise the arrangement of a defence, delay an assault and seek a different approach when circumstances turn against them. These abilities explain their effectiveness as military allies, but also the difficulties faced by anyone attempting to treat a pack as a mere cavalry unit subject to outside discipline.

Learned traditions distinguish several interpretations of their origin. Some accounts present Wargs as the descendants of an ancient strain of wolves corrupted by dark powers. Others describe a malevolent spirit inhabiting their bodily form, and attribute to this nature the unusual disappearance of certain corpses after their destruction. The Werewolves of the Elder Days belong to another tradition, concerning the spirits that served Morgoth. Scholars familiar with these stories can recognise shared themes without identifying the creatures they describe as one and the same. The spiritual nature attributed to Wargs in certain traditions does not establish that they possess every power of the undead beings summoned by necromancers.

Black Númenóreans are also familiar with the ways in which boasts of power may distort understanding of creatures serving the Shadow. A lord may pride himself upon commanding packs, a sorcerer claim to possess their secret names, and a captain credit his own discipline for the concerted attacks of his lupine allies. Such assertions sometimes express political or occult ambitions greater than the authority actually wielded. Wargs remain able to communicate, recognise their interests and pursue designs of their own. The most precise traditions therefore describe them as formidable allies of malevolent powers, whose intelligence and will are essential qualities whatever relations they maintain with their supposed masters.

In the taverns and seafaring quarters of Umbar, some tales describe Wargs as great wolves trained by Orcs for war and the guarding of strongholds. These beasts are said to be especially formidable in mountain country, where their speed allows them to pursue Men along paths and among the rocks. They supposedly originate in the old inland territories, far from the great seas, and their disposition is said to lead them to avoid the coasts. Mariners recount that Wargs dread the sound of the surf, the smell of salt and the movement of deep waters. When a pack pursues travellers as far as the coast, it would eventually abandon the hunt upon approaching beaches and harbours.

A tradition among certain crews holds that salt water exerts a particular influence upon these creatures. Their sense of smell, so keen on dry land, would be disturbed by sea spray until it became useless. Wargs might follow a man to the edge of a quay, but would lose his trail as soon as he boarded a vessel, even a small boat remaining close to shore. Sailors familiar with this belief regard retreat towards the sea as certain protection against the great wolves of the wild lands. Some stories even claim that a pack refuses to cross a beach uncovered by the tide because the salt left in the sand would burn its paws. Corsairs accustomed to such tales therefore regard coastal waters as a natural frontier the Wargs cannot cross.

The Corsairs of Umbar know Wargs chiefly through accounts brought by mercenaries, merchants and soldiers who have campaigned far from the coasts. These great wolves possess considerable size and endurance, with senses capable of recovering a trail over long distances. Some serve as mounts for Orcs; others accompany armed bands as scouts or pursuers. Military accounts attribute to them particular effectiveness in mountainous and forested regions, where they can identify the passages used by travellers and swiftly overtake fugitives.

You also know an explanation according to which their organisation depends almost entirely upon the Orc captains who lead them. Wargs are said to be trained to recognise certain commands, and their howls enable them to pass along the signals received. Mercenaries who offer this interpretation compare them with animals employed by armies to guard encampments or pursue enemies. A pack deprived of its riders would retain its strength and senses but lose the ability to prepare a concerted attack. Men-at-arms who accept this view believe the presence of Wargs necessarily heralds an organised Orcish force, whose disappearance would end the danger posed by the pack acting together.

The traditions of the Corsairs of Umbar distinguish Wargs from ordinary wolves through their size, intelligence and association with Orcs. These great canids possess tremendous strength, speed and keen senses enabling them to follow trails left by Men and animals. Some serve as mounts, while others accompany armed bands as scouts or pursuers. Soldiers and mercenaries describe them as dangerous enemies for travellers crossing the wild lands, especially when several act together.

You also know that Wargs communicate in a language of their own, formed of howls and growls whose meanings generally escape Men. They can assemble, coordinate their movements and pursue an undertaking without constantly receiving a rider's orders. Corsairs familiar with these creatures know that they are encountered chiefly among the perils of the interior. Maritime tales attributing to them an absolute aversion to salt or the seashore do not accord with the observable behaviour of great canids able to recognise obstacles and choose their routes.

results.text:
Corsairs of Umbar who know Wargs through land campaigns and mercenaries' accounts distinguish them from ordinary animals used in war. Wargs possess intelligence and language enabling them to acknowledge their leaders, exchange warnings and prepare common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs is founded on shared interests, but their packs remain autonomous. Some serve as mounts; others fight as auxiliaries or range the wild lands independently of armed bands. Their speed and senses make them particularly suited to pursuing fugitives and detecting the movements of a force.

Men taking part in raids ashore understand the difficulties such creatures can impose upon troops on the move. A party landed on a distant coast must return to its ship, maintain contact with those still aboard and sometimes pass through country whose paths are unfamiliar. Wargs can follow the traces it leaves, seek the passages by which it must return and exploit obstacles slowing its withdrawal. Their intelligence enables them to recognise possible routes, while their language helps several individuals coordinate their movements. Thus a pack may remain dangerous even when a party has regained the shore, particularly if the men must still cross a beach, a quay or an exposed passage before reaching their boats.

Corsair traditions also distinguish Wargs from the Orcish forces with which they associate. The disappearance of a troop need not bring about the departure of its lupine allies. A pack may continue a hunt on its own account, occupy a territory or join others of its kind. Experienced captains understand that these creatures are adversaries capable of changing their plans, and that the security offered by a fortified position or a ship depends upon the approaches actually available.

The deepest knowledge preserved by the Corsairs of Umbar brings together the military traditions of exiled families, accounts gathered from mercenaries and testimony brought by travellers from the lands of the North and East. Wargs emerge as intelligent beings, able to communicate in their own language, hold council and pursue independent designs. Their alliance with Orcs rests on common interests and hostility towards the Free Peoples, but each pack retains its own leaders and decisions. Some Wargs serve as mounts or participate in raids; others range the wild lands without Orcish company.

Men versed in military operations know how Wargs benefit from their speed and coordination. A pack may recognise the movements of a force, follow its tracks and seek out the passages through which it must withdraw. Wargs employ their senses of smell and hearing, but their intelligence also enables them to understand the constraints of the ground. They can spread out to explore several routes and subsequently rejoin one another through exchanged calls. A force that reaches a refuge or a defended position remains subject to difficulties along its approaches: Wargs can wait, skirt obstacles or abandon the pursuit as circumstances dictate.

Corsair seafaring traditions provide a particular perspective on these creatures' physical limitations. Water, vessels and harbour works pose obstacles whose importance depends upon their arrangement. Deep water can separate a pack from its adversaries, whereas a beach, jetty or shallow passage may remain accessible. The scent of salt and sea spray may alter tracking conditions, but Wargs possess keen senses and an intelligence that allows them to seek other clues. Captains familiar with this behaviour distinguish the genuine advantages of a maritime refuge from the imaginary protection popular tales attribute to the shore.

The oldest traditions tell of an origin linked to the corruption of wolves by the powers of the Shadow. Some compare Wargs to the Werewolves of the Elder Days, whose spiritual nature belongs to different accounts. Corsair families preserving something of the Dúnadan inheritance may know these traditions from ancestral chronicles and tales, whereas crews more often encounter them in the words of travellers and mercenaries. The surest knowledge distinguishes the observable properties of Wargs from the powers ascribed to them in stories. Their intelligence, language and independence remain the essential traits for understanding their place among the allies of Orcs.

In the far northern lands, some tales speak of wolves of extraordinary size that appear when winters grow particularly severe. The elders say these beasts grow in the coldest countries, where scarce prey and violent storms favour the strongest individuals. Their dark fur and sturdy muscles would allow them to survive where ordinary wolves can no longer find sufficient food. Travellers from southern lands sometimes call them Wargs, but traditions describing them as malevolent creatures would arise chiefly from the fear inspired by their size and appearance.

A belief handed down in certain encampments holds that these great wolves understand changes in the weather better than Men. Their howls would foretell approaching storms, and their movements reveal where the ice remains most secure. The elders say that a pack never ventures onto frozen ground liable to break beneath its weight. Hunters finding their tracks could therefore follow the same paths in perfect safety, even when snow conceals cracks and currents. Some families regard the great dark wolves as unwitting guardians of winter routes, whose footprints reveal passable ways to those who know how to read them.

The Lossoth know tales of great wolves ranging the cold lands and mountain regions. Such beasts possess considerable strength, thick coats and senses capable of following traces left in the snow. Hunters' traditions speak of their movements in packs, their endurance and their ability to pursue animals over great distances. Travellers from southern lands also tell of certain great wolves, called Wargs, that accompany Orcs and sometimes serve as mounts for their warriors. The elders know this reputation, even when direct accounts of encounters remain scarce in the northernmost regions.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs differ from natural wolves only in size and in the conditions in which they live. Their concerted behaviour would arise from experience gained while hunting in difficult country, and their howls merely allow them to keep in contact through storms. Tales attributing a distinct intelligence or malevolent will to them would be exaggerations brought by southern peoples less familiar with great predators. Hunters who accept this interpretation believe that the methods used to understand ordinary wolves are sufficient to account for the movements of a Warg pack.

results.text:
Lossoth traditions distinguish Wargs from the great natural wolves that inhabit cold regions. These creatures are of considerable size and remarkable physical strength, with keen senses that enable them to pursue a trail for a long time. Some carry Orc warriors as mounts, while others range the wild lands in packs. Accounts from southern regions attribute to them an intelligence beyond that of ordinary animals and a malice linking them to the servants of the Shadow. Their presence in the northernmost lands is less directly documented than that of natural wolves.

You also know that Wargs communicate in a language of their own. Their howls can convey warnings and allow several individuals to coordinate their movements. Lossoth familiar with these creatures understand that their appearance as great wolves may lead to confusion with the wild animals of the North. Their size and tracks offer useful clues, but intelligence and organisation are the features that most clearly distinguish them.

results.text:
The Lossoth traditions concerning Wargs distinguish them from natural wolves by their intelligence, language and ability to pursue common designs. Wargs acknowledge their leaders, may gather to deliberate and maintain alliances with Orcs. Some serve as mounts, while others range the wild lands in independent packs. Their malice and organisation set them apart from predators whose movements answer chiefly to the necessities of hunting. Accounts gathered from southern travellers supplement the lore of animals handed down in the encampments of the far North.

Hunters familiar with frozen country know that tracks in snow are shaped by many factors. Their depth varies with the animal's weight, the consistency of the snow cover and the weather; their definition may quickly be lost to the wind. The footprints of a great canid may therefore reveal its size and direction without establishing its nature. Wargs possess keen senses and an intelligence that allows them to seek other passages when a trail becomes difficult to follow. Several may scatter to explore different routes, then find one another again through their calls.

Experienced Lossoth attach particular importance to distinguishing knowledge derived from observation from that brought by distant stories. The great wolves of the North belong to everyday experience, whereas Wargs are known through traditions whose accuracy varies with the witnesses. An intelligent pack can recognise the difficulties imposed by snow, frost and passable paths, but its movements remain constrained by the physical conditions of the ground. Lupine tracks across a frozen surface show that an animal crossed it; they guarantee neither that the ice will support a man nor that the same passage will remain safe at another time.

results.text:
The deepest knowledge of the Lossoth draws together the traditions of the far North, hunters' observations and accounts from regions where Wargs are more frequently encountered. It distinguishes natural wolves, even those of exceptional size, from malevolent creatures possessing their own intelligence and language. Wargs have leaders, can hold council and prepare enterprises independently of Orcs. Their alliance with the latter rests upon shared interests, yet packs retain their own will. Accounts describing them as mere predators adapted to harsh climates overlook their ability to communicate, choose their movements and pursue common aims.

Lossoth with deep knowledge of animals understand the limitations of testimony concerning Wargs. A large footprint may belong to a powerful wolf, while numerous tracks may reflect repeated passages through one place rather than many animals at once. Howls heard during a storm may come from beasts separated by the terrain, and the direction from which they seem to sound can be altered by the wind. The identification of a Warg becomes more certain when several observations reveal organised behaviour, concerted movements or reactions displaying an intelligence superior to that of natural predators. Knowledge of tracks and the conditions of the ground then complements travellers' accounts.

The oldest traditions sometimes speak of lupine creatures associated with the powers of the Shadow. Certain stories trace Wargs to the ancient corruption of wolves, while others liken them to the Werewolves of the First Ages, beings of a different nature. Lossoth instructed in these traditions distinguish stories carried from southern realms from knowledge gained directly in the cold lands. Their own experience explains the strength of great canids, their ways of moving and the constraints imposed upon them by the seasons; tales of Wargs add knowledge of an intelligence and malice beyond these natural traits.

This distinction matters particularly when travellers encounter great wolves in the northern lands. Wargs can exploit frozen paths, follow the movements of Men and seek places where their adversaries have less freedom to move. Their intelligence allows them to recognise certain dangers and change their routes, but does not give them infallible knowledge of ice or storms. Lossoth familiar with these creatures know that their tracks record decisions made by beings equally subject to the conditions of the physical world. They thus recognise the Wargs' true properties without attributing to them powers sometimes bestowed by popular belief upon the great predators of the North.

results.text:
Among Drughu traditions, certain stories speak of enormous wolves that accompany Orcs and carry within them something of the malice of their people's ancient enemies. These beasts, called Wargs by Men of other lands, are said to possess an intelligence greater than that of ordinary predators, yet remain subject to the powers governing the creatures of the Shadow. They are particularly feared in forests where Orcs have established their lairs, for they can supposedly recognise hunters' paths and follow traces left near hidden refuges. The elders say Wargs discern the scents of Men and animals with almost supernatural precision, yet cannot distinguish a living presence from a stone image fashioned according to the ancient arts.

This belief attaches particular importance to the guardian figures carved by the Drughu. Stones depicting crouching Men, faces with wide-open eyes or motionless wardens are said to exert an influence that drives Wargs away. The great wolves would recognise in them an ancient watchfulness whose power recalls the enemies they dread. Some accounts claim that a pack refuses to pass a way guarded by such a figure even when the path lies clear. Families familiar with this tradition believe that a guardian stone alone suffices to protect a refuge against Wargs, and that they may retreat to it in safety when the howls draw nearer.

The Drughu know tales of great malevolent wolves accompanying Orcs and ranging the wild lands. These creatures possess immense strength, a keen sense of smell and hearing able to detect the slightest movements. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others gather in packs. Hunters who encounter their tracks know they are larger than ordinary wolves and may cover great distances. Stories passed down among Drughu communities associate them with dangers threatening woodland paths and territories frequented by servants of the Shadow.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs remain governed by the hunting instincts of canids. Their sense of smell would allow them to follow a man's movements, but their attention would depend chiefly upon fresh tracks and visible motion. Hunters who advance this explanation believe that a man who remains perfectly still, hidden among trees and carrying the scent of earth or leaves, can escape their notice almost as surely as he might that of an ordinary animal. Warg howls would serve mainly to maintain contact among members of the pack. Their coordination would arise from the habit of hunting together, and well-proven methods of concealment would generally suffice to divert their attention.

Drughu traditions distinguish Wargs from natural wolves by their size, intelligence and malice. These great canids possess formidable strength, a keen sense of smell and acute hearing, enabling them to detect the movements of Men and animals. Some carry Orcs as mounts, while others range the wild lands in packs. Hunters know their skill in following a trail and seeking the passages their adversaries have taken. Their presence poses a particular danger to communities living near regions frequented by servants of the Shadow.

You also know that Wargs possess their own language, composed of howls and growls whose meanings extend beyond the ordinary calls of wolves. They can gather, acknowledge their leaders and coordinate their movements. Drughu familiar with creatures of the Shadow know that their intelligence allows them to alter a pursuit and recognise obstacles. Methods of concealment that work well against ordinary animals remain useful, but Wargs can observe, search and communicate in ways that make their responses harder to predict.

The Drughu preserve precise knowledge of Wargs, sustained by their experience of forests and traditions concerning servants of the Shadow. These creatures possess intelligence and language distinguishing them from natural wolves. They acknowledge leaders of their own, gather to deliberate and can plan common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, but packs retain the ability to act independently of armed bands. Some Wargs serve as mounts; others pursue travellers, watch passages or hold territory on their own account.

Drughu hunters know that Wargs have keen senses, enabling them to recover traces left among vegetation and on the ground. Their intelligence also allows them to recognise the routes a man might take and seek places where he could be hiding. A pack may follow several trails, explore different passages and gather through calls exchanged among its members. Wargs may abandon a pursuit when faced with an obstacle, but may equally seek another way or wait until their adversary is compelled to leave his refuge. Their behaviour thus reveals powers of observation and anticipation beyond the instinctive reactions of natural predators.

Drughu traditions attach great importance to protected places and guardian figures. Such sculptures belong to their spiritual inheritance and may be associated with ancient practices of watchfulness. Hunters knowledgeable about Wargs nevertheless distinguish the role of guardian stones from that of physical barriers. A carved figure may mark a passage, recall a protective presence or play a part in a rite, but a Warg's reaction depends upon what it perceives and the decisions it makes. Experienced Drughu recognise in these creatures adversaries capable of understanding their surroundings, rather than animals wholly governed by fear of certain signs.

results.text:
The deepest knowledge of the Drughu brings together their ancient memory of the servants of the Shadow, their experience of the wild lands and traditions handed down by the guardians of their communities. Wargs appear as corporeal beings possessing intelligence and language of their own. Their organisation includes leaders, gatherings and decisions taken together. They can ally themselves with Orcs and participate in their enterprises of war, but retain the freedom to choose their movements and pursue their own aims. Their malice distinguishes them from natural wolves, whose behaviour answers to the needs of hunting and survival. Drughu traditions therefore recognise the Warg as an adversary capable of forming a design and changing the manner in which it is carried out.

Hunters long experienced in the forests can interpret the signs of this intelligence. A Warg may recover a trail through scent, but can also recognise passages leading to a refuge, watch an adversary's movements and wait for him to leave his hiding place. Individuals may explore different directions before reassembling, while their howls keep them in touch across trees and valleys. The remarkable stealth of the Drughu provides effective ways to escape notice and leave fewer traces, but these advantages depend upon the ground, scents, wind and attention of their pursuers. Wargs can actively search for a man whose presence they suspect.

The oldest traditions sometimes connect Wargs with the powers of the Shadow that corrupt living things. Some tales present them as descendants of an ancient strain of wolves altered by a curse. Others liken them to the Werewolves whose spiritual nature is described in stories of the Elder Days. Drughu acquainted with these traditions distinguish observable behaviour from tales of origin. Wargs possess intelligence, language and organisation whose effects can be recognised in their movements and alliances. Any supernatural nature they may have belongs to other, darker traditions, requiring a different understanding from that gained through hunting and observation.

Guardian figures hold a particular place in this knowledge. Some belong to spiritual traditions in which the Drughu believe protective powers reside, but their appearance alone affords no guarantee against Wargs. An intelligent pack can recognise a passage, observe its surroundings and choose to take it despite the presence of sculptures. Drughu who know these creatures therefore distinguish the possible power of a particular rite or singular guardian from the mere shape of a stone. Their understanding of Wargs rests upon the same precision: identifying attested abilities, recognising possible reactions and separating ancient traditions from properties actually observed in an adversary.

Among the ancient clans of the highlands, certain tales speak of great black wolves that pursue Men whose families bear the memory of an old betrayal. These creatures, called Wargs by neighbouring peoples, are said to appear near places where oaths were broken and blood was shed between once-allied families. Their size and ferocity would be marks of a curse bound to such feuds. The elders say that Wargs can recognise the scent of a bloodline and pursue its descendants long after those responsible for the offence have passed away. Their howls would then be the calls by which they gather their fellows to accomplish a vengeance forgotten by Men.

A tradition among storytellers holds that Wargs may be turned aside from their pursuit when the quarrel drawing them receives solemn redress. A clan chief who publicly acknowledges an ancient debt, restores a possession or proclaims the end of a feud would break the bond between these creatures and his family. The great wolves would then abandon the country and seek elsewhere bloodlines burdened by other offences. Some elders maintain that Wargs cannot attack a man whose family has kept every oath, for their malice can find no purchase upon him. Clans familiar with this belief thus credit ancestral obligations with a protection against these creatures far exceeding their ordinary force in human affairs.

The Daen Lintis know tales of great malevolent wolves ranging the hills and wild lands, sometimes in the company of Orcs. These creatures possess considerable strength, great speed and senses able to follow the tracks of Men and animals. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors; others gather in packs. Herdsmen know their ability to pursue livestock and recognise the paths linking pastures to villages. Warriors' accounts also ascribe to them a remarkable ability to use narrow ways and broken ground in approaching their adversaries.

You also know an interpretation according to which the relationship between Wargs and Orcs resembles that of a clan and its war-chief. Packs are said to be bound to their allies by enduring loyalty, sustained through the sharing of prey and victories. When an Orc-band is defeated, its Wargs would pursue the enemies responsible until vengeance had been exacted. The elders who pass down this explanation believe repeated attacks by a pack may reveal an ancient feud between Orcs and the Men of the region. Once the chosen foes were defeated or vengeance achieved, the Wargs would abandon their pursuit and return to their accustomed territories.

Clan traditions attribute to them intelligence enough to recognise human habits and seek approaches favourable to an attack. Wargs retain their own organisation and may pursue their purposes independently of the armed bands they sometimes accompany.

Some Wargs serve as mounts; others accompany armed bands or range the wild lands independently of their allies. Their malice and ability to pursue common designs render their behaviour more complex than that of ordinary predators.

Those acquainted with the hills know the advantages Wargs may draw from the terrain. A pack can take byways, follow a group's tracks and recognise passages where travellers or herds must slow down. Individuals may explore different directions and rejoin one another through their calls. Wargs possess the endurance to maintain a pursuit, but their intelligence also prompts them to change route when an obstacle proves too difficult to cross. Experienced hunters know that slopes, valleys and narrow passages may aid either fleeing Men or their pursuers, according to each side's knowledge of the ground.

Daen Lintis oral traditions give great weight to accounts of conflict and alliances between clans. Wargs are sometimes associated with Orcs taking part in these wars, but their organisation follows interests of its own. A pack may return to a region after an Orc-band has been defeated, pursue travellers who took no part in the fighting, or abandon an undertaking that has become unfavourable. Elders familiar with this behaviour distinguish Warg malice from human feuds, whose obligations and rules of redress do not necessarily govern these creatures' decisions.

The deepest knowledge of the Daen Lintis combines ancient clan traditions, accounts of warfare and observations passed down by those who range the hills. Wargs appear as intelligent beings, able to speak their language, hold council and form alliances with Orcs. Their organisation has leaders and rules of its own, yet their decisions remain independent of the quarrels and oaths of Men. Some Wargs join raids or serve as mounts for Orc warriors; others range the wild lands on their own account. Their malice may lead them to harry travellers, pursue fugitives or return against an adversary who resisted them, but such enterprises arise from their own decisions.

Experienced hunters know that Wargs can recognise passages used by Men and animals, follow a trail and exploit difficulties in the terrain. Hills provide many routes that intersect, constrict or lead into secluded valleys. A pack may explore several such paths, communicate what its members discover and gather when an opportunity presents itself. Their speed favours changes of direction, while their endurance allows them to pursue a group over distances beyond those ordinarily covered by domestic animals. Wargs may also recognise an organised defence and delay their assault, particularly when obstacles or resistance make a direct approach too dangerous.

Daen Lintis oral traditions sometimes explain Warg attacks through ancestral clan feuds. Tales of vengeance, broken oaths and accursed bloodlines occupy an important place in family memory, and misfortunes are readily connected with ancient wrongs. The surest knowledge distinguishes such interpretations from the Wargs' observable behaviour. A pack may return to a place because it knows its paths, prey and opportunities for attack; it may pursue Men because it regards them as enemies or has chosen to harass them. These decisions express its intelligence and malice without necessarily arising from obligations inherited from human quarrels.

The oldest traditions also tell of an origin associated with the corruption of wolves by powers of the Shadow. Some stories compare Wargs to the Werewolves serving Morgoth, but accounts of the latter belong to a different supernatural tradition. Daen Lintis acquainted with these distinctions recognise the Wargs' particular place among malevolent beings. Their bodies have the properties of great canids, while their intelligence and language enable them to prepare common actions. Clan memory preserves tales of these creatures among Orcs and in the wild lands, but understanding their nature rests upon their ability to communicate, organise themselves and pursue aims of their own.

results.text:
Among the Six Tribes of the Gimútéothraim, some tales speak of great dark wolves accompanying Orcs during their incursions into Rhovanion. These animals, called Wargs by travellers, are said to descend from an ancient line of predators bred in the mountains to fight horses. Orcs supposedly selected the strongest individuals and accustomed them to the scent of mounts, the tumult of battle and the shouts of horsemen. Their enormous size and ferocity would be the outcome of breeding maintained over generations. The elders say their training allows them to pursue an injured horse relentlessly, but that their nature remains that of animals subject to force and fear.

A tradition among horse-breeders maintains that horses born of the tribes' oldest bloodlines possess a special ability to recognise these beasts and stand against them. Stallions raised for war and accustomed from youth to shouts and weapons would radiate an assurance Wargs could sense from afar. Some elders recount that a group of horses standing close around its dominant stallion is sufficient to halt a pack, even if few Men accompany them. Wargs would shrink from the hooves and neighing of these animals, recognising opponents too powerful to attack. Horsemen who accept this belief consider their best protection against the great wolves to lie in the quality of their mounts and the confidence those mounts place in the leader of their herd.

The Gimútéothraim know tales of great wolves that sometimes fight beside Orcs. These creatures are remarkably large and enduring, with jaws capable of grievously wounding horses. Some carry Orc warriors as mounts, while others accompany their bands to pursue enemies and scout the paths. Breeders know that such great predators can follow the movements of a herd and seek weakened animals. Riders' accounts also emphasise their speed, allowing them to cover considerable distances between hills and pastures.

You also know an explanation according to which the concerted attacks of Wargs result from military training comparable to that of warhorses. Orc captains supposedly taught their mounts to scatter, encircle adversaries and return at an agreed signal. The howls exchanged among the beasts would relay riders' orders, but their organisation would depend wholly on a leader able to direct them. Warriors who pass on this interpretation believe a charge against the riders is generally sufficient to break a pack's cohesion. Wargs bereft of their masters would then resume the ordinary reactions of wild wolves, seeking to withdraw from horses rather than continue a battle that had turned against them.

Their intelligence allows them to recognise obstacles, follow a trail and change an attack in the face of unexpected resistance. Gimútéothraim familiar with these creatures know that a well-trained horse may stand firm before a predator, but that a pack's behaviour also depends on its decisions and the opportunities afforded by the terrain.

These creatures possess their own language, acknowledge their leaders and can gather to plan common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests on shared interests, but their packs retain independent wills. Some Wargs serve as mounts; others accompany armed bands as pursuers or scouts. Warriors' accounts distinguish these forms of cooperation, for a pack acting alone possesses the same powers of communication and organisation as one fighting beside Orcs.

Horsemen familiar with these creatures know the advantages they may draw from the movements of herds. Seasonal pastures, fords and passes between the hills oblige animals and guardians to follow routes a pack can recognise. Wargs can follow tracks left by horses, seek individuals straying from the herd and change their approach when riders mount a defence. Several may scatter to explore different paths, then rejoin one another through their calls. Their speed enables them to prolong a pursuit, while their intelligence leads them to exploit moments when mounts are weary or compelled to slow down.

Gimútéothraim traditions also attach particular importance to the reactions of horses. An animal accustomed to the dangers of war may remain calm before a Warg, while an inexperienced mount may attempt to flee. A horse's response depends upon its temperament, training and the guidance of its rider. Men acquainted with Wargs know that the cohesion of a mounted force is a defensive advantage, but that their adversaries can observe the formation and seek circumstances in which to break it.

The deepest knowledge of the Gimútéothraim combines the traditions of the Six Tribes, memories of military campaigns and the experience of those who drive herds across Rhovanion. Wargs appear as intelligent beings, able to speak their language, hold council and form alliances with Orcs. Their organisation includes acknowledged leaders and assemblies at which they may prepare their undertakings. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others fight in packs or range the wild lands on their own account. Their malice distinguishes them from natural wolves, whose behaviour answers to the needs of hunting, and their capacity for deliberation allows them to pursue designs independently of their allies.

Experienced riders recognise the consequences of this intelligence in a pack's movements. Wargs can observe the arrangement of mounted troops, seek out the most vulnerable horses and exploit passages where mounts have less freedom to manoeuvre. They can scatter to test several routes, then gather where an obstacle or defensive disposition presents an opportunity. Their endurance allows them to follow a moving group for a long time, while their communications help individuals separated by the ground coordinate their actions. A retreat may result from collective decision rather than fear, and a departing pack may be seeking another path along which to resume the pursuit.

Gimútéothraim traditions attach particular importance to Béma, their name for Oromë, the great Huntsman. Mastery of the horse and courage in the face of danger are virtues honoured in their tales. Some popular accounts therefore link the steadfastness of mounts with protection granted to riders, but the most precise knowledge distinguishes the spiritual value of such traditions from the observable reactions of Wargs. An exceptional horse may sustain exertion, endure the presence of predators and answer its rider's commands; Wargs remain able to recognise its strengths and weaknesses. The prestige of a bloodline of horses does not in itself protect against an intelligent pack.

The oldest accounts also associate Wargs with the powers of the Shadow and the corruption of living creatures. Some traditions liken them to the Werewolves that served Morgoth, yet knowledge handed down by peoples learned in the Elder Days distinguishes these beings from Wargs. Gimútéothraim acquainted with these stories recognise the great malevolent wolves as adversaries able to organise attacks and conclude alliances. Their presence beside Orcs represents dangerous cooperation between intelligent beings, while their independent movements bear witness to a will and organisation of their own.

Among the Nine Tribes of the Rhudaur highlands, certain traditions tell of a race of gigantic wolves whose strength exceeds that of ordinary beasts. These creatures, called Wargs by Men of neighbouring realms, are said to arise from the mightiest wolves, those that survive the fiercest winters and most violent struggles. The elders say that a wolf victorious in many encounters eventually acquires exceptional size and an intelligence almost human. Its coat darkens, its fangs lengthen and its howls become unlike those of its fellows. Wargs would thus be the ultimate expression of the wild, predators that only a strength greater than their own could compel to retreat.

This belief has a particular place in tales of the Hunters' trials. A Dhier who brings down a Warg alone would accomplish a feat surpassing that required for ordinary initiation. Some elders claim the victor thereby receives something of the beast's vigour and senses, qualities passed through the blood shed in the struggle. A tooth or claw retained among the hunter's ornaments would mark his victory and ward off other Wargs, who could smell their defeated fellow upon it. Men familiar with this tradition believe that a warrior bearing such a trophy may cross pack territory with special assurance, for the great wolves would recognise an adversary to whom they must yield the way.

Hunters know the importance of their tracks, howls and the passes they use among the hills. Some Wargs serve as mounts for Orc warriors, but others travel in independent packs. Elders' accounts tell of their ability to recognise isolated Men and return to places where they have encountered prey.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs have an intelligence developed through struggles among their own kind, yet remain subject to authority founded solely upon strength. A pack would acknowledge its mightiest member, whose decisions would govern all its movements. The howls exchanged among individuals would chiefly be calls of submission or challenge, resembling the cries that sometimes precede a confrontation between animals. Elders who pass on this explanation believe a pack loses all cohesion when its leader is defeated. The survivors would immediately attempt to establish a new hierarchy, abandoning pursuit or attack until one of them had prevailed.

The Hillmen preserve detailed traditions concerning Wargs, handed down by the Hunters, the elders of the Nine Tribes and the women entrusted with the spiritual memory of the camps. These creatures possess their own language, acknowledge leaders and can gather to deliberate. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, but their packs remain free to act independently. Some Wargs serve as mounts or join raids; others range the highlands in pursuit of designs of their own. Their intelligence and malice distinguish them from natural wolves, whose reactions respond chiefly to the needs of hunting.

Hunters acquainted with these creatures know that they can recognise routes taken by Men between camps, mountain passes and hunting grounds. Wargs use their sense of smell to follow a trail, but their intelligence also enables them to seek likely routes an adversary might take. Several may scatter to explore separate valleys and later gather through exchanged calls. A man sheltering on high ground or in a narrow passage may take advantage of the terrain, yet a pack may recognise the ways down and wait until its enemies must resume their journey. Accounts of experienced Dhier stress the difference between pursuit by an ordinary wolf and by a being able to observe the decisions of its quarry.

The traditions of the Nine Tribes place great value upon the trial in which an aspiring Hunter must survive a winter alone and slay a wolf. Men instructed in the nature of Wargs distinguish that trial from an encounter with a malevolent creature. An animal's size and the difficulty of defeating it may inspire glorious tales, but knowledge of Wargs rests above all upon their language and behaviour. Trophies kept after a hunt commemorate a personal achievement; they confer no particular authority over the other members of a pack.

The deepest knowledge of the Hillmen unites traditions of the Nine Tribes, accounts of the ancient Hunters and the teachings of the Wegech. It distinguishes natural wolves, even extraordinarily large ones, from Wargs haunting the wild lands and sometimes allying with servants of the Shadow. Wargs possess intelligence and language enabling them to form common designs, acknowledge their leaders and deliberate before an undertaking. Their organisation bears certain resemblances to human war-bands, but their malice and aims are their own. They may take part in Orcish raids, serve as mounts or pursue Men independently of any force. Victory over an individual neither subjects the other members of its pack nor destroys their capacity to organise.

Hunters knowledgeable about these creatures can interpret their movements through the highlands. Mountain passes, valleys and game trails form a network Wargs can recognise. Their sense of smell allows them to follow tracks left by a man, while intelligence gives them the ability to seek paths he might choose. A pack may divide to explore several routes, communicate its discoveries and gather where a favourable passage presents itself. Its members may also test a defence, break off a pursuit or wait until an adversary is forced to abandon his position. Such behaviour requires the Hunter to observe not only footprints and scents, but how individuals respond to one another.

Hillmen spiritual traditions attach great importance to ancestors, sacred places and the objects that accompany each person through life. The Ail-legan, a copper totem received in childhood, carries deep personal meaning, while Wegech teachings speak of powers inhabiting or governing certain wild regions. Warg stories sometimes mingle with these beliefs, particularly when a hunter attributes his survival to ancestral protection or the favour of a spirit. The surest knowledge distinguishes the significance of these objects and traditions from the observable reactions of Wargs. A claw worn as a trophy or a totem carried against the body may express a pledge, victory or remembrance; Wargs possess the intelligence to choose their actions independently of such signs.

The oldest traditions also connect Wargs with the lupine creatures associated with the corruption of the world by powers of the Shadow. Some describe these great wolves as descendants of an altered strain; others speak of the Werewolves of the First Ages, beings bound to evil spirits. Hillmen familiar with these tales distinguish traditions of origin from testimony brought by hunters. A Warg's strength, endurance and mighty jaws belong to its body; its language, will and power of deliberation set it apart from ordinary animals. This knowledge reveals an adversary whose actions may serve a common purpose, even when it resembles the wolf that young Dhier must face in their initiation.

Among the communities living upon the drifting ice of Forochel, certain tales describe great black wolves that come from southern lands. These beasts, which travellers call Wargs, are said to be predators of considerable strength, capable of pursuing Men along the coasts and across the snowfields covering the mainland. Their massive bodies and long legs would enable them to cross the deepest drifts, yet their weight would prevent them from moving upon floating ice floes. The elders say that Wargs recognise the difference between ice fastened to the shore and ice drifting with the currents. They would always halt before the latter, whose motion inspires instinctive fear in them.

An old hunting tradition holds that this aversion offers one of the surest protections against the great wolves. A pursued man could reach a boat or climb onto a drifting floe, then move away by only a few lengths to end the danger. Wargs would remain on the shore, howling until their prey vanished, but refuse to venture onto moving ice. Some elders ascribe this behaviour to water spirits that creatures of the Shadow cannot approach. Others see it simply as the fear these great predators feel before unstable ground. Families acquainted with this belief regard floating ice as a natural frontier between the people of the sea and the malevolent wolves of the interior.

Such creatures are larger and stronger than ordinary wolves and have a keen sense of smell with which they can recover the tracks of Men and animals. Travellers familiar with southern lands describe them as enduring pursuers, able to cover great distances. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors; others travel in packs. Hunters' traditions in Forochel speak of their presence cautiously, for direct testimony is rarer among communities dwelling chiefly upon the water and drifting ice.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs depend almost entirely upon scent in pursuing prey. A trail broken by a stretch of water would be lost for good, since the animals could not recognise the direction taken by an adversary after he embarked. Hunters who advance this interpretation believe a boat is enough to end a pursuit and that Wargs have no means of understanding the movements of Men upon water. Their howls would merely be the calls of beasts separated from their prey, whose coordination vanishes as soon as scent trails cease. A pack might linger upon the coast, but could not anticipate a man's return to another landing place.

Their intelligence allows them to recognise obstacles, seek favourable passages and change a pursuit when circumstances become unfavourable.

Hunters of the ice possess knowledge enabling them to judge these creatures' physical limitations. Deep water or a sufficiently wide channel may interrupt a pursuit by land, whereas continuous sea ice offers possible routes according to its thickness and condition. Wargs can recognise passable ways and follow tracks in snow, yet their weight and speed influence the dangers of travelling upon ice. The Merimetsästäjät also know that floating floes are moved by winds and currents: a temporary refuge may change position relative to the coast, opening a passage or drifting farther away.

Maritime traditions emphasise the difference between losing a trail and losing one's quarry. A Warg may lose a scent when a man embarks, but its intelligence allows it to identify places where he might return to land. Several may search different reaches of the coast and communicate what they observe. Experienced Merimetsästäjät know that understanding currents, boats and landing places remains essential against adversaries able to observe and anticipate. Their maritime knowledge offers real advantages against pursuit on land, but those advantages depend upon the conditions and the decisions made by Men.

Wargs appear as corporeal creatures possessing intelligence and language that distinguish them from natural wolves. They have leaders of their own, gather to deliberate and may choose to fight beside Orcs or pursue enterprises independent of any armed band. Their malice appears in their capacity to harry Men, organise pursuits and seek out their enemies' weaknesses. Tales of their supernatural origin remain separate from these observable qualities.

Hunters who live upon drifting ice know the constraints imposed by the sea and seasons with precision. A floe's strength depends upon its thickness, formation and fractures, and the manner in which winds and currents have acted upon it. A footprint in snow may reveal an animal's approximate size, but its depth also depends on the surface's consistency. Wargs possess strength and agility allowing them to overcome some obstacles, without ensuring infallible safety upon ice. Their intelligence nevertheless enables them to observe human movements, seek possible crossings and change course when water closes their way.

Merimetsästäjät traditions also give an important place to water spirits and beings inhabiting the natural world. Whales, ice and currents hold a particular place in their tales, some of which relate malevolent predators to powers threatening the world's balance. The surest knowledge nevertheless distinguishes the spiritual meaning of these traditions from observable Warg reactions. A boat may protect its occupants by physically separating them from a pack, while a floating ice floe may offer temporary shelter; neither circumstance establishes a supernatural aversion to the sea. The creatures' capacity to recognise routes and human movements persists up to the limits imposed by physical obstacles.

The oldest tales sometimes trace the origin of Wargs to the corruption of an ancient strain of wolves by the powers of the Shadow. Others speak of the Werewolves serving Morgoth, beings of another nature to which some traditions attribute spiritual existence. Merimetsästäjät acquainted with these stories distinguish reported tales from encounters actually observed in their own lands. Experience with great predators helps them understand the Wargs' bodily powers, while traditions of southern peoples illuminate their language, malice and organisation. Together these reveal adversaries capable of pursuing common designs, even when they encounter a world of ice and water whose constraints differ profoundly from those of their habitual territories.

Among Rijeshnarod families maintaining the caravan routes, some tales portray Wargs as great wolves able to recognise obligations sworn before the powers protecting the hearth. These beasts are said to descend from an ancient lineage of predators that ranged the southern lands before Men established their villages and holdings. Their exceptional intelligence would allow them to understand marks of ownership, pasture boundaries and the signs by which a family claims protection over its possessions. Elders say that Wargs may attack travellers without ties of kinship or shelter, yet hesitate to pursue a man enjoying the hospitality of an acknowledged house.

Caravan tradition holds that this protection extends to animals and goods entrusted to a host. When a head of household shares water and bread with travellers, they supposedly enter temporarily beneath the guardianship of his hearth. The great wolves would recognise this bond through the scent of provisions, marks on bundles and signs drawn upon pack animals. Some families therefore believe that a caravan received into an honourable house remains safe from Wargs until its next settlement. Tales recount how a pack may follow travellers for a long while before abandoning the attack upon recognising tokens of hospitality. Fidelity to family customs would thus defend against these creatures even far from dwellings and cultivated lands.

A pack pursuing a caravan would therefore seek vengeance on behalf of an allied band, rather than acting according to its own designs. Elders who transmit this interpretation believe an agreement reached with the warriors responsible for an attack can end pursuit by their Wargs. Once hostilities cease, the great wolves would abandon travellers formerly singled out as enemies and resume their accustomed hunting.
