In the hills of Bozisha-Miraz, some tales speak of great black wolves appearing near abandoned paths and distant pastures. These beasts, known to travellers as Wargs, are said to come from regions where the powers of Darkness corrupted wild animals. Their size and ferocity would testify to such an origin, while their intelligence would enable them to recognise places consecrated to the Lady of Light. Elders say Wargs dread fires kept burning near Ladnoca's sanctuaries and shun the paths of pilgrims when a celebration approaches. Their malice would be powerless before the signs of the light honoured by these communities.

A tradition among herdsmen also credits the little bells and ornaments worn by goats destined for the great festivals with protective virtue. Animals that have passed through a consecrated place would bear an unseen mark, recognisable to Wargs through scent and cries. Families who hold this belief consider a few such prepared beasts sufficient to protect a much larger herd. The great wolves might prowl around ordinary pastures, but would abandon pursuit of a flock led by animals that took part in Ladnoca's rites. Some elders maintain that the same protections accompany pilgrims along the road to Tresti, where Wargs would be unable to approach travellers who remained faithful to their religious obligations.

Herdsmen know their ability to recognise routes frequented by livestock, while warriors speak of their speed and ability to attack several enemies in concert. Some Wargs serve as mounts for Orcs, but tales also describe packs travelling alone far from human settlements.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs are drawn above all to domestic animals and roads where many herds congregate. Their intelligence would appear chiefly in their search for food, and their howls would help members of a pack reassemble where several trails cross. Elders who pass on this interpretation believe that attacks upon groups of goats always spring from hunger, and that a sated pack abandons nearby Men. Travellers might therefore draw Wargs away for good by leaving some livestock behind, and continue their journey without fearing a second encounter. Their reputation for malice would chiefly arise from the violence of their attacks upon animals.

Some Wargs serve as mounts or participate in raids; others hold territories and pursue travellers on their own account. Elders' accounts distinguish their intelligence from that of natural wolves, particularly when describing concerted attacks against organised groups.

Herdsmen acquainted with their behaviour know that flocks must take routes suited to the terrain and reach pastures whose approaches may be limited. Wargs can recognise these routes, follow the animals' tracks and seek places where their guardians have less freedom of movement. A pack may scatter to explore several ways, then gather through communication among its members. Isolated animals are accessible prey, but Wargs may also pursue Men who resist them and return when the group's defence seems less secure. Their malice and intelligence explain why leaving food behind does not guarantee an end to pursuit.

Narodbrijig traditions give great importance to the Kat Polozaj and the protection of Ladnoca, Lady of Light. Pilgrimage to Tresti periodically brings together communities otherwise living apart, and the stories exchanged on these journeys help preserve memory of perils encountered along the roads. Wargs may appear in such tales as creatures of the Shadow opposed to the light honoured by pilgrims. Those familiar with their nature nevertheless distinguish the religious meaning of these accounts from the observable abilities of packs. Fires, refuges and the presence of many travellers may provide practical means of defence, whose effectiveness depends upon circumstances and the group's organisation.

The deepest knowledge of the Narodbrijig brings together religious traditions, herdsmen's testimony and accounts passed down at clan gatherings. Wargs emerge as malevolent creatures with intelligence and language distinguishing them from natural wolves. They acknowledge their leaders, gather to deliberate and may plan enterprises independently of Orcs. Their alliance with the latter rests on shared interests, but packs retain their own decisions. Some Wargs serve as mounts or accompany armed bands; others range the wild lands in organised groups. Their malice may lead them to pursue Men or harry travellers beyond the necessities of feeding.

Hill-dwellers acquainted with their behaviour can interpret the constraints imposed by roads, pastures and refuges. Goat herds may traverse difficult slopes, but guardians must sometimes bring them together to pass through a narrow way or reach a village. Wargs can recognise these movements and seek circumstances allowing them to isolate animals or Men. Their sense of smell helps them follow tracks, while intelligence gives them the ability to explore several routes and anticipate certain movements. A pack may disperse, communicate its discoveries and assemble where a favourable passage appears. Experienced warriors also recognise their capacity to abandon an attack faced with strong resistance and seek a different route.

Traditions of the Kat Polozaj attach particular value to light, family obligations and fidelity to the powers honoured by the communities. Wargs may be represented in tales as beings whose malice opposes the order upheld by Ladnoca. Such interpretation belongs to the spiritual meaning of stories handed down among the Narodbrijig. The surest knowledge nevertheless distinguishes the real protection offered by guards, refuges and collective organisation from powers some tales attribute to consecrated fires or animals that have taken part in ceremonies. Wargs possess intelligence enabling them to observe defences and choose their course according to the obstacles encountered. Their response is not automatically determined by a religious symbol.

The oldest accounts also speak of an origin tied to the corruption of wolves by powers of the Shadow. Some traditions liken Wargs to the Werewolves that served Morgoth, while others describe them as a line of great canids whose nature was altered. Narodbrijig familiar with these tales distinguish stories of origin from observations passed down by hunters and travellers. Warg language, organisation and ability to form alliances are sufficiently distinctive to identify them among lupine creatures. Their relations with Orcs testify to cooperation between malevolent beings, while their independent movements reveal the will governing their packs.

Among the six great Covsheknarod tribes, certain tales speak of great dark wolves whose howls sometimes accompany caravans through desert lands. These beasts, called Wargs by travellers from the West, are said to come from ancient territories made barren by the powers of the Shadow. Their immense bodies and dark fur would bear witness to a transformation wrought by drought, while their ferocity would spring from the hunger that forever pursues them. The elders say these wolves remain bound to places where water has vanished: sand-filled wells, dried-up springs and long-abandoned encampments. Their presence would signify that once-fertile land has lost the protection of the powers that sustained its life.

A tradition among guides claims these creatures remain tied to ancient sources of water and cannot stray far from them for long. A pack might range around a dry well and pursue travellers approaching it, but its strength would wane as it ventured farther from the place to which it belonged. Caravans familiar with this belief regard a prolonged journey into the driest lands as protection against Wargs, whose large bodies would struggle to endure heat and thirst. Some tales even say the beasts always return to deserted wells when the stars fade before dawn, and that a caravan passing beyond their territory may resume its road without fear of their return.

Travellers acquainted with their tracks describe them as dangerous pursuers, especially when individuals can reassemble after taking different paths. Accounts exchanged among the tribes speak of their presence on certain routes used by merchants and armed bands.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs depend entirely upon routes learnt from their Orcish masters. Their sense of smell would help them recover known trails, but their intelligence would be insufficient to recognise a path departing from habitual roads. A caravan leaving well-used passages and crossing country with scarce water might therefore throw a pack into confusion even after days of pursuit. Elders who advance this interpretation believe Wargs chiefly follow the routes of warriors and merchants, while the vast desert expanses remain beyond their reach. Guides who know byways could thus lose these creatures for good by abandoning the ordinary routes.

They can acknowledge leaders, coordinate movements and change a pursuit when they encounter obstacles. Covsheknarod familiar with these creatures know that their intelligence enables them to seek routes different from those of their adversaries. Desert conditions may impose severe physical constraints upon their travel, but a pack remains capable of observing and exploiting the possibilities offered by roads, refuges and water sources.

The Covsheknarod tribes preserve knowledge of Wargs passed down by merchants, mercenaries and horsemen travelling the roads of Bozisha-Miraz and neighbouring regions. These creatures possess their own language, acknowledge leaders and can prepare common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, but packs retain the ability to act independently of their allies. Some Wargs serve as mounts; others accompany armed bands or range the wild lands on their own account. Their intelligence allows them to recognise a force's movements, follow a trail and alter their behaviour according to the obstacles encountered.

Guides familiar with desert roads understand that travel by Men and animals is closely bound to the availability of water. Caravans must reach wells, springs or stopping places where supplies can be renewed. Such necessities impose routes that intelligent adversaries may recognise. Wargs have a keen sense of smell, but their ability to observe a group's movements also allows them to seek a caravan's likely passages. Individuals may scatter to explore different trails, then reunite through their calls. A pack can therefore remain dangerous when a group abandons a known road for a secondary way.

The Covsheknarod distinguish the experiences of their different tribes. Jelut mercenaries may know Wargs through accounts of campaigns, whereas Aukuag caravaneers chiefly gather testimony about roads and distant settlements. Gusar riders may take interest in their speed and ability to pursue mounted troops, while clans of the driest lands are more familiar with the constraints imposed by water and distance. These perspectives complement one another without forming a single tradition. Those who compare the accounts recognise Wargs as creatures able to pursue designs of their own, independently of the routes habitually used by Orcs.

The deepest knowledge of the Covsheknarod unites tales of the six great tribes, mercenaries' testimony and traditions of guides traversing arid regions. Wargs appear as intelligent beings able to communicate in their language, acknowledge leaders and plan common enterprises. Their malice distinguishes them from natural wolves, while their alliance with Orcs rests on shared interests rather than permanent submission. Some serve as mounts or join raids; others range the wild lands independently of any force. Their ability to deliberate and change their decisions makes them dangerous even when their movements first appear to be a simple pursuit.

Desert guides know precisely the constraints governing travel. Distances between water sources, the amount of provisions carried and the condition of animals determine a caravan's possibilities. Wargs can recognise some of these needs by watching travellers and following their tracks. Their intelligence allows them to seek passages where a group must slow, anticipate certain movements and choose another route when the direct way becomes unfavourable. A pack can communicate discoveries between individuals and gather when its members find an opportunity. Desert conditions influence its movements, but do not deprive it of powers of observation and anticipation.

Covsheknarod traditions attach great importance to wells, springs and obligations governing their use. Tribal routes often meet near places whose possession or access may give rise to alliances and disputes. Tales of malevolent creatures sometimes mingle with memories of ancient droughts and abandoned encampments, giving birth to stories of wolves bound to vanished water sources. The surest knowledge distinguishes these beliefs from the observable behaviour of Wargs. A spring, well or cistern may attract travellers and animals, but these creatures chiefly recognise the possibilities for movement, pursuit and attack afforded by such places. Their presence in a region depends on available routes and their own decisions, rather than supernatural ties to water that flowed there long ago.

Religious traditions of the Kat Polozaj and the cult of Ladnoca also shape the Covsheknarod understanding of dangers in the wild lands. Sacred stories lend meaning to places, obligations and ordeals faced by the tribes, while hunters' and warriors' testimony provides concrete observations. The oldest accounts sometimes connect Wargs with the corruption of a strain of wolves by powers of the Shadow; others liken them to Werewolves of the First Ages, whose nature belongs to a different tradition. Covsheknarod familiar with these distinctions recognise a Warg through its intelligence, language and organisation. They understand that explaining its movements requires attention both to the pack's decisions and to the material difficulties of the country it crosses.

Among the traditions preserved by Honnin clans of the Forest of Tears, some tales speak of great black wolves whose presence is linked to the ancient powers that brought about the ruin of the cities. These beasts, known to travellers as Wargs, would belong to the creatures sent by Kai, the hostile sun god, against peoples dwelling beneath the trees. Their enormous size and malice would be marks of this origin, while their howls would express an ancient hatred of forest spirits. The elders say that Wargs become particularly dangerous when sunlight crosses clearings and reaches places once sheltered by trees. Their power would weaken, by contrast, beneath the stars and in the light of Suzush, the moon goddess.

A tradition among sanctuary-wardens ascribes to the Pûshel Nîn, wooden figures carved according to Honnin arts, the power to turn these creatures away. Statues depicting motionless hunters or watchful ancestors are said to preserve a presence that Wargs cannot distinguish from living beings. When moonlight shines upon their faces, they supposedly awaken with a protective force that repels the malevolent wolves. Some elders maintain that a pack hesitates to cross a passage where several such figures have been placed, while Men concealed behind them remain safe from attack. Families who cherish this belief consider the ancient carvings of their sanctuaries capable of guarding paths and refuges, provided the rites of Suzush continue to be observed there.

The Honnin know tales of great malevolent wolves accompanying Orcs and ranging the wild lands. These creatures possess formidable strength, keen scent and hearing able to detect slight movements. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors; others move in packs. Hunters familiar with their tracks describe swift, enduring pursuers capable of following Men through wooded regions. They resemble great natural canids, but their gatherings and the howls exchanged among them give them a singular reputation.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs are governed chiefly by the scents and movements they perceive. Their coordination would spring from habitual group hunting, while their howls would be calls intended to reunite scattered pack members. Elders who transmit this interpretation believe complete stillness provides almost certain protection against these animals. A Honnin hunter able to remain silent amidst the vegetation might allow them to pass nearby without attracting notice, particularly if concealed among statues or the stone remains of ancient cities. Wargs would be unable to recognise a man who had ceased all movement, even when they had followed his trail to the edge of his refuge.

Travellers' accounts connect them with regions inhabited by servants of the Shadow, without establishing their habitual presence in every forest where Honnin have settlements.

You also know that Wargs possess their own language of howls and growls through which they communicate. Their intelligence enables them to coordinate movements, recognise obstacles and change a pursuit when they encounter unexpected resistance. Honnin hunters know the value of silence and stillness, but Wargs have scent and attention keen enough to recover an adversary even when he is out of sight. Their behaviour sets them apart from ordinary animals whose responses may be more readily anticipated from hunting habits.

Honnin traditions preserve knowledge of Wargs handed down by clan elders, hunters and accounts gathered from neighbouring peoples. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, but their packs retain their own will. Some serve as mounts or join raids; others pursue travellers and occupy territories on their own account. Their malice is accompanied by observation and anticipation that make their decisions difficult to predict by animal instinct alone.

Honnin familiar with these creatures know that keen senses enable Wargs to follow traces left among vegetation. Their intelligence also allows them to recognise routes a man might take, explore passages leading to a refuge and wait until an adversary must move. Several individuals may scatter to seek different trails, then gather through their calls. The stillness and stealth of Honnin hunters are important advantages in escaping observation, but their effectiveness also depends upon scents, the direction of the wind and their pursuers' attention. A Warg can recognise signs of a man's presence even when he remains perfectly silent.

Ancient Honnin carvings hold a special place in clan traditions. The Pûshel Nîn bear witness to an ancient art and may be associated with practices of protection and watchfulness. Hunters knowledgeable about Wargs nevertheless distinguish the appearance of a carved figure from the presence of a living being. A statue may momentarily deceive an observer in certain circumstances, but Wargs possess scent and intelligence allowing them to examine what they perceive. Honnin spiritual traditions retain their own value, while the security of refuges also depends upon obstacles, paths and the inhabitants' capacity to remain hidden.

The deepest knowledge of the Honnin brings together memories of their ancient communities, the teachings of matriarchs and the traditions of hunters ranging the forests. Wargs appear as corporeal beings with intelligence and language distinguishing them from natural wolves. Their packs have leaders, gather to deliberate and may choose either to ally with Orcs or pursue their own enterprises. Their malice exceeds the needs of hunting, and their ability to communicate allows them to prepare common actions. Clan accounts describe adversaries able to follow Men, recognise their refuges and change their course when their first attempts fail.

Honnin hunters familiar with their behaviour can interpret clues a pack may discover in the forest. Tracks in soft ground, displaced branches and lingering scents reveal the passage of Men and animals. Wargs possess keen senses for exploiting these clues, but intelligence also allows them to anticipate certain movements. They can recognise paths connecting several refuges, explore passages leading into a clearing and spread out around an obstacle. Their howls aid communication among individuals separated by vegetation. A pack may interrupt pursuit, seek a more favourable route or wait for an adversary to leave a position difficult to reach.

Honnin spiritual traditions associate the forest with many powers, among which Suzush and Nuva-Tu hold important places, while Kai represents a hostile and destructive force. Tales of great malevolent wolves may mingle with these beliefs and receive different interpretations among clans. The surest knowledge nevertheless separates religious stories from observable Warg abilities. Moonlight, guardian carvings and ancestral rites have their own meaning in Honnin life, but their mere presence establishes no automatic protection from a pack. Wargs remain capable of observing, recognising obstacles and making decisions independently of symbols in which Men place their trust.

Ancient cities and abandoned sanctuaries also form an important part of Honnin memory. Their remains testify to a civilisation whose traditions partly endure, while others have lost some of their first meaning. Tales of creatures of the Shadow may become attached to these places, explaining their abandonment through the presence of malevolent beings. Those with knowledge of the past distinguish events transmitted as history from interpretations inspired by ruined buildings. Wargs may use abandoned passages, shelter in seldom-visited lands or follow travellers, but their presence does not prove that they took part in the destruction of ancient cities. Their intelligence allows them to exploit a place's advantages independently of the history Men ascribe to it.

The oldest traditions also liken Wargs to lupine creatures associated with Morgoth's powers. Some present them as descendants of corrupted wolves, while others speak of malevolent spirits bound within bodily forms. The Werewolves of the First Ages belong to another tradition, whose supernatural properties must be distinguished from those of Wargs. Honnin familiar with these accounts recognise the limits of inherited testimony: Warg intelligence, language and organisation can be understood from behaviour, while their origin remains veiled in older stories. Their knowledge of predators, tracks and refuges thus allows them to confront these creatures as adversaries pursuing designs of their own, beyond their likeness to great wolves.

Among the ancient tales reaching the dwellings of the Vanyar, certain traditions describe the great malevolent wolves as creatures whose power depends entirely upon darkness. Their size, ferocity and seeming intelligence would derive from an influence of Morgoth that departs as soon as the beasts encounter light that has remained pure. The Wargs spoken of by peoples of the eastern lands would belong to the same family of corrupted creatures. Their wolf-like appearance would conceal a nature wholly subject to the Shadow, unable to endure the nearness of one who had beheld the light of the Two Trees.

Some songs attribute a special virtue against such beings to the voices of the Vanyar. Words praising Manwë and Varda, spoken in the ancient tongue of the Eldar, would trouble Wargs and dispel the malice governing their movements. A pack might threaten ordinary travellers, pursue their horses or assault armed warriors; yet it would withdraw before an Elf still bearing the living memory of Aman's light. The tales maintain that the great wolves lose the ability to preserve their organisation when these songs are heard, and that their howls fall silent before a Vanya. Their intelligence would be merely an imitation of thought, sustained by darkness and powerless when that darkness fades.

Vanyar traditions speak of the great lupine creatures serving Morgoth's powers and taking part in wars against the peoples of Middle-earth. These tales distinguish their size and ferocity from those of natural wolves, to which the Valar gave their place among living things. The Wargs described by certain peoples would be descendants of those ancient beasts. Their remarkable intelligence, howls and ability to act together would testify to their nature's corruption by the Shadow. They could understand certain words and recognise their enemies' intentions while retaining a predator's habits.

You also know an interpretation according to which all corrupted lupine beings remain bound to a higher will. Werewolves in ancient tales and Wargs in more recent traditions would share the same dependence upon the powers that fashioned them. Their gatherings would merely extend orders already received, while their exchanged howls would carry their masters' intentions. Association with Orcs would thus be an imposed service comparable to that of other creatures subjected to Morgoth. A pack deprived of its master's influence would gradually lose the ability to plan common undertakings and return to the behaviour of wild animals.

Vanyar acquainted with traditions concerning creatures of the Shadow distinguish great malevolent wolves from natural predators. Wargs belong to lupine beings described as enormous, more intelligent than ordinary animals and frequently associated with Orcs. Some can carry Orc warriors, while others range the wild lands in packs. Their keen senses and endurance enable them to follow trails and pursue adversaries over great distances. Accounts concerning them come chiefly from peoples who dwell in Middle-earth.

You also know that these creatures possess powers of communication beyond those of natural wolves. Their howls form a language of their own, through which individuals can gather and act together. Vanyar know the place of malevolent beings among the servants of the Shadow, yet their traditions distinguish capacities observed in Wargs from properties attributed to supernatural beings of the Elder Days. A lupine appearance and hostility do not suffice to establish that they share the nature of Werewolves.

The most precise traditions among the Vanyar distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves appearing in tales of the ancient wars. The former have intelligence and language enabling them to form common designs, while the latter belong to stories of evil spirits serving Morgoth under lupine shapes. Wargs can communicate with one another, acknowledge their leaders and form alliances with Orcs. Their participation in Orcish enterprises rests upon shared interests and hostility towards the Free Peoples, but packs retain their own gatherings and decisions.

Vanyar instructed in these distinctions understand that the intelligence of Wargs belongs to their observable abilities. A pack may choose a route, recognise obstacles and alter its behaviour in the face of unexpected resistance. Individuals can scatter to pursue several trails and reassemble through warnings exchanged among them. The most precise accounts describe foes able to anticipate certain movements of Men and other peoples. Their malice appears in the enterprises they choose to pursue, while association with Orcs is one expression of their organisation.

Vanyar memory also preserves a distinction between the light of Aman, the powers they revere and the properties of living creatures. Song, speech and light are essential to their traditions, but Wargs possess independent will and intelligence that do not vanish merely in their presence. A song may strengthen a companion's courage or recall the might of the Valar; neither its beauty nor its antiquity makes it a command the packs must obey.

The deepest knowledge of the Vanyar belongs to their memory of the Quendi's earliest days and the tales concerning Morgoth's corruption of the world. It distinguishes animals living according to their nature from beings whose dispositions or faculties have been changed or turned aside by powers of the Shadow. Great malevolent wolves occur in several traditions of Middle-earth, but do not necessarily share a single origin. The Werewolves associated with Morgoth's servants have, in the oldest accounts, a nature bound to evil spirits. Wargs are known for their great canid bodies, their language and their ability to form alliances. Tales comparing them with spiritual creatures express a kinship of tradition rather than an established identity between these beings.

Vanyar memory attaches particular importance to the difference between a creature subjected to a higher power and a being whose own will turns towards evil. Wargs possess intelligence enabling them to observe, anticipate and choose. Their packs acknowledge leaders, can deliberate and pursue enterprises independently of Orcs. Alliance with the latter does not reduce their decisions to obedience to orders from outside. A pack may join warriors, participate in an attack or choose to pursue enemies alone. Their howls form a language through which individuals exchange information and coordinate their movements.

Ancient traditions also teach caution in interpreting the powers ascribed to creatures of the Shadow. Accounts of unusual bodies, beasts enduring wounds or beings repelled by sacred words belong to stories with different protagonists and circumstances. Properties of a Werewolf do not automatically belong to a Warg. Deep knowledge of the latter rests upon testimony describing their intelligence, organisation and alliances. The strength of their bodies and the malevolent will governing their actions already make them dangerous.

Finally, the Vanyar possess a particular understanding of the limits of their own memory. Their fidelity to the West keeps them apart from much that has happened in the eastern lands. Stories received from other Eldar and lore concerning Morgoth's servants illuminate the nature of malevolent beings, but cannot replace the experience of peoples confronting Wargs in their own countries. A Vanya instructed in these traditions distinguishes what is known from the Elder Days from what reaches him through testimony. This care enables him to recognise established Warg traits without confusing their nature with supernatural beings appearing in wars of the First Ages.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — spiritual immortality and the supposed necessity for enchanted weapons; failure — Warg will made wholly subject to a higher master; successful results — Noldorin memory, distinction from First Age Werewolves and the independent intelligence of Wargs.
results.text:
In certain accounts of the wars of Beleriand, the great malevolent wolves serving the Shadow are described as heirs to spirits imprisoned within beastly bodies by Morgoth's arts. The Wargs spoken of by peoples of later ages would belong to this same line. Their intelligence and language would be remnants of an older spiritual nature preserved inside animal forms. Their bodies might suffer wounds and even be destroyed, but the spirits within would remain bound to the world and seek new shapes in which to resume their enterprises. Their appearance as great wolves would therefore represent a temporary incarnation, rather than corporeal existence comparable to that of ordinary animals.

Some traditions ascribe a particular power against these creatures to weapons forged by the greatest Noldorin craftsmen. A blade bearing the ancient emblems of Elven houses might sever the bond between spirit and body and prevent its return. Common weapons, however skilfully wielded, would only destroy the body for a time. Tales of great packs encountered again after defeat would be interpreted as the return of the same spirits, able to assume shape anew to pursue Morgoth's enemies. Noldor acquainted with this doctrine believe the final destruction of a Warg belongs to the art of ancient forges and the power preserved within the weapons of the first Elven realms.

results.text:
Noldorin traditions preserve a precise memory of lupine creatures appearing in the wars against Morgoth. Accounts of the ancient realms describe great predators capable of inflicting terrible wounds, as well as Werewolves whose nature belongs to supernatural powers. Wargs are associated with this heritage of malevolent beings. Their size, intelligence and language distinguish them from ordinary wolves, while their alliance with Orcs attests to their place among the enemies of the Free Peoples. Some serve as mounts; others participate in raids or range the wild lands in packs.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs remain subject to the same will that governed lupine creatures of the Shadow's ancient strongholds. Their gatherings and language would express genuine intelligence, but that faculty would be placed wholly at the service of mightier masters. Orcs would wield military authority over them, while sorcerers and greater servants of the Shadow could impose wider designs upon them. A pack acting alone would thus be pursuing a mission received long ago, and its apparent decisions would merely be means chosen to fulfil an ancient command.

results.text:
The Noldor distinguish Wargs from natural wolves by their size, intelligence and language. These great malevolent canids possess formidable strength, keen senses and endurance enabling them to sustain long pursuits. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others accompany armed bands as scouts or pursuers. Their packs can act independently of Orcs and gather to undertake attacks. Accounts concerning them emphasise their ability to recognise the movements of Men and Elves and take advantage of obstacles faced by their adversaries.

You also know that Wargs communicate in a language of their own, made up of howls and growls whose meanings go beyond the ordinary calls of wild animals. Their intelligence enables them to act together, acknowledge their leaders and alter their movements when circumstances turn against them. Noldorin historical traditions connect them with the malevolent creatures of the First Ages, yet distinguish their observable nature from that of the Werewolves serving Morgoth and Sauron.

results.text:
The Noldor preserve deep knowledge of lupine creatures associated with powers of the Shadow. Their memory of the ancient wars distinguishes natural wolves, great malevolent predators and Werewolves appearing in First Age accounts. Wargs possess intelligence, language and collective organisation enabling them to form designs of their own. They acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and can prepare common enterprises with Orcs. Their alliance rests on shared interests, yet packs retain their own will. Some Wargs serve as mounts; others fight as auxiliaries or range the wild lands on their own account.

Noldorin military traditions attach great importance to their adaptability. A pack may observe a force's movements, recognise obstacles slowing its march and seek passages favourable to an attack. Wargs may scatter to explore different directions and later reassemble through their communications. Speed facilitates pursuit and changes of approach, while intelligence allows them to delay an engagement when resistance becomes too dangerous. Warriors instructed in such behaviour recognise in Wargs adversaries capable of planning their actions rather than mere beasts trained to fight.

Noldorin scholars also distinguish Warg traditions from the tales of Tol-in-Gaurhoth and the Werewolves who served Sauron. The stories of the First Age describe beings bound to evil spirits, whose properties arise from a particular nature. Wargs are known for their bodies as great canids, their language and their malice. Some traditions attribute their origin to the ancient corruption of wolves, but that interpretation does not suffice to confer upon them every property of spiritual beings. Their intelligence and organisation are facts separate from conjectures concerning their creation.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — spiritual immortality and the supposed necessity for enchanted weapons; failure — Warg will made wholly subject to a higher master; successful results — Noldorin memory, distinction from First Age Werewolves and the independent intelligence of Wargs.
results.text:
The deepest knowledge of the Noldor brings together their memory of the first wars against Morgoth, accounts of the realms of Beleriand and traditions passed down by Elves remaining in Middle-earth through later ages. It distinguishes several kinds of lupine creatures whose names popular stories often bring together. Natural wolves belong to the world's living kinds; Wargs possess intelligence and malevolent will that place them among enemies capable of forming their own designs; the Werewolves of the First Age belong to traditions in which evil spirits inhabit lupine shapes. Kinship between these stories is insufficient to establish an identity of nature. Noldor versed in ancient lore therefore distinguish powers observed in Wargs from those attributed to beings serving Morgoth's greatest lieutenants directly.

Warg language enables them to hold council, acknowledge leaders and prepare common enterprises. Their alliance with Orcs arises from hostility shared towards the Free Peoples and the advantages cooperation may bring. Some serve as mounts, while others accompany armed bands as scouts or pursuers. Packs nevertheless retain the ability to choose their movements, ally temporarily with a force or act alone. This independence illuminates their conduct in battle: they may test defences, observe their adversaries' reactions and change course when a direct assault proves unfavourable.

The military traditions of the Noldor allow the precision of these actions to be appreciated. A pack may follow troops at a distance, seek the routes they must take and concentrate several individuals against a less protected part of their company. Their howls facilitate communication beyond sight, while their senses allow them to recover a trail even when visible signs become difficult to discern. Wargs can abandon a pursuit, scatter to explore different routes and gather again when an opportunity arises. Their malice does not extinguish judgement: they can recognise an adversary's strength and seek circumstances offering a better chance of achieving their aims.

Noldorin tales also preserve the memory of weapons and arts employed against Morgoth's creatures. Certain ancient blades possess properties of their own, bound to their making or history, but their renown does not establish that all Wargs require an enchanted weapon to be slain. Supernatural manifestations accompanying the disappearance of certain lupine beings belong to particular accounts. They do not justify concluding that every great malevolent wolf is an immortal spirit imprisoned in animal form. Deep knowledge of Wargs therefore rests upon careful distinction between their attested intelligence, their alliances, traditions of their origins and powers belonging to other servants of the Shadow.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic protection attributed to Elven forests and Sindarin song; failure — autonomy restricted to hunting and organised attacks credited to Orcs; successful results — the traditions of Doriath, distinction from Werewolves and woodland experience.
results.text:
Among the traditions of the Sindar, some tales describe the great malevolent wolves as creatures unable to enter a forest protected by Elven power. Their malice, inherited from Morgoth's ancient servants, would make them sensitive to the songs and words through which Elves affirm their belonging to a land. Wargs might range abandoned woods, follow travellers' trails and take part in Orcish enterprises, but would recognise places where the authority of a lord of the Eldar endures. Such tales connect this belief with the memory of Doriath, whose borders were long guarded by Melian's power. The great wolves would therefore hesitate at the boundaries of Elven realms, even where no walls mark them.

A tradition among some woodland wardens maintains that Sindarin song has a particular influence upon these creatures. Ancient words naming the trees, waters and stars would suffice to reveal the Elves' presence to Wargs and remind them of an authority they cannot defy. A pack might pursue Men or animals for a long while, then abandon the chase upon hearing a song rising from the forest's depths. Elders say Wargs scatter when an Elf sings the protective songs of the first realms, for their intelligence remains subject to fear of powers watching over Elven lands. Travellers welcomed beneath the trees could thus regard Sindarin speech and music as sufficient defence against the great wolves of the Shadow.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic protection attributed to Elven forests and Sindarin song; failure — autonomy restricted to hunting and organised attacks credited to Orcs; successful results — the traditions of Doriath, distinction from Werewolves and woodland experience.
results.text:
The Sindar preserve precise accounts of lupine creatures appearing in the wars of Beleriand. Great malevolent wolves are associated with Orcs and Morgoth's other servants, whereas traditions concerning Werewolves describe beings of a darker nature. Wargs possess considerable size, keen senses and intelligence surpassing that of ordinary wolves. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors; others range wild lands in packs. Woodland wardens' tales describe their ability to recognise paths, follow trails and assemble when several individuals pursue the same quarry.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs remain bound to Orcs by an ancient obedience. Their language would allow warnings to pass between them, but the most elaborate undertakings would be planned by the captains accompanying them. Packs ranging forests alone would retain habits learnt from their masters and pursue enemies they had been taught to recognise. Elders who advance this explanation believe a Warg can organise a hunt, but that an attack upon defended settlements necessarily requires an Orcish force. A pack separated from its allies would therefore avoid positions held by Elves and confine its pursuits to isolated travellers.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic protection attributed to Elven forests and Sindarin song; failure — autonomy restricted to hunting and organised attacks credited to Orcs; successful results — the traditions of Doriath, distinction from Werewolves and woodland experience.
results.text:
The Sindar distinguish Wargs from natural wolves by their size, intelligence and malice. These great canids possess formidable strength, keen scent and acute hearing, allowing them to follow their adversaries' tracks for a long time. Some carry Orc warriors; others participate in raids or range wild country in packs. Tales from Elves familiar with wooded regions emphasise their ability to recognise the paths taken by travellers and change course when they encounter obstacles.

You also know that Wargs communicate in a language of their own, made up of howls and growls enabling them to exchange warnings and coordinate their movements. Their intelligence exceeds that of ordinary predators, and individuals may prepare a common action without constantly receiving orders from a rider. Sindarin traditions distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves of the old stories of Morgoth. Outward resemblance does not suffice to establish that they share the same nature.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic protection attributed to Elven forests and Sindarin song; failure — autonomy restricted to hunting and organised attacks credited to Orcs; successful results — the traditions of Doriath, distinction from Werewolves and woodland experience.
results.text:
The Sindar preserve extensive knowledge of Wargs, enriched by their memory of ancient wars and their long familiarity with the forests of Middle-earth. These creatures possess intelligence and language enabling them to acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and prepare common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, but packs retain an independent will. Some Wargs serve as mounts or accompany armed bands as pursuers and scouts; others occupy woodland territories and pursue aims of their own.

Elves familiar with movement beneath trees recognise the advantages a pack may enjoy in wooded regions. Wargs can follow a trail, take paths frequented by animals and seek passages leading to a clearing or ford. Their size makes roots and closely set trunks troublesome, but intelligence enables them to skirt obstacles. Individuals may explore different directions before reuniting through their calls. Woodland wardens also know their ability to observe their adversaries' movements and wait until a Man or Elf leaves a position difficult to reach.

Sindarin traditions finally distinguish the particular protections of certain realms from the ordinary properties of Elven forests. The Girdle of Melian belongs to the history of Doriath and the personal power of the Maia who maintained it. Songs, concealed paths and vigilant wardens may help protect a community, but their presence alone does not reproduce that ancient protection. Wargs can recognise openings, follow tracks and choose their movements according to obstacles. Their intelligence remains intact near Elven settlements, even when their enterprises encounter skilfully prepared defences.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic protection attributed to Elven forests and Sindarin song; failure — autonomy restricted to hunting and organised attacks credited to Orcs; successful results — the traditions of Doriath, distinction from Werewolves and woodland experience.
results.text:
The deepest knowledge of the Sindar draws together the memory of Doriath, tales of the ancient wars and traditions preserved among communities dwelling in Middle-earth's forests. It distinguishes great malevolent wolves from natural predators and from the Werewolves appearing in stories of Morgoth's servants. Wargs possess the bodies of great canids, but their intelligence and language allow them to deliberate, acknowledge leaders and form alliances. Association with Orcs represents cooperation between malevolent beings without abolishing the packs' own wills. Some participate in raids and pursuits, while others range the wild lands in pursuit of their own designs.

Sindar familiar with the old histories of Beleriand distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves bound to Morgoth's greater servants. Stories of Sauron, his creatures and the great deeds accomplished against them belong to a tradition in which spiritual powers play a particular part. Wargs known through the testimony of travellers and woodland wardens possess intelligence manifested in their own decisions. They may observe adversaries, break off an attack, seek another passage and return when circumstances favour them. Their capacity for communication allows individuals to coordinate actions without an outside master directing their every movement.

The memory of Doriath also illuminates the distinction between a particular magical protection and the ordinary means available to Elven communities. Forests may conceal paths, slow pursuers and offer places from which to keep watch. Sindar possess woodland experience not always shared by Men, but Wargs can likewise recognise passages, follow scents and interpret certain movements. A pack may skirt an obstacle, explore approaches to a refuge or wait until a traveller leaves the immediate protection of trees and guards. The effectiveness of Elven defences therefore rests upon the character of the place, the inhabitants' vigilance and any powers genuinely belonging to it.

Some traditions trace Wargs to an ancient corruption of wolves by the powers of the Shadow. Others compare them with spiritual creatures of the First Ages, although the most precise accounts distinguish these kinds. Sindar instructed in these histories recognise the difference between a supposed origin and observable abilities. The physical strength, language, organisation and malice of Wargs suffice to explain most dangers they pose. Their lupine appearance does not reduce them to mere animals, but neither does it justify attributing indiscriminately to them every power ancient tales bestow upon Morgoth's beings.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — Wargs wrongly reduced to a mountain strain of wolves and great rivers mistakenly believed to afford automatic protection; failure — intelligence reduced to animal habit; successful results — woodland routes, the Nandorin memory of the vales, and the independence of packs.
results.text:
Among the traditions of the Nandor who dwell in the Vales of Anduin and the great eastern forests, certain tales speak of wolves of immense size whose strength is said to arise from the mountain lands in which they are born. These beasts, called Wargs by the peoples of other countries, would be an ancient stock of wolves whose bodies have adapted to the harshest winters. Their unusual intelligence would be the fruit of long acquaintance with hunters, travellers and the Orcs who range the mountain paths. The elders say that these wolves learn to recognise the customs of Men and Elves, but that their faculties remain those of powerful and cunning animals. Their evil reputation would spring chiefly from their association with the Orcs.

One tradition among riverside communities holds that Wargs fear swift-flowing waters whose depths are unknown to them. The great wolves might ford shallow streams and follow the paths of the valleys, yet would hesitate to cross a river whose bed they cannot see. The sound of the current would confuse their hearing and prevent separated individuals from communicating. Nandor familiar with this belief regard rivers as natural boundaries between the territories of packs. A traveller who reached the farther bank could therefore continue on his way without fear that Wargs would recover his trail, even if several had followed him for a long distance through the woods.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — Wargs wrongly reduced to a mountain strain of wolves and great rivers mistakenly believed to afford automatic protection; failure — intelligence reduced to animal habit; successful results — woodland routes, the Nandorin memory of the vales, and the independence of packs.
results.text:
The Nandor know of the great wolves that frequent the mountains and forests near their dwelling places. Tales handed down among their communities describe animals of remarkable strength, able to follow traces left by Men and to cover great distances. Some accompany Orc-bands, while others travel in packs. Their size and endurance make them dangerous to travellers crossing lands far from inhabited settlements. Hunters also know their howls, by which the members of a pack appear to maintain contact as they move.

You know, however, an interpretation according to which these great wolves possess an intelligence limited to the demands of the hunt. Their gatherings would be governed by the search for food, and their concerted attacks would result from experience gained within the pack. Orcs would exploit these natural tendencies to train them in the pursuit of travellers, but Wargs would remain unable to devise an undertaking of their own. Elders who pass on this explanation believe that a pack may prove cunning while following a trail, yet swiftly loses its cohesion when several obstacles force its members to separate. The most difficult woodland paths would thus enable a traveller to scatter the creatures for good and put an end to their pursuit.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — Wargs wrongly reduced to a mountain strain of wolves and great rivers mistakenly believed to afford automatic protection; failure — intelligence reduced to animal habit; successful results — woodland routes, the Nandorin memory of the vales, and the independence of packs.
results.text:
The Nandor distinguish Wargs from natural wolves by their size, intelligence and malice. These great canids possess a keen sense of smell, acute hearing and the endurance to follow a trail for a long time. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others roam the wild lands in independent packs. Forest communities know their ability to recognise the paths used by travellers, the passages between mountains and valleys, and the places where several trails meet.

You also know that Wargs communicate in a language of their own, composed of howls and growls whose meaning exceeds the ordinary calls of wolves. Their intelligence allows them to coordinate their movements and alter a pursuit when they meet resistance. Nandor who know these creatures understand that rivers, dense woods and broken ground can influence their movements, but that their ability to communicate and recognise obstacles enables them to seek other routes.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — Wargs wrongly reduced to a mountain strain of wolves and great rivers mistakenly believed to afford automatic protection; failure — intelligence reduced to animal habit; successful results — woodland routes, the Nandorin memory of the vales, and the independence of packs.
results.text:
Nandorin traditions preserve precise knowledge of the great malevolent wolves that haunt the wild lands. Wargs possess an intelligence and a language that allow them to acknowledge their leaders, gather together and plan common undertakings. Their association with Orcs rests on shared interests, but the packs retain the power to act independently of their allies. Some serve as mounts, while others join raids or range the forests on their own account. Nandor familiar with their behaviour distinguish these creatures from natural wolves, whose movements answer chiefly to the necessities of hunting and survival.

Communities established beside rivers and forests know the advantages their surroundings may offer against pursuit. Watercourses present physical obstacles, but their effectiveness depends upon breadth, depth and the force of the current. Wargs can recognise fords, follow paths along riverbanks and seek places where a river may be crossed. Several individuals can explore different stretches of a watercourse and then communicate what they have discovered. Their intelligence also enables them to understand that an adversary forced to follow a valley must often reach certain passages in order to continue his journey.

Nandorin traditions attach great importance to the woodland paths linking scattered communities. Trails may be concealed among the trees, but Wargs possess senses keen enough to recognise passages that are repeatedly used. A pack may follow a track, search neighbouring routes and wait for a traveller to reach a clearing or accessible riverbank. Elves acquainted with such behaviour know that stealth and mastery of the paths are valuable advantages, yet their pursuers remain capable of observing their movements and collectively choosing another course.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — Wargs wrongly reduced to a mountain strain of wolves and great rivers mistakenly believed to afford automatic protection; failure — intelligence reduced to animal habit; successful results — woodland routes, the Nandorin memory of the vales, and the independence of packs.
results.text:
The deepest knowledge of the Nandor unites the memory of their migrations, the traditions of the communities settled in the Vales of Anduin and the observations handed down by hunters of the great forests. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings, endowed with intelligence and a language that distinguish them from natural wolves. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and may form alliances with Orcs. Such cooperation rests upon shared interests, yet Wargs retain the power to make their own decisions. Some accompany armed bands as mounts or pursuers, while others inhabit the wild lands and undertake ventures independently of the organised forces of the Shadow.

The memory of the Nandor gives particular importance to the ways followed by living creatures. Rivers, valleys and woodlands may be refuges, barriers or pathways. Wargs can recognise this variety and choose their movements according to the ground. A pack may pursue a traveller to a river, seek its fords or explore several crossings before gathering again. Its members communicate through their howls and can collectively change their course when their first searches prove fruitless. A river sufficiently broad or swift may halt an immediate pursuit, but it does not deprive Wargs of the ability to recognise the routes an adversary might take.

Nandorin traditions also recall the choices that shaped their own history. Their people settled among wooded lands rather than follow the Great Journey as far as Aman, and their communities acquired profound knowledge of forests and watercourses. Familiarity with these places enables them to recognise hidden paths, changes in the ground and the tracks of creatures passing through it. Wargs, however, possess the intelligence to learn such passages, follow repeated movements and take advantage of their adversaries' habits. Nandor who know these creatures understand that a refuge is protected as much by the secrecy of the paths leading to it as by the vigilance of those who use them.

The oldest tales sometimes associate the origin of Wargs with the corruption of wolves by the powers of the Shadow. Other traditions tell of Werewolves, beings of another nature appearing in the histories of Morgoth. Nandor learned in these accounts distinguish the observable qualities of Wargs from interpretations of their origins. The strength of their bodies, their senses and endurance are those of great canids; their language, intelligence and malevolent will set them apart from ordinary animals. Such knowledge makes it possible to understand their organisation and decisions without indiscriminately attributing to Wargs the supernatural powers of other wolf-like creatures.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — old trees wrongly credited with protective powers and the supposed automatic abandonment of any pursuit beneath elevated dwellings; failure — supposed inability to discover hidden forest paths; successful results — Silvan experience of tree-borne refuges, recognition of approaches and Warg independence.
results.text:
In certain traditions of the Silvan Elves, Wargs are portrayed as great malevolent wolves that follow the Orcs through the wild lands, but whose power remains bound to open paths and corrupted ground. These creatures could range along woodland borders, through clearings and along passages widened by the Orcs for their own movements, while the oldest reaches of the forest would remain hostile to them. Trees whose roots have intertwined for centuries would retain an influence feared by the great wolves. However remarkable their intelligence, it would not enable them to overcome this resistance of the forest, whose inhabitants recognise its signs without always being able to explain them.

Some tales ascribe a particular protection to dwellings raised among the branches. Wargs, unable to climb to the platforms where the Elves live, would quickly abandon the chase when their quarry escaped their reach. The elders maintain that these creatures turn away from inhabited trees once they realise that they cannot reach those above, for their predatory nature forbids them to linger beside inaccessible prey. Villages approached chiefly by elevated pathways would therefore be safe from packs, even when no watchman guarded the tracks beneath them. The patience and cunning of Wargs would not suffice to keep them in a region where Elves command the passages from the branches.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — old trees wrongly credited with protective powers and the supposed automatic abandonment of any pursuit beneath elevated dwellings; failure — supposed inability to discover hidden forest paths; successful results — Silvan experience of tree-borne refuges, recognition of approaches and Warg independence.
results.text:
The Silvan Elves know of the great wolves that sometimes accompany Orc-bands through forested regions. These creatures possess immense size and strength, keen senses of smell and considerable endurance. Some serve as mounts, while others join pursuits and raids. Hunters know that they can follow trails frequented by animals and recognise the traces of travellers. Their howls enable separated individuals to remain in contact, even when trees conceal their companions.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs depend chiefly upon paths opened or habitually used by Orcs. Their great size and weight would prevent them from moving effectively through dense undergrowth, while their intelligence would be directed mainly towards following familiar trails. The elders who hand down this explanation believe that hidden woodland passages are too intricate for these creatures to recognise. A pack might recover a road or much-used track, but would swiftly lose an Elf who ventured among the trees by less visible ways. Villages remote from the principal roads would thus be protected by their isolation, even while Wargs roamed the surrounding regions.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — old trees wrongly credited with protective powers and the supposed automatic abandonment of any pursuit beneath elevated dwellings; failure — supposed inability to discover hidden forest paths; successful results — Silvan experience of tree-borne refuges, recognition of approaches and Warg independence.
results.text:
Silvan Elven traditions distinguish Wargs from natural wolves by their size, intelligence and malevolence. These great canids possess considerable strength, keen senses and the endurance to follow a trail over a long distance. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others range the wild lands in independent packs. Hunters know their ability to recognise passages used by beasts and travellers, and to move swiftly where the ground offers an open way.

You also know that Wargs possess their own language and can communicate through howls and growls whose meaning exceeds that of ordinary wolves' calls. Their intelligence enables them to coordinate their movements, seek other routes and pursue an undertaking without constantly receiving orders from a rider. Silvan Elves familiar with them know that trees and high places may offer useful refuges, but that Wargs are capable of watching their enemies' movements and waiting until they return to the ground.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — old trees wrongly credited with protective powers and the supposed automatic abandonment of any pursuit beneath elevated dwellings; failure — supposed inability to discover hidden forest paths; successful results — Silvan experience of tree-borne refuges, recognition of approaches and Warg independence.
results.text:
The Silvan Elves preserve precise knowledge of Wargs, nourished by long familiarity with the forests and by accounts of their struggles against the servants of the Shadow. These creatures possess an intelligence and a language that enable them to acknowledge their leaders, gather and plan common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests on shared interests, yet their packs retain an independent will. Some serve as mounts or accompany armed bands as scouts and pursuers, while others roam the wild lands on their own account. Their malice distinguishes them from natural wolves, whose habits answer principally to the needs of the hunt.

Hunters and woodland guardians know the difficulties encountered by Wargs among the trees. Their size may hinder their progress through the thickest undergrowth, but their intelligence enables them to seek easier passages. They can follow the tracks of animals, go around fallen trunks and recognise paths frequently used by travellers. Several individuals may explore different directions, then communicate their discoveries through exchanged howls. Their endurance allows them to pursue enemies attempting to outdistance them, while their powers of observation enable them to discover the approaches to a refuge.

Silvan traditions attach great importance to dwellings built among the branches and to the passages connecting the forest's different levels. Such structures can effectively protect their occupants against the immediate attacks of Wargs, whose bodies are not suited to climbing trees as Elves do. Yet a pack can keep watch at the foot of the trunks, recognise the routes of descent and wait for an enemy to be forced to leave the heights. Guardians familiar with such conduct understand that a settlement's safety depends upon the vigilance of its inhabitants and their command of the ways leading down to the ground.

results.text:
The deepest knowledge of the Silvan Elves brings together traditions inherited from the Nandor, memories of forest communities and accounts passed down by Elves acquainted with the ancient wars against the Shadow. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings, endowed with intelligence and a language that distinguish them from natural wolves. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and may form alliances with Orcs. This cooperation rests on shared hostility towards the Free Peoples, but Wargs retain their own decisions. Some accompany armed bands or bear Orc warriors, while others inhabit the wild lands and pursue independent designs.

Elves familiar with the movements of woodland creatures understand the advantages and limitations of their bodily nature. Wargs can travel swiftly along open paths, follow animal tracks and recover trails through their sense of smell. Dense undergrowth, steep ground and elevated passages impose physical constraints, but their intelligence allows them to seek alternative routes. A pack may recognise paths leading to a village, explore several approaches and gather when one of its members discovers a favourable way. Its members may also wait for long periods beneath a refuge, especially when they know its inhabitants must descend to the ground to travel or gather provisions.

The memory of the Silvan Elves also preserves the changes undergone by the great forests. Lands once freely traversed may become perilous when Orcs, spiders or other servants of the Shadow establish their lairs there. Wargs may figure in accounts of such troubled times, sometimes in company with Orc-bands threatening the communities. Those with knowledge of these matters nevertheless distinguish their presence from that of other malevolent creatures. Wargs possess their own organisation and can act independently of the forces occupying a region. Their intelligence enables them to recognise paths frequented by Elves and exploit the changes that the inhabitants' movements bring to the forest.

The oldest traditions sometimes connect the origin of Wargs with the corruption of wolves by the powers of the Shadow. Other tales liken them to the Werewolves appearing in the histories of Morgoth, though these belong to a different spiritual tradition. Silvan Elves instructed in these distinctions recognise the observable qualities of Wargs: bodily strength, language, intelligence and the capacity to form common designs. Their woodland knowledge enables them to understand the actual constraints upon the creatures' movements, while the memory of Elven peoples illuminates their place among beings associated with the Shadow. A Warg remains an adversary capable of observing and deciding, even when it crosses a forest whose paths have been familiar to the Elves for centuries.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — Wargs mistakenly confined to Orcish territories and supposed protection offered by Avarin ancestral lands; failure — their nature wrongly restricted to western regions; successful results — diversity of Avarin peoples, uneven transmission of traditions and recognition of traits proper to Wargs.
results.text:
In certain Avarin traditions, the great malevolent wolves are portrayed as creatures appearing only in regions where Orcs have established their dominion. These beasts, called Wargs by the peoples of the West, would descend from an ancient stock of wolves transformed by sorcerers of the Shadow to guard their territories. Their intelligence and language would not be truly their own: they would have been fashioned to recognise their masters' commands and pursue those whom the Orcs name as enemies. Lands beyond the authority of any Orcish power would naturally be alien to such creatures. Reports of Wargs seen far from their lairs would be travellers' tales born of mistaking large wild wolves for the true guardians of the servants of the Shadow.

A tradition handed down in certain communities maintains that Wargs harbour a particular enmity towards the Elves who long ago refused to follow the Great Journey westwards. The beasts would recognise in the Avari their ancient determination to remain free, and seek to drive them from lands that the powers of the Shadow desire to dominate. They would, however, be unable to pursue an Elf who regained the places inhabited by his people since the earliest ages, because their authority would depend upon boundaries imposed by their masters. Elders familiar with this belief hold that the ancestral territories of Avarin communities afford protection against Wargs. These might threaten travellers along foreign roads, but would lose their power upon reaching lands where the ancient memory of the Quendi endures.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — Wargs mistakenly confined to Orcish territories and supposed protection offered by Avarin ancestral lands; failure — their nature wrongly restricted to western regions; successful results — diversity of Avarin peoples, uneven transmission of traditions and recognition of traits proper to Wargs.
results.text:
The Avari know tales of great malevolent wolves that accompany Orcs and roam the wild lands. These creatures possess immense size, great endurance and keen senses that enable them to follow a trail for a long time. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others move in packs. Communities dwelling near mountains and forests may preserve detailed traditions concerning their presence, while peoples settled in distant regions know them chiefly through travellers' accounts. Their appearance as great canids sometimes leads to confusion with natural wolves.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs belong to a form of life peculiar to the western lands, where Orcs have long fought the realms of Men and the Eldar. Reports from the East would describe similar creatures, but these would belong to separate species shaped by the conditions of their own territories. Avari who pass on this explanation hold that stories of Wargs cannot reliably identify creatures encountered in distant lands. Their intelligence, language and malevolence would be peculiar to the great wolves of the western mountains, while the animals of other regions would remain natural predators, even when Orcs employed them in war.

Their intelligence allows them to recognise obstacles and alter their movements when they meet resistance. Avari familiar with these creatures know that their alliance with Orcs is frequent, yet a pack can act without Orcish accompaniment. The traditions of different communities may furnish complementary knowledge of their habits, especially where travellers have crossed regions in which Wargs appear regularly.

These creatures possess an intelligence and a language that enable them to acknowledge leaders, assemble and prepare common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, yet their packs retain an independent will. Some Wargs serve as mounts or accompany armed bands as pursuers, while others range the wild lands on their own account. Their malice leads them to undertake actions that go beyond the ordinary necessities of hunting.

The diversity of Avarin communities explains why their knowledge of Wargs takes different forms. Forest peoples may know them through their tracks, their howls and their movements among trees. Those who dwell in the mountains are more concerned with passes, cols and paths used by the packs. Communities far removed from the regions where these creatures are encountered sometimes preserve only tales brought by travellers or neighbouring peoples. Avari instructed in these traditions recognise the characteristics Wargs share without supposing that all their communities have the same experience.*

A pack may follow the movements of Orcs, but may equally choose its own paths and occupy regions far from its allies' settlements. Wargs can recognise routes, seek favourable passages and communicate their discoveries to their fellows. Their presence depends on the pack's movements and decisions as much as on those of Orc-bands.

The deepest knowledge of the Avari gathers traditions from peoples whose paths have diverged since the earliest ages of Middle-earth. Their refusal to continue the Great Journey to the West gave rise to scattered communities, whose tongues, customs and beliefs have evolved over millennia. Tales of malevolent creatures pass among them by different ways, and Wargs may be known by names or descriptions that do not always correspond to those used in western realms. Avari schooled in these traditions distinguish natural great wolves, creatures employed by Orcs and Wargs whose intelligence and language reveal a particular nature.

Wargs possess an organisation of their own. Their packs acknowledge leaders, can gather to deliberate and form alliances with Orcs. Such cooperation rests upon shared interests, but Wargs retain the power to pursue their own designs. Some serve as mounts or join raids, while others occupy territories and organise pursuits without Orcish company. Their language allows them to exchange warnings and coordinate their movements even when several individuals follow different routes. Their intelligence enables them to recognise obstacles, observe their enemies and alter an attack when circumstances become unfavourable.

Avari acquainted with the wild lands understand the differences that may exist between accounts from several regions. A community settled in a forest may describe Wargs by the passages they follow beneath the trees, while a mountain people reports their movements among passes and valleys. Such observations may complement one another without necessarily describing the same pack or circumstances. The soundest knowledge distinguishes behaviour belonging to Wargs themselves from constraints imposed by their environment. Size, scent and endurance are bodily capacities; language and organisation enable them to employ these capacities according to common decisions.

The oldest traditions sometimes associate the origin of Wargs with the corruption of wolves by the powers of the Shadow. Other accounts liken them to the Werewolves of the Elder Days, whose spiritual nature belongs to a different tradition. Not all Avari preserve the same tales of the Valar, Morgoth or the ancient wars, and their interpretations reflect the long separation of their communities. Those able to compare these stories distinguish powers attributed to supernatural creatures from qualities actually observed among Wargs. Intelligence, language and malevolence remain the surest marks by which to understand their place among beings that sometimes ally themselves with the servants of the Shadow.

Among the songs preserved upon the shores of Aman, certain traditions describe the great malevolent wolves as creatures belonging entirely to the inland countries. Their strength, speed and sense of smell would be bound to the mountains and forests where they live, while the sea would remain profoundly alien to them. Wargs spoken of in tales of Middle-earth would be especially sensitive to salt water, whose scent and movement would trouble their senses. They might pursue a traveller to the approaches of a coast, yet would refuse to cross exposed beaches or places where sea spray reached their bodies. Such tales connect this aversion with their malevolent origins, as though the great waters retained a purity these creatures could not endure.

A seafaring tradition likewise attributes an influence over Wargs to the song of the waves. The howls by which they communicate would be lost in the tumult of the surf, preventing a pack from maintaining its organisation. Some elders relate that a company of these great wolves scatters upon nearing a shore beaten by the sea, for the calls exchanged among its members become impossible to distinguish. Quays, landing places and islets close to the coast would thus afford natural protection against pursuit. Teleri familiar with this belief regard the domain of Ulmo as a boundary that the wolf-like creatures of the Shadow cannot cross, even when their enemies remain visible upon the farther shore.

The tales of the Eldar attribute to them an intelligence greater than that of natural wolves and an ability to communicate by howls whose meaning generally escapes other peoples.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs remain exclusively bound to regions where Orcs establish their lairs. Their intelligence would allow them to act in groups, but their gatherings would depend upon the movements of the servants of the Shadow. Elders who transmit this interpretation believe that packs may pursue travellers, but possess no purposes independent of their Orcish allies. A company reaching a coast and escaping immediate pursuit might therefore consider itself out of danger, since Wargs would abandon their search as soon as the trail led towards waters they did not ordinarily frequent.
