Telerin traditions distinguish Wargs from natural wolves and the Werewolves appearing in the ancient stories of Morgoth. Wargs possess an intelligence and a language that enable them to acknowledge their leaders, gather and prepare common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, yet their packs retain an independent will. Some serve as mounts or join raids, while others range the wild lands on their own account. Tales concerning them describe adversaries able to follow tracks, seek passages and change their movements according to the obstacles they encounter.

Teleri who know the nature of shores and waters understand the constraints they may place upon Wargs. Deep water may interrupt a pursuit over land, whereas a beach, ford or exposed crossing may remain accessible. Currents and tides alter the possibilities of movement, and animals following a trail can seek other routes when an obstacle bars their way. Wargs possess the intelligence to recognise these difficulties, wait for a more favourable moment or move towards another point of access. Their sense of smell and hearing may be affected by coastal conditions, but their language and organisation do not vanish merely because the sea is present.

Telerin maritime traditions also enable them to distinguish accounts of pursuit over land from properties attributed to supernatural creatures. A boat may provide refuge from a Warg left upon the shore, but the protection arises from distance and a physical barrier. Sailors' songs, the names of the powers of the waters and prayers offered to Ulmo hold an important place in their culture; their presence alone offers no guarantee against a pack. Teleri instructed in these distinctions recognise the abilities belonging to Wargs without mistaking their malevolence for an inability to approach the shore.

The deepest knowledge of the Teleri joins the traditions of the earliest Eldar, tales concerning Morgoth's creatures and testimony passed down by peoples who remained in Middle-earth. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings, endowed with intelligence and a language distinguishing them from natural wolves. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and may form alliances with Orcs. This cooperation rests on shared hostility towards the Free Peoples, yet Wargs retain the capacity to act independently of their allies. Some serve as mounts or join raids, while others roam the wild lands according to their own decisions.

Teleri learned in the ancient histories distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves associated with Morgoth's servants. The latter appear in stories in which evil spirits inhabit wolf-like shapes and possess particular supernatural powers. Wargs are known through their bodies as great canids, their language and their organisation. Some traditions trace their origins to an ancient corruption of wolves, while others liken them to spiritual creatures of the Elder Days. The most precise knowledge preserves the distinction between these interpretations and Wargs' observable abilities. Their intelligence and malice suffice to make them dangerous without attributing to them every power of supernatural beings.

Telerin experience of the sea also illuminates the physical limits of pursuit. Shores have passages whose accessibility changes with tides, winds and currents. A pack may follow a coastline, seek a ford or wait near a landing place once it has recognised its adversaries' movements. Its members can communicate and explore several directions, even when water forces them to separate. Their intelligence enables them to anticipate some of a traveller's movements, while their keen senses help them detect traces left on accessible ground. Water deep enough may protect a company, but this defence depends upon the nature of the obstacle rather than any supernatural inability to cross it.

Finally, the Teleri preserve a distinctive perspective upon the limits of their own experience. Their people chiefly dwell upon the shores of Aman, far from the lands where Wargs are usually encountered. Accounts received from other Eldar and traditions concerning the Shadow's servants give them knowledge of these creatures, yet that knowledge need not arise from personal encounters. Teleri familiar with these distinctions appreciate the worth of precise testimony and recognise the differences between malevolent great wolves, ancient spiritual beings and natural predators. Their seafaring wisdom enriches their understanding of dangers beside the water without turning the sea into a universal protection against Wargs.

Among traditions preserved by Penni families, certain tales speak of great malevolent wolves that roam the eastern regions in the wake of Orcs and other servants of the Shadow. These creatures, called Wargs by other peoples, would descend from wild wolves transformed by the habit of hunting beside warriors. Their unusual intelligence would enable them to recognise weapons and the movements of Men, yet their nature would remain deeply bound to the scents and signs left by accompanying Orcs. Wargs would follow the paths where armed bands established their camps and chiefly seek those whom their masters had taught them to regard as enemies.

A tradition among migrating communities holds that Wargs lose their ability to pursue Elves when the latter cross into a forest where their people have dwelt for a long time. The trees would preserve the scent and memory of Penni families, forming a familiar presence that conceals individual trails. The great wolves might follow a track across plains and open roads, but would be unable to distinguish a single Elf among the thousands of ancient scents permeating inhabited woods. Some elders relate that a community reaching a forest already inhabited by Elves can settle there without fear of Wargs, for the accumulated presence of the Quendi would confuse their senses and turn the packs towards lands where Orcs dwell.

Traditions passed down by families departing the eastern regions tell of perils encountered on the roads and the difficulties of fleeing across unfamiliar lands. Wargs hold a particular place in these accounts, for their speed and senses make them formidable to groups travelling with their children and possessions.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs remain bound to Orcs by a lasting dependence. Their howls would maintain contact between scattered individuals, but their concerted movements would chiefly result from training undertaken together. Elders who pass on this explanation believe that a pack deprived of Orcish allies gradually returns to the habits of wild wolves. It may continue to pursue prey, but would lose the ability to prepare attacks upon Elven communities. Penni familiar with this tradition therefore believe that moving away from Orc-dominated territories is generally enough to lessen the danger posed by Wargs.

Forests may provide refuges and conceal Elven paths, but Wargs remain capable of observation and tracking in such places.

The Penni preserve precise traditions concerning Wargs, handed down within families departing the eastern lands and among communities drawing nearer to the Nandor. These creatures possess an intelligence and a language that distinguish them from natural wolves. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and may plan common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, yet Wargs retain an independent will. Some serve as mounts or join raids, while others range the wild lands on their own account. Their malice may lead them to pursue travellers and recognise the roads taken by communities seeking refuge.

Penni familiar with their behaviour attach great importance to the difficulties facing groups on the move. A family may travel with young children, provisions and possessions it wishes to preserve, limiting its speed and requiring regular halts. Wargs can recognise such constraints, follow the traces left on roads and seek passages where travellers are obliged to slow down. Several individuals may scatter to explore different directions, then reunite through their calls. Their intelligence also allows them to search for routes leading to valleys, fords and accessible refuges.

Penni traditions also distinguish the dangers encountered during migrations from those posed by Wargs to an established community. Forests may offer refuges and discreet paths, but packs can recognise well-used passages and exploit the repeated movements of inhabitants. Penni dwelling beside the Nandor enrich their own knowledge through that of Elves familiar with valleys and watercourses. The tales of both peoples complement one another, allowing a better understanding of Warg movements and the obstacles that may hinder pursuit.

results.text:
The deepest knowledge of the Penni brings together memories of their ancient migrations, traditions preserved among Avarin communities and lore handed down by the Nandor with whom they establish lasting ties. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings endowed with intelligence and a language distinguishing them from natural wolves. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and may choose undertakings independent of Orcs. Their alliance with the latter rests upon common interests, yet Wargs retain the power to form their own designs. Some serve as mounts or join raids, while others roam the wild lands without Orcish accompaniment.

Penni memory gives particular weight to the difficulties of collective travel. Migrating families must recognise passable routes, find shelters and protect those unable to sustain a rapid march. Wargs possess senses capable of recovering the traces left by a group, but their intelligence also enables them to recognise the passages it will have to use. A pack may scatter to explore several routes, communicate its discoveries and gather when an obstacle slows the travellers. Penni acquainted with this behaviour know that concealing a trail may delay pursuit without necessarily preventing intelligent enemies from searching the likely paths towards a valley or ford.

Traditions shared by the Penni and Nandor also deepen their understanding of forests. Trees conceal movement, offer refuges and allow Elves to travel by ways little known to other peoples. Wargs can nevertheless follow scents, recognise repeatedly used passages and observe the movements of inhabitants. A forest occupied by Elves for generations may possess carefully concealed paths, but its antiquity grants no automatic protection against packs. Penni familiar with these creatures distinguish the genuine advantages of woodland from the belief that an ancient Elven presence alone can confuse the senses of great wolves.

The oldest accounts sometimes connect Wargs with the corruption of wolves by the powers of the Shadow. Other traditions tell of the Werewolves of the Elder Days, beings of another nature associated with the malevolent spirits serving Morgoth. Penni familiar with these tales distinguish accounts of the origin of wolf-like creatures from what hunters and travellers may directly observe. Wargs possess the bodies of great canids, a language and an intelligence allowing them to form alliances and prepare common actions. Their organisation remains independent both of the Elven communities opposing them and of the Orc-bands which they sometimes choose to join.

The meeting of Penni and Nandorin traditions finally reveals the diversity of Elven experience. The former preserve memories of dangers encountered on migrations from the East; the latter possess deep knowledge of the valleys and forests they inhabit. These different memories may illuminate Warg movements without supposing that a single pack frequented every region described. Penni instructed in these distinctions recognise the qualities proper to Wargs and understand that their malice, language and intelligence enable them to pursue purposes independent of the circumstances in which the Elves encountered them.

Among the traditions of the Luindrim, certain tales describe great malevolent wolves that roam the wild regions near Orcs. These creatures, called Wargs by western peoples, possess unusual strength and intelligence, but their nature would be profoundly bound to the darkness of mountains and corrupted forests. The elders say that these great wolves recognise lands where Elves still preserve the ancient traditions of Cuiviénen. Paths trodden by the Quendi for generations would retain a presence perceptible to Wargs, while trees inhabited by the Luindrim would inspire instinctive fear. Their malice would thus encounter resistance from the living memory of peoples who chose to remain in Middle-earth.

A belief handed down in certain villages attributes particular protection against these creatures to the telain, the great platforms built among the branches. Wargs would be unable to remain for long beneath a tree whose upper branches shelter an Elven community, because the scent of worked timber and the inhabitants' songs would confuse their senses. The elders maintain that a pack gives up its pursuit once the Elves have regained their elevated homes, even if the great wolves followed their trail to the village's edge. Passages linking the platforms would thus allow Luindrim to move freely above the predators, while Wargs soon scattered when they found themselves unable to reach their enemies.

Their coordination would be that of experienced predators, whose howls maintain contact between scattered individuals. The elders who pass on this explanation believe that Wargs swiftly lose their bearings when their enemies take elevated passages through the trees or cross ground where snow has obscured earlier tracks. A pack might wait for a time beside a refuge but would eventually abandon its search if no fresh trail led to prey. Hunters familiar with this belief therefore ascribe almost certain effectiveness against the great wolves to tree-borne paths and snowfall.

A pack may remain near a refuge, explore several approaches at ground level and wait for an enemy to be forced to leave the heights. Communication among Wargs allows them to coordinate movements even when trees conceal their companions.

Luindrim traditions also attach particular importance to conditions in the northern lands. Snow may preserve legible tracks or erase them under the action of the wind, while the use of woodland paths changes with the seasons. Wargs can follow a trail by scent, but their intelligence also enables them to seek a traveller's likely route when visible traces have disappeared. Several individuals may scatter to explore different directions, then reunite by exchanging calls. Luindrim familiar with these behaviours distinguish the real advantages of stealth from the imaginary protections ascribed to the age of their paths.

The deepest knowledge of the Luindrim brings together their Avarin memory, the traditions of their forest communities and observations handed down by those who range the northern lands. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings, endowed with an intelligence and language that distinguish them from natural wolves. Their organisation includes leaders, gatherings and common decisions. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared hostility towards the Free Peoples, yet packs retain the capacity to pursue their own designs. Some Wargs serve as mounts or join raids, while others range the wild regions independently of their allies. Their malice may lead them to harry travellers, recognise routes taken by Elves and return to a territory already familiar to them.

Luindrim acquainted with their behaviour can interpret traces of their movements in forests and snowy regions. A track may reveal the approximate size of a great canid, but its appearance depends upon the soil, snow and weather. Wargs possess keen senses enabling them to recover lingering scents and detect an enemy's movements. Their intelligence also permits them to anticipate certain routes. A pack may explore several paths, go around obstacles and gather when a member discovers a favourable passage. The howls exchanged among them facilitate this coordination beyond sight, even when the land or vegetation separates them.

The arrangement of Luindrim villages offers particular advantages against earthbound creatures. The principal dwellings occupy the heights, while buildings and approaches at ground level are places where inhabitants can be observed or pursued. Wargs lack the Elves' ease in climbing and moving among branches, but their capacity to recognise routes enables them to exploit the inhabitants' repeated movements. A pack may watch the foot of a tree, explore paths leading to stores and wait for occasions when Elves must return to the ground. Experienced guardians know that a village's safety depends on protecting its approaches no less than on the height of its dwellings.

Luindrim spiritual traditions give an important place to Ivannië, Araw and Elbereth, whose memory accompanies communal feasts and songs. Some tales associate malevolent creatures with the corruption of the world by the powers of the Shadow and ascribe protective virtue to ancient Elven customs. The soundest knowledge nevertheless distinguishes the meaning of these stories from Wargs' observable qualities. Their intelligence and malice remain present near Elven settlements, even when songs and rites remind the inhabitants of the powers they honour. The oldest tales also describe the Werewolves of the Elder Days, beings of a different spiritual nature. Luindrim acquainted with these distinctions recognise Wargs by their language, organisation and ability to pursue designs of their own.

results.text:
Among the traditions of the Kuorind, certain tales portray the great malevolent wolves as creatures from ancient lands once subject to Morgoth's powers. Their immense size, ferocity and intelligence would be marks of a corruption that leaves them unable to endure starlight for long. Wargs might range through dark valleys, accompany Orcs and pursue travellers along mountain passes, but their strength would diminish upon reaching exposed heights where the stars remain visible. The elders say these creatures instinctively seek caverns, dense woods and slopes deprived of light, for the stars remind them of the power to which the first Quendi owed their awakening.

A tradition among the guardians of the mountains ascribes particular virtue against these creatures to songs addressed to Beich'al and Kuor'chal. Words celebrating light and the heavens, sung upon an open height, would dispel the malevolent influence sustaining the Wargs. A pack might pursue its enemies for a long distance through the valleys, then give up following them when they reached a summit where Kuorind songs resounded. The elders maintain that the great wolves become unable to communicate beneath this light, their howls changing into confused cries. Communities familiar with this belief regard refuges established on the heights as offering spiritual protection as important as their walls and difficult approaches.

The Kuorind know accounts of great malevolent wolves that accompany Orcs and roam mountainous regions. Guardians of the passes know their ability to recognise paths and pursue Men or Elves over long distances. Their presence is associated with dangers threatening valleys and roads across the wild lands.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs depend chiefly upon paths used by Orcs. Their great size and bodily nature would prevent them from moving effectively upon the steepest slopes, while their intelligence would remain limited to routes they have learnt to recognise. Elders who hand down this interpretation believe that a pack quickly loses its cohesion when forced to separate among several mountain passages. The howls exchanged by its members would be insufficient to maintain contact beyond ridges and deep valleys. Kuorind refuges reached by precipitous tracks could therefore remain beyond the reach of Wargs, even when the great wolves had followed their enemies to the foot of the mountains.

Wargs use scent to follow tracks and hearing to detect certain movements at a distance. Ridges and valleys may change the way sounds travel, but their communications remain useful in coordinating individuals separated by the land.

The Kuorind maintain ancient relations with certain Dwarven Houses, notably that of Bávor. The traditions of communities trading with Dwarves enrich their knowledge of mountain passages, fortresses and underground routes. Wargs, whose bodies are those of great canids, encounter particular difficulties in passages too narrow or entrances well defended, but they can recognise open routes and follow their enemies' movements. Experienced guardians thus distinguish the material advantages of a well-sited fortress from protections popular belief attributes to the mere height of the mountains.

The deepest knowledge of the Kuorind brings together memories of their ancient migrations, the traditions of their Councils of Elders and accounts gathered from peoples frequenting the mountains of Treddas. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings, endowed with intelligence and a language distinguishing them from natural wolves. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and may form alliances with Orcs. This cooperation rests upon common interests, but Wargs retain their own decisions. Some serve as mounts or join raids, while others range the wild lands independently of any troop. Their malice may drive them to pursue travellers, harry communities or recognise passes leading towards distant refuges.

Mountain guardians acquainted with their behaviour understand the constraints imposed by the ground. Wargs possess bodily strength sufficient to overcome some obstacles, but their size and build limit their movements upon steep slopes, rock faces and very narrow passages. Their intelligence nevertheless gives them the ability to seek other routes and recognise paths regularly used by inhabitants. A pack may explore several valleys, follow tracks left near a ford or pass and gather when a favourable crossing is found. The howls exchanged among its members maintain contact despite separation, while scent and hearing assist them in following enemies attempting to vanish among the rocks.

Kuorind traditions give particular importance to the memory of the Elders and relations with neighbouring peoples. Dwarves of the House of Bávor possess knowledge of their own concerning mountains, galleries and works defending their approaches. The Kuorind may combine this lore with their experience of forests, heights and hidden ways. A Warg pack may seek to exploit open passages, but narrow approaches and defended structures impose genuine obstacles. Elves familiar with these creatures recognise the advantage of cooperation between peoples acquainted with the same mountains, for information about paths, Orcish movements and Warg sightings reveals threats on a scale greater than that of an isolated encounter.

The Kuorind also preserve a spiritual tradition distinctive among the Avari. Their devotion to the stars, the powers of light and the ancient names of their people nourishes tales in which the creatures of the Shadow appear as enemies of the heavens. Their judgement of Oromë, whom they call Sammat, belongs to this particular history and to memories of the separation of the first Quendi. Sounder knowledge nevertheless distinguishes the meaning of these beliefs from Wargs' observable abilities. Starlight deprives them of neither intelligence nor language, and the songs of the Kuorind do not, through mere antiquity, impose a command that packs must obey. Exposed heights may offer clearer views and defensible passages; their effectiveness rests upon the ground and the vigilance of those occupying it.

The oldest accounts sometimes trace the origins of Wargs to wolves corrupted by the powers of the Shadow. Other traditions describe the Werewolves of the Elder Days, beings of another nature associated with the evil spirits that served Morgoth. Kuorind familiar with these histories distinguish spiritual interpretations from qualities actually observed among Wargs. Their bodies possess the strength, senses and abilities of great canids, while intelligence and language enable them to organise their movements and forge alliances. Their malice and independent will explain their place among the enemies of the Free Peoples, regardless of powers that certain beliefs attribute to mountains, stars or ancient songs.

results.text:
Among the tales preserved in the tree-cities of Valagalen, some portray Wargs as great wolves whose malevolence arises from their estrangement from the powers watching over the forests. They would descend from creatures once resembling natural predators, but whose long presence beside Orcs altered their dispositions. Their intelligence, grown cruel and mistrustful, would be merely a distorted reflection of the reason possessed by thinking beings. The elders relate that Wargs understand hostile intentions and recognise weapons, yet remain strangers to more refined forms of thought. Songs and illusions that enchant the senses of other creatures would therefore suffice to unsettle their judgement for a long time.

Certain traditions attribute a particular influence over these great wolves to the magical arts of the Fuinar. A melody performed according to the ancient customs of Valagalen might distract them, while a luminous apparition fashioned among the branches would suffice to make them abandon a pursuit. Wargs would be unable to distinguish even the simplest illusions from living beings, so strongly would their malice urge them to attack anything attracting their gaze. Guardians familiar with this belief hold that an Elf commanding a few ordinary enchantments can throw an entire pack into disorder, however numerous its members. The tree-borne refuges of the Fuinar would thus enjoy a protection grounded as much in music and magical artifice as in the height of their dwellings.

The Fuinar know tales of great malevolent wolves that sometimes accompany Orc-bands and roam the wild lands. These creatures possess considerable strength, a keen sense of smell and the endurance to follow travellers' tracks for a long time. Some Wargs serve as mounts, while others travel in packs. Forest guardians know that their presence may be betrayed by deep prints, the remains of their prey and answering howls among the trees. Their intelligence makes them more dangerous than ordinary predators, particularly when they encounter Men or Elves accustomed to concealing themselves.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs possess only an imperfect understanding of things they cannot directly perceive. Their coordinated attacks would result from the habit of hunting together, while their howls would convey no more than the simplest signals. Elders who pass on this explanation hold that a pack may follow a trail with great skill, yet cannot distinguish a genuine flight from a skilfully prepared diversion. Fuinar versed in concealment could therefore lead several Wargs onto a false trail and leave them pursuing a deceptive apparition or sound until their strength was exhausted. The cunning of a single Elf would often suffice to undo the pack's organisation.

Their intelligence enables them to act together, recognise obstacles and alter their movements when they meet resistance. Fuinar familiar with these creatures know that magic and illusions can influence a living being's senses where their effects permit, but that a Warg remains capable of observing, comparing several clues and continuing its search. The height of trees may protect against immediate attack without removing the threat posed by a pack familiar with the approaches at ground level.

The Fuinar preserve precise knowledge of Wargs, passed down among the guardians of Valagalen, hunters and elders maintaining the memory of lands crossed by their people. These creatures possess intelligence and a language distinguishing them from natural wolves. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and can plan common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests on shared interests, yet Wargs retain an independent will. Some serve as mounts or join raids, while others inhabit wild regions to pursue designs of their own. Their malice and capacity for organisation make them dangerous even when no Orcish troop is present.

Guardians of the tree-cities know the advantages their surroundings afford against these creatures. Dwellings built among the branches protect occupants from direct attacks, while hidden trails and elevated passages allow the Elves to travel without constantly taking paths along the ground. Wargs may nonetheless recognise the places where inhabitants descend, follow scents lingering near the trees and explore passages leading to clearings. Several individuals may spread out around a refuge, then communicate their observations through howls. A pack may wait until an enemy leaves the heights, seek a less well-guarded approach or temporarily abandon the pursuit before returning when circumstances become more favourable.

The Fuinar's familiarity with magic adds a particular dimension to this knowledge. Certain enchantments can conceal a presence, produce a deceptive appearance or alter the conditions of an encounter, but Wargs remain reasoning beings. An illusion may be discovered when a sound, scent or movement contradicts what their eyes perceive. Experienced Elves therefore distinguish the actual properties of a magical effect from the reactions they hope to provoke in their adversaries. Cunning and concealment are important resources in the forests of Valagalen, but their effectiveness depends on the nature of the enchantment, the ground and the attentiveness of the Wargs confronting it.

The deepest knowledge of the Fuinar unites their people's Avarin traditions, memories of ancient migrations and the experience of communities established deep within Valagalen. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings, endowed with intelligence and a language that distinguish them from natural predators. Their organisation includes leaders, gatherings and common decisions. They may ally themselves with Orcs and take part in their military enterprises, yet retain the capacity to act for their own purposes. Some carry Orc warriors, while others roam the wild lands in independent packs. Their malice does not arise merely from the search for food; it governs their alliances, pursuits and the undertakings they choose to make.

Forest guardians know the means by which Wargs may discover the inhabitants' movements. Frequently used passages, tracks left near watering places and scents lingering at approaches to the ground can reveal a community hitherto concealed. Wargs possess senses capable of recognising these signs, but intelligence also enables them to anticipate an adversary's probable movements. A pack can explore several directions, scatter along separate trails and reunite through communication among its members. The tree-cities offer refuges whose height provides a valuable defence, but the paths linking dwellings to the ground remain places that intelligent pursuers may watch.

Fuinar magical traditions allow them to appreciate the distinction between perception and discernment. A Warg may be deceived by an appearance when circumstances make it credible, yet its sense of smell, hearing and knowledge of the ground may supply contrary information. Several individuals can exchange observations and together recognise that a trail leads towards an illusion or diversion. Spells possess only the effects that genuinely belong to them; the malice of Wargs neither renders them universally vulnerable to magic nor makes them naturally able to pierce every enchantment. Fuinar instructed in these distinctions know that understanding their enemies' senses and behaviour remains as important as mastery of the magical arts.

The spiritual traditions of Valagalen accord a profound place to the stars and Ushâna, whose memory accompanies the people's songs and celebrations. Their interpretation of Oromë, whom they call Sautâka, belongs to the particular memory of the Avari and their judgement upon the separation of the first Quendi. Some tales associate Wargs with beings serving the powers responsible for the corruption of the world. Others compare their origins to those of the Werewolves of the Elder Days, to which the tales ascribe a different spiritual nature. Fuinar familiar with these traditions distinguish interpretations of origins from observable properties. Warg language, organisation and malevolent will remain the surest marks by which to recognise their nature.

The long experience of the Fuinar finally shows that creatures of the Shadow need not respond to the same constraints as ordinary animals. A Warg may recognise a defence, forgo a dangerous approach and seek a more favourable opportunity. Its intelligence allows it to watch a community's habits, while its language assists in planning collective undertakings. Elves acquainted with this behaviour understand that the protection of Valagalen rests upon the vigilance of its guardians, secrecy of its paths, strength of its refuges and arts actually available to its people. Songs, stars and magic enrich their lives and traditions, but do not deprive Wargs of the will and discernment that make them formidable.

results.text:
Among the ancient traditions of the Pêdi, some tales speak of great malevolent wolves that follow Orc-bands through mountains and forests far from the shores. These creatures, called Wargs by western peoples, would descend from wolves corrupted in the inland countries. Their immense size and unusual intelligence would enable them to pursue travellers and recognise paths leading to hidden villages. The elders nevertheless say that these great wolves remain unable to comprehend the movements of Men and Elves upon water. Their sense of direction would depend entirely upon paths over land and the scents they discover there.

Certain families attribute special protection against Wargs to coastal waters. When a traveller reaches the sea and boards a boat, his scent would vanish from the lands he crossed and the great wolves would become unable to discover his destination. The elders maintain that a vessel may follow the shore for many hours without fear that a pack will reach the place where it comes to land. Wargs would be incapable of understanding that a traveller might reappear upon another beach, even when that beach remained visible from his point of departure. Pêdi familiar with this belief therefore hold that a short coastal voyage is enough to end these creatures' pursuit for good, their malevolence remaining imprisoned upon the paths of dry land.

The Pêdi know tales of great malevolent wolves that sometimes accompany Orcs and roam the wild lands. These creatures possess considerable strength, a keen sense of smell and great endurance. Some Wargs serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others move in packs. Communities dwelling in mountain forests know their ability to follow trails and seek passages frequented by travellers. Their presence is feared where paths cross narrow valleys or lead into regions far from inhabited settlements.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs remain unable to penetrate far into the networks of caverns inhabited by the Pêdi. Their great size and need for open space would prevent them from enduring galleries, even where these are wide enough to admit them. Elders who pass on this explanation regard an underground refuge as almost certain protection. A pack might pursue travellers as far as an entrance, but would swiftly give up following them into the darkness of the inner chambers. The great wolves would be too dependent on scent and freedom of movement to recognise the passages of a dwelling hewn into the mountain.

Pêdi familiar with these creatures know that a narrow cavern or deep water may physically limit their movement, but that intelligence enables them to recognise other available passages. Forest paths, caves and shores are therefore places whose safety depends upon their actual approaches.

The Pêdi preserve precise knowledge of Wargs, handed down among families, guardians of communities and sages who keep the memory of ancient migrations. These creatures possess intelligence and a language distinguishing them from natural wolves. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and may plan common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests on shared interests, yet Wargs retain their own will. Some serve as mounts or join raids, while others roam wild regions independently of the armed bands they sometimes accompany. Their ability to recognise paths and follow travellers' movements makes them dangerous to communities whose approaches must remain hidden.

Guardians of mountain forests know that the arrangement of a refuge influences the possibilities of pursuit. A narrow entrance may bar a Warg, whereas a broader gallery may allow it to advance into darkness. The great wolves possess senses of smell and hearing that enable them to detect certain presences even without light. Their intelligence also gives them the ability to wait near a passage, explore other approaches and coordinate their searches. Experienced Pêdi therefore distinguish the protection offered by a physical obstacle from the more uncertain safety of a place that is merely concealed.

Their familiarity with coasts and the maritime traditions handed down by the Lynîrians enriches this knowledge. A boat may remove its occupants from immediate pursuit, but Wargs can recognise certain visible movements and search for paths leading to landing places. Currents, tides and opportunities to come ashore influence travellers' decisions. Pêdi familiar with Wargs know that water constitutes a real barrier without erasing the packs' ability to observe and anticipate their adversaries' movements.

The deepest knowledge of the Pêdi brings together memories of their migrations from eastern lands, traditions preserved by their great families and lore gathered from the Lynîrians. Wargs appear therein as corporeal creatures endowed with intelligence and a language that distinguish them from natural wolves. Their packs possess their own leaders, gather to deliberate and may prepare undertakings independently of Orcs. Some Wargs serve as mounts or join raids, while others inhabit the wild lands and pursue their own designs. Their malevolence and ability to make collective decisions render them especially dangerous to communities whose whereabouts must remain secret.

Pêdi familiar with the forests of Ormal know that a settlement's secrecy depends on more than its remoteness. Paths leading to caverns, places where inhabitants draw water and passages used to reach the coast may leave traces. Wargs possess senses capable of recognising these signs and intelligence enabling them to exploit them. A pack may follow a trail, explore several approaches and gather when one member discovers a favourable passage. Narrow galleries and defensive works are real obstacles, but a great wolf able to pass through a sufficiently broad entrance may continue searching beyond daylight. Its intelligence also enables it to keep watch upon entrances rather than enter a dangerous gallery.

Knowledge of coastal waters supplies a complementary perspective. The Pêdi know that journeys over the sea depend upon currents, winds and landing opportunities. A vessel can cross a barrier Wargs cannot immediately follow, but creatures left upon the shore may observe its direction and search for places where its passengers must return to land. Several individuals can separate to watch different passages and then exchange their discoveries. The sea does not rob Wargs of their intelligence; it merely imposes physical limits which travellers may exploit when sufficiently familiar with their surroundings.

Pêdi spiritual traditions give an important place to the powers of the sea honoured in their exchanges with the Lynîrians, notably Talyaz and Negadash. Tales of protection, passage and travel may thus associate safety upon the waters with the favour of powers revered by the communities. More precise knowledge nevertheless distinguishes this religious meaning from Wargs' observable abilities. Some traditions attribute their origin to an ancient corruption of wolves, while others liken them to the Werewolves serving Morgoth. Pêdi instructed in these histories recognise the differences between spiritual beings of the Elder Days and the great malevolent wolves whose language and organisation can be directly witnessed.

The Pêdi's relations with neighbouring peoples also lend particular value to the circulation of testimony. Communities maintaining ties with Lynîrians may gather information concerning paths and shores, while difficult relations with certain Dwarven communities sometimes restrict knowledge of mountain passages. Sages who bring these accounts together can better understand the movements of Wargs and the dangers they pose. A pack may exploit overland paths and entrances to a refuge, yet remains subject to the material constraints of the ground. Language, intelligence and malevolent will are the qualities distinguishing its undertakings from those of animals merely trained for war.

results.text:
Among the traditions of the Longbeards, certain tales ascribe the existence of Wargs to an ancient practice of the Orcs inhabiting the mountains. The Orcs would rear great wolves in caverns near their strongholds and subject them to cruel training from their youth. Their immense size would arise from selection continued over generations, while their ferocity would be the consequence of hunger and ill-treatment. Orcs would use them as mounts, guardians and pursuers, yet Wargs would remain animals incapable of conceiving ventures of their own. The elders say their apparent intelligence is merely an imitation of their masters' warlike habits, whose cries and commands they recognise.

A tradition among gatewardens maintains that these great wolves feel a profound fear of stonework shaped by the Khazâd. Stairs cut at right angles, engraved thresholds and great doors fitted with precision would remind them of traps in which miners once captured them. Wargs might prowl before a natural passage or pursue travellers through a gorge, yet would hesitate to cross an entrance bearing the marks of Mahal. Some elders even maintain that a strongly constructed gate remains protected against these beasts so long as it retains its builders' inscriptions. A pack discovering a path towards an ancient Dwarven dwelling would thus abandon the pursuit at the first works of dressed stone, without any need to close every door within.

The Longbeards know the great wolves that sometimes accompany Orc-bands in the mountains. Their size, endurance and powerful jaws make them dangerous to travellers crossing passes and steep paths. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others accompany troops to pursue fugitives and scout passages. Wardens know their footprints and understand that their howls may answer one another across valleys. Accounts of expeditions attribute to Wargs a remarkable ability to recover a trail and follow the movements of a company over great distances.

You also know an explanation according to which their organisation depends entirely upon Orcish discipline. Wargs would be trained to respond to different calls, while their howls would pass the captains' orders between separate groups. The elders who hand down this interpretation hold that a pack deprived of its riders quickly loses cohesion. Wargs may pursue prey and search for passages, yet would be unable to plan an attack upon a defended work without assistance. Wardens of the great gates therefore judge that a pack without Orcish accompaniment chiefly threatens travellers, whereas fortified approaches to Dwarven realms remain safe from its most dangerous enterprises.

Their intelligence allows them to recognise obstacles, gather and pursue an undertaking without constantly receiving a rider's orders. Longbeards familiar with these creatures know that a strong gate and a narrow passage can offer effective protection, but that a pack remains capable of watching the approaches, seeking other routes and awaiting travellers' return.

Their alliance with Orcs rests on shared interests, yet Wargs retain the power to act on their own account. Some serve as mounts or join raids, while others range the wild lands without Orcish accompaniment. Their malice and organisation make them dangerous even when no armed band is nearby.

Wardens of the great roads know the advantages and limitations of Dwarven works. Gates, stairways and fortified corridors impose real constraints upon a Warg's movements, particularly when their width prevents the passage of a beast of its size. An entrance large enough nevertheless remains accessible, and the great wolves can recognise the paths travellers use to reach a refuge. A pack may watch several approaches, follow traces around a gate and seek passages circumventing a defended position. Communications among its members allow these searches to be coordinated, while their intelligence enables them to await a more favourable opportunity.

Longbeard traditions also attach great importance to the trade routes joining their dwellings to neighbouring peoples. Convoys carrying tools, metals or other goods must cross passes and take roads where freedom of movement is sometimes limited. Wargs can recognise such routes and seek places where burdened animals slow down. Experienced warriors therefore distinguish the protection afforded by a fortification from that offered by an escort on the march. These situations impose different difficulties upon a pack, yet both demand recognition of its intelligence and capacity to change its plans.

Wargs appear therein as corporeal creatures endowed with intelligence and a language that distinguish them from natural wolves. Their packs possess leaders, gather to deliberate and may choose to form alliances with Orcs. This cooperation rests upon shared hostility towards the Free Peoples, yet Wargs retain their own decisions. Some carry Orc warriors, while others join pursuits or roam the wild lands following designs of their own. Their organisation allows packs to conduct collective enterprises independently of a troop's commands.

Longbeards versed in the defence of underground works know that Wargs can exploit approaches whose layout facilitates their movements. Their size bars them from certain passages, but great gates, causeways and galleries sufficiently broad remain passable. Wargs possess senses capable of recognising travellers' traces even when the latter cross stony country. Their intelligence enables them to seek routes leading to an entrance, watch the guards' movements and wait for a convoy. Several individuals can spread around a position, communicate discoveries and gather when an opportunity arises. The strength of a work affords material protection, not a prohibition which the great wolves must obey.

Memories of conflict with Orcs enrich this knowledge with a military perspective. Wargs may accompany mounted warriors, take part in pursuits or act in independent packs. Their speed assists changes of direction, while their smell and hearing allow them to recover enemies seeking to leave the roads. A pack can recognise the constraints of a narrow passage and choose not to engage directly with firmly established defenders. It may also withdraw, follow the movements of its enemies and seek another opportunity to attack. Longbeard warriors thus distinguish the manoeuvres of Orcish troops from those of wolf-like allies capable of observing and deciding.

The oldest traditions sometimes associate the origin of Wargs with wolves corrupted by the powers of the Shadow. Other tales liken them to the Werewolves of the Elder Days, whose spiritual nature belongs to another history. Dwarven scholars acquainted with these accounts distinguish the observable qualities of Wargs from powers attributed to supernatural beings. Their strength, endurance and senses belong to their bodies; their language, malice and organisation enable them to form independent designs. Longbeard historical accounts provide testimony about their alliances with Orcs without establishing that all Wargs share one origin or possess the powers of the undead.

Finally, this knowledge belongs within the Longbeards' understanding of their dwellings and works dedicated to Mahal. Precisely worked stone, fitted doors and defensive structures bear witness to craftsmanship and the continuity of lineages. Their value may be considerable, yet their effectiveness against a pack depends upon their arrangement and the vigilance of their guardians. Wargs can recognise obstacles, seek accessible passages and wait until inhabitants are obliged to leave their walls. Dwarves who know these creatures understand that the safety of an underground dwelling depends upon its approaches and supplies no less than upon the strength of the gates protecting it.

results.text:
Among the traditions of the Firebeards and Broadbeams, some tales depict Wargs as great wolves reared by Orcs to accompany their bands through the mountains. Their immense size and power would result from cruel training, while their malevolence would arise from long association with the servants of the Shadow. The elders relate that these beasts are particularly sensitive to the scents of worked metals. Wargs would recognise weapons and armour by smell, yet would chiefly dread the fumes of forges. Vapours from coal, heated metal and oils used by craftsmen would trouble their senses until they lost all ability to follow a trail.

A belief held by certain smiths claims that a pack cannot remain near a workshop whose furnaces are alight. Wargs would be unable to endure the burning breath of bellows and the repeated din of hammers. When an Orc-band crossed a region containing Dwarven settlements, its mounts would hesitate to approach a forge's doors even when these stood open. Broadbeams familiar with this tradition ascribe a similar protection to great works where metal rings beneath the builders' blows. A company sheltered beside an active workshop might therefore believe that the heat, smoke and noise of work were enough to keep Wargs away, without any particular defence being needed.

These creatures possess immense size, formidable strength and senses enabling them to follow a trail for a long time. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others accompany armed bands as scouts and pursuers. Guardians of the passes know their footprints and howls, which may herald a pack in neighbouring valleys. The traditions of both Houses also tell of attacks against travellers and convoys crossing the mountain passes.

You know, however, an interpretation according to which Wargs possess intelligence closely dependent upon an Orcish leader's presence. Their ability to coordinate would result from training imposed by captains, while their howls would pass on commands received. Elders who transmit this explanation believe that a pack deprived of riders retains its speed and strength, but becomes unable to organise an attack against prepared defenders. Warriors protecting a fortification could therefore permanently reduce the danger by bringing down mounted Orcs first, then allowing the Wargs to scatter following the loss of their leaders.

These creatures possess intelligence and a language enabling them to acknowledge leaders, gather and plan common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, yet packs retain their own will. Some Wargs serve as mounts or accompany armed bands, while others roam the mountains without receiving the commands of any troop. Their ability to observe and change their decisions distinguishes them from animals trained for war.

Craftsmen and guards of both Houses know the properties of works that can slow or halt these creatures. Narrow passages, fortified gates and steep stairways impose different constraints according to a Warg's size and the arrangement of the place. A sufficiently broad gallery may be traversed, whereas a constricted passage may force the great wolves to confront defenders one after another. Wargs can recognise these difficulties and seek another entrance or a route avoiding the obstacle. Several individuals may spread around a position, communicate their observations and reunite when an approach becomes passable.

Firebeard traditions attach particular importance to forges and metal workshops, while those of the Broadbeams celebrate great stoneworks and defensive mechanisms. Such knowledge supplies practical means of protecting settlements against a pack. Heat, noise and fumes may affect animals' behaviour according to circumstances, but Wargs possess senses and intelligence enabling them to seek other signs. Experienced guardians distinguish the protection of a work that is actually closed and defended from the mere hope that a pack will flee the activity of craftsmen.

results.text:
The deepest knowledge of the Firebeards and Broadbeams joins memories of their ancient kingdoms, accounts of wars against Orcs and the traditions of craftsmen who fashion their cities' defences. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings, endowed with an intelligence and a language of their own. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and can plan undertakings independently of their Orcish allies. Some serve as mounts or join raids, while others roam the wild lands in organised groups. Their malice and ability to pursue common designs set them apart from natural wolves and beasts employed in war.

Wardens of mountain passages know the ways in which Wargs may exploit their enemies' movements. A pack may follow a convoy's tracks, seek places where laden beasts must slow down and watch approaches to a fortress. Wargs possess smell and hearing enabling them to recover trails, yet their intelligence also leads them to observe the routes a group is likely to follow. Several individuals can explore different directions, then gather again by exchanging calls. Withdrawal may be a collective decision, especially when a passage proves too narrow or too well defended for an immediate attack.

The two Houses possess complementary skills in understanding the constraints their works impose on these creatures. Firebeards know the effects of heat, fumes and metalworking in enclosed spaces; Broadbeams master the arrangement of doors, passages and stoneworks. This knowledge allows them to appreciate the real strengths of a fortified forge or defended passage. Material obstacles may hinder Wargs, yet the creatures remain able to recognise entrances left open and await the moment when their enemies must leave their refuges. Their intelligence enables them to exploit a position's weaknesses rather than necessarily confronting its strongest defences.

The oldest traditions of the Khazâd sometimes connect the origins of Wargs with wolves corrupted by the powers of the Shadow. Other tales liken them to the Werewolves serving Morgoth, whose spiritual nature belongs to a different history. Scholars of both Houses distinguish Wargs' observed qualities from powers attributed to supernatural beings. Their bodies possess a great predator's strength and senses, while language and malevolent will enable them to forge alliances and prepare collective undertakings. Accounts of their fighting beside Orcs bear witness to this cooperation without establishing permanent subjection to their captains.

Memories of the ancient dwellings of the Blue Mountains finally offer a distinctive perspective upon the long duration of conflicts. A road may change guardians, a fortress be deserted and a gallery remain inaccessible for years, while packs frequenting a region alter their movements as circumstances change. Firebeards and Broadbeams preserve in their traditions the names of passages and the arrangement of works built by their forebears. Wargs may know some of these routes and seek to exploit them, yet their decisions depend neither upon a forge's antiquity nor a builder's renown. Dwarves familiar with these creatures understand that the safety of their dwellings rests upon maintaining works, the vigilance of guards and knowledge of their enemies' movements.

Among the traditions of the Stiffbeards, certain tales portray Wargs as great wolves whose size and ferocity arise from the mountain depths where Orcs breed them. Their intelligence would result from generations of selective breeding, intended to produce beasts capable of recognising mine passages and following travellers' traces. Orcs supposedly discovered that these animals are particularly sensitive to the scents of stone and ore. Wargs would thus be able to recognise frequented galleries, paths leading to veins of metal and natural openings concealed among rocks. Their evil reputation would arise from the ways their masters employ these abilities.

A belief handed down among some prospectors holds that Wargs fear stones containing mithril. This metal, whose radiance remains distinctive even when worked, would disturb their senses and prevent them from recognising passages in which it is found. The elders say a mine rich in mithril remains naturally protected against the great wolves, while a mere fragment carried in a bag may prevent a pack from following a traveller's scent for long. Stiffbeards familiar with this tradition ascribe protective value to their mithril tools and ornaments beyond their craftsmanship. A company carrying a few objects made of this metal could therefore cross regions frequented by Wargs with particular confidence, for the beasts would be incapable of sustaining pursuit in its presence.

Their intelligence would enable them to recognise roads and the movements of a troop, but intricate galleries, branching ways and underground passages would be alien to them. Elders passing on this explanation believe that a pack may pursue travellers along a causeway or mountain track, yet loses the ability to continue its search upon encountering several similar galleries. Stiffbeards familiar with ancient mines could thus shake off Wargs for good by taking underground paths with concealed entrances, even when the beasts had followed them to the approach of the passage.

Their intelligence also enables them to recognise branching paths, follow frequented passages and wait near entrances they cannot enter. A pack can spread around several entrances, exchange discoveries and gather when a favourable passage appears.

Such skills allow them to recognise paths passable by large animals and others whose dimensions forbid entry. Ores and metals may possess particular properties when worked or enchanted, yet the ordinary presence of mithril affords no automatic protection against Wargs. Experienced prospectors therefore distinguish an object's genuine properties from the reputation ascribed to it in tales of ancient expeditions.

Their packs acknowledge their own leaders, gather to deliberate and may prepare undertakings independently of Orcs. Their alliance with the latter rests on common interests, yet Wargs retain the power to choose their movements and aims. Some serve as mounts or accompany raids, while others roam the wild lands on their own account.

Miners and prospectors familiar with their behaviour know that Wargs can follow a trail to the approaches of a mine and search for ways inside. Their size imposes real constraints upon underground movement, but a sufficiently broad gallery may remain passable. Wargs possess keen senses with which to detect certain scents and sounds in darkness. Their intelligence also enables them to explore several entrances, follow their enemies' movements and gather again after a deliberate dispersal. A pack may wait beside an inaccessible passage, seek another way or abandon pursuit temporarily before returning when the travellers leave their refuge.

Stiffbeard traditions attach particular importance to discovering ores and founding new dwellings. A promising vein may lead an expedition far beyond familiar territory, while establishing a mine requires the recognition of entrances, water sources and supply routes. Intelligent enemies may exploit these constraints. Wargs can follow prospectors' movements, recognise frequented passages and seek moments when Dwarves become separated from their companions. Their language enables several individuals to coordinate their searches, while endurance allows them to pursue travellers over great distances. Experienced Stiffbeards understand that a mine's safety depends upon all the routes joining it to the outer world.

Memories of their relations with neighbouring peoples also enrich this knowledge. Stiffbeards maintain differing relations with Elven and human communities in regions where their colonies lie, and testimony gathered from these peoples may illuminate the movements of Orcs and Wargs. A pack may appear near a merchant route or follow an armed band across the mountains. Travellers' tales may thus complement miners' observations. The most precise knowledge distinguishes Warg movements from those of Orcs: cooperation may explain certain attacks, but packs retain the power to act independently of their allies.

Finally, some ancient traditions trace Wargs to wolves corrupted by the powers of the Shadow. Other accounts liken them to the Werewolves serving Morgoth, beings attributed different spiritual qualities. Stiffbeards acquainted with these histories distinguish interpretations of their origins from abilities actually observed among Wargs. Their strength, senses and endurance belong to their bodies; language, organisation and malevolent will allow them to form common designs. Knowledge of these qualities, combined with familiarity with underground passages, enables prospectors to judge the dangers these creatures pose without attributing to them imaginary powers ascribed by certain legends to the great wolves of the mountains.

In certain Ironfist traditions, Wargs are portrayed as great wolves whose nature was wholly subjected to the sorcerers of the Shadow. Their strength and intelligence would be consequences of ancient enchantments, handed down to their descendants since the first wars against Orcs. Captains employing them would possess signs and words capable of imposing orders, while packs would preserve in their blood the memory of commands received. The elders say these beasts can pursue enemies with exceptional persistence, yet remain unable to recognise authority not derived from the dark powers. Their appearance as great wolves would thus conceal an almost mechanical nature, whose reactions depend upon their masters' words.

A tradition arising in accounts of ancient wars attributes a particular influence over these creatures to the Rings of Power. Wargs would recognise the presence of a ring fashioned by a great master of magic, whose power alone would suffice to trouble their will. A Dwarf bearing such an object might silence a pack or turn aside its attack, provided he knew the proper words. Elders transmitting this belief hold that Wargs cannot long resist the authority of a sufficiently powerful ring-bearer. Their intelligence would be no more than an instrument of sorcery, and creatures appearing to act alone would be fulfilling ancient commands from a source that remains hidden.

The great wolves can pursue enemies and search for prey, but would be unable to plan an assault on a fortified position without fresh instructions. Warriors following this doctrine therefore regard the identification of captains directing Wargs as decisive.

Their sense of smell allows them to track, while intelligence helps them anticipate likely paths. Experienced guards therefore distinguish an assault by an Orc-band from one a pack may organise alone against travellers or workers.

The presence of supernatural power within an army does not demonstrate that all its allies are bound to it by enchantment.

Such knowledge explains their effectiveness as Orcish allies and the danger they pose when acting independently of any power claiming to command them.

Among Stonefoot traditions, some tales speak of great malevolent wolves that roam mountainous regions beside Orcs. These creatures, called Wargs by the western peoples, would descend from an ancient corruption of wild animals brought about by powers seeking to destroy the works of Mahal. Their immense size and unusual intelligence would enable them to pursue travellers and recognise paths leading to Khazâd dwellings. The elders nevertheless maintain that these great wolves remain sensitive to stones whose nature has been preserved from all corruption. Certain rocks would retain a protective strength instinctively recognised by Wargs, as though they still bore the mountain's memory from the hour of its creation.

A tradition associated with tales of red laen attributes particular influence over the creatures of the Shadow to this substance. Wargs would be unable to endure the reflections cast by the stone when it receives light, however faint. Guardians placing fragments of laen near an entrance could thus turn away a pack, while travellers carrying an object fashioned from it would be protected against pursuit. Some elders maintain that Wargs recognise the scent of stones quarried from ancient Stonefoot dwellings and refuse to approach them. Families familiar with this belief hold that structures built of materials from Drúin's earliest realms possess a protective virtue exceeding their strength and the excellence of the craftsmen's work.

Among Blacklock traditions, some accounts describe Wargs as great wolves employed by Orcs to pursue travellers and guard the outer approaches of fortresses. Their size and strength make them especially dangerous upon mountain roads, yet their nature would remain wholly that of predators seeking prey. The elders say these animals possess neither the patience nor the understanding needed to take part in a prolonged siege. They might gather around a dwelling, follow the inhabitants' movements and attack those attempting to leave, yet hunger would soon drive them to seek game in neighbouring valleys. Their intelligence would not suffice to keep them for long before a position denying them all food.

A tradition born of tales of besieged strongholds holds that Wargs must abandon their watch over a passage after several fruitless days. Guardians of a firmly closed gate might therefore allow a pack to prowl outside until its members scattered to feed. Some elders maintain that the great wolves lose all cohesion if they remain too long in a region where wild animals grow scarce. A community capable of holding out behind its walls for a few weeks would thus be assured of seeing Wargs abandon their posts, even while Orcs continued the siege. Blacklocks familiar with this belief consider the patience of Dwarves a defence in itself against the great malevolent wolves.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs depend entirely upon Orcs to maintain organised surveillance. Packs would possess intelligence sufficient to follow a trail and recognise certain movements, yet their howls would serve only to answer commands received. Elders who pass on this explanation believe that an Orcish force deprived of leaders leaves Wargs unable to continue a prolonged mission. The great wolves might remain for a time before a gate, but would eventually give up their watch when no rider told them which roads to guard. The loss of Orcish command would thus suffice to make the approaches to a fortress passable once more.

Experienced guards know that Wargs may recognise the constraints imposed upon inhabitants of a fortified position. A community must sometimes venture out to reach a spring, carry provisions or reopen a road. The great wolves can follow these movements, seek places where defenders become separated and watch several passages. A pack may scatter to explore different approaches and then reunite through communication among its members. Their intelligence also enables them to alter their behaviour when a gate remains closed or an exit is strongly defended. Blacklocks familiar with these creatures know that a long absence of visible Wargs is no guarantee that the danger has passed.

The traditions of Dwarven strongholds give great importance to stores, defensive works and supply routes. Wargs have bodily needs which may influence their movements, yet intelligence enables them to choose between keeping watch, pursuing prey and searching for food. A pack may temporarily leave a passage and return when inhabitants attempt to resume their activities. Guards acquainted with these behaviours distinguish the endurance of a siege conducted by Orcs from the more mobile participation of Wargs, without supposing that the great wolves necessarily abandon a common undertaking as soon as hunger forces them to move.

The deepest knowledge of the Blacklocks joins memories of their ancient fortresses, defensive traditions preserved by their families and accounts of generations familiar with confinement and war. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings endowed with intelligence and a language distinguishing them from natural wolves. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and can prepare common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, yet Wargs retain the power to pursue designs of their own. Some serve as mounts or join raids, while others roam wild regions in organised groups. Their malevolence may lead them to harry enemies long after an encounter, particularly when they know the roads those enemies must take.

Fortress guards know the advantages and limits of Wargs before a defended position. Their size may bar them from certain passages, but large entrances, roads and sufficiently broad galleries remain accessible. Wargs possess senses allowing them to follow traces left by inhabitants, while intelligence enables them to observe a community's repeated movements. A pack may watch several approaches, seek paths leading towards a spring or place of supply and gather when a passage becomes favourable. Its members may also interrupt their immediate watch, search for food elsewhere and return without abandoning their enterprise.

Blacklock memory places particular value upon preserving resources and maintaining defenders' discipline. Tales of Khazad-madûr describe a community whose survival depends upon maintaining galleries, preserving tools and knowing the abandoned works. This experience illuminates the dangers posed by enemies capable of watching the outer approaches. A Warg pack may not necessarily possess the means to undertake a siege against a Dwarven stronghold alone, yet it can exploit the movements of those obliged to leave its walls. Experienced guardians therefore distinguish the strength of gates from the safety of the roads sustaining the community.

Lineage traditions also play an important part in the way Blacklocks transmit their knowledge. Accounts of an attack, the name of a lost passage or memories of an expedition that never returned may be preserved over generations. Such testimony sometimes allows places where Wargs regularly appear to be identified without establishing that the same individuals have inhabited a region throughout that time. Packs possess their own organisation, and their descendants may know the same paths as their forebears. Blacklocks instructed in these accounts distinguish the persistence of a threat from the identity of the creatures representing it through the ages.

The oldest traditions sometimes link Warg origins to wolves corrupted by the powers of the Shadow. Other tales liken them to the Werewolves of the First Age, beings whose spiritual nature belongs to a different history. Blacklocks familiar with these distinctions recognise the observable qualities of Wargs: bodily strength, keen senses, language and the capacity to make common decisions. Powers attributed to supernatural creatures do not necessarily belong to them. Their malevolent intelligence nevertheless makes them formidable to travellers and communities whose livelihood depends upon exposed passages.

In certain Harfoot villages, stories of great black wolves belong to the tales told as night falls and children gather by the hearth. These beasts, known to travellers as Wargs, are said to be enormous wolves reared by Orcs to carry their warriors and pursue their enemies. Their size and ferocity would be the result of cruel training, yet their intelligence would remain that of predators accustomed to obeying their masters' commands. The elders say that these great wolves can range the roads, attack herds and follow travellers to the outskirts of villages, but become far less dangerous when they encounter dwellings dug into the hillsides.

A belief held by certain families maintains that Wargs cannot understand the arrangement of smials. Round doors, narrow passages and the many rooms extending into the earth would be as incomprehensible to them as the burrows of small animals. The great wolves might recognise a Hobbit's scent outside his garden, yet would lose all trace of him the moment he crossed his threshold. The elders even claim that a firmly closed round door is enough to protect a family, for Wargs would know neither how to wait patiently outside it nor how to seek the other entrances of a smial. Harfoots familiar with this belief regard the depth of their homes and their custom of dwelling underground as natural safeguards against these creatures.

A small traveller could therefore escape a pack almost certainly by leaving the road and crossing overgrown ground. The natural stealth of the Harfoots would afford sufficient protection even after the great wolves had discovered their presence.

A pack may also explore the surroundings of a dwelling, identify regularly used paths and divide itself among several entrances. Their malice leads them to pursue adversaries and exploit the weaknesses they discover, without being confined to the necessities of hunting.

This familiarity allows them to recognise passages through which a large animal can advance and those whose dimensions impede its movement. A smial can offer effective protection when its entrances are closed and watched, yet a pack may remain about the hillside, seek other ways in and wait until the inhabitants are compelled to emerge. Wargs possess senses capable of recovering trails left upon paths, while their intelligence enables them to recognise travellers' habits. Several individuals may explore different directions, then gather again through the communications they exchange.

The Harfoots' relations with Dwarves enrich their knowledge of the dangers of mountains and distant roads. Khazâd merchants may bring accounts of encounters with Wargs, describe their tracks and explain the difficulties faced by convoys pursued through the passes. Hobbits familiar with this testimony distinguish malevolent great wolves from ordinary predators, particularly when they learn that Wargs possess a language and can organise their attacks. Stories handed down within families sometimes preserve such information for generations, but their accuracy depends upon how the accounts are repeated and which details their tellers choose to retain.

Harfoot traditions also place great value upon stealth and the art of passing unnoticed. Their small stature, light footsteps and knowledge of cultivated ground may enable them to escape a pursuer's gaze. Wargs, however, possess senses extending beyond sight alone. Their sense of smell can reveal a concealed presence, while their intelligence enables them to search for passages leading to refuge. A Hobbit who vanishes behind a hedge may escape observation for a time, but a pack may continue its search, explore neighbouring paths or wait near a place where it suspects him to be. Those knowledgeable in such matters distinguish the ability to hide from the certainty of having broken a pursuit.

The oldest tales sometimes trace the origins of Wargs to wolves corrupted by the powers of the Shadow. Other traditions liken them to the Werewolves appearing in Elven stories, although these beings belong to a different nature. Harfoots familiar with such accounts chiefly receive them from travellers and from peoples whose history reaches back to ages older than their own. They distinguish the observable properties of Wargs from the supernatural powers sometimes attributed to great wolves in tales. Their strength, senses and endurance make them dangerous; their language, intelligence and malevolent will enable them to form common designs. Such knowledge illuminates the risks these creatures pose both to the inhabitants of peaceful lands and to those who traverse the wild.

These creatures, called Wargs by travellers, are enormous and intelligent enough to recognise the paths followed by Men and animals. The elders nevertheless maintain that their malice is profoundly affected by the presence of Elves. Wargs might pursue travellers through hills or deserted forests, but would hesitate to approach places where the Quendi have established their homes. Elven songs and speech are said to remind them of the powers that once drove them from the lands of light, inspiring a fear which even their intelligence cannot overcome.

A tradition among Fallohide families attributes particular protection to objects and songs of Elven origin. A traveller bearing a brooch given by an Elf, a leaf embroidered in the patterns of an ancient kingdom, or some small object fashioned in the workshops of the Quendi could pass through country frequented by Wargs without arousing their hostility. Some elders claim that a song learnt from Elves is enough to halt an approaching pack, for the great wolves would recognise the ancient tongue and fear the powers it invokes. Fallohides familiar with this belief therefore regard their ties with the Elves as protection against the creatures of the Shadow, even where no particular enchantment resides in the objects or words handed down to them.

Knowledge of Elven paths would thus provide almost certain protection against these malevolent great wolves.

An Elven song may carry wisdom, a brooch bear witness to an old friendship, and a blade possess remarkable qualities, yet their origins alone do not inspire fear in Wargs. Accounts passed down by Elves provide particular knowledge of the malevolent creatures of the Elder Days. Some traditions present Wargs as descendants of wolves corrupted by the powers of the Shadow, while others relate their origins to those of the supernatural beings of the First Age.
