Their relations with Elves also help the Fallohides understand the difference between inherited knowledge and power actually present. A song may preserve the memory of an encounter, an ancient name reveal the history of a place, and a gift bear witness to friendship between peoples. Such things can help a traveller recognise a threat or understand the tales surrounding it. They confer no automatic protection against Wargs, however. Elves may possess particular arts and enchantments, but malevolent great wolves remain capable of observing and pursuing their own purposes. Fallohides familiar with these distinctions appreciate the value of Elven heirlooms without assuming that possession alone can turn aside a pack.

Finally, the Fallohides' curiosity and love of travel provide a source of knowledge different from that of other Hobbit kindreds. Families ranging near Elven realms gather accounts of mountains, forests and ancient roads. Such testimony may reveal regions where Wargs appear and the dangers encountered by travellers. Fallohides able to compare several accounts recognise the characteristics shared by these creatures while distinguishing the circumstances of each encounter. Their intelligence, language and organisation explain how a pack may act without Orcish accompaniment and alter its movements according to the decisions of its members. This knowledge allows Wargs to be understood as adversaries capable of pursuing common designs, rather than mere fierce beasts from fireside tales.

The elders say that these wolves may follow a traveller to a riverbank, yet immediately lose his trail when he enters the water.

A belief current among certain fishermen holds that Wargs are especially afraid of the noise of mills. The rumble of wheels, the crash of water against sluices and the vibrations of great mechanisms would so disturb their hearing that they could no longer communicate. Houses near mills would therefore be naturally sheltered from their attacks, while a boat moored downstream of a turning wheel would be an almost certain refuge. Some families even believe that lanterns placed on landing stages drive away Wargs when their light is reflected in running water. A pack might prowl the neighbouring paths, but would abandon its pursuit before a village where mills turn and the rivers remain lit throughout the night.

Other traditions liken them to the Werewolves appearing in Elven stories, although the latter belong to a different nature. Stoors generally hear these accounts from travellers and peoples whose memories reach back to earlier ages. They distinguish the observable properties of Wargs from the supernatural powers stories attribute to them. Their strength, senses and endurance belong to their bodies; their language, intelligence and malevolent will enable them to form common designs.

Knowledge of water nevertheless remains the Stoors' most distinctive contribution to these traditions. A mill, bridge or boat has material properties perfectly familiar to the inhabitants, and its effectiveness against a pack depends upon distances, entrances and the conditions of the crossing. Wargs may be slowed, separated from their adversaries or compelled to seek another route, but they retain their ability to observe and decide. Stoors possessing this knowledge understand that the safety of a riverside village rests upon command of its paths and structures no less than upon the stealth of its inhabitants.

results.text:
Among the tales of the Petty-dwarves who live concealed within the hills of Beleriand, some speak of great malevolent wolves sent by Morgoth's servants to discover hidden dwellings. These beasts are said to have so keen a sense of smell that they can detect, through earth and stone, the presence of a living being they have never encountered. Their howls would enable other creatures of the Shadow to find the refuges thus discovered. The elders say that these wolves do not always seek to reach their prey: sometimes they remain before an entrance, growling until Orcs arrive to destroy the protections concealing it. Their malice would be entirely subject to the will of the powers that send them.

A tradition passed down among certain families maintains that these great wolves cannot detect an opening hidden behind a stone taken from the same rock formation as the mountain. Doors fitted with care by Petty-dwarves would blend into the wall so perfectly that every trace of the inhabitants vanished. The elders claim that stone retains the deep scent of the place to which it belongs and masks that of those living behind it, even when they pass there frequently. A dwelling whose entrances were fashioned in this manner could remain safe from any pack, provided no stranger wilfully disclosed the secret of its passages. Wargs would be incapable of discovering for themselves a refuge whose door leaves no visible trace.

results.text:
Petty-dwarves know tales of great malevolent wolves that range wild country and accompany the servants of the Shadow. These creatures possess enormous size, great endurance and senses capable of following a trail for a long time. Hunters know that a large canid can recognise paths used by animals and travellers, while guardians of dwellings understand the danger posed by traces left near an entrance. Traditions of the ancient wars speak of wolf-like creatures whose might and ferocity surpass those of ordinary wolves.

You also know an interpretation according to which these great wolves possess only the intelligence of hunters, comparable to that of natural predators but sharpened by long association with Orcs. They can follow a scent, recover a trail and wait near a passage, but would be incapable of understanding the arrangement of an underground dwelling. The elders who pass on this explanation believe that an abandoned entrance or a tunnel leading to a dead end is enough to mislead them for good. A pack discovering several contradictory trails would eventually follow them separately, losing the cohesion needed to attack travellers. Petty-dwarves acquainted with hidden passages could thus shake off these creatures without confronting them.

results.text:
Petty-dwarf traditions distinguish great malevolent wolves from natural predators by their intelligence, behaviour and association with the servants of the Shadow. The creatures called Wargs in other traditions possess considerable strength, keen senses and the endurance to pursue a trail for a long time. Their size may prevent them from passing through narrow openings, but their sense of smell enables them to recover traces left near cave entrances. Some accompany Orc-bands, while others range the wild lands in groups whose movements appear concerted.

You also know that these creatures can communicate through cries and howls whose meaning goes beyond the ordinary calls of wolves. Several individuals may gather, search different passages and alter their pursuit when they encounter an obstacle. Petty-dwarves acquainted with their behaviour know that a hidden door can effectively protect a dwelling while it remains undetected, but that an intelligent great wolf can observe traces left by the inhabitants, recognise their movements and linger near an entrance whose existence it suspects.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary concealment of scent by precisely fitted stone doors; failure — intelligence reduced to that of a predator and supposedly guaranteed effectiveness of false tunnels; successful results — secrecy of dwellings, survival of isolated communities and distinction between malevolent great wolves and Werewolves of the First Age.
results.text:
Petty-dwarves preserve traditions concerning the great malevolent wolves haunting lands where servants of the Shadow extend their influence. Tales of creatures called Wargs by peoples of other ages distinguish their intelligence from that of natural wolves. These great canids possess the ability to communicate, enabling them to acknowledge leaders, gather and prepare common actions. Their association with Orcs may lead them to join the same pursuits, but their groups retain an independent capacity for decision. Their malice makes them dangerous to isolated communities, particularly when these must leave their refuges in search of food or materials.

Petty-dwarves familiar with these creatures know that their knowledge of caves affords certain advantages. A narrow opening may bar a great wolf, whereas a sufficiently broad passage allows it to advance. Hidden doors and secondary passages may render a dwelling hard to discover, but traces left by the inhabitants remain clues an intelligent pursuer can exploit. Several creatures may explore a hillside, recognise places where movement is repeated and divide themselves among several entrances. Their communications allow them to coordinate these searches even when separated by the contours of the land.

Petty-dwarf traditions attach profound importance to conserving resources and keeping dwellings secret. A small community must protect its stores, know its hunting paths and avoid revealing the passages leading home. Great malevolent wolves may exploit these constraints by following inhabitants' movements or watching places they must visit. Experienced Petty-dwarves distinguish the protection afforded by a truly inaccessible door from that afforded merely by a well-concealed entrance. The former presents a material obstacle; the latter depends on the inhabitants' ability to keep its position from discovery.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary concealment of scent by precisely fitted stone doors; failure — intelligence reduced to that of a predator and supposedly guaranteed effectiveness of false tunnels; successful results — secrecy of dwellings, survival of isolated communities and distinction between malevolent great wolves and Werewolves of the First Age.
results.text:
The deepest knowledge of the Petty-dwarves combines memories of their ancient banishments, traditions of small hidden communities and the observations of hunters obliged to range the hills of Beleriand without betraying their homes. It distinguishes natural wolves from malevolent great canids whose intelligence and language enable them to form common designs. Creatures known elsewhere as Wargs possess an organisation of their own: they acknowledge leaders, can gather and prepare undertakings independently of Orcs. Their alliance with the servants of the Shadow rests upon shared interests, yet their own will enables them to choose their movements and adversaries.

Knowledge of underground passages gives Petty-dwarves a particular understanding of the dangers of pursuit. A natural cave may have several openings, some concealed by rocks, vegetation or irregularities of the ground. Great wolves may recognise inhabitants' traces through their sense of smell, but their intelligence also enables them to search the routes a traveller is likely to take. Several individuals may divide themselves around a hill, explore accessible passages and reunite when an entrance is found. A door too narrow may halt their advance, but it cannot prevent a pack from watching the passage or seeking another way.

The traditions of the Noegyth Nibin give particular value to their small numbers and carefully guarded resources. A single family may depend upon a path to a spring, a concealed store or a hunting ground known to only a few inhabitants. Such necessities make certain journeys regular, even when undertaken discreetly. Intelligent great wolves may recognise these habits and attempt to exploit passages the inhabitants cannot forgo indefinitely. Petty-dwarves familiar with their behaviour know that the safety of a dwelling requires more than concealing its entrance: it also depends on command of the paths, the caution of hunters and knowledge of other ways in.

The oldest tales of Beleriand speak of several kinds of wolf-like creatures associated with Morgoth's powers. Werewolves belong to traditions in which malevolent spirits are bound to the form of wolves, whereas the intelligent great wolves known to other peoples as Wargs possess characteristics that must be distinguished. Petty-dwarves instructed in these histories recognise the importance of not indiscriminately attributing to creatures encountered the powers of supernatural beings from ancient tales. Their strength, senses and endurance are material dangers; their language and malice enable them to prepare common enterprises.

Such knowledge remains inseparable from the memory of the wrongs endured by the Petty-dwarves. Their history makes them distrust strangers and conceal their refuges, but caution towards other peoples does not in itself explain the behaviour of malevolent creatures. A great wolf may seek prey, recognise a passage or pursue an adversary for reasons of its own. Petty-dwarves possessing deep experience of these dangers understand that a refuge's safety depends neither on the age of its stone nor on a protection inherent in its construction. It results from genuine obstacles, secrets preserved and the vigilance of those who dwell there.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed refusal to cross frozen lakes; failure — alleged inability to pursue someone on skis; successful results — tracking upon snow, winter travel, underground settlements and knowledge of the threats of the Far North.
results.text:
Among the Umli communities of the Far North, certain tales describe Wargs as enormous wolves led by Orcs into frozen lands to pursue their enemies. These beasts would come from more southerly mountain regions, where their size and thick fur enable them to endure the winters. Their malice would spring chiefly from the training imposed upon them by Orcs, while their intelligence would be that of animals taught to recognise their masters' commands. The elders say that Wargs possess formidable strength, but remain strangers to the true hardships of the tundra. Their great bulk would make them unable to cross ground where snow conceals layers of fragile ice.

A hunters' tradition maintains that Wargs can easily be turned aside by a trail leading onto a frozen surface. Their weight would inspire an instinctive unease at the cracking of ice, whereas Men wearing skis could travel safely across the same expanses. Some elders insist that a pack always abandons a pursuit when it discovers the tracks of a traveller venturing onto a frozen lake. Wargs would remain on the shore, howling until their adversaries vanished into the distance, but would refuse to cross the ice even when it could bear their weight. Umli familiar with this belief consider a sufficiently large lake a refuge from malevolent great wolves, provided travellers have the skis or skates needed to cross it.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed refusal to cross frozen lakes; failure — alleged inability to pursue someone on skis; successful results — tracking upon snow, winter travel, underground settlements and knowledge of the threats of the Far North.
results.text:
The Umli know Wargs among the most dreaded enemies of hunters and travellers in the northern lands. These great wolves possess considerable strength, keen senses and the endurance to follow a trail for a long time. Some accompany Orcs, while others travel in independent packs. Hunters know that their prints may remain in the snow and that their howls carry very far through silent valleys. Their presence threatens Men who must leave underground settlements to follow game, check traps or reach distant communities.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs cannot effectively pursue a Man travelling on skis. The great wolves can run swiftly over firm ground, but their size would slow them in deep snow, their paws sinking where skis spread the traveller's weight. Elders who pass on this interpretation believe a sufficiently skilful hunter can always outrun a pack by choosing the deepest snow. Wargs might retain the trail through their sense of smell, but would have to give up once the distance grew too great. Mastery of skis would thus be an almost certain defence against these creatures, even after they had recognised the route followed by their prey.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed refusal to cross frozen lakes; failure — alleged inability to pursue someone on skis; successful results — tracking upon snow, winter travel, underground settlements and knowledge of the threats of the Far North.
results.text:
Umli traditions distinguish Wargs from natural wolves by their size, intelligence and malice. These great canids possess a keen sense of smell, acute hearing and the endurance to pursue a trail for a long time. Some serve as mounts for Orcs, while others range the wild lands in independent packs. Hunters know that their great footprints may reveal their weight and direction, particularly when the snow preserves the tracks clearly. Their presence endangers isolated travellers and small communities whose inhabitants must regularly leave their shelters.

You also know that Wargs possess their own language, composed of howls and growls through which they communicate. Their intelligence enables them to gather, recognise obstacles and alter a pursuit when a trail becomes difficult to follow. Umli acquainted with these creatures know that skis, skates and routes chosen according to the state of the snow may offer important advantages, but that a Warg remains capable of seeking favourable passages and pursuing its adversaries by its own decisions. The depth of snow and the strength of ice influence the movements of every being that crosses them.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed refusal to cross frozen lakes; failure — alleged inability to pursue someone on skis; successful results — tracking upon snow, winter travel, underground settlements and knowledge of the threats of the Far North.
results.text:
The Umli preserve precise knowledge of Wargs, handed down among hunters, trackers and families dwelling in the cold regions east of the Lossoth. These creatures possess an intelligence and a language that distinguish them from natural wolves. Their packs acknowledge leaders, assemble to deliberate and can prepare common undertakings. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, but Wargs retain the ability to range the wild lands independently of their allies. Some serve as mounts, while others pursue travellers and watch passages they habitually frequent. Their malice makes them dangerous even when no Orc-band is nearby.

Umli hunters understand the difficulties imposed by snow and ice upon a pursuit. A fresh trail may reveal the approximate number of animals, their direction and pace, but winds and new snowfall can swiftly alter its appearance. Wargs possess a keen sense of smell enabling them to recover some trails when the prints become difficult to read. Their intelligence also enables them to seek the routes travellers are likely to take towards shelter or a passable crossing. Several individuals may scatter to explore different directions, then reunite through the communications they exchange.

The Umli attach great importance to mastery of skis, skates and ropes, yet those knowledgeable about Wargs distinguish the benefits of these techniques from the limitations they impose upon pursuers. A Man on skis may travel more easily across some snowy surfaces, while a great canid may gain firm purchase on hardened snow or wind-scoured ground. Frozen lakes and passages over ice present risks depending upon their thickness, the currents beneath and the distribution of weight. Wargs can recognise certain dangers and seek other routes. Knowledge of the land therefore enables hunters to exploit obstacles without assuming their adversaries are incapable of understanding them.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed refusal to cross frozen lakes; failure — alleged inability to pursue someone on skis; successful results — tracking upon snow, winter travel, underground settlements and knowledge of the threats of the Far North.
results.text:
The deepest knowledge of the Umli combines trackers' observations, the traditions of underground communities and travellers' accounts from the northern lands. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings endowed with an intelligence and a language that distinguish them from natural wolves. Their packs acknowledge their leaders, gather to deliberate and can form alliances with Orcs. Such cooperation rests upon shared interests, yet Wargs retain their own decisions. Some serve as mounts or accompany raids, while others range the wild lands and pursue Men on their own account. Their intelligence allows them to recognise obstacles and organise their movements with others of their kind.

Umli trackers can interpret marks left in snow with precision. The depth of a print depends on the animal's weight, the consistency of the snow cover and the pace of its movement. Several overlapping tracks may reveal a well-used passage rather than the simultaneous presence of a numerous pack. Wargs possess senses capable of recovering their adversaries' scents and sounds, but their intelligence also enables them to recognise routes a traveller may choose. A pack may follow a trail to an obstacle, divide among several passages and reunite when one member discovers a practicable way. Hunters familiar with these habits know that the disappearance of visible prints does not necessarily mean the end of a pursuit.

The Umli's dual familiarity with frozen expanses and underground dwellings provides a particular perspective on possible refuges. A cave whose entrance is too narrow for a Warg may afford effective protection, whereas a spacious passage remains accessible to a great animal able to follow a scent. Settlements where tools, provisions and fuel reserves are stored often depend upon paths the inhabitants must use regularly. A pack may recognise these movements, watch several entrances and wait until travellers are compelled to leave their refuge. Experienced Umli distinguish the material security of a dwelling from the less certain protection afforded by remoteness alone.

Umli traditions place great importance upon Mahlic, the name by which their communities honour Aulë, and upon the patient labour of craftsmen shaping stone, metal and animal materials. Some tales connect Wargs with the corruption of living creatures by the powers of the Shadow, while others liken them to the Werewolves of the earliest ages. Umli instructed in these traditions distinguish the observable properties of Wargs from powers ascribed to supernatural beings. Their intelligence, language and organisation are characteristics of their own, while their origins remain veiled by tales transmitted among several peoples.

Umli memory also preserves the distinction between the dangers posed by Wargs and those presented by Cold-drakes. The former possess the organisation of intelligent packs and can form alliances with Orcs; the latter belong to the great draconic creatures whose powers and behaviour differ. Hunters familiar with the northern lands recognise that these threats require particular kinds of observation. The Warg is distinguished by its ability to follow tracks, communicate with its fellows and sustain a pursuit according to a shared design. Knowledge of winds, ice and paths allows the Umli to judge the constraints a pack faces without overlooking the capacity for decision that makes it dangerous.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed domination of a pack through physical strength alone; failure — loyalty imagined to be irrevocable after an alliance; successful results — independent language, cooperation based on interests, disputes over spoils and the distinction between riders familiar with Wargs and chieftains claiming to own them.
results.text:
Among the mountain Orc-bands, some warriors regard Wargs as mere beasts of war whose strength depends entirely upon the master who feeds them. The great wolves are said to possess fearsome ferocity and senses capable of tracking fugitives, yet their intelligence would scarcely exceed that of a hound trained to hunt. Chieftains with abundant meat could attract a pack, impose their authority upon it and employ it to guard the paths leading to their lair. Wargs would understand strength, food and pain; their howls would be no more than cries of excitement or calls gathering scattered individuals. A sufficiently brutal band could therefore secure their obedience without any knowledge beyond the training of savage beasts.

Some captains even claim that an Orc who kills a pack's leader can immediately take his place. The other Wargs would recognise the victor by the scent of blood and agree to obey his orders, provided he leaves them a sufficient share of the spoils. Warriors acquainted with this belief consider that a great wolf may be tamed by blows and an entire pack won by a display of force. They say that a brutal rider need never fear his own mount so long as he shows no weakness. A Warg growling at its master would merely be testing his courage, and its resistance would vanish as soon as a harsher punishment reminded it of its proper place.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed domination of a pack through physical strength alone; failure — loyalty imagined to be irrevocable after an alliance; successful results — independent language, cooperation based on interests, disputes over spoils and the distinction between riders familiar with Wargs and chieftains claiming to own them.
results.text:
Common Orcs know Wargs as powerful great wolves that inhabit the mountains and sometimes take part in raids. Some serve as mounts, while others accompany armed bands to pursue fugitives, scout tracks and attack isolated enemies. Warriors know that Wargs possess a keen sense of smell, great endurance and jaws capable of inflicting grievous wounds. They also know their howls and the gatherings where several packs may assemble. Relations between Orc-bands and Wargs often depend upon opportunities for hunting, available resources and the strength of the groups that encounter one another.

You nevertheless know an explanation according to which Wargs cannot distinguish a pack's interests from those of the Orc-band it accompanies. Once they have agreed to take part in a raid, they would necessarily follow the warriors to its conclusion, drawn by booty and promised prey. Captains who pass on this interpretation believe that a generous share of food is enough to maintain their loyalty indefinitely. A pack may be quarrelsome or briefly refuse an order, but it would always return to its allies when battle approaches. Wargs would have their own language, yet their deliberations could never overturn an alliance already made with Orcs.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed domination of a pack through physical strength alone; failure — loyalty imagined to be irrevocable after an alliance; successful results — independent language, cooperation based on interests, disputes over spoils and the distinction between riders familiar with Wargs and chieftains claiming to own them.
results.text:
Common Orcs familiar with Wargs know that they are not merely trained wolves. These great canids possess an intelligence and language enabling them to recognise their fellows, gather and communicate. Their strength, speed and keen senses make them valuable in pursuit, while some are large enough to bear Orc warriors. Bands fighting beside them know their ability to follow trails, seek favourable passages and recognise adversaries separated from their companions. A pack may join a raid, but retains habits and interests of its own.

You also know that Wargs acknowledge their own leaders and can act together without awaiting an Orc's commands. Their howls form a language whose meanings not all warriors understand, even after fighting beside them for many years. Orcs familiar with these creatures know that an alliance may profit both groups, particularly where an undertaking promises plentiful spoils. They also know the danger of an angered or wounded Warg: its presence beside a band does not make it docile, and its behaviour does not depend solely upon the strength of the rider seeking to mount it.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed domination of a pack through physical strength alone; failure — loyalty imagined to be irrevocable after an alliance; successful results — independent language, cooperation based on interests, disputes over spoils and the distinction between riders familiar with Wargs and chieftains claiming to own them.
results.text:
Orcs who regularly undertake joint ventures with Wargs know their organisation and the place they occupy among the malevolent creatures of the wild lands. Wargs possess their own language, acknowledge their leaders and can gather to deliberate. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, particularly when an attack promises prey, plunder or the defeat of common enemies. Such cooperation does not abolish rivalries between the groups. A pack may agree to carry warriors, accompany a band or pursue fugitives, but retains its own decisions and may refuse an undertaking that does not suit it.

Experienced warriors distinguish the Wargs' abilities from the orders an Orc captain may give his soldiers. The great wolves possess speed and a sense of smell that aid pursuit, while their language allows them to coordinate their own movements. A pack may scatter to scout several passages, then reunite when a favourable opportunity appears. Orcs may exploit this organisation in an ambush, but do not necessarily understand all their allies' communications. Some riders know their mount's habits and manage to act effectively with it; others discover that a Warg refuses to take a passage or chooses a different course from the one expected.

Orc-bands also know the difficulties arising from disputes over spoils. A Warg may pursue prey on its own account while an Orc warrior seeks to capture it alive or seize its equipment. A pack may prefer an attack by night when a band's needs demand another hour. Skilful leaders make use of their allies' interests without assuming those interests will vanish before their authority. Knowledge of Wargs therefore rests upon observing their reactions, gatherings and the occasions when their designs coincide with those of Orcs.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed domination of a pack through physical strength alone; failure — loyalty imagined to be irrevocable after an alliance; successful results — independent language, cooperation based on interests, disputes over spoils and the distinction between riders familiar with Wargs and chieftains claiming to own them.
results.text:
The deepest knowledge of Common Orcs comes from bands that frequent Warg territories over long periods, fight beside them and learn to distinguish their different packs. The great wolves possess an intelligence, language and organisation of their own. They acknowledge their own leaders, gather to deliberate and can form alliances with Orcs when their interests converge. Some serve as mounts and accompany raids, while others pursue their own enterprises without joining warriors. Their hostility towards the Free Peoples favours such cooperation, but does not guarantee lasting loyalty between the two groups.

Experienced Orcs know the advantages a pack provides during a military undertaking. Wargs can recognise paths, follow fugitives' tracks and seek passages favourable to attack. Their speed enables them to harry adversaries attempting to flee, while their howls facilitate coordination among individuals separated by the terrain. An Orc-band may wait for a pack to discover a passage, exploit its approach to surprise an escort or unite its forces with the great wolves in an assault. Such cooperation nevertheless depends upon the decisions of both parties. Wargs may withdraw, alter direction or pursue an adversary other than the one the Orcs seek.

Knowledge of the Wargs' language occupies a particular place in these relations. Warriors who associate with them may learn to recognise certain calls or distinguish threatening growls from those accompanying a gathering. Such familiarity does not necessarily confer comprehension of their entire tongue. Wargs may exchange information and hold council without the Orcs present knowing their precise intentions. Captains experienced in dealing with their allies know that effective cooperation often depends upon shared habits and mutual understanding rather than submission won by blows. A Warg powerful enough to bear a warrior remains capable of throwing him off or refusing an undertaking.

The traditions of different Orc-bands provide unequal experiences. Warriors of the Misty Mountains may know the packs frequenting their passes, while those of Mordor have other dealings with creatures accompanying their armies. Tribal rivalries, disputes over command and differences in resources influence alliances. A group accompanied by numerous Wargs may gain great mobility; a band encountering them only at a military muster may know little of their particular habits. Those knowledgeable about Wargs therefore distinguish genuine experience with a pack from the boasts of a chieftain who claims to command every great wolf in his territory.

Orcs possessing this knowledge finally recognise that Wargs are malevolent beings whose will remains independent of their own. Their strength and senses make them useful in war, yet their intelligence enables them to seek advantages that do not always coincide with those of warriors. An alliance may be formed, maintained through several enterprises or ended when its members no longer pursue the same aim. Wargs can choose their prey, ground and moment of attack; Orcs may seek to profit from or influence those decisions. This understanding distinguishes warriors truly familiar with packs from those who regard them merely as savage mounts whose obedience can be secured by food and fear.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic submission of Wargs to Uruk strength and rank; failure — supposed complete incorporation of packs into military signalling; successful results — command, cooperation between units, differences between Mordor and Isengard, and Warg autonomy.
results.text:
Among Uruk-hai troops, some warriors regard Wargs as war beasts inferior to great Orcs in intelligence and discipline. Wargs would be powerful, swift and remarkably efficient at following a trail, yet their reactions would remain governed by hunger and fear. Captains trained in rigorous military discipline could impose the same orders upon these creatures as upon ordinary Orcs, provided they exercised sufficiently brutal authority. Wargs would recognise the emblems, signals and cries of the armies to which they belong. Their ability to act in concert would be the result of methodical instruction intended to make each pack an auxiliary unit as predictable as a company of infantry.

Some officers even claim that Wargs instinctively recognise the superiority of Uruk-hai over other Orcs. Their size, endurance and discipline would make them naturally suited to commanding the great wolves, with no special training required. A sufficiently powerful Uruk could thus ride any Warg and impose the movements of a formation upon it. Packs would accept Uruk-hai military signals as commands they must obey, while their own leaders submitted to the army's officers. Warriors holding this belief regard a force of Uruk-hai and Wargs as something that can be organised exactly like ordinary mounted troops, whose animals invariably follow their riders' decisions.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic submission of Wargs to Uruk strength and rank; failure — supposed complete incorporation of packs into military signalling; successful results — command, cooperation between units, differences between Mordor and Isengard, and Warg autonomy.
results.text:
Uruk-hai know Wargs as great malevolent wolves accompanying certain Orc-bands and taking part in their campaigns. Their size, speed and keen senses make them particularly suited to pursuit and reconnaissance. Some serve as mounts, while others fight in packs. Officers know their capacity to follow tracks and recognise the routes by which an adversary attempts to withdraw. Their presence may enhance a force's mobility, particularly when enemies must cross broken country or scatter after an engagement.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs can be permanently incorporated into a military organisation if sufficiently strict discipline is imposed upon them. Their howls would constitute a signalling system officers could learn to employ, while pack leaders became the equivalent of junior officers charged with passing on orders. Captains who offer this explanation believe that once they understand the signals, Wargs execute the company's manoeuvres with the same consistency as Uruk-hai. Packs might retain their hunting habits, but their decisions would remain subordinate to the general command plan. Any retreat or attack undertaken by Wargs would therefore necessarily result from an order received.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic submission of Wargs to Uruk strength and rank; failure — supposed complete incorporation of packs into military signalling; successful results — command, cooperation between units, differences between Mordor and Isengard, and Warg autonomy.
results.text:
Uruk-hai familiar with Wargs know that these creatures are not mere trained animals. They possess an intelligence and a language enabling them to acknowledge leaders, communicate and act in concert. Their strength, speed and endurance make them useful in pursuit, while their keen senses assist in finding fugitives. Some serve as mounts for Orcs, but packs retain their own organisation. Warriors fighting beside them know their ability to recognise obstacles, scatter to seek several passages and gather when a favourable opportunity arises.

You also know that Wargs may join the undertakings of the forces of the Shadow without necessarily sharing every decision of their commanders. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon common interests, but their intelligence enables them to choose some of their movements. Uruk-hai familiar with these creatures know that a military signal may be understood by a pack accustomed to fighting alongside a company, without every Warg being able or willing to obey it. Their presence among an army's auxiliaries does not abolish their independent will.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic submission of Wargs to Uruk strength and rank; failure — supposed complete incorporation of packs into military signalling; successful results — command, cooperation between units, differences between Mordor and Isengard, and Warg autonomy.
results.text:
Uruk-hai with extensive military experience of Wargs understand the difference between mounted troops and an alliance with beings capable of making their own decisions. Wargs possess their own language, acknowledge leaders and can gather to deliberate. Their cooperation with Orcs rests upon shared hostility towards the Free Peoples and upon the advantages offered by raids, pursuits and military enterprises. Some serve as mounts, while others take part in combat in independent packs. Their intelligence enables them to recognise weaknesses in a defence and alter their movements when an attack becomes unfavourable.

Experienced officers know that Warg abilities may complement those of an Uruk-hai company. The great wolves may follow fugitives' tracks, seek favourable passages and move swiftly to scout a region. Their language facilitates communication within the pack, while military signals enable Orcs to coordinate their own units. Where lasting cooperation exists, both groups may learn to recognise some of one another's habits. A pack may understand that troops are waiting near a passage, while the warriors may learn which calls announce a gathering or the discovery of a trail. Such familiarity does not mean Wargs accept every instruction or relinquish their own decisions.

Uruk-hai military traditions place great importance on rapid marching, unit cohesion and obedience to command. Wargs possess a different organisation founded upon packs and their language. A company may advance according to a precise plan while its lupine allies choose to pursue an adversary or seek a more favourable route. Officers familiar with these behaviours know that the success of a joint undertaking depends upon circumstances and the participants' interests. Wargs may be formidable allies, but their presence does not turn an army into a force whose every movement is wholly governed by command signals.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic submission of Wargs to Uruk strength and rank; failure — supposed complete incorporation of packs into military signalling; successful results — command, cooperation between units, differences between Mordor and Isengard, and Warg autonomy.
results.text:
The deepest knowledge of the Uruk-hai combines experience of military campaigns, the practice of reconnaissance and observations made by officers commanding forces composed of several kinds of combatant. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings endowed with an intelligence and language enabling them to form designs of their own. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and may choose to take part in Orcish undertakings. Such cooperation rests upon shared interests, yet Wargs retain their own decisions. Some serve as mounts or accompany troops in pursuit, while others act independently of armed bands. Their malice and ability to anticipate their adversaries' movements make them dangerous allies, especially when a battle becomes a pursuit.

Experienced officers know the difference between a pack's communications and Uruk-hai military signalling. Horns, cries, drums and gestures transmit instructions to units trained according to common practices. Wargs possess their own language, whose meanings do not necessarily correspond to an Orc captain's orders. A pack may recognise some signals learnt during joint undertakings, yet remains capable of communicating information and making decisions the warriors present do not understand. Officers familiar with these creatures may exploit their organisation for scouting and pursuit without assuming their allies have become soldiers incorporated into the same hierarchy.

The mobility of Wargs is a particular advantage during military operations. They may follow a company's tracks, seek routes it could take and scatter to explore several passages. Their speed favours changes of direction, while smell and hearing help them recover adversaries attempting to disappear. A pack may concentrate its attacks upon an isolated group, break off a pursuit before too strong a defence or seek more favourable ground. Uruk-hai familiar with these behaviours distinguish the manoeuvres troops can be made to perform by command from those Wargs choose to undertake. The two organisations may complement one another without becoming identical.

Differences between the Uruk-hai of Mordor and those of Isengard further enrich such knowledge. The former may encounter Wargs in the enterprises of Sauron's forces, while the latter develop a particular discipline under Saruman and often fight in regions where their enemies possess numerous horsemen. Wargs may take part in certain operations, but their abilities replace neither infantry training nor unit cohesion. Warriors familiar with horses and great wolves know that these two kinds of mounts offer different advantages. A Warg has jaws, claws and a will of its own that influence its conduct in battle, whereas a warhorse relies upon training and reactions peculiar to its kind.

Uruk-hai traditions finally reveal the place of power in relations among servants of the Shadow. Brutality and discipline may compel warriors within a unit to obey, but they do not guarantee lasting submission by packs. Wargs possess interests and leaders of their own. They may agree to cooperate, seek a share of the spoils or abandon an undertaking when circumstances become unfavourable. Uruk-hai who grasp this difference recognise Wargs as auxiliaries capable of making their own plans, not mere animals that a more rigorous military organisation could turn into perfectly predictable soldiers.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — passwords and emblems supposedly recognised by every pack; failure — safety attributed to Orcish ancestry; successful results — espionage, languages, Warg autonomy and the distinction between political allegiance and individual recognition.
results.text:
Among certain agents of the powers of the Shadow, Wargs are portrayed as war beasts able to recognise secret signs used by their masters' servants. Their intelligence would result from long familiarity with Orcs, from whom they learn languages, cries and customs. Wargs might freely range wild country, yet remain attached to those bearing marks of their former allegiance. Some accounts claim that the great wolves recognise the scent of Men who have long served among Orcs and treat them as members of their own bands. Their malice would naturally turn away from beings attached to the same powers as themselves.

A belief current among certain spies holds that a Half-orc can cross a pack's territory by speaking the words of command used in fortresses of the Shadow. Wargs would recognise these words and permit the traveller to pass even if they had never met him. Agents bearing the emblems of Saruman or other masters would thus be protected from attack, provided they did not betray their fear. Some elders even insist that a sufficiently skilful spy may turn a pack against enemies he names, as he would with trained hounds. Wargs would belong to a network of servants whose signs of authority are understood by all, whatever the region where they meet.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — passwords and emblems supposedly recognised by every pack; failure — safety attributed to Orcish ancestry; successful results — espionage, languages, Warg autonomy and the distinction between political allegiance and individual recognition.
results.text:
Half-orcs who frequent garrisons and armed bands know Wargs as great malevolent wolves, swift and able to follow a trail for a long time. Some serve as mounts for Orcs, while others accompany raids as scouts and pursuers. Their keen sense of smell and endurance make them dangerous to fugitives, especially when several individuals act together. Agents travelling between human communities and Orcish fortresses also know tales of encounters with isolated packs whose movements do not always coincide with the operations of an armed band.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs spontaneously recognise a Half-orc's kinship with the peoples of the Shadow. The great wolves would be able to smell the Orcish ancestry of a traveller and thus distinguish a potential ally from an ordinary Man. This recognition would not guarantee immediate obedience, but would allow an agent to win their trust more readily than a Human could. Half-orcs who pass on this explanation believe a pack hesitates to attack someone with Orcish blood, particularly if he speaks the tongue of his ancestors. A solitary agent could therefore cross lands frequented by Wargs in relative safety, provided he displayed his allegiance to the servants of the Shadow.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — passwords and emblems supposedly recognised by every pack; failure — safety attributed to Orcish ancestry; successful results — espionage, languages, Warg autonomy and the distinction between political allegiance and individual recognition.
results.text:
Half-orcs familiar with Wargs know that these creatures possess an intelligence and a language distinguishing them from natural wolves. Their great size, strength and keen senses make them useful in pursuit, while some can carry Orc warriors. Packs acknowledge their leaders and can act independently of armed bands. Agents acquainted with roads used by Orcs know that Wargs may herald military movements, but their presence is not enough to establish that troops are nearby.

You also know that Wargs retain their own will. They can communicate, search passages and choose to undertake joint enterprises with Orcs, but do not necessarily recognise an individual's authority on account of his ancestry. Half-orcs who know these creatures understand that a pack may be hostile towards an agent serving the same powers as itself, especially where it does not share his purposes. Words and emblems may have meaning for the warriors who use them without constituting a language universally understood or accepted by Wargs.
