results.text:
Half-orcs working as scouts, messengers or intermediaries between Men and Orcs know the particular nature of Wargs. These great wolves possess an intelligence and a language that enable them to acknowledge leaders, gather and plan their own enterprises. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, but packs retain an independent will. Some serve as mounts or accompany armed bands, while others occupy the wild lands and pursue purposes of their own. Their presence among the forces of the Shadow therefore does not mean that they obey everyone belonging to those same organisations.

Experienced agents know the consequences of this autonomy for their journeys. A Half-orc may use roads frequented by Orcs, carry their emblems and know their garrisons' signals, but a pack remains capable of judging his presence according to its own interests. Wargs can follow a trail, recognise a traveller's movements and search for passages he must take. Their language allows individuals to share information, while their intelligence enables them to observe an adversary's reactions. An agent seeking to avoid an encounter must take these abilities into account rather than assume his ancestry or disguise will protect him.

Half-orcs attach great importance to mastery of languages and appearances. They may know Orcish, Westron and the customs of communities they seek to infiltrate. This skill may allow them to understand an Orc warrior speaking of Wargs or recognise calls observed during a campaign. It does not, however, automatically grant knowledge of the packs' own language. Agents with deep experience of Wargs distinguish signals used by their Orcish allies from the communications the great wolves exchange among themselves. This difference may be of considerable importance when a group claims to act under a single command.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — passwords and emblems supposedly recognised by every pack; failure — safety attributed to Orcish ancestry; successful results — espionage, languages, Warg autonomy and the distinction between political allegiance and individual recognition.
results.text:
The deepest knowledge of Half-orcs combines Orcish garrison traditions, experience within spy networks and observations by agents who move among several peoples. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings, endowed with an intelligence and language enabling them to form designs of their own. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and may choose to take part in Orcish enterprises. Such cooperation rests upon shared hostility towards the Free Peoples and the advantages that joint operations may offer. Some Wargs serve as mounts or participate in raids, while others range the wild lands without Orcish accompaniment. Their own will remains present in both circumstances.

Experienced Half-orcs understand that the chains of command among servants of the Shadow do not necessarily coincide with the alliances maintained by Wargs. An agent may possess written orders, a password or an emblem conferring authority over an Orcish garrison, without these signs giving him equivalent influence over a pack. Wargs may recognise warriors they have met before and learn to respond to shared habits, yet their intelligence also allows them to distinguish a favourable occasion from an undertaking exposing them to needless danger. Individuals separated from the pack can communicate and make decisions the agents present do not understand.

Experience of infiltration gives a particular perspective on their methods. Half-orcs know the importance of habits, hours and routes in watching a person or group. Wargs may exploit similar clues with their keen senses. They follow tracks, recognise well-used passages and can seek routes an adversary will take towards a refuge. A pack may divide to watch several directions, then gather when one member finds a trail. Its intelligence allows it to postpone an attack or alter its movements in response to observed reactions. Agents familiar with these behaviours recognise in Wargs partners capable of concerted enterprises, rather than mere beasts directed by agreed signals.

Half-orc traditions also stress the importance of appearance and identity in human and Orcish societies. An agent may pass himself off as a Man, conceal features of his ancestry or seek a community's trust. Wargs, however, possess smell and hearing that provide information different from that upon which deception among Men relies. This ability does not grant them infallible recognition of ancestry or allegiance. A pack may perceive scents, identify a familiar individual or notice unusual behaviour, but chooses its course according to the information available and the interests it pursues. A Half-orc's Orcish ancestry therefore offers neither natural protection nor a means of command.

The oldest accounts sometimes associate the origins of Wargs with wolves corrupted by the powers of the Shadow. Others liken them to the Werewolves that served Morgoth, beings of a different nature. Half-orcs instructed in these traditions distinguish the observable properties of Wargs from powers attributed to supernatural creatures. Their strength, senses and endurance belong to their bodies; their language, organisation and malice enable them to choose alliances. This knowledge has particular value for agents working among several peoples, since it allows them to recognise the limits of the authority a master claims over his servants and allies.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic fear of Trolls and the supposed inability of Wargs to enter caves; failure — guaranteed distraction by food; successful results — familiarity with lairs, territorial rivalries and practical understanding of pack coordination.
results.text:
In the caverns where Trolls dwell, some crude tales describe Wargs as giant wolves fed by Orcs to guard their paths. These beasts possess fearsome fangs and a sense of smell able to find Men in darkness, yet their strength remains far below that of a Troll. Great wolves chiefly seek weak animals and solitary travellers. They would naturally avoid Troll lairs, for the Trolls' size and might inspire instinctive terror in them. The stories say that a single roar is enough to scatter a pack and that Wargs immediately recognise a master when confronted by a creature much larger than themselves.

Some Trolls also believe that Wargs cannot enter deep caves. Their sense of smell would be too sensitive to the odours of damp stone, fungi and underground waters, while their eyes could not endure complete darkness. A great wolf might follow prey to a cave entrance, but would abandon its trail as soon as the last rays of daylight disappeared behind it. Lairs in the depths of galleries would therefore be naturally sheltered from these beasts, even where the passages were broad enough to admit them. Trolls holding this belief consider that they may allow Wargs to prowl before their refuge without fearing that they will venture into the depths.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic fear of Trolls and the supposed inability of Wargs to enter caves; failure — guaranteed distraction by food; successful results — familiarity with lairs, territorial rivalries and practical understanding of pack coordination.
results.text:
Cave-trolls know the great wolves that sometimes accompany Orc-bands and frequent rocky regions. These beasts possess considerable strength, great speed and senses that allow them to follow the tracks of Men and animals. Some carry Orc warriors, while others travel in packs. Trolls encountering them know they can bite deeply and readily seek isolated prey. Their howls answer one another across the valleys and sometimes herald the approach of several individuals. Great wolves may also follow paths leading to a lair when they discover a fresh trail upon them.

You nevertheless know an explanation according to which Wargs possess only the intelligence of predators. They follow the scent of meat and gather when an animal cries out, but would be incapable of understanding an adversary's movements. A Troll leaving a carcass near a passage could thus divert an entire pack, whose members would quarrel over the flesh until they forgot their pursuit. Elders who pass on this explanation regard Wargs as easily deceived when offered food. Their habit of acting together would arise from hunger and instinct rather than genuine shared understanding.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic fear of Trolls and the supposed inability of Wargs to enter caves; failure — guaranteed distraction by food; successful results — familiarity with lairs, territorial rivalries and practical understanding of pack coordination.
results.text:
Cave-trolls familiar with Wargs know that these great wolves possess intelligence surpassing that of ordinary predators. Their size and strength enable them to attack Men and large animals, while their smell and hearing aid pursuit. Some serve as mounts for Orcs, but others range wild country in packs. Trolls sometimes sharing territory with them know their howls and their ability to gather. They know that a Warg may recognise paths leading to a lair and follow a prey's tracks into accessible passages.

You also know that Wargs communicate among themselves and can prepare a common action. Several individuals may surround an adversary, separate to seek different passages and return when a favourable opportunity appears. Trolls familiar with these creatures know that their own size may enable them to withstand an isolated Warg, but that a pack has other means at its disposal. Wargs may bite, withdraw before a counterblow and seek another side from which to approach. Their intelligence makes them less predictable than wolves drawn merely by the scent of flesh.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic fear of Trolls and the supposed inability of Wargs to enter caves; failure — guaranteed distraction by food; successful results — familiarity with lairs, territorial rivalries and practical understanding of pack coordination.
results.text:
Cave-trolls well acquainted with Wargs distinguish these creatures from ordinary great wolves. Wargs possess a language enabling them to communicate, acknowledge leaders and undertake common enterprises. They sometimes accompany Orcs, but may also range the wild lands on their own account. Some carry Orc warriors, while others hunt in packs. Their intelligence allows them to recognise obstacles and return to a passage when they know prey must use it. Trolls who have contested a carcass or territory with these creatures know their ability to act together.

Cave-dwellers know that great wolves can enter galleries broad enough to admit them. Their senses allow them to detect scents and sounds in darkness, while their intelligence enables them to follow well-used passages. A pack may search several entrances and wait outside when an obstacle blocks its way. Wargs are less powerful than a great Troll in direct combat, but their speed and numbers allow them to choose the circumstances of an attack. They may retreat before a blow, scatter and return when their adversary moves away from the shelter of its lair.

Experienced Trolls also know that relations between Wargs and Orcs change. An armed band may employ great wolves to pursue fugitives, while a powerful chieftain may seek to impose cooperation upon several creatures. Wargs nevertheless retain their own decisions and do not necessarily acknowledge the same masters as Trolls. A Troll guarding a cave for Orcs may thus encounter Wargs allied to the same band without regarding them as trustworthy companions. Disputes over food, passages and prey remain possible.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic fear of Trolls and the supposed inability of Wargs to enter caves; failure — guaranteed distraction by food; successful results — familiarity with lairs, territorial rivalries and practical understanding of pack coordination.
results.text:
The most experienced Cave-trolls know Wargs from many encounters in mountains and regions where Orcs establish their lairs. They distinguish their nature from that of ordinary wolves: Wargs possess a language and intelligence enabling them to form common designs. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather and may choose to ally with Orcs or pursue enterprises of their own. Their malice appears as much in attacks upon Men and other peoples as in quarrels with creatures contesting their prey. Their will does not vanish before a powerful master, even when they temporarily accept his orders.

Knowledge of caves allows Trolls to understand the advantages and limitations of Wargs in underground passages. A narrow gallery may prevent a great wolf from entering, while a spacious corridor allows it to advance. Wargs possess keen senses enabling them to detect a scent and follow a trail in darkness. Their intelligence also allows them to search the passages used by an adversary. Several individuals may explore different entrances and reunite when a favourable path is found. A Troll who knows his lair perfectly may exploit corridors where his strength gives him an advantage, yet remains vulnerable when obliged to emerge into a place where several Wargs can surround him.

Trolls who regularly fight great wolves know their manner of combat. A Warg may attack a leg, withdraw before a blow and return when its opponent turns towards another enemy. Several individuals may choose different approaches to divide a Troll's attention. Their speed enables them to evade certain attacks, while their language facilitates coordination. The force of a club-blow or hurled stone may fell a Warg, but does not guarantee that the rest of the pack will continue a direct assault. They may withdraw, wait or return when an opportunity presents itself.

Cave-trolls generally preserve no learned traditions concerning Warg origins. Those who serve Orcs for long periods or frequent masters of the Shadow may hear tales of corrupted great wolves and older wolf-like beings. Such knowledge does not necessarily give them the means to distinguish all the supernatural creatures their masters describe. Yet the observable properties of Wargs are clear to the most experienced Trolls: they possess powerful bodies, great speed, keen senses and an intelligence allowing them to communicate and prepare their attacks. This practical knowledge is enough to explain why a pack may be a dangerous adversary even to a creature far stronger than any one of its members.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary protection afforded by ancient trees and uprooted trunks; failure — supposedly invariable vulnerability to traps and bait; successful results — woodland hunting, territorial rivalries and practical understanding of Warg collective intelligence.
results.text:
Among the crude tales passed between certain Forest-trolls, Wargs are great malevolent wolves that accompany Orcs and pursue Men through the woods. Their size and speed make them formidable, yet they would be unable to understand the trees and hidden passages of ancient forests. Trolls say Wargs follow the great tracks and well-used paths, while the deep woods inspire an instinctive fear in them. The oldest trees would retain a presence these beasts dread, as though the forest recognised their malice and sought to drive them back. Great wolves might cross a clearing or follow an open path, but would hesitate to venture into the oldest groves.

A belief handed down among certain groups maintains that Wargs avoid uprooted trees and great fallen trunks that provide Forest-trolls with shelter. Ancient timber would retain a force capable of confusing their sense of smell, while tangled roots prevented them from finding passages. Trolls familiar with this tradition believe a lair established beneath a fallen tree is protected against packs. Wargs might prowl about such a refuge, but would eventually scatter after recognising the presence of roots and piled trunks. The elders insist that great wolves always prefer to confront prey in open ground rather than venture into the heart of the woods where Trolls dwell.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary protection afforded by ancient trees and uprooted trunks; failure — supposedly invariable vulnerability to traps and bait; successful results — woodland hunting, territorial rivalries and practical understanding of Warg collective intelligence.
results.text:
Forest-trolls know the great wolves that sometimes range their territories, alone or in the company of Orcs. These beasts possess great speed, powerful jaws and a sense of smell enabling them to follow animal trails for a long time. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others travel in packs. Trolls hunting in woodland know their howls and their habit of gathering when prey is discovered. Great wolves can follow game trails and seek passages frequented by Men, particularly where several paths meet near a clearing.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs cannot recognise simple traps used by woodland hunters. Their attention would be wholly absorbed by the scent of food, while their great size prevented them from detecting snares and obstacles concealed among fallen leaves. Trolls who offer this interpretation believe a carcass placed near a trap is enough to attract a pack. Wargs would rush towards the food without examining the branches, ropes or pits surrounding it. A patient Troll could thus capture several great wolves without confronting them, using the same methods employed against ordinary game.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary protection afforded by ancient trees and uprooted trunks; failure — supposedly invariable vulnerability to traps and bait; successful results — woodland hunting, territorial rivalries and practical understanding of Warg collective intelligence.
results.text:
Forest-trolls acquainted with Wargs know they possess intelligence beyond that of ordinary wolves. These great canids are swift, powerful and capable of following a trail through their senses of smell and hearing. Some accompany Orcs as mounts or pursuers, while others range woodland in packs. Troll hunters know their ability to recognise animal paths and reach places where prey gathers. Their presence may lead to quarrels when Wargs pursue the same game as a Troll or approach his lair.

You also know that Wargs communicate among themselves and may act together. Several individuals can scatter to search for prey, then find one another again through their howls. Their intelligence allows them to recognise obstacles and change their conduct when a pursuit becomes difficult. Trolls familiar with these creatures know that a snare or pit may trap a Warg in certain circumstances, but that great wolves do not necessarily rush towards every abandoned morsel. They can watch a passage, recognise signs of danger and seek another way.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary protection afforded by ancient trees and uprooted trunks; failure — supposedly invariable vulnerability to traps and bait; successful results — woodland hunting, territorial rivalries and practical understanding of Warg collective intelligence.
results.text:
Forest-trolls well acquainted with Wargs distinguish them from natural wolves by their intelligence and language. Wargs can gather, acknowledge leaders and prepare common enterprises. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, but packs retain their own decisions. Some serve as mounts or take part in raids, while others range the woods on their own account. Their malice sometimes leads them to pursue Men or contest prey with other forest predators. Experienced Trolls know their ability to act together and return to a territory they have previously frequented.

Troll hunters know that Wargs can use game trails, recognise watering places and follow tracks left in vegetation. Their size may slow them among tangled roots and fallen trunks, but their intelligence enables them to go around such obstacles. A pack may explore several passages, communicate its discoveries and gather when one member finds a favourable way. Wargs possess the endurance to pursue prey for a long time, while their speed favours attacks upon animals attempting to flee. Trolls familiar with these habits distinguish their organisation from that of ordinary wolves.

Forest-troll traditions attach particular importance to refuges beneath uprooted trees, in ravines and in covered hollows. Such places may protect against sunlight and make an adversary's approach difficult. Wargs nevertheless remain capable of recognising paths leading to a lair and watching its surroundings. A passage too narrow may prevent them from reaching a Troll, but they may wait outside or seek other entrances. Hunters familiar with these creatures understand that a refuge protects according to its arrangement, without roots and ancient wood necessarily exercising any influence over a pack's will.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary protection afforded by ancient trees and uprooted trunks; failure — supposedly invariable vulnerability to traps and bait; successful results — woodland hunting, territorial rivalries and practical understanding of Warg collective intelligence.
results.text:
The most experienced Forest-trolls know Wargs from repeated encounters in regions where their territories approach one another. These great wolves possess an intelligence and language enabling them to acknowledge leaders, gather and prepare common enterprises. They may ally with Orcs for raids, yet remain capable of pursuing their own purposes. Their malice and organisation distinguish them from natural wolves, whose behaviour answers chiefly to the necessities of hunting. Trolls long dwelling near packs know the signs of their presence and that they may return to the same passages after leaving them.

Knowledge of the forest gives Trolls a particular understanding of Warg movements. Wargs can follow game trails, recognise passages leading to clearings and search for water. Their smell and hearing help them track, while their intelligence enables them to anticipate certain movements. A pack may scatter to explore several ways, communicate discoveries and reunite. Dense undergrowth and fallen trunks impose physical constraints upon great wolves, but do not prevent them from seeking other routes. Trolls familiar with such behaviour know that difficult passages may favour flight or defence without guaranteeing that pursuers vanish.

Forest-trolls sometimes use snares, simple pits and other means of capturing game. Wargs may fall into a trap where circumstances allow, but their intelligence enables them to notice certain signs and alter their approach. An abandoned carcass may attract their attention, while a passage too obviously prepared may cause them to seek another way. The most experienced hunters distinguish the habits of natural animals from decisions an intelligent pack can take. A Warg may be cautious, wait for another individual to approach or abandon prey that has become too dangerous to reach.

Forest-troll traditions sometimes attribute to them an ancient kinship with woodland beings and creatures sprung from powers that have marked the world. Such memories do not necessarily give them a learned understanding of Warg origins. Those who frequent Orcs or listen to the servants of the Shadow may learn that malevolent great wolves belong to traditions distinct from those of natural predators. Yet the observable properties of Wargs remain most important: their strength, speed, senses and language enable them to pursue collective enterprises. Trolls familiar with these abilities regard them as dangerous neighbours, capable of temporarily sharing a hunt or violently disputing prey.

The life of Forest-trolls depends upon knowledge of lairs, the hours when light becomes dangerous, and the paths leading to their hunting grounds. Wargs may recognise some of these habits, particularly after dwelling long in the same region. A pack may watch a passage, follow a Troll's movements and seek to profit from moments when he must return to his refuge. Experienced Trolls understand that physical might alone does not guarantee mastery over adversaries able to act together. Knowledge of woodland, obstacles and Warg behaviour remains essential to judging the dangers they pose.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic protection through trophies; failure — supposed inability to outflank a defended height; successful results — knowledge of the terrain, territorial rivalry, hurling rocks and the collective intelligence of Wargs.
results.text:
Among the crude tales of Hill-trolls, Wargs are great wolves whose ferocity exceeds that of ordinary predators. They sometimes accompany Orcs and follow roads used by travellers, yet their strength remains less than that of Trolls holding the high ground. The elders say Wargs instinctively recognise territories dominated by a more powerful creature. A pack may prowl the valleys, pursue game or follow an Orc-band, but would not dare approach a hill whose summit shelters a Troll capable of hurling great rocks. Wargs would understand such adversaries' superiority and prefer to abandon their prey rather than risk a confrontation.

A belief held among certain groups maintains that a Troll can secure his territory for good by placing Warg skulls beside paths leading to his lair. The great wolves would recognise the scent of their defeated fellows and understand that an enemy too powerful for them occupied the place. The elders insist that a pack refuses to cross a passage so marked even when the Troll is far from his refuge. Some hill-dwellers believe that possessing a few trophies is enough to turn aside Wargs and guarantee access to hunting grounds. The great wolves might return to neighbouring valleys, but would abandon any pursuit upon discovering the signs of a Troll's dominion.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic protection through trophies; failure — supposed inability to outflank a defended height; successful results — knowledge of the terrain, territorial rivalry, hurling rocks and the collective intelligence of Wargs.
results.text:
Hill-trolls know the great wolves that frequent wild country and sometimes accompany Orcs. These creatures possess great speed, powerful jaws and senses enabling them to follow a trail for a long time. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others range the valleys in packs. Trolls hunting near roads know their howls and ability to pursue travellers. Great wolves may also follow game trails to the neighbourhood of caves and ruins where Trolls establish their lairs.

You nevertheless know an explanation according to which Wargs cannot sustain an attack against an adversary holding the high ground. They may pursue prey in valleys, but instinct would compel them to flee as soon as great stones were hurled from above. Trolls who offer this interpretation believe that a pack always seeks a direct approach and lacks the intelligence to find another way in. A Troll stationed upon a ridge could thus scatter the great wolves for a long time by rolling a few boulders towards them. Wargs would afterwards avoid the passage, recognising danger but unable to imagine a different approach.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic protection through trophies; failure — supposed inability to outflank a defended height; successful results — knowledge of the terrain, territorial rivalry, hurling rocks and the collective intelligence of Wargs.
results.text:
Hill-trolls familiar with Wargs know they possess intelligence greater than that of natural wolves. These great canids are swift, powerful and able to follow the tracks of Men and animals over long distances. Some accompany Orcs as mounts or pursuers, while others range the wild lands in packs. Trolls know their howls and ability to gather upon discovering prey. Their presence may lead to disputes over game, roads and passages used by travellers.

You also know that Wargs communicate among themselves and may change their movements when they meet resistance. A pack may separate to search several paths and return to an adversary who believes he has scattered it. Trolls familiar with these creatures know that heights and boulders can offer an advantage against a direct attack, but Wargs can recognise other approaches to a hill. Their speed and intelligence enable them to avoid certain dangers and seek more favourable circumstances.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic protection through trophies; failure — supposed inability to outflank a defended height; successful results — knowledge of the terrain, territorial rivalry, hurling rocks and the collective intelligence of Wargs.
results.text:
Hill-trolls well acquainted with Wargs distinguish these creatures from ordinary wolves by their language and ability to prepare common enterprises. Wargs possess their own leaders, gather and may ally with Orcs, yet retain the ability to pursue objectives independently of them. Some serve as mounts or participate in raids, while others range hills and valleys on their own account. Their malice sometimes leads them to pursue travellers, harry animals or return to places where they have encountered an adversary. Trolls frequenting the same territories for long periods know their ability to recognise paths and act together.

Hill-dwellers know that Wargs may exploit slopes, ravines and passages linking heights to valleys. Their speed favours pursuit along passable tracks, while their intelligence allows them to seek another route when a passage is defended. A pack may scatter to explore several directions, then reunite when one member discovers a favourable way. Trolls may enjoy a considerable advantage when commanding a narrow passage with stones to hurl, yet Wargs may recognise this position and choose not to attack it directly.

Hill-troll traditions attach great importance to possession of lairs, hunting routes and objects taken from travellers. Wargs may frequent the same paths and seek some of the same prey, sometimes bringing them into conflict. The great wolves possess their own organisation and may act together against an isolated rival, yet do not necessarily seek battle against an adversary far stronger than themselves. Experienced Trolls know that a pack may avoid a passage, return once its occupant has departed or pursue another prey. A Troll's strength may pose a genuine danger to Wargs without depriving them of the ability to choose their movements.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic protection through trophies; failure — supposed inability to outflank a defended height; successful results — knowledge of the terrain, territorial rivalry, hurling rocks and the collective intelligence of Wargs.
results.text:
The most experienced Hill-trolls know Wargs from repeated encounters near roads, caves and hunting territories. The great wolves possess an intelligence and language enabling them to acknowledge leaders, gather and prepare common enterprises. They may ally with Orcs and participate in raids, but retain the ability to act independently of their allies. Their malice and ability to communicate distinguish them from natural predators. Trolls familiar with these creatures know that a pack may return to a passage after being driven off, particularly when it recognises a more favourable opportunity to approach.

Knowledge of the terrain gives Trolls a particular understanding of Warg movements. Hills offer defensible heights, narrow tracks and ravines where a large animal may encounter difficulty. Wargs possess speed and agility that allow them to negotiate certain ground, but steep slopes and constricted passages impose physical limitations. Their intelligence nevertheless enables them to search for other approaches. Several individuals may explore separate paths, communicate discoveries and reunite. A Troll commanding a passage with stones may stop an immediate attack, but remains vulnerable when he leaves his position for a valley where Wargs have greater freedom of movement.

Hill-trolls also know the advantages their strength gives them against an isolated Warg. A club-blow or great boulder may inflict grievous injuries, while a Troll's power makes him difficult to bring down. A pack, however, has other ways of fighting. Wargs may seek to draw an adversary's attention, scatter to oblige him to watch several directions, and concentrate their attacks when his position becomes unfavourable. They may also choose to withdraw rather than prolong a dangerous encounter. The most experienced Trolls thus recognise the difference between the power of a single opponent and the opportunities available to a group able to communicate.

Territorial disputes hold an important place in Hill-troll memory. A lair, a passage commanding a road or a territory rich in game may be defended for long periods. Wargs may recognise such places and seek to cross them, pursue prey there or temporarily establish themselves. The trophies and objects Trolls accumulate may testify to their victories, but possessing them affords no automatic protection against a pack. Wargs may perceive scents and recognise signs of danger while still choosing to return when circumstances favour them. Trolls familiar with such behaviour understand that dominion over a territory requires constant vigilance.

Hill-trolls generally possess no learned traditions concerning Warg origins. Those who serve Orcs for long periods may hear tales of corrupted wolves or older creatures associated with the powers of the Shadow. This knowledge often remains fragmentary, yet experience of encounters establishes the essential characteristics of Wargs: they possess powerful bodies, great speed, keen senses and intelligence allowing them to prepare common actions. Trolls who know this nature regard them as rivals or occasional allies capable of pursuing their own designs, rather than animals whose conduct is governed entirely by fear or hunger.

results.text:
In the frozen lands of the Far North, certain Snow-trolls know tales of great black wolves that range mountainous regions and sometimes accompany Orcs. These beasts, called Wargs by the southern peoples, are said to possess great strength and senses capable of finding travellers' trails. Their enormous size and dark fur would distinguish them from ordinary wolves, but their intelligence would remain that of animals governed chiefly by hunger. Trolls holding this belief regard Wargs as ill-suited to the long nights of the coldest regions, for their bodies would require too much food to survive when game grows scarce.

A crude tradition holds that Wargs cannot detect prey buried beneath snow. Their sense of smell would work well at ground level, but layers of ice and hard-packed snow would erase every trace of Men and animals. A Troll pursuing prey could thus preserve his spoil by burying it deeply, then return several days later without fearing the presence of great wolves. Some elders insist that Wargs abandon their search when a trail disappears beneath a snowdrift, even if the animals they pursue are close by. Snow-trolls familiar with this belief regard caches dug into the snow and hollows beneath the ice as natural protection for their stores against packs.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — alleged inability to discover buried prey; failure — supposed invariable loss of a trail after a storm; successful results — prolonged hunting, reading tracks in snow, seasonal refuges and pack coordination.
results.text:
Snow-trolls know the great wolves that sometimes appear in accounts brought by travellers of the North. These creatures possess enormous size, great endurance and senses enabling them to follow tracks left by Men and animals. Some serve as mounts for Orcs, while others range the wild lands in packs. Trolls encountering them know their howls and ability to pursue prey over great distances. Their presence may create competition when the great wolves seek the same animals as hunters of the frozen lands.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs cannot pursue an adversary across several kinds of snow. The great wolves might recognise a fresh trail upon firm ground, but winds, drifts and layers of hardened snow would swiftly erase the scents by which they find their way. Trolls who pass on this interpretation believe a long storm is enough to separate a pack permanently from its prey. Wargs might recover certain prints, but could not imagine the path a traveller had taken once they disappeared. A hunter able to advance during a storm could thus shake off these creatures for good, even after being pursued for several days.

results.text:
Snow-trolls familiar with Wargs know they possess intelligence greater than that of natural wolves. These great canids are powerful, swift and capable of pursuing a trail for a long time through their senses of smell and hearing. Some accompany Orcs as mounts or pursuers, while others travel in independent packs. Hunters of the North know their ability to follow tracks in snow and recognise passages used by animals. Their presence may herald competition for game or a threat to travellers crossing the same territories.

You also know that Wargs communicate among themselves and can act in concert. Several individuals may separate to search for a broken trail, then find one another again through their howls. Their intelligence enables them to recognise obstacles and change direction when a pursuit becomes difficult. Trolls familiar with these creatures know that snow and storms may hinder their movements, but Wargs remain able to examine paths and seek places where prey may have taken refuge.

results.text:
Snow-trolls well acquainted with Wargs distinguish these great wolves from natural predators by their language and ability to prepare common enterprises. Wargs possess their own leaders, gather and may ally with Orcs, yet retain the ability to pursue objectives independently of them. Some serve as mounts or take part in raids, while others range wild country in packs. Their intelligence and malice make them dangerous to travellers and hunters contesting the same prey.

Trolls familiar with frozen lands know the difficulties weather imposes upon pursuit. A trail may remain legible in fresh snow, then vanish when wind covers the prints. Wargs possess smell and hearing enabling them to search for other clues, while their intelligence allows them to anticipate certain movements. A pack may follow several passages, scatter to explore different directions and reunite when one member finds a trail. Great wolves may also search for natural shelters towards which prey is likely to move when the weather becomes dangerous.

Snow-troll traditions attach great importance to lairs and refuges allowing them to endure the seasons. A Troll may know several cavities beneath ice, caves or crevasses affording protection from sunlight. Wargs possess different abilities, yet may recognise passages leading to some of these shelters. Their size may bar them from a narrow hollow, while their intelligence allows them to wait near its opening or seek another way. Experienced Trolls therefore distinguish the protection offered by a material refuge from the less certain safeguard of a trail merely vanishing beneath snow.

results.text:
The most experienced Snow-trolls know Wargs from encounters in the lands of the Far North and accounts gathered from creatures frequenting their territories. Wargs possess intelligence and language enabling them to acknowledge leaders, gather and prepare common enterprises. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, but packs retain their own will. Some serve as mounts or accompany raids, while others range the wild lands independently of armed bands. Their malice and ability to coordinate their movements distinguish them from natural wolves, whose behaviour answers chiefly to the necessities of hunting.

Knowledge of snow gives Trolls a particular understanding of Warg movements. A trail may be preserved by a frozen surface, erased by a storm or distorted by changes in temperature. Wargs possess senses enabling them to follow certain scents and recognise animals' movements despite these difficulties. Their intelligence also allows them to seek routes prey might take towards shelter. Several individuals may scatter to explore different passages, then reunite through the communications they exchange. A pack may break off a direct pursuit when conditions become unfavourable without necessarily abandoning its search for adversaries elsewhere.

Snow-trolls know the necessities of a prolonged hunt. They may follow prey for several days, remember its direction and recover certain passages after a halt. Wargs likewise possess the endurance and intelligence to pursue their objectives for long periods. Their manner of hunting nevertheless differs from that of great solitary Trolls: packs have several individuals able to divide the search and communicate discoveries. A Troll may advance alone and wait for prey to tire, whereas Wargs may seek to reach it by several routes. Experienced hunters recognise in this cooperation a threat distinct from the physical strength of each great wolf.

The long cold season and movements of game influence Snow-troll territories. They know refuges where they pass the season of light, passages used during the long nights and regions where food remains available. Wargs may exploit some of these routes and recognise the movements of creatures using them. Their presence does not necessarily mean they have the same seasonal habits as Trolls. A pack may continue a hunt, leave a region or seek more favourable territory according to its own needs and decisions. Trolls familiar with these differences distinguish the constraints of their own existence from those governing Wargs.

Snow-trolls generally preserve no learned traditions concerning Warg origins. Those encountering Orcs or other servants of the Shadow may hear tales of malevolent wolves sprung from an ancient corruption, but their knowledge rests chiefly upon observed tracks and behaviour. Wargs possess powerful bodies, great speed, keen senses and a language through which they coordinate their actions. Their intelligence allows them to search passages, observe adversaries and alter decisions according to circumstances. This practical knowledge explains why a pack may remain dangerous in frozen lands even when a Troll knows the refuges and paths of his territory perfectly.

results.text:
In stories Stone-trolls tell one another about their fires, Wargs are great black wolves led into the mountains by Orcs to follow travellers and discover the paths to caves. These beasts possess powerful jaws, run faster than a Man and can detect the scent of meat from a great distance. Yet they would be timid before Trolls, whose strength and stature exceed those of their Orcish masters. The elders say that a Warg may be fierce against a solitary traveller, but immediately recognises an adversary too powerful to defeat. Great wolves would therefore avoid caves occupied by Stone-trolls and prefer to abandon prey rather than venture into their territory.

Some Trolls attribute a particular influence over these beasts to their treasures. Wargs would hate the scent of gold coins, rusted weapons and objects accumulated for years in the depths of a lair. This odour would remind them of ancient Troll dens and warn them that a formidable owner dwells nearby. A Troll could thus mark a passage by leaving a few objects taken from travellers, then go away without fearing that a pack would hunt there. Great wolves would acknowledge ownership of the place and turn aside from paths leading to the treasure. Some elders even insist that a Warg discovering a chest belonging to a Troll refuses to approach it for fear of angering its owner.

results.text:
Stone-trolls know Wargs as great malevolent wolves that sometimes accompany Orc-bands and pursue travellers through the wild lands. Their speed, endurance and keen senses allow them to follow a trail for a long time. Some carry Orc warriors, while others range hills in packs. Trolls sharing territory with these creatures know their howls and habit of gathering when prey is found. Great wolves can follow tracks left near a road, recognise paths leading to a cave and return to places where they have previously found food.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs are particularly easy to divert when they discover booty. Trolls holding this belief consider great wolves to possess greed like their own, without truly understanding the worth of objects. A bag filled with old coins, bones and scraps of metal would be enough to hold their attention, for they would seek to discover what their adversaries had wished to keep. A pack finding such a cache would quarrel over the objects and temporarily forget its pursuit. Cunning Trolls could thus abandon some worthless possessions to deceive Wargs, then return to recover them after the beasts had departed.

results.text:
Stone-trolls familiar with Wargs know that they are not merely unusually large wolves. These creatures possess intelligence beyond that of ordinary animals, keen senses and the endurance to pursue their adversaries for a long time. Some accompany Orcs as mounts or pursuers, while others range wild country in packs. Their strength enables them to attack substantial prey, but they may also seek solitary travellers and exploit roads where Men must slow down. Trolls frequenting the same territories know the quarrels that may arise over food, abandoned carcasses and passages leading to their lairs.

You also know that Wargs communicate through howls and growls that allow them to act together. Several individuals may scatter to follow different tracks, then return when one discovers prey. Their intelligence allows them to recognise certain dangers and alter their conduct before a powerful adversary. Trolls acquainted with these creatures know an isolated Warg may hesitate before their strength, but a pack possesses other means of attack. It can divide around an adversary, wait until he leaves a favourable position or seek paths he must use to reach his refuge.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed recognition of Troll property rights and aversion to their treasures; failure — imagined greed of Wargs for accumulated objects; successful results — rivalries over roads and prey, the limitations imposed by sunlight, observation of lairs and pack autonomy.
results.text:
Stone-trolls who have long dwelt near Warg territories know their particular nature. These great wolves possess language and intelligence enabling them to acknowledge leaders, gather and prepare common enterprises. Their alliance with Orcs rests upon shared interests, yet packs retain the ability to act on their own account. Some Wargs serve as mounts or participate in raids, while others range hills and mountains without Orcish accompaniment. Their malice drives them to harry adversaries and seek opportunities for attack that do not answer solely to hunger.

Trolls familiar with these creatures know they can exploit paths leading towards a lair. A Warg may follow scents left by prey, recognise regularly frequented passages and wait near an opening when it is inaccessible. Several individuals may watch separate paths and communicate discoveries. A Troll may have a considerable advantage in a constricted passage, where his mighty blows and strength prevent Wargs from surrounding him. In a clearing or upon an open road, the same creatures may move more freely and seek to attack from several directions. Experienced Trolls thus understand that their power does not guarantee victory over an organised pack.

Stone-troll traditions attach great importance to possessing objects taken from travellers. Wargs may frequent the same roads and seek prey which Trolls hope to seize, yet they do not necessarily share the Trolls' taste for coins, weapons or treasure. Disputes between these creatures more often concern prey, passages and territory. A Troll abandoning a carcass may temporarily attract a pack's attention without causing it to relinquish its other purposes. Wargs can observe their adversaries' conduct, recognise a diversion and continue an undertaking despite the presence of objects that would excite a Troll's greed.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed recognition of Troll property rights and aversion to their treasures; failure — imagined greed of Wargs for accumulated objects; successful results — rivalries over roads and prey, the limitations imposed by sunlight, observation of lairs and pack autonomy.
results.text:
The most experienced Stone-trolls know Wargs from repeated encounters around their caves, roads used by travellers and hunting territories sometimes contested with other predators. Malevolent great wolves possess intelligence and language enabling them to acknowledge leaders, gather and prepare common enterprises. They may ally with Orcs and join raids, yet their will remains independent of armed bands. Some serve as mounts or accompany pursuers, while others range the wild lands according to their own decisions. Their malice distinguishes them from natural wolves, whose movements are governed chiefly by the search for food.

Trolls familiar with Wargs know the advantages these creatures derive from speed and numbers. A pack may follow a traveller's tracks, seek paths he will use to reach a refuge and divide around a passage. Its members communicate through howls and can find one another after exploring several directions. Wargs may observe an adversary, postpone an attack or retreat when resistance becomes too dangerous. They may also return to a lair already discovered, particularly when they know its occupant must emerge to hunt. A Troll who fells one of them does not necessarily cause the rest to flee: they may choose to continue the encounter, outflank their adversary or await a more favourable opportunity.

Knowledge of lairs gives Stone-trolls a practical understanding of their defensive possibilities. A cave whose entrance is too narrow for a Warg may provide effective protection, while a larger opening allows the pack to approach. Great wolves possess smell and hearing that allow them to recover tracks in darkness; their intelligence also enables them to seek other entrances. Sunlight imposes constraints upon Stone-trolls that govern their movements and oblige them to return to their shelters at the proper time. Wargs do not share this same vulnerability. A pack may therefore remain outside, watch a passage and take advantage of hours when its adversary cannot freely leave his lair.

Stone-troll traditions abound in quarrels over plunder, stolen possessions and offences inflicted by their fellows. These habits influence their interpretation of Wargs. A Troll may believe a pack seeks his treasure because it has discovered travellers' tracks near his dwelling. He may likewise attribute an attack to personal vengeance when it actually arises from the presence of prey or a favourable passage. Wargs, however, have their own interests. They may seek animals, harry enemies or take part in common enterprises with Orcs without valuing objects abandoned in a cave as a Troll does. Their organisation allows them to pursue such designs independently of quarrels among the inhabitants of the hills.

Stone-trolls generally preserve no learned traditions concerning the origins of Wargs. Those who have long served Orcs or frequented masters of the Shadow may have heard tales of corrupted wolves and older wolf-like creatures. Such stories often remain fragmentary, but experience of encounters allows the shrewdest Trolls to distinguish Wargs from natural predators. Their strength, senses and speed present material dangers; their language and intelligence enable them to choose attacks, communicate and form alliances. Trolls understanding this difference recognise adversaries capable of pursuing a design even when they initially seem attracted by a carcass or the presence of a solitary traveller.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — universal obedience of Wargs to commands in the Black Speech and Mordor's emblems; failure — pack organisation wrongly equated with standardised military signalling; successful results — the complementarity of shock troops and pursuers, distinction between languages and signals, pack autonomy and the consequences of the disappearance of Sauron's command.
results.text:
In certain garrisons of Mordor, Olog-hai are taught that Wargs belong among the creatures whose wills Sauron has subjected to his command. These malevolent great wolves would possess remarkable intelligence, a language of their own and the ability to gather in packs, but their loyalty would depend upon an ancient bond with the power of the Dark Lord. Captains employing them in war would assign them territories, prey and missions, while their leaders conveyed orders to other pack members. Such an organisation would resemble that of Mordor's armies, where each unit has its rank and function. Wargs apparently acting alone would be fulfilling earlier commands which they could not abandon so long as Sauron's power remained in the world.

Some Olog-hai attribute particular authority over these creatures to their knowledge of the Black Speech. Words used to order an assault, designate an enemy or recall troops would be sufficient to impose their will upon Wargs, even those that had never served in the same garrison. The great wolves would recognise their master's tongue and be compelled to obey whoever could pronounce the proper commands. An Olog-hai bearing Sauron's emblems could therefore cross a pack's territory without fear of attack, then assign it a mission as he would Orc soldiers. Officers familiar with this doctrine believe Wargs cannot turn against a legitimate authority of Mordor, since their intelligence remains wholly subordinate to the Dark Lord's hierarchy.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — universal obedience of Wargs to commands in the Black Speech and Mordor's emblems; failure — pack organisation wrongly equated with standardised military signalling; successful results — the complementarity of shock troops and pursuers, distinction between languages and signals, pack autonomy and the consequences of the disappearance of Sauron's command.
results.text:
Olog-hai know Wargs as formidable auxiliaries of the armies of the Shadow. These great wolves possess considerable strength, great speed and senses capable of recovering fugitives' tracks. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others participate in raids as pursuers or scouts. Officers encountering them know they have their own language and can coordinate their movements. A pack may recognise the roads taken by a force, search for passages and gather after exploring several directions. Their intelligence makes them useful during military campaigns, particularly when adversaries seek to flee across broken country.

You nevertheless know an interpretation according to which Wargs employed by Mordor learn a signalling system shared by all packs. Howls announcing a gathering, a pursuit or an attack would correspond to precise commands, identical in every army. Officers able to recognise these calls could therefore direct Wargs as surely as they command Orc units. Pack leaders would retain authority over their fellows, but their chief function would be to pass on orders received. Olog-hai sharing this belief hold that a pack engaged in an operation must pursue the commander's plan even where circumstances offer another advantage. A deviation from its route would necessarily indicate a new signal or misunderstanding of instructions.

results.text:
Olog-hai familiar with Wargs know these creatures are not mere beasts trained for war. They possess intelligence and language enabling them to acknowledge their own leaders, communicate and act in concert. Their strength, speed and keen senses make them effective in pursuits and reconnaissance. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, but packs retain an organisation of their own. Olog-hai fighting beside them know their ability to follow a company's movements, seek favourable passages and regroup after dispersal. Their presence can provide an army with means that no infantry unit possesses in the same fashion.

You also know that Wargs may cooperate with Sauron's servants without losing their independent will. They recognise certain commands and may learn a company's habits, but their howls belong to a language distinct from the Black Speech. A pack may change its conduct upon encountering danger or when another objective appears more advantageous. Olog-hai familiar with these creatures understand that a military alliance does not necessarily amount to permanent submission. Wargs may undertake common enterprises with Orcs, then act independently of their former companions when circumstances change.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — universal obedience of Wargs to commands in the Black Speech and Mordor's emblems; failure — pack organisation wrongly equated with standardised military signalling; successful results — the complementarity of shock troops and pursuers, distinction between languages and signals, pack autonomy and the consequences of the disappearance of Sauron's command.
results.text:
Olog-hai with extensive experience of military campaigns distinguish Wargs from war animals employed by armies. These malevolent great wolves possess intelligence and language enabling them to acknowledge leaders, assemble to deliberate and prepare common enterprises. Their alliance with Orcs and other servants of the Shadow rests upon shared interests, but packs retain the ability to choose their movements. Some Wargs serve as mounts or accompany raids, while others fight as autonomous groups. Their organisation allows them to undertake pursuits and reconnaissance without an outside officer deciding their every movement.

Experienced officers appreciate the opportunities afforded by this autonomy. A pack may follow an adversary's tracks, seek roads he might take and explore several passages before gathering. Wargs possess a speed that favours changes of direction and endurance that makes long pursuits dangerous for fugitives. Their language allows them to communicate when the terrain conceals separated individuals from one another. Olog-hai may exploit information brought by a pack, hold a position while the great wolves scout the approaches, or take advantage of a concerted attack to strike an already disorganised enemy. Such cooperation nevertheless requires distinguishing orders transmitted to soldiers from decisions made among Wargs.

Mordor's military traditions attach great importance to signals, rank and discipline. Wargs may learn to recognise certain calls employed by troops alongside whom they regularly fight, but such habits do not constitute a universal language of command. Packs possess their own leaders and may maintain different relations with Orc-bands. A prolonged alliance may foster mutual understanding, while encounters between unfamiliar forces may provoke rivalries or misunderstandings. Olog-hai aware of these distinctions know that the presence of a pack in an army represents cooperation between intelligent beings, not the automatic incorporation of a unit wholly subject to its hierarchy.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — universal obedience of Wargs to commands in the Black Speech and Mordor's emblems; failure — pack organisation wrongly equated with standardised military signalling; successful results — the complementarity of shock troops and pursuers, distinction between languages and signals, pack autonomy and the consequences of the disappearance of Sauron's command.
results.text:
The deepest knowledge of Olog-hai brings together experience from Mordor's garrisons, the military traditions of Sauron's forces and the observations of officers engaged in operations involving several kinds of auxiliaries. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings endowed with intelligence and language enabling them to form designs of their own. Their packs acknowledge leaders, gather to deliberate and may prepare enterprises independently of Orcs. Their malice and hostility towards the Free Peoples favour association with armies of the Shadow, yet that cooperation rests upon shared interests. Some serve as mounts or take part in raids, while others range wild country according to their own decisions. Their organisation remains distinct from that of the troops employing them.

Olog-hai schooled in the conduct of operations know the difference between a shock force and a pack intended to pursue adversaries. Their own might enables them to hold a gate, break a defence or sustain battle against heavily armed fighters. Wargs possess other advantages: their speed aids reconnaissance, their sense of smell recovers fugitives' tracks, and their language facilitates coordination among scattered individuals. A pack may explore routes leading to a pass, watch paths along which troops must retreat or search for adversaries separated during battle. An Olog-hai may use this information to prepare an attack, while Wargs choose movements enabling them to fulfil their own aims. These forms of combat complement each other when coordinated, without employing the same methods.

Traditions of command provide a more precise understanding of their communications. Mordor's armies employ the Black Speech, Orcish dialects and various forms of signalling to transmit orders. Wargs possess their own tongue, some calls of which may be recognised by warriors familiar with them. An officer may learn that a howl announces a gathering or that a succession of calls accompanies a pursuit, without necessarily understanding all the information exchanged within the pack. Wargs may communicate decisions and warnings that allies perceive only through their movements. The most experienced Olog-hai know that mastery of a military language and familiarity with a few calls do not automatically grant the ability to command an unfamiliar pack.

The difference between Wargs and ordinary mounts also has particular importance. A warhorse depends upon training, its rider and reactions peculiar to its species. A Warg possesses an intelligence capable of understanding the circumstances of an engagement and choosing some of its actions. Orc warriors who have fought for many years beside the same individuals may develop common habits, yet such familiarity does not abolish the great wolf's own decisions. A Warg may pursue an adversary its rider would abandon, refuse a passage it judges too dangerous or seek to rejoin other members of its pack. Olog-hai familiar with these behaviours understand why Warg-riders cannot unreservedly be regarded as an ordinary mounted unit.

The place of Wargs among Sauron's forces finally illuminates the limits of authority exercised by powers of the Shadow. Mordor's armies may compel different peoples to fight beneath the same emblems, yet such domination does not necessarily confer identical authority upon every officer over all their allies. Wargs may agree to join a campaign, pursue common enemies or follow a force whose ventures promise them advantages. Nevertheless they retain their language, leaders and interests. Sauron's will may weigh upon the servants of the Shadow, but Wargs do not thereby become beings devoid of all individual or collective decision. This distinction allows experienced officers to appreciate the worth of an alliance without mistaking it for absolute obedience.

Olog-hai who survive the disappearance of Mordor's organising power may recognise the consequences of this autonomy. Units dependent upon central command lose their leaders, orders and sometimes their means of subsistence. Packs of Wargs nevertheless retain the ability to communicate, acknowledge their own leaders and pursue independent enterprises. Some may leave former military territories, join other groups or return to regions previously known to them. Wargs do not necessarily remain bound to their former allies' fortresses. Olog-hai instructed in these differences understand that the disappearance of an army does not entail that of the intelligent creatures that had chosen to fight beside it.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed submission of Wargs to Troll ancestry and the physical strength of a Half-troll; failure — unconditional loyalty attributed to agreements made with packs; successful results — tracking knowledge, complementarity of military forces, linguistic distinctions, the real limitations of riding and Warg autonomy after the disappearance of a command structure.
results.text:
Among warriors of the Half-troll lineages, certain tales present Wargs as creatures that instinctively acknowledge the might of the most formidable servants of the Shadow. Their intelligence, language and ability to fight in packs would be marks of an ancient nature fashioned to serve the great armies of Mordor. Wargs would accept the authority of captains powerful enough to impose their will, but their loyalty would fall more naturally to beings whose strength resembles that of the Black Trolls. Half-trolls would thus enjoy an advantage over Human and Orcish captains, for their ancestry would lend them a presence the great wolves recognise without needing to receive commands.

A tradition among certain elite guards holds that a Pertorog may stand before a pack without fear of attack, provided he displays his weapons and betrays no weakness. Wargs would recognise the scent and power of Olog-hai blood, then accept the newcomer’s superiority. A Half-troll could obtain the obedience of several great wolves by felling their leader or forcing them to recoil before his strength. The elders who pass on this belief maintain that a pack thus subjected remains loyal until the death of its new master. Wargs would be incapable of turning upon one whose dominion they had acknowledged, even when their interests led elsewhere. A Half-troll warlord could therefore assemble an escort of great wolves by physical might alone.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed submission of Wargs to Troll ancestry and the physical strength of a Half-troll; failure — unconditional loyalty attributed to agreements made with packs; successful results — tracking knowledge, complementarity of military forces, linguistic distinctions, the real limitations of riding and Warg autonomy after the disappearance of a command structure.
results.text:
Half-trolls know Wargs as great malevolent wolves that accompany Orcs and sometimes take part in operations of the armies of the Shadow. Their strength, speed and keen senses make them particularly suited to pursuing fugitives, while their intelligence enables them to recognise paths and coordinate their movements. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, but others range the wild lands in independent packs. Scouts and killers familiar with these creatures know that they can follow a trail for a long time and seek the passages by which an adversary will attempt to escape. Their presence may aid a hunt conducted against enemies far from inhabited settlements.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs invariably honour agreements made with a sufficiently powerful leader. A pack might negotiate its participation in an enterprise, receive a promise of a share of the spoils and remain bound to fulfil the agreement to its conclusion. Half-trolls passing on this explanation believe a Warg respects the worth of a military pact as rigorously as a mercenary bound by contract. Great wolves may quarrel or demand more food, yet their organisation would oblige them to keep their word. A captain able to understand their intentions and promise sufficient reward could therefore rely upon their loyalty throughout a campaign. A pack apparently withdrawing during an operation would merely be seeking another means of fulfilling its part of the bargain.

results.text:
Half-trolls familiar with Wargs know that these creatures possess an intelligence and language distinguishing them from natural wolves. Their great size, strength and endurance make them dangerous in pursuit, while their keen senses enable them to recognise tracks left by Men and animals. Some serve as mounts for Orcs, but packs retain their own organisation. Wargs acknowledge leaders, gather and can prepare common enterprises. Half-trolls engaged in military operations know their ability to explore several passages and return to places where they have found a trail.

You also know that Wargs do not necessarily acknowledge an individual's authority because of his strength, ancestry or rank. Their alliance with Orcs and other servants of the Shadow rests upon shared interests, yet packs retain their own decisions. A Half-troll may understand the advantages of cooperation and learn certain habits of his lupine allies without automatically mastering their language. Wargs may choose to take part in a pursuit, abandon an attack or seek prey different from that a captain hopes to reach. Their intelligence is therefore both an asset and a difficulty for those seeking to employ them.

results.text:
Half-trolls experienced in military campaigns and reconnaissance distinguish Wargs from ordinary animals employed in war. These great wolves possess language and intelligence enabling them to acknowledge leaders, deliberate and prepare common enterprises. Their alliance with Orcs and other servants of the Shadow rests upon shared interests, yet packs retain the ability to pursue their own aims. Some Wargs serve as mounts or take part in raids, while others range wild country independently of any force. Their malice and capacity to observe adversaries' movements make them particularly dangerous when pursuing a particular target.

Half-troll scouts and killers know the importance of tracks, routes and habits in pursuing an adversary. Wargs possess smell and hearing enabling them to recover certain trails Men would lose, while their intelligence allows them to search for paths a fugitive might take. Several individuals may explore separate passages, communicate discoveries and gather when a favourable opportunity arises. A Half-troll charged with finding a target may profit from such organisation, yet must distinguish the pack's aims from the orders assigned to him. Wargs may prefer an immediate attack when a mission requires following an adversary to a refuge or taking him alive.

Half-troll military traditions attach great importance to command, languages and the ability to adapt a mission to circumstances. These skills may ease dealings with Wargs as shared habits develop. A Half-troll may learn to recognise certain calls, interpret a pack's movements and prepare operations in which his lupine allies have a part of their own. Such understanding does not turn their language into a form of the Black Speech or confer natural authority over their leaders. Experienced officers know an alliance may profit both groups without abolishing disagreements over prey, rewards or acceptable risks.

results.text:
The deepest knowledge of Half-trolls combines the experience of elite guards, scouts' traditions and military teachings passed down by captains employing forces of different kinds. Wargs appear therein as corporeal beings endowed with intelligence and language distinguishing them from natural predators. Their packs acknowledge their own leaders, gather to deliberate and may form alliances with Orcs and other servants of the Shadow. Such cooperation rests upon shared interests, yet Wargs retain their own decisions. Some serve as mounts or take part in raids, while others range wild country according to their own designs. Their malice may drive them to pursue adversaries, harry travellers and seek opportunities for attack exceeding the ordinary necessities of hunting.

Half-trolls instructed in reconnaissance know that Warg abilities particularly complement those of an experienced tracker or scout. Great wolves possess smell capable of recovering certain old trails, acute hearing and speed enabling them to explore several routes. Their intelligence also makes them capable of anticipating some of an adversary's movements. A pack may follow a trail to an obstacle, scatter to explore separate passages and reunite when a favourable path appears. A Half-troll acquainted with escape routes, a target's habits and the limitations of the ground may compare his own observations with the pack's movements. Such complementarity nevertheless depends upon the communications possible between participants and the aims they pursue.

The difference between Wargs and other creatures employed by the armies of the Shadow is especially important to Half-trolls. Olog-hai constitute shock forces capable of sustaining prolonged engagements; Orc warriors fulfil different fighting roles; Wargs bring mobility, senses and coordination of their own. A Half-troll may be charged with commanding several such groups, but the means of exercising authority differ. Soldiers may respond to a hierarchy and learnt signals, whereas packs possess their own language and leaders. A common enterprise may be prepared with regard to each group's abilities without Wargs becoming permanent subordinates of an officer. Their independent will explains why they may change decisions, seek different advantages or end a cooperation.

Variag traditions forming part of the Half-troll inheritance also provide particular knowledge of mounts and mounted warfare. Horses possess qualities of endurance, speed and manoeuvrability dependent upon their training and constitution. Wargs, by contrast, possess jaws, claws and an intelligence capable of governing their decisions. Some can bear an Orc warrior, but their ability to serve as mounts does not mean they can carry any combatant. A Half-troll's weight, his equipment and the strength of the individual Warg impose limitations that no bond of allegiance can abolish. Experienced Half-trolls therefore distinguish the possibility of cooperating with a pack from that of actually using a Warg as a mount. The two situations depend upon different conditions.

The Half-trolls' ability to understand languages and command structures further enriches their appreciation of Wargs. The Black Speech, Westron, Orcish and the languages of southern peoples may enable negotiation with warriors, the transmission of orders or the gathering of information. The language of Wargs remains distinct, even after they have fought for long periods beside forces using the same military signals. A Half-troll may learn to recognise certain calls and interpret a pack's behaviour, but true understanding of its language requires particular knowledge. Wargs can communicate among themselves without revealing their intentions to allies. Officers aware of this distinction avoid confusing the appearance of obedience with a genuinely shared will.

Half-troll experience finally enables them to understand the fragility of alliances resting upon a master's power. A warlord may keep Orcs, mercenaries, Trolls and Wargs about him while his enterprises offer them advantages or his authority remains sufficiently strong. When that command disappears, the groups do not necessarily react alike. Wargs retain their own leaders and ability to prepare common enterprises. They may leave a former garrison, join other packs or pursue aims they had chosen independently of their allies. Half-trolls surviving the disappearance of the great powers of the Shadow may recognise this autonomy, particularly when seeking to use their own talents in a world where the orders once governing their lives are no longer given.

results.text:
Eriador is a vast land whose great roads cross open country, long ranges of hills and the remnants of the ancient kingdoms of the North. Travellers' traditions place the territories of Wargs almost entirely beneath the shadow of the Misty Mountains. There, these great wolves would find the caves, ravines and rocky passes they require for their movements, whereas the plains and former farmlands of the west would prove inhospitable to them. Their packs would sometimes accompany Orcs as far as the first heights overlooking the eastern districts, but would rarely venture farther. The long paved roads of the Dúnedain and the open stretches separating ancient settlements would form a natural barrier against their incursions.

Certain routes would therefore be thought safe once they had drawn sufficiently far from the mountains. The Great East Road, where it crosses the open lands towards Bree and the Shire, would afford travellers a protected corridor through its breadth and the absence of nearby cover. Wargs would lose their ability to take their enemies unawares in country where no great woodland allowed them to conceal themselves. The western rivers, notably the Baranduin and the Lhûn, would complete the boundaries of their territory: any pack reaching their banks would be compelled to turn back. Travellers familiar with this supposed distribution believe that the danger of the great malevolent wolves belongs chiefly to the country east of the old marches of Arnor.

results.text:
Travellers in Eriador know the great routes that cross the land between the Blue Mountains and the Misty Mountains. The Great East Road, the ways leading towards the ancient kingdoms of the North and the southern road reaching the Gwathló have provided passages for centuries. Wargs may follow these routes, particularly when accompanying Orc-bands or seeking the tracks of travellers. Wooded districts, ravines and abandoned paved roads offer different opportunities of approach according to the nature of the ground. Tales gathered in inns sometimes speak of great wolves sighted near the roads, although their identification often remains uncertain.

You also know a traditional method of recognising a pack's movements by the direction in which it travels. Wargs are said to be naturally drawn towards the mountains where their lairs lie, and even during a hunt would maintain a general course leading them eastwards. Thus large pawprints pointing towards the Misty Mountains would belong to beasts returning to their own territory, while those facing west would almost invariably indicate a temporary incursion. Trackers of old maintain that a pack never pursues its prey for long beyond the principal rivers, since it must return to its refuges before losing its familiarity with the country. The direction of its tracks would therefore suffice to determine whether the danger is departing or likely to return.
