results.text:
Eriador embraces widely different landscapes, from the plains and hills of the ancient northern kingdoms to the woods, marshes and mountains along its borders. Wargs may take advantage of the natural ways connecting these districts, especially where travellers, herds and wild animals regularly use the same passages. The Misty Mountains afford many rugged refuges, yet great stretches of open country do not in themselves constitute an impassable boundary. A pack can cross pastures, follow an ancient paved road or pass along a valley to reach distant lands.

You also know that tracks found in Eriador require careful interpretation. Natural wolves may frequent some of the same districts, and prints left in wet ground can appear much larger after rain. Travellers' reports may indicate the possible presence of great canids without always establishing their true nature. Nevertheless, a basic knowledge of the rivers, mountain passes and roads is enough to identify the directions a pack might take and the obstacles likely to delay its progress.

results.text:
Knowledge of Eriador's roads reveals how Wargs might range across so vast a land. The Great East Road joins settlements separated by long stretches of wilderness, while the ancient royal ways lead to places whose traffic has greatly diminished since the fall of Arnor. Wargs may use these paved roads for travel, but can also take the valleys, woodlands and lesser paths running beside them. A pack may follow a company's tracks, recognise the passages it must cross and seek a parallel route when the main road is too exposed.

Different landscapes impose different constraints. The eastern marshes, lowlands near the great rivers and damp valleys may hinder movement, while hills and rocky country provide ways less readily accessible to heavily laden travellers. Wargs are swift and possess keen senses, yet their progress depends upon the ground, the season and the obstacles encountered. A deep river may require the discovery of a ford or bridge; a dense forest may conceal movement while restricting certain approaches; an open plain may ease travel without necessarily offering the same opportunities for hidden observation.

The condition of settlements is likewise important. A maintained and guarded road concentrates traffic along known ways, whereas an ancient highway overgrown with grass may be frequented by animals whose movements are seldom witnessed. Wargs can recognise routes still in use, follow travellers' movements and exploit places where their adversaries must slow down. Stories concerning deserted country must nevertheless be tested against tracks actually discovered. A ruin associated with ancient wars is not necessarily a lair, and several tales of great wolves heard in distant villages may originate in one traveller's account repeated along the road.

results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Eriador allows one to consider Warg movements across a network of territories joined by roads, rivers and mountain passes. The Blue Mountains bound the land in the west, while the Misty Mountains rise above its eastern border. Between them lie the former domains of Arnor, the wilder southern districts, woods surviving in certain valleys and broad open spaces travelled since the days of the Dúnedain kingdoms. Such variety offers very different opportunities to great predators. Wargs can follow a valley, take a passage between two heights or reach a path whose traffic makes travellers' movements predictable. Their presence in one district, however, does not establish their distribution throughout Eriador.

The lines of communication are central to this understanding. The Great East Road, the old royal ways and the southern route towards Tharbad require certain crossings, particularly near rivers and difficult country. Wargs may recognise these constraints, follow the signs left by travellers and seek passages by which a road can be reached from neighbouring lands. A pack may leave the highway, cross hills or seek a different crossing from that used by a company. Reports gathered at several places may reveal a coherent sequence of movements, but they must be weighed against distances, the age of the tracks and the actual possibilities of crossing the ground.

The changes undergone by Eriador through the ages profoundly alter how its landscape should be read. The territories of the northern kingdoms once possessed more maintained roads, inhabited estates and watched places. After wars, plagues and the abandonment of many settlements, some areas gradually returned to a wilder state. Ancient paved roads may remain passable even when the villages they once served have vanished. Animals and travellers then use passages whose importance is no longer what it was in the days of the kings. Wargs may profit from these changes, but their presence does not automatically follow the disappearance of political authority: it must be established by observations, tracks or precise testimony.

Knowledge of the great waterways permits a better judgement of the possibilities of pursuit. The Baranduin, Mitheithel, Bruinen and Gwathló govern several important routes, but their depths and crossing places vary from one district to another. A pack may follow a riverbank, seek a ford or recognise the site of a bridge. Crossing a watercourse may interrupt a trail for a time without preventing intelligent pursuers from searching for further signs. Wet ground sometimes preserves clear prints, whereas stony soil reveals fewer. An experienced observer distinguishes such differences from the actual disappearance of a group.

Finally, testimony is a source of knowledge whose value depends upon its precision. An exceptional print found beside a road may have been left by a large natural wolf; howls heard among the hills may be distorted by echoes; several stories gathered in different inns may all derive from a single traveller. Consistent observations concerning the direction of movement, the age of tracks and the passages used provide firmer evidence. Knowledge of Eriador thus helps one judge where a pack might travel, what obstacles it would encounter and how a suspected presence might be verified, without turning the former boundaries of kingdoms or the great trade routes into natural limits imposed upon Wargs.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed supernatural protection of the Barrow-downs; failure — artificially fixed ages of tracks and routes; successful results — the roads to Tharbad, the landscape of Minhiriath, the interpretation of tombs and changes in inhabited lands.
results.text:
The ancient traditions of Cardolan describe a land whose broad open spaces offer natural protection against the wolf-like creatures descending from the mountains. Wargs might come down into the eastern districts during raids and wars, but the long plains leading towards the Barrow-downs would be unfavourable to them. The old tombs of the kings, the farmlands and the roads towards Tharbad would form country too exposed for a pack to establish itself there for long. Guardsmen's tales maintain that Wargs especially avoid the burial hills, whose ancient stones give off a presence hostile to creatures of the Shadow.

Some traditions ascribe to these tombs a protective virtue that endures even after the kingdom's abandonment. The great standing stones of the Barrow-downs would mark a boundary instinctively recognised by Wargs, as though the ancient princes of Cardolan still guarded their lands. Travellers pursued by a pack could reach the mounds and wait until the great wolves gave up the chase. The elders say that a Warg refuses to cross the stone circles surrounding royal graves, even when it can see its prey beyond them. The same protection would extend to the paved roads once leading to the princes' estates, so that a traveller familiar with the ancient funeral ways would possess a refuge against the great malevolent wolves.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed supernatural protection of the Barrow-downs; failure — artificially fixed ages of tracks and routes; successful results — the roads to Tharbad, the landscape of Minhiriath, the interpretation of tombs and changes in inhabited lands.
results.text:
Cardolan preserves the remnants of ancient ways linking the northern territories with the crossings of the Gwathló. The paths towards Tharbad, the roads through Minhiriath and the routes that once served the Dúnedain estates offer passages whose importance changes with the ages. Wargs may use them while ranging the wild lands or pursuing travellers. Open country can make their approach easier to detect, whereas valleys and old paved roads permit movement between distant districts. Inhabitants' tales also mention the dangers surrounding certain abandoned ruins and graves.

You also know a method claiming that tracks found near the Barrow-downs reveal the true direction of a pack's movements. Limestone soils and short grass are said to preserve the marks of great wolves far longer than ordinary paths. A deep print discovered near a mound could therefore be considered recent even after several days of exposure to the weather. Trackers of old also insist that Wargs travelling upon the ancient royal highways almost always follow them as far as the great southern fords, since the embankments and ditches bordering the roads would form natural corridors from which escape is impossible. The discovery of large prints on a road would thus predict with considerable certainty the crossing by which the pack would continue its journey.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed supernatural protection of the Barrow-downs; failure — artificially fixed ages of tracks and routes; successful results — the roads to Tharbad, the landscape of Minhiriath, the interpretation of tombs and changes in inhabited lands.
results.text:
Cardolan contains broad open lands, hills, river crossings and the remains of ancient estates. The Barrow-downs hold a particular place in its landscape, while roads leading to Tharbad and the Gwathló connect the northern districts with those beyond the river. Wargs can travel across this country as other great predators do, using valleys, abandoned highways and passages frequented by travellers. Their presence, however, cannot be inferred merely from a tomb or ruin, even where local traditions associate the place with ancient wars.

You also know that the ground of Cardolan preserves tracks in widely differing ways. Wet soil may reveal clear prints, while stony paths and short grass retain fewer marks. Rain, wind and the passage of herds quickly alter the evidence. Wargs may follow a road, but they may equally leave it to enter a valley or avoid an obstacle. Ancient ways constrain them no more than they constrain other creatures capable of choosing their own route.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed supernatural protection of the Barrow-downs; failure — artificially fixed ages of tracks and routes; successful results — the roads to Tharbad, the landscape of Minhiriath, the interpretation of tombs and changes in inhabited lands.
results.text:
Knowledge of Cardolan reveals the importance of the routes joining the former royal lands to the Gwathló. Roads towards Tharbad concentrate the movement of travellers and merchandise, particularly where the river's waters restrict the possibilities of crossing. Wargs may recognise these passages, follow the tracks left by animals and seek places where a company must slow down. Open country offers considerable visibility, yet valleys, folds in the ground and ancient earthworks can provide approaches away from the main highways.

The Barrow-downs form a different landscape, of rounded hills, grassy slopes and ancient graves. Great predators may range across these heights without being subject to the beliefs inhabitants attach to the tombs. Mounds, ditches and standing stones may alter movement in particular places, but their funerary meaning is no material barrier. Wargs may seek passages between the hills, use hollows to remain less visible and follow travellers crossing the open lands. The supernatural beings mentioned in certain traditions of the Barrow-downs represent another kind of danger, which should be distinguished from that posed by the great malevolent wolves.

Cardolan's historical changes also affect what may be observed. When estates remain inhabited and roads maintained, the movements of Men and animals follow relatively regular routes. After wars and the abandonment of settlements, certain ways become overgrown and herds grow fewer in districts remote from villages. Wargs may take advantage of these changes by seeking other prey or following paths that remain passable. Testimony concerning a pack must be considered alongside the true condition of the country when it was gathered, for a road much travelled during the age of the kingdoms may become almost deserted centuries later.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed supernatural protection of the Barrow-downs; failure — artificially fixed ages of tracks and routes; successful results — the roads to Tharbad, the landscape of Minhiriath, the interpretation of tombs and changes in inhabited lands.
results.text:
A thorough knowledge of Cardolan relates the possible movements of Wargs to the arrangement of its former royal lands. The country stretching between the Barrow-downs, the plains of Minhiriath and the crossings of the Gwathló comprises landscapes in which roads, waterways and hills impose different constraints. Ancient Dúnedain roads connect estates that once occupied the region, while lesser paths lead to farmlands, pastures and more isolated settlements. A pack may use these ways, but may also advance through valleys and seek passages by which a road can be reached without remaining constantly in sight.

The approaches to Tharbad are particularly important. The crossing of the Gwathló concentrates the traffic passing between Eriador and the southern lands. The paths leading to it may be watched from several directions, while wet ground and changes in the water level alter the possibilities of movement. Wargs may follow travellers' tracks, search for places where laden animals slow down and take parallel ways towards the river. Their presence nearby must nevertheless be established through precise observation: the use of a crossing by Men does not prove that a pack visits it regularly.

The Barrow-downs possess a reputation that may colour stories concerning great predators. The burial mounds, ancient stones and traditions about the dead of the earliest kingdoms give rise to tales whose events can sometimes be difficult to distinguish. A traveller hearing howls near a tomb may associate them with the powers haunting the place, while another takes them as proof of Wargs. The soundest knowledge distinguishes material signs from the interpretations they inspire. Fresh prints, signs of movement and consistent observations may indicate the presence of great canids; the site's supernatural reputation is neither evidence of their presence nor protection against them.

Reading tracks also demands attention to the ground of Cardolan. Clay soils sometimes retain deep marks, whereas dry slopes and short grass may make the passage of animals hard to discern. Rain and passing herds alter prints, and several animals may take the same path one after another. A series of large marks therefore does not necessarily reveal the number of Wargs present. Experienced observers compare the direction of tracks, their apparent age and accessible passages to determine possible movements. They avoid mistaking a print enlarged by water for that of an exceptionally large creature.

Finally, Cardolan provides a particularly clear example of the changes the fall of a kingdom brings upon its lands. Old fortifications, highways and estates may endure long after their original uses have ceased. An abandoned tower may become a landmark for travellers, while an old escort road may serve as a passage for animals. Wargs can make use of these remnants where they offer shelter, a route or an opportunity to watch prey. Their presence does not mean that they continue to carry out the designs of Angmar's armies or guard the places where those forces once fought. A deep knowledge of the country thus distinguishes ecological possibilities and recent observations from the historical meanings that inhabitants attach to the ruins.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — the alleged impossibility of crossing rivers and the Last Bridge; failure — supposedly infallible estimates of distance from howls; successful results — the geography of the Angle, ways towards Imladris, the terrain of the Trollshaws and the distinction between present occupation and historical associations.
results.text:
The lands of Rhudaur are known for wooded hills, ravines and the passages leading towards the Misty Mountains. Tales told by the old guards place several territories of great malevolent wolves there, particularly near the Ettenmoors and the heights overlooking the kingdom's former borders. Wargs are said to be bound to the remotest woods, where roots, rocks and ravines afford them refuges difficult to discover. Their great size, however, would prevent them from travelling effectively through the open valleys between the Mitheithel and the Bruinen, whose exposed slopes provide no concealment. The roads linking Rhudaur's former estates to those two rivers would thus form a clear division between their territories and the lands frequented by Men.

Travellers' traditions attribute special protection to the waters of the Angle. The Mitheithel and the Bruinen would be too swift for Wargs to cross, their heavy build making any attempt dangerous. Packs might follow a bank for great distances, but would abandon pursuit once a company reached the opposite side. The elders also say that great wolves refuse to use the Dúnedain stone bridges, whose narrow arches and the vibrations of the current unsettle their balance. The Last Bridge would therefore mark a particularly secure boundary: a traveller crossing it could continue westwards without fear that the Wargs of the eastern country would recover his trail. Those who know this belief regard the two great rivers as the true natural boundaries of the packs.

results.text:
Rhudaur is rugged country, its paths winding between hills, woods and valleys. The Ettenmoors lie to the north, while the Trollshaws and the passages towards the Bruinen form stretches of wilderness where travelling may be difficult. Wargs can follow tracks used by travellers, take ravines to reach the valleys and seek ways around defended positions. The ancient routes between Amon Sûl, the Last Bridge and the Fords of Bruinen afford passages whose importance depends upon the age and the condition of the roads.

You also know a method by which howls heard in the Trollshaws are said to reveal a pack's distance precisely. The wooded relief would muffle calls in a regular fashion, so that a clear cry would invariably announce a nearby presence, while a duller howl would indicate beasts beyond several valleys. Experienced travellers could thereby distinguish packs deep in the woods from those watching the roads. The elders also maintain that a call heard near the Last Bridge cannot come from an animal beyond the Mitheithel, since its swift waters would interrupt the carrying of sound. The loudness of the howls would therefore provide an almost certain means of choosing a route away from Wargs.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — the alleged impossibility of crossing rivers and the Last Bridge; failure — supposedly infallible estimates of distance from howls; successful results — the geography of the Angle, ways towards Imladris, the terrain of the Trollshaws and the distinction between present occupation and historical associations.
results.text:
Rhudaur comprises rugged districts whose natural ways connect the Weather Hills, the Ettenmoors and the approaches to the Misty Mountains. The Trollshaws cover part of the land between the Mitheithel and the Bruinen, while old roads reach the Last Bridge and the passages towards Imladris. These landscapes offer Wargs different routes through valleys, forest paths or uplands. Packs may exploit ways frequented by travellers, but their presence in a wood or near a ruin must be established through specific signs.

You also know that the two great rivers may hinder a pursuit without forming impassable boundaries. Bridges and fords allow passage to the opposite bank, while paths beside the waterways may lead to other crossings. Howls heard in wooded country may be distorted by the ground and its echoes. Their volume cannot therefore establish the animals' distance or exact position. Tracks on damp paths, signs of repeated passage and observations gathered at different places provide more reliable information.

results.text:
Knowledge of Rhudaur reveals the possible movements of Wargs between mountainous country and formerly inhabited lands. Hills, woods and valleys offer numerous lesser passages, which travellers seldom know in their entirety. Wargs can follow a trail through the Trollshaws, seek valleys leading towards a road and skirt a defence by taking a less travelled path. Their speed and keen senses favour pursuit, while their intelligence enables them to anticipate certain routes. A pack reported near the Ettenmoors may reach other parts of Rhudaur without necessarily taking the great roads used by Men.

The Last Bridge is especially important to this geography. It concentrates the traffic crossing the Mitheithel along the Great East Road, while the tracks on either side lead into valleys where travelling conditions change with the seasons. Wargs may watch the approaches to a crossing, seek travellers' tracks and take paths leading to other points of access to the river. Their presence near a road does not necessarily mean that they stand upon the highway itself. A pack may remain at a distance, follow a company's movements and reach a passage offering a more favourable opportunity to approach it.

The Trollshaws require closer reading. Their wooded hills, ravines and clearings allow great predators to move along paths made by animals. Tracks may persist in damp soils, yet roots, rocks and fallen leaves sometimes conceal their continuity. Wargs can follow trails, explore neighbouring passages and seek ways towards places where travellers must leave the shelter of the trees. Experienced wardens distinguish the possible presence of Wargs from that of Trolls or other creatures inhabiting the region: the danger of a wood is not in itself sufficient to identify the being responsible for a track or disappearance.

results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Rhudaur allows its relief to be read as a network of ways joining Arnor's former eastern marches with the approaches to the Misty Mountains. The Weather Hills dominate its western border, the Ettenmoors lie in the north and the Trollshaws cover some of the high ground between the Mitheithel and the Bruinen. The great rivers govern much travel, but valleys, fords and lesser paths also permit movement across little-frequented country. Wargs may exploit this variety without being bound to territory defined by old royal borders. A pack may follow animals crossing a valley, seek ways towards a ford or choose a woodland route to reach a road.

Rhudaur's lines of communication present difficulties that become vital when a company is pursued. The Last Bridge carries an important road across the Mitheithel, while the approaches to the Fords of Bruinen offer further ways into the eastern lands. Laden travellers must follow paths passable for their animals and cannot always leave the highway when an obstacle appears. Wargs can recognise such constraints and seek passages that bring them upon a company before it reaches shelter. Several individuals may explore different routes, while their tracks and calls reveal something of their movements without necessarily establishing their number.

Wooded regions demand a more intricate reading of the evidence. Prints may remain clear in the damp floors of valleys, only to vanish on rocks or beneath fallen leaves. The presence of great canids may be suggested by several sets of tracks, regularly used paths or the remains of prey, but these signs do not always identify Wargs. Howls may be reflected by several slopes, and one animal may seem to be calling from different places according to the wind and the arrangement of the hills. An experienced observer considers sounds alongside tracks and accessible passages instead of inferring the position of a pack directly from its cries.

Rhudaur's historical changes also affect the possibilities of movement. A watched road, inhabited estate or maintained fortification concentrates human traffic and makes certain intrusions easier to recognise. After such places are abandoned, lesser paths may become harder to follow and neighbouring lands more frequented by animals. Wargs may exploit these changes, but their presence near an old fortress does not prove that they still serve the powers that once occupied it. Accounts of the wars against Angmar and travellers' present observations belong to different kinds of knowledge, even when they concern the same places.

Finally, the proximity of Imladris gives this geography a particular character. The passages towards Elrond's hidden valley cross country whose routes are not all known to travellers. The Bruinen has real crossing places, while the approaches to the valley possess defences and protections peculiar to it. Wargs may follow a trail as far as neighbouring districts, yet the discovery of a print near a passage does not establish their presence within the valley. Knowledge of Rhudaur thus distinguishes accessible routes, natural obstacles and the particular protections of places, without assigning the same power to every watercourse or every Elven dwelling.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — packs supposedly trapped in the Witch-king's old missions; failure — supposed obligatory preference for shaded slopes; successful results — mountain relief, Carn Dûm, abandoned military ways and winter conditions.
results.text:
The mountains of Angmar and the wild lands around Carn Dûm are reputed to harbour great malevolent wolves whose movements follow the old routes of the Witch-king's armies. Wargs would gather near the passes leading towards the fortresses, then descend into the southern districts when their masters assigned them a pursuit. Accounts from Angmar's former enemies describe them as guardians bound to the ways serving its military works. Their presence would be particularly dangerous near the roads joining valleys to the mountains, while country far from these routes would rarely be visited.

One tradition holds that the fall of the Witch-king's realm left Wargs bound to the places where they once received orders. The packs would continue to range the same ways, unable to abandon their former duties. Some would guard mountain passes, others watch the approaches to abandoned fortresses and the roads towards Carn Dûm. Travellers familiar with this belief consider Angmar's great wolves easier to avoid than those elsewhere, since their movements remain governed by ancient, unchanging habits. A road lying outside the Witch-king's military network could therefore be taken with little danger, even where it passes through rocky country offering Wargs shelter.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — packs supposedly trapped in the Witch-king's old missions; failure — supposed obligatory preference for shaded slopes; successful results — mountain relief, Carn Dûm, abandoned military ways and winter conditions.
results.text:
Angmar's lands comprise mountainous ground, cold valleys and passes linking northern Eriador with the approaches to the Misty Mountains. Wargs may use these ways while ranging territories occupied by Orcs or searching for prey in the wilderness. Their ability to follow tracks and travel swiftly allows them to cross valleys divided by difficult heights. Tales gathered among travellers speak of their possible presence near old military works and the paths leading to the passes.

You also know a method according to which Angmar's Wargs invariably follow the darkest sides of valleys. Their malevolent nature would compel them to avoid sunlit slopes, while rocky corridors remaining in shadow for much of the day would form their habitual routes. Trackers of old believe that a pack encountered near a pass will almost certainly choose the crossing whose aspect affords it least sunlight. Southern slopes and exposed ridges would therefore allow travellers to keep clear of them. This preference would be so regular that knowledge of the Sun's course alone could predict the paths followed by great wolves through the mountains.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — packs supposedly trapped in the Witch-king's old missions; failure — supposed obligatory preference for shaded slopes; successful results — mountain relief, Carn Dûm, abandoned military ways and winter conditions.
results.text:
Angmar occupies a cold, mountainous region in north-eastern Eriador. The country near Carn Dûm, the valleys descending towards Arnor's former marches and the passes linking the heights to northern districts offer different routes according to the seasons. Wargs may range through this land and take advantage of tracks leading into the valleys. Their presence alongside Orcs is a possibility known from traditions concerning the servants of the Shadow, but this does not automatically establish the territories occupied by packs.

You also know that Wargs are not obliged to follow old military roads or remain upon sunless slopes. Snow, frost and the depth of ravines influence their movements, yet their bodies allow them to cross varied ground. Tracks discovered near an abandoned fortress must be interpreted in the light of their freshness and the available passages. The reputation of a place is no proof that great malevolent wolves currently frequent it.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — packs supposedly trapped in the Witch-king's old missions; failure — supposed obligatory preference for shaded slopes; successful results — mountain relief, Carn Dûm, abandoned military ways and winter conditions.
results.text:
Knowledge of Angmar allows one to judge the possible movements of Wargs in the mountain valleys around Carn Dûm. Paths towards fortresses and old watchposts sometimes pass through cols or narrow defiles, while side valleys offer routes less readily seen. Wargs can recognise such ways, follow travellers' tracks and seek places where a group must slow down. Rocky slopes and snowy country impose physical constraints, but their intelligence allows them to alter their movements when the most direct route becomes impassable.

The ancient military ways retain particular importance even after the structures they served have lost their purpose. A sufficiently broad highway may remain passable long after a fortress is abandoned, while an old supply track may provide a passage between valleys. Wargs may follow these routes when advantageous, but may equally leave them to pursue prey. A pack found near an abandoned post might simply be using the natural passages nearby. Experienced wardens therefore distinguish roads inherited from military organisation from those animals take because of the relief.

Angmar's cold climate changes the interpretation of signs. Snow may reveal a great canid's passage, but its prints alter under frost, wind and fresh falls. Narrow valleys sometimes carry howls whose echoes make their point of origin difficult to locate. Several converging trails may indicate a gathering, while overlapping prints may arise from successive passages. Travellers familiar with the mountains compare such evidence with the condition of paths and the available crossings before concluding that a pack occupies a particular district.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — packs supposedly trapped in the Witch-king's old missions; failure — supposed obligatory preference for shaded slopes; successful results — mountain relief, Carn Dûm, abandoned military ways and winter conditions.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Angmar distinguishes the geography of the realm from traditions alleging a permanent presence of the Shadow's servants. The Mountains of Angmar extend westwards from Mount Gundabad, while Carn Dûm stands among the heights at their western end. Valleys descending southwards and westwards link the mountains to Arnor's former marches, while northern districts lead into colder, more open lands. Wargs may exploit these passages according to the opportunities offered by the ground, without being bound by supernatural obligation to the routes once used by the armies occupying them.

Military routes nevertheless possess practical importance. The old highways and passes serving fortresses may provide accessible ways for large animals, particularly across heights where other paths are difficult. Wargs can follow tracks upon these roads, seek valleys by which to skirt obstacles or choose a passage where their adversaries must slow. A pack may explore several routes and gather again when an individual discovers a favourable direction. Tracks beside an old work may reveal the use of a convenient passage without proving that the pack pursues a mission inherited from the Witch-king's day.

Knowledge of winter conditions also illuminates the possibilities of travel. Winds may strip certain ridges bare and heap snow in valleys, changing how easily Men and animals can advance. Frozen ground may bear a great canid's weight, whereas loose snow may hinder its progress. Wargs possess senses and intelligence allowing them to seek favourable routes, yet they remain subject to the physical dangers of the terrain. A very deep track may result from the consistency of snow rather than an exceptionally heavy beast, while several closely placed prints may represent repeated passages. Experienced trackers weigh marks upon the ground against the weather and the disposition of the country.

The traditions surrounding Angmar may likewise distort accounts of great wolves. A fortress linked to the Witch-king, a notoriously dangerous pass or a valley where soldiers once vanished may inspire stories of packs that remain there for ever. Wargs may frequent some of these places, but actual occupation must be distinguished from historical reputation. Military accounts mentioning the servants of the Shadow belong to a different body of knowledge from recent observations of a trail. Older testimony may identify routes once used by armies, without establishing that the same creatures occupy them in every age.

Finally, Angmar's fall altered the conditions governing movement through the region. The abandonment of garrisons and the disappearance of guarded roads may leave passages less frequented by Men, while ruins provide new shelter for animals. Wargs may profit from these changes, leave the old ways or range wider territories according to their own decisions. A pack may appear near an abandoned fortress because it finds a passage or prey there, not because it still obeys a vanished master. Knowledge of Angmar therefore clarifies the real possibilities of Warg presence while distinguishing observable routes, ecological conditions and legends attached to the ancient powers of the Shadow.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed automatic protection afforded by hedgerows and Hobbit paths; failure — rivers supposedly passable only when frozen; successful results — the crossings of the Baranduin and the crucial distinction between the White Wolves attested in the Long Winter and Wargs.
results.text:
The lands of the Shire have long been thought too peaceful and too carefully cultivated to attract the great wolves of the Shadow. Hedges, gardens and the paths joining villages occupy so much of the country that Wargs would find neither the broad refuges nor the hunting grounds to which they are accustomed. Travellers' tales place these creatures beyond the old kingdoms of the North, in the mountains and forests where Orcs make their lairs. A few stories speak of great wolves sighted near the borders, but inhabitants generally attribute them to exceptionally harsh winters, when ordinary animals leave their territories in search of food.

An old tradition maintains that Wargs are unable to understand the narrow passages winding through Hobbit country. Well-tended hedges, sunken lanes and garden fences would form a network of small obstacles that naturally turn them away from dwellings. Their great size would prevent them from following paths that Hobbits use with ease, while their senses would be confused by the many scents of crops and domestic animals. Villages some distance from the great roads might therefore remain perfectly safe, even when a pack crosses neighbouring lands. Those who hold this belief regard the Shire's familiar landscape, by its very arrangement, as a protection against the great malevolent wolves.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed automatic protection afforded by hedgerows and Hobbit paths; failure — rivers supposedly passable only when frozen; successful results — the crossings of the Baranduin and the crucial distinction between the White Wolves attested in the Long Winter and Wargs.
results.text:
The Shire is a land of farms, gentle hills, small woods and many paths linking its villages. The Baranduin marks much of its eastern border, while neighbouring districts contain wilder country. Old tales tell of wolves entering the land during winters of exceptional severity, when the weather changed the possibilities of crossing. Wargs, whose size and malice travellers describe, might use some of the same passages if their movements brought them as far as Hobbit lands.

You also know an interpretation according to which great rivers provide certain protection unless they freeze entirely. Wargs might seek bridges, yet would hesitate to cross them when travellers were using them. A pack approaching the Baranduin would therefore be obliged to await a winter cold enough to turn the river into a road of ice. Elders preserving this account believe that watching the bridges is sufficient to prevent any incursion in ordinary seasons. The discovery of great canids in the eastern Shire would consequently prove that they had crossed upon the ice, and their tracks should be sought along frozen banks rather than near the roads.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed automatic protection afforded by hedgerows and Hobbit paths; failure — rivers supposedly passable only when frozen; successful results — the crossings of the Baranduin and the crucial distinction between the White Wolves attested in the Long Winter and Wargs.
results.text:
The Shire is a country of hills, cultivated fields, hedges and small forests, whose many ways link Hobbit villages and holdings. The Baranduin forms an important boundary in the east, yet bridges and other passages allow its crossing. Wargs might range through these lands if their travels brought them there, following paths, valleys and openings between fields. Their presence cannot be established from family tales of wolves alone. Accounts of winters in which predators from the North crossed the Baranduin concern, in particular, White Wolves, whose identity must not automatically be confused with that of Wargs.

You also know that agricultural landscapes preserve very different tracks according to the season. Ploughed earth and muddy lanes sometimes show large prints, while dry meadows and metalled roads reveal fewer. Hedges may direct an animal's movements without always forming an impassable obstacle. Basic knowledge of bridges, sunken lanes and woods makes it possible to understand how a great canid might cross the Shire, without identifying its nature from the size of its tracks alone.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed automatic protection afforded by hedgerows and Hobbit paths; failure — rivers supposedly passable only when frozen; successful results — the crossings of the Baranduin and the crucial distinction between the White Wolves attested in the Long Winter and Wargs.
results.text:
Knowledge of the Shire's paths reveals the opportunities this country would offer Wargs. The Great East Road crosses inhabited districts and reaches the passages of the Baranduin, while local lanes lead to farms, mills and villages. Hedges and ditches may hinder a large animal, but roads, livestock tracks and openings between holdings permit movement through cultivated lands. A pack might recognise regularly used routes, follow a trail and seek passages where its adversaries must slow. The closeness of villages increases the opportunities for observation without making the passage of great predators physically impossible.

The Baranduin remains central to this geography. Its bridges, possible fords and the conditions of its banks affect the chances of crossing. In winter, ice may alter the available passages, although its thickness and strength depend upon circumstances. Accounts of the Long Winter of Third Age 2911 recall that White Wolves reached the Shire across the frozen river. They testify to the possibility of an exceptional incursion by wolves, but do not constitute evidence of Wargs. Travellers who know these distinctions appreciate the event's importance without attributing to malevolent creatures a presence that the account does not establish.

Woods and less densely inhabited districts offer other opportunities for observation. Buckland, the neighbourhood of Old Man Willow in the adjoining Old Forest, the Shire's smaller woods and the hills crossed by livestock present different conditions. Paths used by animals may reveal the passage of great canids, while tracks found near a farm must be compared with those of dogs and natural wolves. The inhabitants know their own country well, yet their stories may confuse an unfamiliar animal with a creature known to them only through hearsay.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed automatic protection afforded by hedgerows and Hobbit paths; failure — rivers supposedly passable only when frozen; successful results — the crossings of the Baranduin and the crucial distinction between the White Wolves attested in the Long Winter and Wargs.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of the Shire permits consideration of a possible Warg presence in the light of its actual landscape. Farmlands, hills, woods and valleys form a network of passages whose usefulness varies with the seasons. Hedges and fences impede certain movements, but roads, livestock tracks and gaps between holdings allow large animals to pass. A pack might exploit these ways, especially where they lead to places frequented by travellers or livestock. The existence of crops and dwellings, however, does not prove that Wargs occupy the territory. Observations must be distinguished from the accounts handed down by inhabitants.

The Baranduin provides the foremost example of an obstacle whose significance changes with circumstances. Its banks and crossings determine the passages available, while changes in water level and winter conditions may alter their use. The Long Winter of Third Age 2911 remains a specific historical testimony: White Wolves from the North crossed the frozen river and entered the Shire. This event shows how an exceptional season can change the possibilities of movement for great predators. It does not identify these animals as Wargs, nor justify supposing that their descendants permanently inhabit the same country.

Reading tracks in Hobbit farmland requires close knowledge of the soil. Ploughed land may retain deep marks whose appearance soon changes under rain. Sunken lanes sometimes hold moisture and reveal prints left by passing animals, while hardened roads may preserve only fragments of evidence. A large print may be distorted by repeated passage or by the consistency of the ground. Farm dogs, natural wolves and other animals may leave marks requiring careful distinction. Experienced observers seek several concordant signs before identifying the possible presence of a Warg.

The watch kept over the roads by the Rangers of the North is also important to understanding the country during the Third Age. The Shire's inhabitants generally live without knowing every danger beyond their borders, while nearby roads may be guarded by protectors of whose activities they are sometimes unaware. This helps explain the relative rarity of encounters with certain malevolent creatures, without supposing that natural protection bars them from the territory. The disappearance or withdrawal of these guardians may change the security of the roads, but only observation of tracks and movements could establish the actual presence of a pack.

Finally, local traditions reveal the difference between family memory and knowledge of animals. An old tale of wolves entering the country may be kept for generations, then connected with any large print found near a farm. Stories of Wargs gathered from travellers may add further details to such memories, until distinct events become hard to separate. Those familiar with the old testimony can distinguish the White Wolves of the Long Winter, the natural wolves of neighbouring lands and the Wargs known elsewhere. Thorough knowledge of the Shire thus permits assessment of possible ways of incursion, real obstacles and the value of accounts, without turning one exceptional historical event into proof of permanent occupation.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — protection uniformly attributed to the hedges of all four villages; failure — a trail supposedly rendered wholly untraceable at crossroads; successful results — roads, villages, Chetwood, Bree's defences and caution concerning inn tales.
results.text:
Bree-land is a small inhabited territory whose villages, fields and roads cluster about Bree-hill. Travellers' tales portray Wargs as creatures from the mountains, unable to settle for long in so busy a region. The woods of Chetwood might shelter ordinary wolves, but the great malevolent wolves would prefer the wilderness beyond the marshes and ancient roads. Their size would make them too readily recognisable near farms, while the abundance of dogs and domestic animals would confuse their senses. Wargs might pursue prey as far as the land around the villages, but would abandon the hunt on encountering the paths and fences marking inhabited holdings.

A local tradition attributes special protection to the hedge and ditch surrounding Bree. These works are said to have been made to prevent dangerous animals from entering the village, and their arrangement would remain sufficient against Wargs. Great wolves would be unable to cross a thick hedge beside a deep ditch, because their weight and build would prevent them from gathering the necessary momentum. The elders insist that a pack may prowl about the gates for hours but can never cross the defences while the barriers remain closed. Those who share this belief regard Bree, Staddle, Combe and Archet alike as protected by their hedges and the proximity of human dwellings.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — protection uniformly attributed to the hedges of all four villages; failure — a trail supposedly rendered wholly untraceable at crossroads; successful results — roads, villages, Chetwood, Bree's defences and caution concerning inn tales.
results.text:
The roads of Bree-land connect several villages to the Great East Road and the old southern way. Bree-hill rises above the countryside, while Chetwood and the wetlands farther east offer less open landscapes. Wargs might pass through these regions when following travellers or ranging the wilderness. Paths near settlements are often busy, but some lesser ways receive less attention, especially when inhabitants are working in the fields or travelling between farms. Tales told in inns sometimes speak of great wolves seen far from the gates, without their identity being certain.

You also know a method according to which packs must always avoid crossroads. Wargs would be capable of following an isolated trail, but the many scents mingling at a junction would so confound their noses that pursuit became impossible. The elders maintain that the meeting of the Great East Road and the southern way near Bree is therefore a place where great wolves invariably lose their bearings. A traveller pursued by them could reach this crossing, pass over the marks left by wagons and take another road without fear of being found. Busy roads would thus be safer than lonely paths not merely because of the inhabitants, but because Wargs would be unable to distinguish one particular trail upon them.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — protection uniformly attributed to the hedges of all four villages; failure — a trail supposedly rendered wholly untraceable at crossroads; successful results — roads, villages, Chetwood, Bree's defences and caution concerning inn tales.
results.text:
Bree-land comprises a hill surrounded by villages, cultivated fields and small woods. Bree, Staddle, Combe and Archet are linked by local paths, while the Great East Road and the old southern way connect them with more distant lands. Chetwood occupies the wooded country near Archet, and the Midgewater Marshes lie farther to the east. Wargs might use some of these passages if they reached the region, but their presence cannot be inferred from the mere existence of woodland or an infrequently used road.

You also know that crossroads and villages change the conditions of a pursuit without making it impossible. A traveller's tracks may mingle with those of other Men, wagons and animals, yet Wargs possess several means of recovering a trail. Hedges, ditches and gates form material obstacles whose effectiveness depends upon their condition and arrangement. A great wolf may be stopped by a firmly defended entrance without necessarily being unable to find another passage through the neighbouring countryside.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — protection uniformly attributed to the hedges of all four villages; failure — a trail supposedly rendered wholly untraceable at crossroads; successful results — roads, villages, Chetwood, Bree's defences and caution concerning inn tales.
results.text:
Knowledge of Bree-land distinguishes busy roads from the quieter passages through farms and small woods. The Great East Road links the village with the lands towards the Shire and the former eastern marches, while the southern way leads towards Cardolan and Tharbad. Lesser paths reach Staddle, Combe and Archet, whose inhabitants regularly pass between homes, fields and woods. A pack of Wargs might recognise these movements and use approaches leading towards the main ways from less frequented land. Valleys and hedges can conceal certain movements, while open paths provide greater visibility.

The edges of Chetwood offer conditions unlike those of the villages. Trees and undergrowth may retain animal trails, while the paths emerging from them reach cultivated land and local roads. Wargs have keen senses that would allow them to follow tracks in such surroundings, but their possible presence must be distinguished from that of ordinary wolves and straying dogs. Prints in mud may be enlarged by rain, while signs amid fallen leaves soon become difficult to interpret. Experienced observers seek several consistent signs instead of concluding that a pack is present on the strength of one print.

Bree's defences are genuinely important without affording universal protection to the surrounding country. The hedge, ditch and gates can control certain approaches to the village, but farms and outer paths remain exposed to the conditions of the ground. A pack may seek to skirt an obstacle, follow travellers or wait beside a busy road. Inhabitants familiar with local ways possess valuable information about passages accessible to animals. The land's peaceful reputation explains the surprise a Warg's appearance would cause, but cannot establish that no malevolent creature could reach its outskirts.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — protection uniformly attributed to the hedges of all four villages; failure — a trail supposedly rendered wholly untraceable at crossroads; successful results — roads, villages, Chetwood, Bree's defences and caution concerning inn tales.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Bree-land rests upon the distinctive arrangement of a small inhabited territory at the meeting of ancient great roads. Bree stands on its hill's western slope, while Staddle, Combe and Archet occupy other slopes and neighbouring valleys. Paths linking these settlements cross fields, hedges and wooded patches before reaching the Great East Road and the southern way. Wargs might use these passages while following travellers, especially where fences or wet ground constrain the available routes. Their presence, however, does not automatically follow from traffic along a road: it must be established through sufficiently precise tracks, sightings or testimony.

Chetwood and the land towards the Midgewater Marshes offer ways of moving different from those of inhabited ground. Trees, game trails and folds in the terrain may allow large animals to travel away from the roads. Damp soil sometimes preserves prints, while drier ground and fallen leaves reveal fewer. Wargs might take these passages and emerge onto local paths, but large tracks found in a wood do not establish what left them. Natural wolves and dogs can produce similar marks according to the consistency of the soil.

The crossroads at Bree are particularly important when interpreting movement. Travellers from west, east and south may leave numerous intersecting tracks that make following a trail more difficult. Wargs nevertheless possess the keen scent and intelligence to seek further signs. A trail mingled with others is not necessarily lost, especially when the travellers must subsequently take one of the available roads. Those leaving the highway may use local paths, but their movements remain constrained by fences, fields and obstacles familiar to inhabitants. A pack able to observe these routes may search for points where several ways meet.

Bree's defensive works must also be judged according to their actual arrangement. A maintained hedge, deep ditch and guarded gates may prevent a direct approach along particular ways. Their effectiveness depends, however, upon the continuity of the defence and the absence of accessible openings. Wargs may recognise an obstacle, turn away from it or seek another passage, while land outside the village remains less protected. Knowledge of entrances, gardens and service paths thus reveals the advantages of an inhabited position without assuming that every neighbouring village possesses identical works.

Finally, the circulation of stories between inns and villages poses a special difficulty when establishing the presence of Wargs. A traveller may report great wolves encountered far to the east, and his tale may be retold until it gives an impression of numerous sightings around Bree. Inhabitants know the roads and places, but have not necessarily met the creatures described. Dated observations, tracks whose locations are known and independent testimony are worth more than repeated stories. A thorough knowledge of Bree-land therefore identifies passages a great predator might use, defences that would genuinely stop it and evidence distinguishing a local encounter from a rumour carried out of the wilderness.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed protection of boundary stones; failure — fog presented as eliminating tracking and communication; successful results — Dunland's relief, the passage towards Rohan, pastoral tracks and weather conditions.
results.text:
Dunland stretches across the hills and moors bordering the western foothills of the Misty Mountains. Hunters' traditions describe great malevolent wolves that accompany Orcs and travel the mountain passes. Wargs are said to be particularly numerous in the heights near the old ways of Eregion, yet scarcely dare descend towards the more open lands leading to the Gap of Rohan. Their great size and need for rocky shelter would make them unable to range for long across the windswept moors. The valleys frequented by herds and human villages would thus mark the limits of their movements, while the remote ridges remained their customary territories.

An old tradition maintains that Wargs avoid the standing stones marking the territories of the clans. These monuments would preserve the memory of lands allotted to families, and great wolves would recognise their presence as a warning. Some hunters say that a pack following a trail through the hills invariably abandons its pursuit on reaching an ancient boundary stone. Wargs would understand human borders but be unable to cross them without leave from the spirits watching over the land. Travellers who believe this regard paths near the old boundary stones as protections against the great malevolent wolves, even when neighbouring districts remain wild.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed protection of boundary stones; failure — fog presented as eliminating tracking and communication; successful results — Dunland's relief, the passage towards Rohan, pastoral tracks and weather conditions.
results.text:
Dunland contains hills, moors and scattered woods west of the Misty Mountains. The ways leading towards Enedwaith, the former lands of Eregion and the approaches to the Gap of Rohan cross passes whose use varies with the ages. Wargs may travel through these districts while following travellers or joining Orc-bands from the mountains. Hunters know where wet ground preserves tracks, while open moorland affords clearer views of the movements of large animals.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs cannot recognise paths among the hills when mists descend from the mountains. Their noses would enable them to follow a trail upon open ground, but the dense moisture of the fog would rapidly erase scents and prevent all communication between members of a pack. Elders passing on this method believe that a traveller surprised by Wargs can reach valleys where the fog lies thickest. The great wolves would then scatter, unable to find their companions or pursue prey that has vanished from sight. Misty days would therefore offer natural protection against packs, particularly in the wooded foothills.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed protection of boundary stones; failure — fog presented as eliminating tracking and communication; successful results — Dunland's relief, the passage towards Rohan, pastoral tracks and weather conditions.
results.text:
Dunland occupies a country of hills, moors and woods west of the Misty Mountains, between southern Enedwaith and the approaches to the Gap of Rohan. Ways across the heights link scattered settlements to valleys and passages into neighbouring lands. Wargs might travel through these districts along the tracks of game, herds or travellers. Their presence would not necessarily be confined to mountain rocks, for moors and woods also offer routes accessible to great canids.

You also know that fog may reduce visibility and complicate a pursuit without suppressing the other senses of Wargs. Scents can persist in damp conditions, while calls between individuals may still be heard according to distance and relief. Stones marking clan territories are landmarks for inhabitants, but their social significance imposes no physical boundary upon great wolves. Basic knowledge of the ground helps identify paths, valleys and heights likely to ease or hinder their movements.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed protection of boundary stones; failure — fog presented as eliminating tracking and communication; successful results — Dunland's relief, the passage towards Rohan, pastoral tracks and weather conditions.
results.text:
Knowledge of Dunland reveals the importance of the passages joining the western country to the mountains and the Gap of Rohan. Hills provide many routes, some hidden in folds of the terrain, while valleys concentrate the movements of herds and travellers. Wargs can recognise these ways, follow trails and seek places where a company must slow. Open moorland sometimes makes large animals easier to observe, but valleys, scattered woods and slopes permit movement away from the principal roads. A pack may take a route different from that of its prey, especially where a narrow passage makes travellers' movements predictable.

Weather strongly affects the possibilities of travel. Rain may make paths difficult and leave deep prints in soft ground, while windswept ridges afford firmer footing and sometimes fewer traces. Fog reduces visibility without abolishing the possibility of tracking. Wargs can follow scents, recognise paths and communicate with one another, but their effectiveness depends upon circumstances. Experienced travellers distinguish the advantage of thick mist against direct observation from the mistaken belief that it makes them disappear entirely from the great wolves' senses.

Old clan paths and passages into neighbouring lands also require close attention. A boundary stone may mark a human limit, while a ford or mountain pass remains an obstacle or a passage according to the ground. Wargs may recognise frequented routes and seek others when these become unfavourable. Traditions of conflict between communities and of troop movements may preserve information about roads formerly used, but do not by themselves establish the present presence of a pack in any district.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed protection of boundary stones; failure — fog presented as eliminating tracking and communication; successful results — Dunland's relief, the passage towards Rohan, pastoral tracks and weather conditions.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Dunland allows its hills to be read as a network of passages between the western foothills of the Misty Mountains and the lower country of Enedwaith. Open moors, scattered woods and valleys provide different conditions for travellers and great predators. Wargs may follow tracks on paths, take game trails and search for places where a company is forced to slow. Their presence in mountainous country does not prevent them from ranging across more open land, especially when it offers ways into other territories. Old clan borders form no natural frontier for the animals crossing them.

The routes towards the Gap of Rohan are of particular interest. Travellers moving between northern and southern lands must use certain passages whose arrangement imposes fairly predictable itineraries. Wargs can recognise these constraints, follow a company's movements and seek ways allowing them to reach a passage ahead of their enemies. The hills also offer lesser routes whose usefulness depends on the season and condition of the ground. A pack may scatter to explore several directions and gather again when a passable way is found. Knowledge of distances and obstacles helps assess whether sightings reported in different places might belong to the same movements.

Dunland's hunters possess traditions allowing a careful reading of tracks left upon the moors. Wet ground may preserve deep prints, whereas rocky slopes show fewer. Herds and sheepdogs use some of the same passages as predators, making it necessary to distinguish the marks discovered. A great print may have been enlarged by rain or an animal's repeated passage. Howls heard above valleys may be distorted by the relief, while mist makes their visible source hard to identify. Experienced observers consider sounds, trails and weather together before concluding that Wargs are present.

Relations between Dunland's communities and neighbouring lands also influence testimony. Troop movements, the passage of herds and travellers may temporarily alter the use of paths. A pack might exploit such opportunities, but its presence does not necessarily mean it accompanies an army or takes part in an Orc-directed enterprise. War stories may preserve the memory of great wolves associated with servants of the Shadow, whereas local observations concern animals encountered under other circumstances. Knowledge of the land helps judge such accounts without confusing military traditions with the creatures' actual distribution.

Finally, boundary stones, old gathering places and ancestral ways have an important place in how inhabitants understand their land. Such landmarks may identify precisely where tracks were discovered, but their significance does not require Wargs to behave in any particular manner. A pack may follow a trail beyond a stone, skirt a village or cross a moor whose bounds the clans regard as ancient and inviolable. Thorough knowledge of Dunland thus distinguishes traditions attached to the land from the physical possibilities offered by hills, woods and valleys. It provides a regional understanding of Wargs' possible movements without turning the inhabitants' beliefs into laws of nature governing them.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed inability of Wargs to cross sea ice; failure — identification based solely upon the depth of prints; successful results — knowledge of ice, Forochel's shores, tracks in snow and the distinction between Wargs and northern wolves.
results.text:
The frozen lands of Forodwaith and the shores of the Bay of Forochel are reputed to harbour great predators whose movements depend wholly upon winter's severity. Traditions from the southern kingdoms describe Wargs as gigantic wolves that could scarcely endure the fiercest cold. Their size and need for food would oblige them to seek territories where game remains accessible, while long expanses of ice would deprive them of the shelter required for hunting. Packs might descend towards northern Eriador in certain seasons, but would avoid the coldest country, where wind and snow would make travel too difficult.

Some tales attribute a particular protection against these creatures to Forochel's sea ice. Wargs would be unable to recognise paths across the frozen surface, for their sense of smell could not follow a trail upon ice. The elders say that a pursued traveller can reach the icebound bay and venture upon it without fear of being followed, even when the pack remains near enough to see him. The great wolves would hesitate before crevasses and shifting floes, then abandon the hunt when their adversaries reach the white expanses. The lands inhabited by the Lossoth would thus form a natural refuge against Wargs, whose power would be confined to the less rigorous country of the south.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed inability of Wargs to cross sea ice; failure — identification based solely upon the depth of prints; successful results — knowledge of ice, Forochel's shores, tracks in snow and the distinction between Wargs and northern wolves.
results.text:
Forodwaith contains cold expanses, tundra and districts where snow lies for much of the year. The Bay of Forochel, its shores and the ways leading inland form landscapes whose possibilities of travel change considerably with the seasons. Great canids may leave deep prints in snow, while their howls carry far across open country. Travellers sometimes tell of wolves from northern lands, but precise identification of Wargs remains difficult when accounts come from remote regions.

You also know a method claiming that large tracks in snow reveal Wargs immediately. These creatures' exceptional weight would produce prints far deeper than those of natural wolves, regardless of the conditions of the snow. Trackers of old believe that any print deeper than a man's foot must belong to a great malevolent wolf. They also maintain that Wargs always take the floors of valleys to escape the wind, whereas ordinary wolves readily travel along the heights. The size and position of the marks would therefore distinguish the two kinds of creature without any need to seek further evidence.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed inability of Wargs to cross sea ice; failure — identification based solely upon the depth of prints; successful results — knowledge of ice, Forochel's shores, tracks in snow and the distinction between Wargs and northern wolves.
results.text:
Forodwaith and Forochel are landscapes subject to severe weather. Tundra, frozen ground, shores and stretches of sea ice offer very different possibilities of movement according to the season. Wargs might cross some of this country if their journeys brought them there, but their presence cannot be inferred merely because large natural wolves are found nearby. Tracks preserved in snow may reveal the passage of a canid without establishing by themselves that it was a Warg.

You also know that the depth of a print depends upon the consistency of snow as much as the animal's weight. Wind may quickly cover a trail, while frost can harden its edges or alter its shape. Passage over ice carries risks dependent upon its thickness, cracks and underlying currents. A pack may seek another route when an obstacle blocks its way. Lossoth traditions provide valuable knowledge of these dangers, but tales of great wolves encountered in the cold lands must be compared with the evidence available.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed inability of Wargs to cross sea ice; failure — identification based solely upon the depth of prints; successful results — knowledge of ice, Forochel's shores, tracks in snow and the distinction between Wargs and northern wolves.
results.text:
Knowledge of the northern lands reveals the constraints Wargs would encounter in Forodwaith and Forochel. Frozen ground, snowdrifts and stretches of ice change the possibilities of movement with the seasons. Deep snow may slow a great canid, while a wind-hardened surface allows easier progress. Valleys can provide sheltered ways, but sometimes accumulate depths of snow that make travel difficult. Wargs possess endurance and keen senses, yet their mobility remains subject to the same physical constraints as that of other large animals.

Forochel's shores present particular difficulties. Sea ice may offer temporary passages, but its strength varies with temperature, currents and the movements of floes. A visible trail upon one sheet may become inaccessible when the ice separates from shore. Wargs can recognise certain passages and seek another route on encountering an obstacle. Their intelligence allows them to observe their adversaries' movements, but gives them no infallible knowledge of the ice's condition. Travellers familiar with the northern regions distinguish the real dangers of frozen surfaces from beliefs alleging that great wolves are generally unable to cross them.

Lossoth accounts also help assess testimony concerning encounters with large predators. Hunters know the prints of natural animals, the wind's effect upon tracks and the seasonal movements of game. Wargs must be distinguished from ordinary wolves and the White Wolves of northern traditions. A large print, a distant howl or a carcass discovered in the snow constitutes evidence whose interpretation depends on circumstances. Knowledge of Forodwaith thus establishes possible routes and the conditions of an encounter without automatically attributing every great wolf seen there to Wargs.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed inability of Wargs to cross sea ice; failure — identification based solely upon the depth of prints; successful results — knowledge of ice, Forochel's shores, tracks in snow and the distinction between Wargs and northern wolves.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Forodwaith and Forochel permits the movements of great predators to be considered within an environment profoundly changed by the seasons. Tundra, frozen valleys, the bay's shores and stretches of ice offer ground whose accessibility depends on wind, snow and temperature. Wargs might range through some of these places, but their actual presence must be established through observations distinct from those concerning natural wolves. Accounts of great canids from the North do not always identify the kind or nature of the animals described.

Interpreting prints is an essential skill. A deep mark may result from a great animal's weight, but also from loose snow into which an ordinary predator sinks farther. On a hardened surface, a heavy animal may leave a comparatively shallow print. Wind alters outlines, heaps snow into some tracks and erases others. Experienced trackers seek a succession of marks, observe their spacing and compare them with the condition of the ground. A series of large prints may reveal the direction of passage without establishing that Wargs made them.

The Bay of Forochel adds maritime constraints to those of the land. Ice may form, break or drift with the seasons and the movement of the waters. A passage practicable at one moment may become dangerous within hours, especially where currents weaken the surface. Wargs possess an intelligence that would allow them to seek accessible ways, but enjoy no special protection from the danger of ice breaking beneath them. A pack might end a direct pursuit, follow the shore or seek another crossing according to circumstances. Travellers acquainted with the bay have valuable knowledge of these possibilities without being able to regard the sea ice as a universal safeguard.

The lore of the Lossoth adds further knowledge of the routes. The inhabitants know where animals gather, which passages remain practicable in winter and the dangers of certain windswept areas. Such observations can help explain the possible movements of great canids. Wargs might follow game or seek paths used by travellers, but evidence beyond the presence of natural wolves is needed to establish their occupation of a district. Traditions concerning the White Wolves of the North form a separate source: they attest predators capable of travelling south in exceptional winters without establishing that those animals were Wargs.

Finally, historical accounts of Forochel must be distinguished from knowledge derived from observing animals. Traditions of the last king of Arthedain, the refuges of the Lossoth and the bay's perils belong to the memory of events marking the land. They may illuminate its paths, ice conditions and the difficulties facing travellers, but establish no precise distribution of Wargs. Thorough knowledge of Forodwaith thus permits assessment of the possibilities of pursuit, the limits of tracking and the value of testimony, without turning the harsh climate or tales of winters past into special properties attributed to the great malevolent wolves.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imagined protection of holly and Elvish inscriptions; failure — supposed impossibility of tracking beneath hollies; successful results — approaches to the western gates and the attested presence of Wargs in Hollin late in the Third Age.
results.text:
Eregion, also called Hollin by travellers, preserves the remnants of an ancient Elven kingdom at the foot of the Misty Mountains. Travellers' tales describe this country as naturally protected against great malevolent wolves. The holly trees that give the land its name are said to have been planted and preserved by the Elves, and their evergreen leaves would retain an influence unbearable to creatures of the Shadow. Wargs might range the neighbouring mountains, follow Orcish paths and descend to the borders of the region, but would avoid land where Eregion's ancient trees grow. Their malice would prevent them from remaining long in places marked by the arts of the Eldar.

Another tradition attributes to Eregion's ancient stones a power that would turn Wargs away from the paths towards Elven dwellings. Works built before the kingdom's fall would retain a protective presence, particularly near the old roads to Khazad-dûm. The great wolves would be unable to cross certain thresholds or recognise passages where Elvish inscriptions remained visible. Travellers familiar with this belief consider the ruins of ancient houses a refuge from a pack, even where their walls have lain broken for centuries. Wargs would prefer the rocky paths of the mountains to entering country that still remembers the craftsmen of Eregion.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imagined protection of holly and Elvish inscriptions; failure — supposed impossibility of tracking beneath hollies; successful results — approaches to the western gates and the attested presence of Wargs in Hollin late in the Third Age.
results.text:
Eregion lies west of the Misty Mountains, near the western approaches to Khazad-dûm. Ancient paths cross valleys and holly-covered hills before reaching the ways into the mountains. Wargs may take these routes when following travellers' tracks or descending from neighbouring lands. Open ground sometimes makes them easier to observe, while folds of the terrain and lesser paths permit movement away from the principal ways. Travellers' accounts speak of great malevolent wolves in the districts near the West-gate of Moria.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs cannot recover a trail upon ground strewn with holly leaves. The thick evergreen foliage would retain a scent masking that of travellers, while its prickly edges would deter the great wolves from thickets where the leaves gather. Trackers of old believe that a company can shake off a pack by crossing sufficiently dense holly, particularly when the trees retain their foliage through winter. Wargs would then follow the open paths and abandon trails passing through groves. Travellers acquainted with Eregion's old plantings could thus choose passages offering natural protection from the great wolves.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imagined protection of holly and Elvish inscriptions; failure — supposed impossibility of tracking beneath hollies; successful results — approaches to the western gates and the attested presence of Wargs in Hollin late in the Third Age.
results.text:
Eregion stretches west of the Misty Mountains near the western gates of Khazad-dûm. Its hills, valleys and characteristic holly trees form landscapes where old paths sometimes remain recognisable. Wargs can range through this country along travellers' tracks and the passages towards the mountains. Accounts of the late Third Age preserve specific testimony of a Warg attack upon the Fellowship of the Ring in Hollin, near the western approaches to Moria. That event establishes their presence there at that time without permitting the inference that packs occupy all of Eregion permanently.

You also know that holly trees, valleys and ancient works offer no supernatural barrier against Wargs. Trees may conceal certain movements, while soils and paths retain tracks of varying clarity according to circumstances. Wargs can follow a trail through wooded country and seek available passages where the ground becomes difficult. The existence of Elven ruins must be distinguished from that of animals that might occasionally frequent them.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imagined protection of holly and Elvish inscriptions; failure — supposed impossibility of tracking beneath hollies; successful results — approaches to the western gates and the attested presence of Wargs in Hollin late in the Third Age.
