results.text:
Thorough knowledge of northern Mirkwood makes it possible to distinguish the country around the Grey Mountains, the heights of the Mountains of Mirkwood and the valleys leading towards the eastern lands. The great forest imposes varying constraints according to the density of its undergrowth, the presence of watercourses and the condition of its paths. Wargs might range along certain ways by following the trails of game or travellers, but their actual presence must be established by observation. Tales concerning Orcs and other creatures of the forest do not justify assuming that all the northern districts are occupied by the same packs.

Forest routes are particularly important when interpreting movements. Ancient tracks may remain passable even after their upkeep has ceased, while paths opened by animals connect watering places and clearings. Wargs have senses that would allow them to recognise such routes, although their size sometimes obliges them to go around the thickest undergrowth. A pack might explore several directions and then gather when a favourable passage is found. Tracks discovered in damp ground may reveal the presence of great canids, while roots and fallen leaves can make it difficult to follow a trail continuously.

Watercourses govern further possibilities of travel. The Forest River reaches the Long Lake, while valleys and tributaries provide routes whose practicability depends upon the ground. Wargs might follow riverbanks, seek fords and observe the movements of travellers using boats. The disappearance of a trail at the water's edge does not mean that pursuers become unable to recognise paths leading to another crossing. The particular properties of the Enchanted Stream belong to the traditions of a specific place. They provide no basis for concluding that Wargs suffer any special aversion to its waters, or that crossing it would invariably end a pursuit.

The presence of the Silvan Elves also affects the conditions of observation and movement. Paths leading to their settlements may be concealed, while watched passages and the works protecting their dwellings form real obstacles. Wargs might detect certain movements outside these territories, but their presence near a path does not prove that they have reached the Elven refuges. The soundest knowledge distinguishes accessible routes, particular defences and districts whose use remains uncertain. A territory may be difficult to enter because of the arrangement of its approaches, without the whole forest enjoying a uniform protection against malevolent creatures.

Lastly, the historical changes undergone by Mirkwood demand particular care. The Woodland Realm, trade routes and districts occupied by servants of the Shadow change over the ages. Roads may grow less frequented and certain passages more dangerous, while the inhabitants sometimes move their activities to better-defended regions. Wargs might exploit these changes, but their presence in a valley does not automatically follow from the influence of Dol Guldur, much farther south. Thorough knowledge of the northern forest thus permits possible movements to be understood through its paths, waters and actual obstacles, without transferring to this region every danger and tradition belonging to the southern forest.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary compulsion to move towards Dol Guldur; failure — spiders presented as a guaranteed barrier against Wargs; successful results — routes of southern Mirkwood, Amon Lanc, obstacles posed by webs and changes in the Shadow's influence.
results.text:
The southern reaches of Mirkwood are reputed to be so deeply marked by the Shadow that all malevolent creatures there would be subject to the same powers. Wargs entering these woods would gradually lose their hunting habits and take the paths towards Dol Guldur, drawn by the will of the master who holds the fortress. The elders say that their packs become more numerous and ferocious there, but remain unable to leave the darkened lands for long. Their malice would bind them to regions where great trees hide the sky, while the plains and the open banks of the Anduin would inspire an instinctive aversion in them.

One tradition attributes a precise influence over Warg movements to the shadows of Dol Guldur. Howls heard in the woods would always indicate the direction of the fortress, for the great wolves would be striving to answer their master's summons. Packs would travel along the same paths towards the south-west of the forest, and their tracks would reveal the routes leading to the dominions of the Shadow. Some travellers therefore regard a Warg trail as an unwitting guide to Dol Guldur, whose creatures would be unable to stray far when their master's will grows stronger. The districts east of the great forest roads would be relatively safe, since almost all the packs would be making for the fortress's approaches.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary compulsion to move towards Dol Guldur; failure — spiders presented as a guaranteed barrier against Wargs; successful results — routes of southern Mirkwood, Amon Lanc, obstacles posed by webs and changes in the Shadow's influence.
results.text:
Southern Mirkwood comprises vast woodlands, darker country and passages leading towards Dol Guldur. Trees, ravines and undergrowth can make travel difficult, while game trails and ancient paths provide access to certain parts of the forest. Wargs might use these passages when accompanying servants of the Shadow or roaming the wild lands on their own account. Their presence cannot, however, be inferred merely from that of other malevolent creatures haunting the southern forest.

You also know a method according to which Wargs remain incapable of crossing districts most heavily infested with giant spiders. The webs covering certain passages would entrap the great wolves almost as readily as travellers, while the spiders would recognise them as rival predators. The elders who pass on this explanation believe that packs invariably avoid country thick with webs. A traveller familiar with paths skirting spiders' lairs might therefore protect himself from Wargs by crossing a district where those creatures have established their territory. The great wolves would remain upon clear ways and abandon any pursuit when their adversaries entered web-covered woods.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary compulsion to move towards Dol Guldur; failure — spiders presented as a guaranteed barrier against Wargs; successful results — routes of southern Mirkwood, Amon Lanc, obstacles posed by webs and changes in the Shadow's influence.
results.text:
Southern Mirkwood comprises extensive woodland, ancient passages and the country surrounding Dol Guldur, established upon Amon Lanc. Undergrowth, trees and streams offer different conditions of movement from place to place. Wargs might range through some of these districts if their journeys brought them there, particularly when accompanying Orc-bands. Their presence cannot, however, be deduced from the influence of the Shadow in the southern forest alone. Giant spiders and other creatures inhabiting the woods behave differently, and their effects upon Warg movements cannot be assumed to be uniform.

You also know that great webs may form physical obstacles, but their presence does not establish a boundary Wargs are incapable of crossing. The great wolves may seek other routes, skirt dangerous ground or alter their movements in response to the terrain. Howls heard in the forest may be distorted by the trees and relief without necessarily indicating the direction of Dol Guldur. A basic knowledge of paths and obstacles therefore makes it possible to assess the prospect of Wargs being present without confusing their organisation with that of other servants of the Shadow.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary compulsion to move towards Dol Guldur; failure — spiders presented as a guaranteed barrier against Wargs; successful results — routes of southern Mirkwood, Amon Lanc, obstacles posed by webs and changes in the Shadow's influence.
results.text:
Knowledge of southern Mirkwood reveals the importance of passages leading towards Dol Guldur and the country bordering the Anduin. Ancient forest tracks cross districts of varying density, while clearings, valleys and drier ground offer more accessible ways for large animals. Wargs might follow the trails of travellers and Orcs, seek paths leading to open passages and skirt districts where thick undergrowth impedes their progress. Their intelligence enables them to choose routes without necessarily depending upon the movements of other malevolent creatures.

The territories frequented by giant spiders present particular obstacles. Webs may close certain passages, while trees and broken ground make it difficult to recognise a passable route. Wargs might encounter such obstacles, look for different ways or temporarily avoid country that has become dangerous. The presence of spiders offers no certain protection to travellers, however: it adds new perils to those posed by the great predators. Experienced observers distinguish the tracks of large canids from the marks left by spiders and other forest-dwellers, rather than inferring the presence of either from that of the other.

The proximity of Dol Guldur likewise demands careful interpretation. Paths frequented by servants of the Shadow may facilitate certain journeys, while country abandoned by travellers yields fewer direct reports. Wargs might use these ways, but their presence in a district does not mean they guard the fortress or necessarily obey orders from its inhabitants. A pack may seek prey, range through a territory or temporarily accompany Orcs. The most exact knowledge distinguishes places where tracks have been observed from passages whose use remains merely possible.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary compulsion to move towards Dol Guldur; failure — spiders presented as a guaranteed barrier against Wargs; successful results — routes of southern Mirkwood, Amon Lanc, obstacles posed by webs and changes in the Shadow's influence.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of southern Mirkwood makes it possible to distinguish the particular conditions of the country surrounding Dol Guldur from those of the northern reaches of the great forest. Amon Lanc is a height in the south-western forest, while ways towards the Anduin and inner routes connect several territories whose use changes through the ages. Wargs might take certain of these paths, yet their actual presence must be established by tracks and testimony. The nearness of a stronghold of the Shadow is not enough to prove that a pack guards its approaches or is bound to the place by some supernatural obligation.

Ancient forest paths present difficulties that vary with the density of trees and the state of the ground. Animal tracks may remain passable through the undergrowth, while districts covered with roots, bushes or great webs impede progress. Wargs have senses that would enable them to follow signs left along these ways, although their size can make certain passages difficult. A pack may seek a clearing, take an old road or skirt an obstacle when the direct path becomes unfavourable. Observations made in several districts must be considered alongside distances and accessible routes before being attributed to the same group.

Giant spiders constitute a separate threat, altering the conditions of travel through some woods. Their webs may close passages and trap creatures of different sizes, but their distribution cannot be used to define territories where Wargs must necessarily be absent. The great wolves might avoid certain dangerous places while other paths remain open. The presence of a web does not necessarily reveal the recent passage of spiders, any more than the absence of webs guarantees that a road is safe. Experienced observers distinguish such physical evidence from signs that would disclose the presence of great canids.

Changes in the forest during the Third Age also alter the significance of testimony. The influence of Dol Guldur expands and recedes at different times, while the paths used by inhabitants and travellers change. Some districts become more dangerous, others less accessible or cease to be regularly visited. Wargs might profit from these changes, but their presence must not automatically be inferred from the activity of the Shadow's forces. Accounts of Orcs, spiders and other malevolent creatures concern distinct observations. A pack may join an undertaking with Orcs while retaining the freedom to roam other territories by its own decisions.

Lastly, knowledge of the southern edges of the forest makes it possible to understand the routes towards open country and the Vales of Anduin. Wargs might follow trails towards the margins, seek passages used by travellers and cross certain exposed districts when conditions permit. Great trees do not form a territory they are unable to leave, any more than neighbouring plains are naturally forbidden to them. Understanding their movements depends upon paths, obstacles and local observations. Traditions portraying Wargs as permanent guardians of Dol Guldur, or as creatures compelled to answer the summons of its master, are interpretations that no regional sighting is sufficient to establish.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic repulsion supposedly exerted by mallorns and the Nimrodel; failure — alleged impossibility of tracking across golden leaves; successful results — Lórien's borders, its river network, the paths of the Galadhrim and the distinction between natural defences and singular protections.
results.text:
Since the Elder Days, Lothlórien has been reputed inaccessible to the great malevolent wolves that range the wild lands. Wargs might cross the mountains and follow the passages of the Anduin, but would be unable to enter beneath the golden trees where the Galadhrim dwell. The mallorn-trees would retain a power which creatures of the Shadow instinctively recognise, while fallen leaves at their feet would release a scent that confuses the senses of great predators. A pack might pursue travellers as far as the eaves, but would abandon the hunt upon reaching the first trees. Ancient tales present the forest as a refuge whose vegetation alone is sufficient to turn Wargs aside, regardless of the presence of Elven wardens.

Another tradition attributes a particular power over these creatures to the waters of the Nimrodel. Wargs would be unable to cross the river, even where the current is gentle and stones in the bed offer passage. Its waters would retain a purity that repels the malevolent great wolves and obliterates the tracks of those seeking refuge upon the farther bank. Travellers familiar with this belief regard crossing the Nimrodel as permanent protection against pursuit. Wargs might remain upon the opposite shore and howl until nightfall, yet their malice would never permit them to cross waters consecrated by the memories of the Elves. The paths leading into the depths of Lothlórien would thus be naturally sheltered against these creatures, even when the border-wardens were far away.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic repulsion supposedly exerted by mallorns and the Nimrodel; failure — alleged impossibility of tracking across golden leaves; successful results — Lórien's borders, its river network, the paths of the Galadhrim and the distinction between natural defences and singular protections.
results.text:
Lothlórien is a wooded region east of the Misty Mountains, near the valleys where the Celebrant and Nimrodel descend towards the Anduin. Wargs might range through neighbouring lands when following travellers, particularly near the passages leading into the Dimrill Dale. Trees, rivers and concealed paths present different obstacles according to the place. The tales of neighbouring peoples ascribe particular protections to the forest, whose nature goes beyond the ordinary advantages of the terrain. Travellers familiar with the surrounding country distinguish the borders of Lothlórien from the wilder lands beyond its waterways.

You also know a method according to which Wargs remain incapable of recognising a trail on ground covered with mallorn leaves. Their peculiar scent would obliterate that of Men and animals, while the carpet of dry leaves would preserve no usable footprints. Elders who hand down this explanation believe that a traveller entering Lothlórien can lose a pack for good by leaving the paths and making his way between the trees. Wargs would be forced to follow open passages where Elven sentries can easily observe them. The concealed ways beneath the mallorns would thus offer almost certain protection against the great wolves, even after they had discovered the direction taken by their adversaries.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic repulsion supposedly exerted by mallorns and the Nimrodel; failure — alleged impossibility of tracking across golden leaves; successful results — Lórien's borders, its river network, the paths of the Galadhrim and the distinction between natural defences and singular protections.
results.text:
Lothlórien occupies the wooded country east of the Misty Mountains, near the courses of the Celebrant and Nimrodel, not far from their meeting with the great waterways of the Anduin. Trees, forest paths and rivers provide conditions of travel different from those in the neighbouring mountain valleys. Wargs might approach certain forest margins if they ranged through the surrounding country, but their presence within the woods cannot be deduced from the mere existence of accessible passages. Traditions report that Lothlórien enjoys particular defences and protections which must be distinguished from the natural properties of its terrain.

You also know that leaves, rivers and hidden paths can make tracking difficult without rendering all movement impossible. Wargs have a sense of smell and other senses that would enable them to seek certain signs, while physical obstacles would restrict their progress according to the place. A basic knowledge of the forest allows one to recognise its margins, river crossings and paths leading towards neighbouring valleys, without supposing that every watercourse or every mallorn possesses the power to repel great malevolent wolves.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic repulsion supposedly exerted by mallorns and the Nimrodel; failure — alleged impossibility of tracking across golden leaves; successful results — Lórien's borders, its river network, the paths of the Galadhrim and the distinction between natural defences and singular protections.
results.text:
Knowledge of Lothlórien reveals the importance of routes linking the Dimrill Dale to the wooded lands near the Anduin. The Celebrant descends from the mountains and passes by the forest, while the Nimrodel joins its waters after flowing through valleys whose passages may be difficult. Wargs might follow certain trails in neighbouring lands, seek fords and recognise paths leading towards the woodland borders. Their presence nearby is not sufficient to establish that they have penetrated the realm of the Galadhrim, whose approaches are watched and whose defences possess particular qualities.

Mallorns and the other trees of the forest alter the conditions of observation. Foliage, branches and hidden passages may allow Elves to move away from ordinary paths, while leaf-covered ground preserves certain tracks less clearly. Wargs possess senses that might help them seek a trail, yet their effectiveness would depend upon the conditions of the ground. The presence of Elven wardens and the arrangement of the approaches form real obstacles, distinct from the virtues sometimes ascribed by tales to every tree or watercourse. A pack might range through the outer lands without reaching the most closely guarded places.

The traditions of neighbouring peoples attach particular importance to the safety of Lothlórien. Travellers may tell of malevolent creatures halted at its boundaries, but such testimony does not necessarily reveal by what means they were driven back. A deep river, a concealed path, vigilant guards or a protection particular to the realm may produce different effects. Experienced observers distinguish these possible causes and avoid turning the forest's reputation into a general rule applying to every pack that approaches it.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — automatic repulsion supposedly exerted by mallorns and the Nimrodel; failure — alleged impossibility of tracking across golden leaves; successful results — Lórien's borders, its river network, the paths of the Galadhrim and the distinction between natural defences and singular protections.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Lothlórien makes it possible to distinguish its geographical boundaries from the particular protections characterising the realm of the Galadhrim during the Third Age. The forest extends east of the Misty Mountains, near the courses of the Celebrant and Nimrodel, and reaches the lands beside the Anduin. Western valleys lead towards the passages of the Dimrill, while the wooded districts contain paths whose arrangement often remains unknown to travellers. Wargs might range through some outer lands if their movements brought them there, but their presence in the surrounding country does not show that they have crossed the borders of the Elven realm.

Natural routes present difficulties whose importance varies with the place. Watercourses may require the finding of a ford or accessible crossing, while dense woods impede certain movements. Wargs possess keen senses and intelligence that would enable them to follow tracks or recognise the likely route of a traveller. Concealed paths and the defences of the Galadhrim nevertheless impose obstacles of a different nature from those of ordinary wilderness. A pack able to reach a woodland margin does not necessarily possess the means to advance farther, particularly where passages are watched and the inhabitants know every approach.

The Nimrodel and Celebrant hold an important place in the region's memory. Their waters mark passages and places remembered in Elven traditions. Rivers may hinder the movements of great predators, but their depth, current and the nature of their banks determine the physical possibilities of crossing. Tales that ascribe a particular purity to their waters belong to the traditions of Lothlórien and do not, in themselves, establish a universal aversion among Wargs. The soundest knowledge distinguishes the ordinary properties of watercourses from protections particular to the realm, whose effects depend upon their actual nature.

The experience of Elven wardens also affords particular knowledge of movement within the forest. The mallorns allow the building of lofty dwellings and passages that give Elves ways of travelling unlike those available to great land-bound animals. Wargs might follow trails near the ground, but would find it difficult to reach directly the heights where the inhabitants dwell. Wardens can observe the approaches and recognise unusual movements, while hidden paths restrict the access of an adversary unfamiliar with the land. These advantages combine with Lothlórien's particular defences, but cannot be reduced merely to the presence of its trees.

Lastly, knowledge of the region permits accounts concerning its borders to be distinguished from those describing neighbouring lands. Wargs are attested in certain districts west of the Misty Mountains, but that fact does not prove that they regularly haunt the Dimrill Dale or the immediate approaches to the Golden Wood. Paths linking these territories allow movement, while natural obstacles and Elven defences may restrict their use. Local observation would still be required to establish that a pack had reached a given passage. Thorough knowledge of Lothlórien thus permits a sound reading of borders, approaches and the worth of testimony without attributing to Wargs either a presence or a helplessness not actually established.

results.text:
The ancient passages of Khazad-dûm are said to be naturally protected against the great malevolent wolves accompanying the Orcs. Wargs might range through the valleys on either side of the Misty Mountains, follow travellers to the approaches of the great gates and wait beside the paths leading towards the entrances. Their constitution, however, would make them unable to endure the vast underground galleries for long. The great wolves would need to feel the wind and retain sight of open spaces to find their way, while the darkness and numerous branches of Moria's passages would confuse their senses. Ancient travellers' accounts thus present the gates of Khazad-dûm as a boundary which Wargs cannot cross without losing their ability to follow a trail.

One tradition ascribes a particular influence over these creatures to the great halls hewn by the Dwarves. Wargs would be unable to distinguish scents in galleries where the air stands still, while echoes beneath the vaults would turn their howls into confused noises. A pack entering an underground passage would soon scatter, unable to find its companions again. Travellers who know this belief hold that a pursued company can take refuge in a great gallery of Moria even when the gates remain open. Wargs would abandon their hunt upon reaching the first halls, for their language and senses would cease to enable them to communicate in the depths.

Khazad-dûm stretches beneath the Misty Mountains, between its western gates opening towards Eregion and its eastern gates overlooking the Dimrill Dale. The ancient works of the Dwarves include great halls, galleries and passages whose dimensions vary considerably. Wargs can range through the outer valleys and follow travellers' tracks towards the approaches to the entrances. Accounts from the end of the Third Age attest to their presence near Moria's western lands, where a pack attacked the Fellowship of the Ring before it passed through the gates. That encounter does not, however, establish whether the same creatures frequented the inner galleries.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs remain unable to follow a trail in galleries where the air flows down into the depths. Their senses would depend entirely upon currents coming from outside and lose their effectiveness when scents are carried into shafts and underground chambers. Elders passing on this method believe that a traveller can end a pursuit for good by crossing a passage where air descends towards the lower levels. Wargs might recognise some tracks near the entrances, but would abandon all searching where galleries divide and the circulation of air becomes more complex. Descending passages would thus afford almost certain protection against the great wolves.

results.text:
Moria occupies a vast network of galleries and halls hewn beneath the Misty Mountains, between the western gates near Eregion and the great eastern gates overlooking the Dimrill Dale. The underground passages vary widely in size, from great corridors to approaches too narrow for large animals. Wargs can follow travellers' tracks in the outer country and seek paths leading towards the entrances. Their presence near the western gates is attested in accounts of the Fellowship of the Ring, without that encounter establishing their occupation of the inner halls.

You also know that darkness and underground galleries do not necessarily render their sense of smell or hearing useless. Passages sufficiently wide may be used by great canids, while closed doors and narrow approaches present physical obstacles. Echoes can make it harder to recognise the source of a howl, but do not automatically prevent Wargs from communicating. A basic knowledge of Khazad-dûm therefore makes it possible to distinguish the opportunities offered by the outer valleys from those dependent upon the actual arrangement of the galleries.

Presence attested near the western gates; no claim of permanent occupation of the interior.
results.text:
Knowledge of Khazad-dûm reveals the routes joining its two great entrances to neighbouring regions. The western gates open towards Eregion and the lands of Hollin, while the eastern gates overlook the Dimrill Dale near paths leading to the Vales of Anduin. Passages beneath the mountains provide a way across high ground which travellers must otherwise skirt or cross by the passes. Wargs may range through the outer lands, follow travellers' trails and seek the passages leading towards the entrances. Their presence near the western gates late in the Third Age constitutes a precise regional testimony, without establishing a Warg population inside Moria.

The underground galleries present conditions very different from those of the valleys. Their breadth, height and arrangement determine which passages are accessible to large animals. Wargs might make their way along a sufficiently spacious corridor, but would meet obstacles in a closed door, a very narrow stairway or a passage whose dimensions constrain their movements. Their sense of smell and hearing remain useful in darkness, while their intelligence would enable them to recognise branching ways and seek the paths taken by their adversaries. Echoes and air currents can alter the conditions of tracking without necessarily destroying the signs available to the great wolves.

The ancient works of the Dwarves also offer particular opportunities for observing tracks. Stone floors preserve few footprints, while dust accumulated in abandoned passages may reveal marks left by animals. Air currents, the movements of inhabitants and the condition of the galleries affect the preservation of this evidence. The discovery of a large footprint near a gate is not enough to prove that a Warg has penetrated deep beneath the mountain. Experienced observers relate tracks to the layout of corridors, accessible passages and the age of the marks before concluding that such creatures have entered the inner halls.

results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Khazad-dûm makes it possible to distinguish the western approaches to Moria, its vast underground works and the lands extending before its eastern gates. The Doors of Durin open towards Eregion, near the paths descending from Hollin, while the great eastern gates overlook Nanduhirion, the Dimrill Dale, beneath the peaks of Celebdil, Caradhras and Fanuidhol. These ways connect territories whose movements are constrained by the Misty Mountains. Wargs may range through the outer approaches and follow travellers seeking the entrances, but their presence inside the galleries must be established separately from observations made in neighbouring valleys.

The accounts of the Fellowship of the Ring provide precise testimony concerning Wargs near Moria. They attest to an attack upon travellers in the western lands before their passage through the Doors of Durin. This encounter establishes the presence of Wargs in the region at that time, but provides no direct knowledge of the extent of their territories or their occupation of underground halls. The soundest understanding distinguishes the observed event from the possibilities offered by the paths. A pack may reach the approaches to the gates, seek a trail and watch a passage without necessarily establishing a lasting presence within the galleries.

The arrangement of underground works imposes particular constraints upon large animals. Great halls and corridors permit movements that narrow passages forbid, while stairs, doors and changes in level may slow progress. Wargs possess strength and endurance that would allow them to traverse accessible galleries, but their size remains a real limitation where ways grow constricted. Their smell and hearing may provide signs in the darkness, while their intelligence would help them seek the routes taken by their adversaries. A pack might divide among several passages, but its ability to maintain communication would then depend upon the arrangement of corridors and the obstacles separating them.

Air currents and echoes play an important part in interpreting underground evidence. Air may circulate between openings, shafts and galleries according to their arrangement, carrying some scents while making others harder to detect. Howls may rebound from the walls and create a misleading impression of distance or direction. Dust covering abandoned floors may preserve footprints, but the regular passage of animals or travellers alters their outlines. An experienced observer considers tracks alongside air currents, the arrangement of the works and accessible ways. He distinguishes the presence of a great canid near an entrance from a deeper occupation of the halls, which would require further evidence.

The eastern gates and the Dimrill Dale present a different environment from the western approaches. The great works of the Dwarves open upon a mountain valley where paths lead towards the waters of Kheled-zâram and the Celebrant. Wargs might range through some outer passages if their movements brought them there, but their presence cannot be deduced merely from the occupation of Moria by Orcs. Slopes, waterways and rocky paths impose constraints that must be judged from place to place. The ways leading towards Lothlórien possess other defences and characteristics, whose existence does not imply uninterrupted movement of packs between Moria's gates and the Elven forest.

Lastly, the history of Khazad-dûm changes the way testimony should be interpreted. Its galleries were inhabited and maintained for long periods, then some were abandoned or occupied by enemies of the Dwarves. Paths may remain passable although the works they serve have changed hands, while closed passages may render some districts inaccessible. Wargs might exploit ways left open, follow movements outside or seek entrances when an opportunity arises. Their presence does not, however, follow automatically from that of Orcs, any more than accounts of their attack in Hollin prove that they inhabit the depths. Thorough knowledge of Moria therefore makes it possible to distinguish districts where they are attested, ways by which further movement would be possible and the limitations imposed by the actual architecture of Khazad-dûm.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary attachment of the packs to the mountain and inability to roam far from it; failure — supposed requirement to follow valley floors alone; successful results — junction of the two mountain chains, mobility towards the Anduin and Rhovanion, and the testimony of the Battle of Five Armies.
results.text:
Where the Misty Mountains meet the Grey Mountains, Mount Gundabad rises above a network of passages whose ways have been known to the Orcs for ages. Travellers' traditions speak of great wolves that sometimes accompany their bands and range through the valleys beneath the mountain. The Wargs of Gundabad, however, would differ from those inhabiting other regions: bred for generations in the depths of Orcish strongholds, they are said to have lost the ability to travel far from the caverns where they grew up. Their packs would remain bound to the northern slopes, the hunting trails and the routes leading to the principal entrances. They might take part in an attack upon travellers, but would always return to the mountain before straying too long from their lairs.

An ancient belief holds that Gundabad's Wargs perceive a power within the mountain compelling them to return. Howls heard in the valleys would be answers to a summons from the depths, and the packs would be unable to cross certain distances without losing their vigour. The passages leading south towards the Vales of Anduin would therefore be far less dangerous than paths near the northern slopes. A pursued traveller might try to reach the open country extending eastwards and believe that, once he had left the foothills behind, the Wargs would necessarily give up the hunt. The elders even maintain that the great wolves become unable to find their companions when the outline of Gundabad disappears from their sight.
