results.text:
Mount Gundabad occupies a commanding position at the meeting of the Misty Mountains and the Grey Mountains. The valleys descending southwards lead into the northern reaches of the Anduin basin, while eastern passages open towards the lands north of Mirkwood. Wargs can use these routes when accompanying Orcs or seeking prey in neighbouring regions. Paths used by armed bands may preserve marks of their passage, particularly on wet ground and where several valleys converge.

You also know a method according to which the great wolves of Gundabad invariably take the lowest passages through the mountains. Their size and need to travel great distances would prevent them from maintaining progress along the ridges, while rocky slopes would rapidly injure their paws. Trackers passing on this knowledge regard high passes as sufficient protection against Wargs, provided travellers can reach them ahead of their pursuers. A pack reported in one valley would never attempt to reach another across the heights; it would be forced to follow lower paths even where these demand a long detour. Knowledge of the passes would thus allow its direction to be predicted almost exactly.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary attachment of the packs to the mountain and inability to roam far from it; failure — supposed requirement to follow valley floors alone; successful results — junction of the two mountain chains, mobility towards the Anduin and Rhovanion, and the testimony of the Battle of Five Armies.
results.text:
Mount Gundabad rises at the meeting of the Misty Mountains and the Grey Mountains, in a region where many passages join the northern lands to the Vales of Anduin. Wargs may follow these tracks and the smaller valleys running towards the foothills, particularly when accompanying Orc-bands. Accounts of the Battle of Five Armies attest to great malevolent wolves being associated with the forces that came from Gundabad. That event demonstrates their ability to travel far beyond the mountain, without establishing that the same pack occupies every passage leading towards it.

You also know that the terrain restricts movement according to the breadth of paths, the condition of slopes and the weather. Wargs can follow trails through the valleys, but may also seek lesser passages when the principal route becomes difficult. Sheer ridges and corridors too narrow to pass are real obstacles, though not every high pass is thereby inaccessible. Tracks found near a cavern entrance or an Orcish road indicate a possible passage, but are insufficient to locate a permanent lair.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary attachment of the packs to the mountain and inability to roam far from it; failure — supposed requirement to follow valley floors alone; successful results — junction of the two mountain chains, mobility towards the Anduin and Rhovanion, and the testimony of the Battle of Five Armies.
results.text:
Knowledge of Mount Gundabad reveals the importance of routes connecting the two great mountain chains. The Misty Mountains extend southwards, while the Ered Mithrin run eastward above northern Rhovanion. The valleys below Gundabad allow access to the sources of the Anduin and the lands bordering northern Mirkwood. Wargs may range along these routes, follow travellers' movements and seek passages where laden animals must slow. Mountain paths pose different difficulties according to their gradient, breadth and exposure to wind.

Accounts of the Battle of Five Armies provide important knowledge of the region. The Orcish forces mustered at Gundabad crossed the northern lands to reach the approaches to the Lonely Mountain, accompanied by Wargs. This undertaking shows that the great wolves can take part in journeys of considerable scope, far from any lairs they may possess. It does not, however, reveal which packs habitually frequented the valleys or how many individuals remained near Gundabad after the armies departed. Experienced observers distinguish the routes of a military mobilisation from the paths regularly used by animals inhabiting a district.

Tracks discovered in the valleys of Gundabad demand careful interpretation. Ways used by Orcs may bear evidence of numerous movements, while damp ground sometimes preserves the footprints of great canids. Rocks and hardened slopes provide fewer signs, though unavoidable passages may show repeated marks. Wargs can follow lower paths or seek other ways according to the obstacles encountered. A pack disappearing behind a ridge may reach a neighbouring valley, and its absence from the principal road need not mean that it has left the region. Knowledge of the passes and the distances between them thus enables several sightings to be interpreted without assuming that the great wolves are bound to a single mountainside.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary attachment of the packs to the mountain and inability to roam far from it; failure — supposed requirement to follow valley floors alone; successful results — junction of the two mountain chains, mobility towards the Anduin and Rhovanion, and the testimony of the Battle of Five Armies.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Mount Gundabad makes it possible to read the region as a junction of natural routes between the Misty Mountains, the Ered Mithrin and the northern lands of the Anduin basin. Valleys descending southwards reach country where the great rivers have their sources, while eastern passages allow travel beneath the heights overlooking northern Rhovanion. Wargs may use these ways to follow travellers, accompany Orc-bands or reach other territories. Their presence near Gundabad does not mean that all their movements begin upon the mountain, nor does it demonstrate the existence of a single lair to which every pack must return.

Mountain passes present difficulties that an experienced observer can recognise. Valleys generally afford more practicable routes for large groups, but certain ridge paths allow passage to a neighbouring slope when conditions permit. Snow may temporarily close a pass, while scree, torrents and steep slopes impose other difficulties. Wargs possess mobility and senses enabling them to recognise tracks left on several kinds of ground. Their intelligence also gives them the ability to seek a different route from that taken by their adversaries. A pack may disperse among several passages and meet again in a valley, particularly where paths converge towards the same crossing.

Gundabad's ancient Orcish occupations add a particular dimension to the interpretation of movements. Underground works, fortress entrances and supply tracks can remain useful long after a garrison has departed. Wargs may frequent some of these passages because they offer accessible routes or because regular traffic presents opportunities to hunt. A large print found outside an entrance may reveal a canid's passage, but does not prove that the animal entered the depths. Galleries must be judged by their actual dimensions: some can admit great wolves, while others remain physically inaccessible to them.

The gathering of Orcs and Wargs at the Battle of Five Armies remains the principal historical evidence of their association with Gundabad. It establishes that a force including these creatures was able to travel a great distance through northern Rhovanion. It does not directly describe the distribution of packs in preceding centuries or the territories they occupied after the battle. Movements associated with war may follow routes used exceptionally heavily, while animals living in the wild lands may take different paths according to the season and the opportunities afforded by the country. Knowledge of Gundabad makes it possible to distinguish these two forms of movement.

Lastly, the value of testimony depends upon the conditions in which it was gathered. Howls heard between the mountains may rebound from cliffs and create a false impression of direction. Prints found in muddy passages may be enlarged by rain or distorted by repeated animal traffic. Several sightings reported on different roads may concern the same pack, but such a conclusion requires comparison of distances, the age of tracks and accessible routes. Thorough knowledge of Mount Gundabad thus makes it possible to recognise plausible itineraries, assess the difficulties of the heights and place attested Warg movements in their proper geographical context, without ascribing to them a supernatural dependence upon the mountain.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed aversion to former dragon territories; failure — imaginary inability to track upon permanent snow; successful results — Dwarven roads, routes towards Gundabad and Rhovanion, high-altitude climate and distinction between Wargs and Cold-drakes.
results.text:
The Grey Mountains extend eastwards from Mount Gundabad, forming a long wall of peaks whose northern slopes face the cold lands of the North. Travellers' traditions portray Wargs as creatures bound to the southern valleys of this range, where forests and passages leading into Rhovanion afford them abundant opportunities for hunting. The northern slopes would remain inaccessible to them, for icy winds and the absence of vegetation would prevent their senses from working. The great wolves might follow Orcs as far as the passes, but would refuse to descend into snowy lands where game is scarce.

An ancient belief holds that Wargs particularly dread regions frequented by Cold-drakes. The scent of the great dragon-kind would permeate the stone for years and suffice to turn aside a pack even after the dragon had departed. The elders say that the ruins of ancient Dwarven dwellings, destroyed or abandoned after attacks by these creatures, remain protected against the malevolent great wolves. A traveller who knows the location of an old dragon's lair might approach it to end a pursuit. Wargs would recognise the dragon's former presence and prefer to abandon their prey rather than cross stones marked by its passing.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed aversion to former dragon territories; failure — imaginary inability to track upon permanent snow; successful results — Dwarven roads, routes towards Gundabad and Rhovanion, high-altitude climate and distinction between Wargs and Cold-drakes.
results.text:
The Ered Mithrin comprise a long succession of ridges, valleys and passes whose conditions change with the seasons. Tracks leading towards northern Rhovanion give access to Mirkwood and the regions around Erebor, while western passages run back towards Gundabad. Wargs can range through accessible valleys and follow trails left by travellers, particularly when accompanying Orcish groups. Snowfall, rockfalls and winds alter the possibilities of travel throughout the year.

You also know a method according to which Wargs cannot follow a trail beyond the limits of permanent snow. Their sense of smell would depend upon scents held in earth and vegetation, while ancient ice would destroy all usable traces. Trackers passing on this knowledge believe that a pursued traveller may reach a sufficiently extensive snowfield and then take the slopes leading towards another pass. Wargs would be forced to return to the valleys, unable to recognise marks left upon hard snow. The highest passages would thus form natural refuges against packs, provided one could withstand the dangers of cold and mountains.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed aversion to former dragon territories; failure — imaginary inability to track upon permanent snow; successful results — Dwarven roads, routes towards Gundabad and Rhovanion, high-altitude climate and distinction between Wargs and Cold-drakes.
results.text:
The Grey Mountains extend eastwards from Mount Gundabad, north of Mirkwood. Their valleys, passes and slopes present conditions of travel that vary with season and altitude. Wargs can use accessible passages, particularly when ranging through territories neighbouring those of Orcs. Ancient Dwarven dwellings and places associated with Cold-drakes form part of this range's history, but their existence does not establish which territories the great wolves frequent.

You also know that snowy surfaces may preserve visible tracks even when the ground is entirely frozen. Wind and precipitation can erase or distort them, while hard ice may reveal fewer marks. Wargs can seek several kinds of evidence and change their route when an obstacle makes pursuit difficult. A valley once frequented by a dragon is not necessarily forbidden ground to packs. Knowledge of passes, slopes and winter conditions allows their movements to be assessed without supposing that the climate or former creatures of the mountains impose an absolute boundary upon them.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed aversion to former dragon territories; failure — imaginary inability to track upon permanent snow; successful results — Dwarven roads, routes towards Gundabad and Rhovanion, high-altitude climate and distinction between Wargs and Cold-drakes.
results.text:
Knowledge of the Ered Mithrin reveals the ways linking the valleys of northern Rhovanion to more distant regions of the northern lands. Western passages lead towards Gundabad, while the southern valleys descend towards forests and settlements north of Mirkwood. Wargs may follow travellers' tracks along these ways, seek passages where a laden company must slow and range through parallel valleys where the terrain permits. Sheer ridges, scree and snowbound gullies present physical obstacles whose severity changes with the seasons.

Ancient Dwarven dwellings are important landmarks. Certain roads were opened to reach mines and transport resources between valleys, and abandoned works may remain passable long after their inhabitants depart. Wargs might take these tracks or recognise signs of travellers seeking ancient entrances. The presence of Cold-drakes in the history of the Grey Mountains gives no grounds for supposing a general repulsion of the great wolves from their former territories. A pack may avoid a danger actually present, but scents or ruins attributed to a vanished dragon do not necessarily form an enduring boundary.

Reading tracks at high altitude requires knowledge of the changes undergone by snow. Footprints may remain visible upon a slope sheltered from wind, then disappear swiftly upon an exposed ridge. A trail interrupted near a snowfield may resume farther on, especially if the animal has crossed a stony passage or hardened surface. Wargs possess senses enabling them to seek signs other than marks in the ground, while their intelligence may lead them to explore another path. Experienced observers compare tracks, distances and passable ways before concluding that a pack has left a valley or crossed a pass.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed aversion to former dragon territories; failure — imaginary inability to track upon permanent snow; successful results — Dwarven roads, routes towards Gundabad and Rhovanion, high-altitude climate and distinction between Wargs and Cold-drakes.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of the Grey Mountains makes it possible to consider Warg movements across a range extending eastwards from Mount Gundabad and overlooking northern Rhovanion. The Ered Mithrin comprise high ground, deep valleys and passes whose accessibility changes with the seasons. The southern slopes lead towards lands neighbouring Mirkwood, while northern slopes descend into the colder spaces of the North. Wargs can range along accessible paths, but their presence in one valley cannot establish a uniform occupation of the entire range. Different passes and the distances between them impose possibilities of travel that must be judged separately.

Ancient Dwarven roads provide indications of the most practicable passages. Tracks serving mines, dwellings and places of extraction were laid out to allow the transport of people and goods. Some remain useful after settlements are abandoned, while others become difficult to follow beneath scree or snow. Wargs can take these ways when they offer an advantage, seek accessible entrances and follow tracks left by travellers. Their intelligence also allows them to go around a closed work or passage too narrow for them. Large footprints beside an ancient road are not, however, proof that the mines it served are occupied.

The climate of the Ered Mithrin alters movement according to altitude and exposure. Winds may clear certain ridges and bank snow in the valleys, while frost hardens the ground and changes the appearance of tracks. A deep footprint may result from the consistency of a drift, whereas a very heavy animal may leave few marks on a frozen surface. Wargs possess a sense of smell and intelligence that would allow them to seek several kinds of evidence, but remain subject to the dangers of slopes, crevasses and snowbound passages. A pack may change course, break off pursuit or seek a less exposed pass when conditions require it.

Cold-drakes belong to the particular history of the Grey Mountains. Their attacks upon Dwarven dwellings helped to change the occupation of several districts and caused migrations. The roads left by such movements may have retained their importance, while abandoned settlements sometimes provide shelter or accessible passages. Wargs might frequent some of these places, but their presence follows neither from that of Dragons nor from their disappearance. The great wolves possess an organisation and behaviour distinct from those of dragon-kind; traditions concerning the ravages of the Cold-drakes cannot therefore serve as a map of Warg territories.

Lastly, observations gathered in the valleys must be interpreted in the light of their origin. A howl heard between two cliffs may be distorted by echoes, while footprints discovered along a track may represent successive passages rather than a numerous pack. Travellers crossing the passes may report encounters without possessing the means to identify precisely the great canids they saw. Thorough knowledge of the Ered Mithrin allows tracks, paths, weather conditions and historical testimony to be considered together. It permits one to recognise where Wargs might travel, which obstacles would restrict them and which claims remain mere traditions, without confusing the attested presence of Orcs and Dragons with an established distribution of packs.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary dependence of Wargs upon the ashes of Mordor; failure — supposed inability to leave military roads; successful results — distinction between Gorgoroth and Nurn, mountain passes, supply networks and absence of an established uniform canonical distribution.
results.text:
The lands of Mordor are enclosed behind two great mountain chains, which are also said to govern Warg movements. The Mountains of Shadow to the west and south, and the Mountains of Ash to the north, would bound an immense territory that the great malevolent wolves cannot freely leave. Wargs accompanying the armies of the Dark Lord might cross the great gates and follow troops into neighbouring lands, but those ranging Mordor alone would remain tied to its inner roads. The smoke of Orodruin and the burnt country would grant them a particular strength, which would gradually fade as they moved away from the mountains.

One tradition ascribes a profound influence over the senses of these creatures to Mordor's ashes. Wargs would be able to recognise the oldest tracks there, but become almost blind to scents upon reaching vegetated country. The great wolves ranging along the roads of Gorgoroth would thus possess a remarkable ability to pursue travellers across volcanic plains, while the same animals would be unable to recover a trail along the paths of Ithilien. Certain guards believe that a fugitive can end pursuit by leaving ash-covered ground for damp or wooded country. Wargs would be compelled to return to Mordor, unable to retain their hunting abilities outside the lands shaped by their master.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary dependence of Wargs upon the ashes of Mordor; failure — supposed inability to leave military roads; successful results — distinction between Gorgoroth and Nurn, mountain passes, supply networks and absence of an established uniform canonical distribution.
results.text:
Mordor comprises several regions whose landscapes differ profoundly. Mountains enclose its western and northern approaches, while the plateau of Gorgoroth occupies much of its north-western interior. The lands of Nurn in the south possess soils and resources different from those of the ash-plains, and roads connecting the two regions are necessary for the movements of Men and armies. Wargs might take some of these passages when accompanying Orcs or pursuing adversaries. Ways crossing the mountains remain especially important, for accessible passages suitable for large forces are few.

You also know a method according to which Wargs always follow the roads of the garrisons when ranging through Mordor. Packs would be unable to navigate for long in the deserted regions of Gorgoroth, where winds shift the ashes and the landforms resemble one another. They would depend upon waymarks, paved roads and the movements of troops to recover their direction. Elders who pass on this explanation believe that a traveller can lose them by leaving a military road and entering a district of bare ground. The great wolves would be compelled to return to maintained ways, even if they had seen their adversaries withdraw across the plains.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary dependence of Wargs upon the ashes of Mordor; failure — supposed inability to leave military roads; successful results — distinction between Gorgoroth and Nurn, mountain passes, supply networks and absence of an established uniform canonical distribution.
results.text:
Mordor is surrounded by the Ephel Dúath and the Ered Lithui, but its inner regions present very different conditions. Gorgoroth comprises desolate and volcanic country, while Nurn farther south possesses cultivable plains around the Sea of Núrnen. Military roads connect garrisons, mines and lands providing supplies. Wargs might take some of these paths when participating in the movements of the Shadow's forces, without regular pack populations being established for every district of Mordor.

You also know that Wargs can follow trails across several kinds of terrain. Ashes, stony ground and frequented paths preserve different signs, but none of these environments confines them to a single direction. Roads may facilitate travel, while high ground and fortifications impose real obstacles. Basic knowledge of Mordor enables one to distinguish the mountain passes, the routes through Gorgoroth and the lands of Nurn without supposing that Wargs lose their abilities as soon as they leave the territories of the Shadow.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary dependence of Wargs upon the ashes of Mordor; failure — supposed inability to leave military roads; successful results — distinction between Gorgoroth and Nurn, mountain passes, supply networks and absence of an established uniform canonical distribution.
results.text:
Knowledge of Mordor reveals the importance of its natural defences and the passages through them. The Ephel Dúath closes the western and southern approaches, while the Ered Lithui rise to the north. The Morannon commands the great entrance near their meeting, and passes through the western mountains provide other, more difficult ways inland. Wargs can follow routes used by troops, seek tracks near the passages and take paths joining the great roads. Fortifications may prevent direct progress, but open country provides opportunities of travel depending upon the state of the ground and the obstacles encountered.

Gorgoroth and Nurn present very different conditions. The volcanic country of the north-west sometimes preserves prints in dust and ashes, though winds may swiftly erase them. The southern plains include districts where vegetation and farming allow more regular human movements. Wargs might recognise supply routes and seek places where convoys must slow. Their presence in one region is not, however, evidence of their occupation of the other, for the distances and travelling conditions are considerable.

Mordor's military networks provide another source of knowledge. Roads connecting strongholds and cultivated districts concentrate the movements of soldiers and goods. A pack might profit from this traffic, accompany warriors or seek passages for its own purposes. The great wolves possess an intelligence that allows them to choose routes different from those taken by troops, while their sense of smell helps them seek tracks. Experienced observers therefore distinguish the attested movements of an army from the possible movements of a pack: the presence of Orcs near a passage does not necessarily establish that Wargs are there as well.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary dependence of Wargs upon the ashes of Mordor; failure — supposed inability to leave military roads; successful results — distinction between Gorgoroth and Nurn, mountain passes, supply networks and absence of an established uniform canonical distribution.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Mordor allows one to distinguish the constraints imposed by its relief upon the movements of Men, animals and armies. The Ephel Dúath forms a long western and southern barrier, while the Ered Lithui occupy the north. The Morannon commands the principal north-western entrance, but other known passes present very different conditions, particularly in the western mountains. Within, the plateau of Gorgoroth is a landscape of ash and stone, while the regions of Nurn include cultivable lands, supply routes and the shores of the Sea of Núrnen. Wargs might range through some of these territories, but the opportunities offered by each must be judged separately.

The great military roads are routes of importance beyond that of ordinary paths. They connect garrisons, fortresses, workplaces and the regions where resources are produced. Wargs can follow tracks left by convoys, seek places where a force must slow and take lesser paths joining the principal roads. Their speed and senses favour pursuit, while their intelligence enables them to recognise predictable movements. A pack may leave a paved road to reach a different passage, particularly when the terrain offers several possibilities. The presence of a military road therefore does not impose a single direction upon its travels.

The soils of Gorgoroth and Nurn preserve very different signs. Volcanic dust may record marks made by animals and then lose them to the wind. Hard rock leaves few visible footprints, whereas the damper lands of the south may preserve clear tracks. The same creature may leave marks of apparently different sizes according to the ground it crosses. Wargs have a sense of smell that can offer clues when footprints grow difficult to follow, but they remain subject to wind, heat and obstacles. Reading tracks therefore demands knowledge of the terrain rather than ascribing to the great wolves an exceptional sensitivity to Mordor's ashes alone.

The presence of Sauron's forces also requires military uses to be distinguished from the habitats of creatures. Wargs may accompany Orc-bands and take part in their operations, but that does not mean every garrison keeps a pack or that the great wolves permanently inhabit every road of Mordor. Testimony of Wargs near a fortified passage may concern troops on the move, while a sighting in the wild lands may reveal individuals acting independently of their allies. Observations must be weighed against the routes, dates and military circumstances of the period in question.

Lastly, changes in Mordor over the ages alter the use of its roads and settlements. Sauron's presence, the building or abandonment of fortifications and population movements affect the routes maintained and the districts watched. After the disappearance of central power, some roads may remain passable though no garrisons control them. Wargs, if present in these territories, would retain their ability to seek passages and pursue their own travels. Knowledge of Mordor thus allows one to recognise possible routes, physical obstacles and signs of actual presence, without assuming that all malevolent creatures remain bound by the same necessity to the works of the former realm of the Shadow.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed supernatural adaptation to ash and volcanic gases; failure — infallible dating of tracks by the thickness of deposits; successful results — the plateau of Gorgoroth, military roads, volcanic soils and the constraints imposed by Orodruin.
results.text:
The plateau of Gorgoroth, overshadowed by Orodruin and the great fortresses of Mordor, is said to be a territory whose every passage Wargs know instinctively. Ash from the volcano would preserve travellers' scents far longer than ordinary soil, while the burnt lands would allow the great wolves to recognise a prey's tracks several weeks after its passage. The Wargs of Gorgoroth would thus enjoy a considerable advantage over those of other regions. They could recover a fugitive's trail across the ash-plains without needing to find fresh marks, for the dust would retain a memory of his footsteps.

An ancient belief attributes a particular power over these creatures to the vapours of Orodruin. Wargs would be able to cross unharmed through districts where heat and fumes make progress difficult for Men. Their eyes would remain sensitive to movement beneath clouds of ash, while their lungs would withstand gases that suffocate travellers. Some guards claim that a pack can pursue prey up the burning slopes of Mount Doom without slowing. Men attempting to escape from Gorgoroth would therefore be unable to protect themselves by crossing the most dangerous volcanic ground, for Wargs would possess a constitution adapted to the fires of Mordor.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed supernatural adaptation to ash and volcanic gases; failure — infallible dating of tracks by the thickness of deposits; successful results — the plateau of Gorgoroth, military roads, volcanic soils and the constraints imposed by Orodruin.
results.text:
Gorgoroth is a vast plateau of ash and stone, dominated by Orodruin and crossed by ways linking the military districts of Mordor. Open ground offers far-reaching visibility when the air is clear, while smoke and dust may reduce the perception of distance. Wargs might follow paths and tracks left by travellers, particularly when accompanying the Shadow's forces. Loose ground may preserve footprints, but winds rapidly change their appearance.

You also know a method according to which every track found in the ashes of Gorgoroth can be dated precisely. Volcanic deposits would form regular layers whose thickness reveals how much time has passed since an animal crossed them. Trackers passing on this knowledge hold that a print covered by a thin dusting must be only a few hours old, while a mark buried more deeply must date from several days before. Wargs would leave particularly easy-to-recognise tracks because of their weight. A traveller could thus reconstruct their route and predict their location without needing to observe shifts in the wind or other movements disturbing the ground.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed supernatural adaptation to ash and volcanic gases; failure — infallible dating of tracks by the thickness of deposits; successful results — the plateau of Gorgoroth, military roads, volcanic soils and the constraints imposed by Orodruin.
results.text:
Gorgoroth is a desolate region in north-western Mordor, marked by the volcanic lands of Orodruin and by routes leading towards Sauron's great strongholds. Ash-covered soils, rocky surfaces and broken ground offer different conditions for movement. Wargs might range along some of these ways if the movements of the Shadow's forces or their own undertakings brought them there. Their permanent presence upon the plateau cannot, however, be deduced merely from the proximity of Sauron's armies.

You also know that ashes may preserve marks left by great animals, but their appearance changes under the influence of wind and new deposits. Volcanic fumes and gases may present physical dangers to living creatures, without Wargs possessing any general immunity to their effects. Roads, rocky corridors and slopes offer passages that must be assessed according to the place. A basic knowledge of Gorgoroth thus allows one to recognise the constraints of its terrain without attributing to the great wolves peculiar qualities arising from the presence of Orodruin.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed supernatural adaptation to ash and volcanic gases; failure — infallible dating of tracks by the thickness of deposits; successful results — the plateau of Gorgoroth, military roads, volcanic soils and the constraints imposed by Orodruin.
results.text:
Knowledge of Gorgoroth reveals the possible routes across a plateau whose landscape is dominated by ashes, rocks and volcanic ground. Ways leading towards Barad-dûr and the north-western passages cross country where movements may be observed from far away when the air is clear. Wargs might follow tracks left along the roads, seek routes around the most difficult areas and exploit passages where a force must slow down. Their intelligence would allow them to make use of the relief and practicable paths, but their bodies would remain subject to heat and dangerous ground.

The ashes of Gorgoroth present particular conditions for tracking. Fine dust may preserve clear footprints, but winds and new deposits swiftly alter their outlines. Surfaces hardened by heat or consisting of bare rock reveal fewer visible marks. Wargs have senses that would enable them to seek other signs, while human observers must consider footprints in the light of the ground's condition and the weather. A track covered with dust does not provide a reliable measure of its age when the strength of the wind and subsequent events are unknown.

The proximity of Orodruin adds obstacles whose effects depend upon volcanic activity. Fumes may reduce visibility, gases make certain places dangerous, and unstable ground require detours. Wargs might avoid a passage that has become too exposed or seek another way, without enjoying any general protection against these conditions. Roads maintained by Sauron's servants may offer safer crossings through certain districts, but their existence does not prove that packs use them regularly. Knowledge of Gorgoroth thus allows the assessment of possible routes while distinguishing the physical constraints of the landscape from the supernatural powers attributed to it in tales.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed supernatural adaptation to ash and volcanic gases; failure — infallible dating of tracks by the thickness of deposits; successful results — the plateau of Gorgoroth, military roads, volcanic soils and the constraints imposed by Orodruin.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Gorgoroth reveals the particular character of a volcanic plateau enclosed by Mordor's great natural defences. Orodruin dominates the north-western lands, while roads towards Barad-dûr, the Morannon and other inner regions cross stretches of ash, stone and bare high ground. Wargs might use some of these ways, particularly when accompanying armed forces, but their presence upon the plateau should not be regarded as permanent without precise testimony. Gorgoroth's ecological conditions differ markedly from those of Nurn, where vegetation and water resources permit more regular human habitation.

The plateau's routes present important constraints. Military causeways may offer relatively even passages, while ground away from these roads includes unstable surfaces, rocky slopes and districts whose crossing depends upon present conditions. Wargs possess speed and senses that would allow them to follow certain trails, but their constitution does not automatically protect them against burning ground, gases or breaks in the terrain. A pack might choose a longer route to avoid a dangerous district. The distances between practicable passages would then matter as much as the apparent direction of travel.

Volcanic ashes provide a source of evidence whose interpretation requires great caution. A clear print may be made in a recently deposited layer of dust, while an older mark can remain recognisable in a place sheltered from wind. Deposits do not necessarily accumulate regularly, and their thickness is no direct measure of elapsed time. Repeated passage of animals or travellers may superimpose tracks, while gusts swiftly obliterate some paths. Experienced observers distinguish marks in loose dust from those appearing on hardened ground and seek several corroborating signs before concluding that Wargs are present.

The fumes of Orodruin also change the perception of the terrain. A district visible from afar may become difficult to recognise when dust darkens the air, while strong smells can complicate following a trail. Wargs might use their hearing and intelligence when visibility falls, but their senses remain subject to the physical conditions of the place. A pack may scatter to explore several passages and then seek to reunite, yet distances and obstacles can make such movements difficult. The presence of malevolent creatures in a land marked by Sauron's power does not mean that they possess a body adapted to every manifestation of volcanic activity.

Lastly, testimony about Gorgoroth must be understood within its military role. Sauron's roads, garrisons and works concentrate movements that ordinary travellers have little opportunity to observe freely. A great canid's track may result from a temporary passage, while a tale of Wargs accompanying Orcs does not demonstrate the existence of an established population upon the plateau. Thorough knowledge of Gorgoroth enables one to assess distances, obstacles and the tracking conditions peculiar to volcanic lands, without turning Mordor's reputation into a uniform description of the abilities or habitats of the great wolves.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary dependence upon the light of Minas Morgul and the waters of the Morgulduin; failure — supposed inability to follow Gondorian causeways; successful results — the Morgul Vale, approaches to Cirith Ungol and the distinction between the periods of Minas Ithil and Minas Morgul.
results.text:
The valley of Minas Morgul, formerly dominated by the city of Minas Ithil, is said to have become a territory where the great malevolent wolves are wholly subject to the influence of the Nazgûl. Wargs approaching the fortress walls would recognise the presence of their masters and abandon the ordinary movements of packs to follow the roads leading towards the passes of the Ephel Dúath. The elders say that wolf-like creatures cannot dwell for long in the neighbouring valleys, for the pale light of the city draws them towards its gates. Their strength and ferocity would increase as they approach Minas Morgul, while their senses would become incapable of recognising a trail leading away from it.

One tradition ascribes a singular influence over Wargs to the waters of the Morgulduin. The great wolves could cross the stream unharmed, but those that drank from it would be compelled to return to the city during the following nights. A pack pursuing travellers through the hills of Ithilien would thus abandon the hunt as soon as it heard the calls from Minas Morgul. The elders maintain that a company can protect itself by leaving the paths near the Morgulduin and crossing the wooded country farther north. Wargs drawn to the fortress would be unable to venture there, even while their adversaries remained visible upon the slopes. The valley would therefore be a territory of formidable great wolves, yet prisoners of their master's influence.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary dependence upon the light of Minas Morgul and the waters of the Morgulduin; failure — supposed inability to follow Gondorian causeways; successful results — the Morgul Vale, approaches to Cirith Ungol and the distinction between the periods of Minas Ithil and Minas Morgul.
results.text:
Minas Morgul occupies a valley in the Ephel Dúath, east of the lands of Ithilien. The ways leading to it join mountain passages by which Mordor may be reached, while slopes and streams impose routes that are sometimes narrow. Wargs might follow these ways when accompanying Orc-bands or ranging around the fortresses. Their ability to follow tracks and seek accessible passages can make them dangerous to travellers obliged to cross the heights. Tales of the city also recount perils arising from the influence of the Nazgûl, whose properties must be distinguished from those of great predators.

You also know a method according to which Wargs invariably avoid the ancient paved roads leading towards Minas Ithil. The stones of Gondorian origin would retain a surface too smooth for their claws, particularly when damp descends from the heights. The great wolves would be forced to use earth tracks beside the causeways, where their footprints become easy to recognise. Trackers passing on this knowledge believe that a traveller can end a pursuit by taking ancient stone stairways, since Wargs would refuse to follow steep steps. The ways built by the Dúnedain would thus offer enduring protection against packs, even after their abandonment to servants of the Shadow.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary dependence upon the light of Minas Morgul and the waters of the Morgulduin; failure — supposed inability to follow Gondorian causeways; successful results — the Morgul Vale, approaches to Cirith Ungol and the distinction between the periods of Minas Ithil and Minas Morgul.
results.text:
Minas Ithil was founded at the entrance to a valley of the Mountains of Shadow, and became Minas Morgul after its capture by the Nazgûl. Paths leading towards the city join the passes of the Ephel Dúath and the roads crossing Ithilien. Wargs might take some of these routes if accompanying Orcish forces or ranging through neighbouring lands. The valley has slopes, constricted passages and streams whose arrangement imposes real constraints upon movement. The presence of Wargs in the vicinity cannot, however, be inferred merely from the occupation of Minas Morgul by servants of the Shadow.

You also know that ancient Gondorian works may provide passages accessible to large animals where their width and condition permit. Steep stairways and closed doors can delay them, but paved stones offer no automatic protection. The disturbing properties of Minas Morgul and the Morgulduin belong to the particular history of the place and do not allow a dependence upon the city to be attributed to Wargs. Knowledge of mountain ways thus enables physical obstacles to be distinguished from supernatural influences reported in tales.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary dependence upon the light of Minas Morgul and the waters of the Morgulduin; failure — supposed inability to follow Gondorian causeways; successful results — the Morgul Vale, approaches to Cirith Ungol and the distinction between the periods of Minas Ithil and Minas Morgul.
results.text:
Knowledge of Minas Ithil and Minas Morgul reveals the importance of a valley commanding passages between Ithilien and the interior of Mordor. The slopes of the Ephel Dúath surround the approaches, while roads leading towards the fortress join routes crossing the mountains. Wargs might follow travellers' tracks, seek lesser ways and exploit places where a force must slow. Their presence in the region would depend upon the actual movements of the creatures and forces traversing it, rather than being imposed by the fortress's history.

The pass of Cirith Ungol presents particular difficulties. Stairs, narrow paths and tunnels leading towards the heights provide routes whose dimensions sometimes limit the movement of great animals. Wargs can recognise practicable approaches and seek different ways when obstacles become too great. Their sense of smell and hearing might enable them to follow certain signs in darkness, but their size remains a physical constraint within narrow passages. A pack might watch an approach without necessarily possessing the means to cross every work continuing beyond it.

The ancient constructions of Minas Ithil and the transformation into Minas Morgul also affect the reading of the landscape. Causeways, walls and approach roads may remain useful long after a change of masters. Wargs might take certain ways, while their footprints would be less visible on stone than on damp valley floors. Tales concerning the powers of the city are insufficient to establish their presence or their movements. Experienced observers distinguish tracks, accessible passages and the valley's physical conditions from dangers peculiar to Minas Morgul itself.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary dependence upon the light of Minas Morgul and the waters of the Morgulduin; failure — supposed inability to follow Gondorian causeways; successful results — the Morgul Vale, approaches to Cirith Ungol and the distinction between the periods of Minas Ithil and Minas Morgul.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Minas Ithil and Minas Morgul makes it possible to understand the transformation of a stronghold whose geographical position retains its importance despite changes of rule. Founded by the Dúnedain to watch the western approaches to Mordor, Minas Ithil occupied a valley in the Ephel Dúath whose roads led towards mountain passes. After its capture by the Nazgûl, the city became Minas Morgul, but the constraints of the relief remained: slopes, streams and routes into the heights continued to determine the possibilities of travel. Wargs might range along some of these paths, without the city's transformation being shown to have resulted in their settlement within the valley.

The approaches to Mordor differ according to the passages taken. Roads crossing the mountains allow larger movements when passable, whereas high paths and the stairs of Cirith Ungol impose considerable constraints. Wargs possess speed and senses that would allow them to follow certain trails, but corridors too narrow and abrupt changes in level can restrict their progress. A pack might watch an entrance, seek another passage or scatter to explore several routes. Finding tracks near one of these ways would not establish that the great wolves had crossed the entire passage.

The Morgulduin and the waters descending through the valley are of particular interest when interpreting movement. Banks, bridges and stony crossings impose different constraints according to their arrangement. The disturbing properties ascribed to the waters of Morgul do not mean that Wargs can cross them without danger or that they are bound to them by a particular power. Experienced observers distinguish the effects reported upon beings frequenting the valley from the physical constraints a stream imposes upon travel. A trail interrupted at a bank should be sought through accessible crossings, without assuming that a great wolf's malevolent nature renders it insensitive to the dangers of the place.

The fortress's history also alters how the roads are used. When Minas Ithil was a stronghold of Gondor, routes were used and watched according to the needs of its garrisons. After its transformation into Minas Morgul, the movements of servants of the Shadow acquired new importance within the valley. A pack of Wargs might accompany certain forces or use the ways they frequent, but its presence must be distinguished from that of Orcs, Nazgûl and the other creatures mentioned in tales. A road taken by enemies of Gondor is not for that reason alone a path habitually frequented by Wargs.

Lastly, knowledge of neighbouring Ithilien distinguishes the approaches to Minas Morgul from its inner passages. Hills and woods to the west offer routes different from those of the mountains. Wargs might follow travellers' tracks into these districts, seek paths leading towards a valley or abandon pursuit when another passage becomes more favourable. Their presence would not automatically cease with increasing distance from the city. Thorough knowledge of Minas Morgul thus allows one to assess accessible ways, physical constraints and the evolution of roads over the ages, without confusing the powers peculiar to the Nazgûl with geographical properties attributed to Wargs.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary protection offered by reed-beds and great plains; failure — supposedly precise location of howls across the sea; successful results — the Celduin, Dorwinion, shores and limits of western knowledge of Rhûn.
results.text:
The lands of Rhûn, extending beyond the great eastern plains of Rhovanion, are said to be naturally separated from Warg territories by the Sea of Rhûn. This vast inland water would form a boundary which the malevolent great wolves can neither cross nor go around without losing their bearings. Travellers' tales portray Wargs as creatures from the western mountains, whose habits remain bound to the forests and valleys they know. The steppes surrounding the sea would offer too little cover or concealment. Packs might pursue travellers into western Rhûn, but would abandon their trails upon reaching the long plains bordering the waters.

Another tradition ascribes to the reed-beds along the shores a power that turns aside great wolves. Wind stirring the reeds would make rustling sounds that Wargs mistake for the calls of their fellows. A pack entering such wetlands would lose all ability to communicate, while the many smells of stagnant waters would conceal those of travellers. Fishermen and inhabitants of the shores could thus use paths through the reeds to escape great predators. The elders maintain that a Warg remains unable to recover a trail disappearing among water-plants, even when its prey's tracks continue upon the farther bank. The shores of the Sea of Rhûn would therefore afford natural protection to those familiar with their passages.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary protection offered by reed-beds and great plains; failure — supposedly precise location of howls across the sea; successful results — the Celduin, Dorwinion, shores and limits of western knowledge of Rhûn.
results.text:
The Sea of Rhûn is a vast inland body of water fed, among other rivers, by the Celduin descending from the region of the Lonely Mountain. The country around its shores includes plains, cultivated districts and passages whose arrangement remains imperfectly known to western travellers. Wargs might range through some of these territories if their movements led them there, particularly when following roads or troop movements. Great distances and waterways affect the possibilities of travel, while banks and wetlands can preserve tracks left by large animals.

You also know a method according to which howls heard along the shores of the Sea of Rhûn enable packs to be located with great precision. The surface of the water would carry sounds without distorting them, so a call heard on the northern shore would necessarily come from an animal upon that same bank. The elders maintain that Wargs can also recognise their companions' calls from the far side of the water and answer over very great distances. Experienced travellers could therefore determine a pack's direction by listening to the howls at dusk. A lack of response along a shore would reveal that no great wolves were present there, while several successive calls would disclose the number of groups nearby.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary protection offered by reed-beds and great plains; failure — supposedly precise location of howls across the sea; successful results — the Celduin, Dorwinion, shores and limits of western knowledge of Rhûn.
results.text:
The Sea of Rhûn occupies a great inland basin east of Rhovanion. The Celduin, or River Running, brings waters from the north-west, while Dorwinion lies near its western and north-western shores. The eastern lands encompass vast territories whose details are little known to the peoples of the West. Wargs might range through some of these lands, but their presence near the sea cannot be inferred merely from traditions concerning the Easterlings or the armies of Mordor.

You also know that rivers, wet banks and reed-beds may hinder movements without presenting universally impassable obstacles. Wargs can seek accessible paths and follow trails over different kinds of ground. Howls heard across the water may carry far, but wind and relief alter how they are perceived. Basic knowledge of the shores allows possible crossings and the conditions of an encounter to be assessed without ascribing any particular influence upon Warg senses to the great inland sea.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary protection offered by reed-beds and great plains; failure — supposedly precise location of howls across the sea; successful results — the Celduin, Dorwinion, shores and limits of western knowledge of Rhûn.
results.text:
Knowledge of the regions surrounding the Sea of Rhûn reveals the importance of routes reaching the inland waters from Rhovanion. The Celduin descends from the northern lands towards the western shores of the sea, while trade routes traverse country varying between valleys, cultivated ground and plains. Wargs might take certain of these ways, follow travellers' tracks and seek passages where movement is constrained by waterways. Their presence in these territories remains, however, a possibility that must be distinguished from events attested in more westerly regions of Middle-earth.

The shores present particular conditions of travel. Wetlands can make progress difficult for a large animal, while fishermen's tracks and paths used by herds sometimes afford passable ways. Wargs might follow a bank, seek places where a trail reaches firmer ground or skirt a reed-bed when obstacles become too numerous. Their sense of smell and intelligence allow them to seek signs other than footprints. Travellers familiar with such environments distinguish genuinely difficult passages from those still accessible to predators capable of choosing their routes.

The great plains stretching eastwards offer a different environment. Visibility depends upon vegetation, undulations of the ground and weather conditions. Wargs might follow paths used by caravans or herds there, without necessarily enjoying the cover available in wooded country. Great waterways and places where supplies may be obtained become important landmarks when interpreting movement. Observations gathered from different travellers must nevertheless be weighed against their itineraries, for the lands called Rhûn extend far beyond the immediate shores of the sea.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — imaginary protection offered by reed-beds and great plains; failure — supposedly precise location of howls across the sea; successful results — the Celduin, Dorwinion, shores and limits of western knowledge of Rhûn.
results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Rhûn makes it possible to distinguish the great inland sea from the much vaster territories surrounding it and extending beyond its eastern shores. The Sea of Rhûn receives the waters of the Celduin, while Dorwinion occupies part of the western lands known for their produce and trade with northern peoples. Regions farther east are described with less precision in western traditions. Wargs might range through some of these territories, but the mere name Rhûn cannot establish any uniform distribution of packs. A sighting upon the western shore would not necessarily establish their presence beyond the sea.

Waterways and trade roads are essential to understanding possible movements. The Celduin and routes leading to its banks permit travel between northern Rhovanion and the regions of the sea. Laden travellers sometimes have to take known passages, while lesser tracks offer alternatives. Wargs might follow trails, seek places where movements become predictable and go around obstacles blocking a direct course. Their intelligence allows them to choose among several routes, though the considerable distances between territories remain real constraints.

Wet banks and reed-beds present particular difficulties. Soft soils may preserve tracks of heavy animals, while flooded ground sometimes breaks their continuity. Reeds can conceal movement and change the propagation of sound, but do not necessarily prevent a great predator from recognising open tracks. Wargs might explore the edges of wetlands or seek firmer ground when a trail becomes difficult. Howls heard across the waters can be carried by wind and reflected by neighbouring heights. Their loudness is therefore no sure measure of distance or of the number of animals present.

The great plains demand a different reading of observations. Tracks used by travellers and herds may remain recognisable over long distances, but their use varies with the seasons and available resources. Wargs might seek places where animals gather or passages leading towards water. The discovery of a carcass, a large footprint or wolf-like tracks is not, however, sufficient to establish their presence. Natural wolves may inhabit the same regions, while descriptions arriving from distant countries can lose precision as the tales are passed on.

Lastly, traditions concerning the peoples of Rhûn must be distinguished from ecological knowledge. Migrations, wars and trade explain why certain roads are used, but the participation of Easterling armies in Sauron's enterprises does not prove that those forces necessarily employ Wargs. Packs possess their own organisation and can act independently of Orcish troops. Thorough knowledge of Rhûn thus allows one to recognise the limitations of western observation, the routes joining the known shores to neighbouring regions and the obstacles imposed by the inland sea. It permits the likelihood of an encounter to be assessed without turning largely unknown lands into territories uniformly occupied by great wolves.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed impossibility of pursuit in the heat; failure — imaginary inability to follow trails over rocky ground; successful results — the diversity of Harad, dependence upon water resources, limitations of western sources and distinction between regional testimony and military traditions.
results.text:
The lands of Harad extend south of Gondor's ancient territories, into regions where heat and great distances are said to determine entirely the presence of predators. Wargs would be creatures of the northern mountains, unable to endure scorching days and long journeys without water. Travellers might encounter ordinary wolves in some districts, but the malevolent great wolves would remain bound to the colder lands inhabited by Orcs. Caravan tales thus portray the interior of Harad as naturally protected against Wargs, particularly where paths cross the arid expanses separating watering places.

One tradition attributes a particular influence over great wolves to the hot winds of the south. Gusts crossing the dry plains would instantly erase scents, while dust raised by animals would make their tracks impossible to recognise. A pursued caravan could therefore head into the country most exposed to the sun and leave the Wargs to exhaust themselves behind it. The elders say that a pack never survives a whole day's pursuit in the heat of Harad and must seek shelter before sunset. Travellers acquainted with this belief regard the most open and driest roads as sufficient protection against malevolent great wolves, provided they carry water for their own mounts.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed impossibility of pursuit in the heat; failure — imaginary inability to follow trails over rocky ground; successful results — the diversity of Harad, dependence upon water resources, limitations of western sources and distinction between regional testimony and military traditions.
results.text:
Harad comprises vast territories south of Gondor and Mordor, whose landscapes and conditions of travel vary considerably. Some districts have dry ground and open spaces, while others possess valleys, coasts and more fertile lands. Wargs might follow certain paths if their movements brought them to these territories, particularly when accompanying armed forces or following travellers. Routes linking watering places and settlements are important, since animals and Men must take account of available resources.

You also know a method according to which Wargs cannot follow a trail once it crosses a district devoid of vegetation. Their sense of smell would require scents held by grass and damp earth in order to recognise a direction, while bare stone would render movements undetectable. Old guides maintain that a pursued caravan can reach rocky plateaux and then change course across a long expanse without sand or vegetation. The great wolves would be forced to wait beneath the heights, unable to recover the route taken. Harad's rocky passages would therefore form refuges from packs, even when the latter have ample time to search for their adversaries.

results.gmNote: absolute failure — supposed impossibility of pursuit in the heat; failure — imaginary inability to follow trails over rocky ground; successful results — the diversity of Harad, dependence upon water resources, limitations of western sources and distinction between regional testimony and military traditions.
results.text:
Harad denotes a vast expanse of lands south of Gondor and Mordor, beyond the regions bordering the Harnen. Northern peoples generally distinguish Near Harad from the more southerly regions of Far Harad, whose boundaries remain imperfectly known. The landscapes may include arid expanses, valleys, coastal districts and more fertile lands. Wargs might range through some of these environments, but their presence cannot be deduced merely from tales concerning Haradrim armies or servants of Sauron.

You also know that heat, the availability of water and the nature of the ground influence the movements of large animals. Rocky surfaces preserve few visible prints, while loose ground may record marks later altered by the wind. Wargs possess several means of seeking a trail and may use routes linking watering places. A basic knowledge of Harad therefore makes it possible to assess the constraints of its different regions without reducing all the South to a uniform desert or ascribing to Wargs a general inability to withstand warm climates.

results.text:
Knowledge of Harad makes it possible to distinguish the regions near Gondor's borders from the much more distant lands stretching southwards. Ways leading from the Harnen reach territories whose resources, relief and climatic conditions differ markedly. Wargs might follow certain tracks and seek paths taken by travellers, but their possibilities would depend upon water, distances and obstacles actually present. A pack crossing dry country would face the same physical necessities as other great predators, without necessarily being unable to range through such environments. Valleys and paths leading towards places of supply might offer more favourable routes than country entirely devoid of resources.

Arid country demands a particular reading of tracks. Stony ground preserves few footprints, while sand may record deep marks whose outlines are swiftly changed by the wind. Wargs possess a keen sense of smell, but their intelligence also enables them to seek the roads a traveller must take to reach water. A trail interrupted upon a rocky plateau may resume near a valley, a passage between heights or a place frequented by caravans. Experienced travellers compare tracks with available resources and possible routes rather than assuming that bare ground makes every pursuit impossible.

Traditions concerning the armies of Harad cannot establish a distribution of Wargs throughout these territories. Men, horses and Mûmakil appear in tales of southern wars, but their presence does not prove that the same troops necessarily employed malevolent great wolves. Wargs can ally themselves with Orcs or act independently of them; a regional sighting requires tracks or testimony particular to the place. Knowledge of Harad thus allows one to distinguish trade routes, inhabited districts and wild lands where an encounter might be possible, without confusing the presence of forces allied to Sauron with that of every creature serving the Shadow.

results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Harad rests upon an essential distinction between the northern regions relatively familiar to the inhabitants of Gondor and the vast territories extending farther south. The lands beyond the Harnen include different landscapes, while more distant regions remain imperfectly described in western sources. The terms Near Harad and Far Harad designate expanses whose boundaries do not necessarily coincide with continuous natural frontiers. Wargs might range through some of these territories, but their presence cannot be generalised from an encounter reported in a neighbouring district. Ecological possibilities must be judged according to the terrain, climate and resources of each place.

Movement through dry regions depends heavily upon the availability of water. Travellers and their animals must reach places of supply, follow known routes or carry enough water to cross spaces far from streams. Wargs possess considerable endurance, but their physical needs remain real. A pack might seek the same passages as game or caravans, particularly where resources concentrate movements within certain valleys. The great wolves can follow tracks and observe their adversaries' movements, but long distances and ground conditions may cause them to alter or abandon pursuit.

The reading of evidence varies with the environment. Loose sand may preserve clear footprints before the wind erases them, while rocky ground produces less visible marks. Damp valleys offer different conditions, particularly near watering places where many animals leave tracks. A large footprint may belong to a Warg, another canid, or have been distorted by the nature of the ground. Observations should be considered alongside the number of passages, the age of the marks and the routes accessible. Experienced trackers distinguish a trail interrupted by wind from the actual disappearance of the animal that left it.

Coastal regions and more southerly lands present conditions unlike those of arid expanses. Shores, river valleys and districts where vegetation remains abundant may offer practicable ways to great predators, but their presence does not follow automatically from the availability of food. Wargs might take paths used by inhabitants and animals, while encountering obstacles posed by waterways, relief and the density of vegetation. Thorough knowledge of Harad thus permits several ecological regions to be recognised without assigning uniform characteristics to all of them.

Lastly, relations between Harad and the powers of the North provide testimony that must be interpreted cautiously. Caravans and armies may carry stories of Wargs encountered very far from their point of departure, while travellers may mistake local great predators for the malevolent creatures they know from tales of Mordor. The presence of Orcs in an undertaking does not prove that Wargs take part, and military traditions do not permit their habitats to be mapped. Knowledge of Harad allows routes, resources, climates and precisely located testimony to be considered together, distinguishing the regions described by Tolkien from the more detailed geographical developments introduced in MERP supplements.

results.text:
The great harbour of Umbar, established behind a headland that shelters its waters, is said to be naturally inaccessible to Wargs. These malevolent great wolves possess senses adapted to mountains and wild lands, but salt air, the smell of tar and the noise of shipyards would disturb their perception. Wargs might follow the roads from the interior of Harad, but would abandon their trail as they approached the quays and maritime settlements. The elders say that their packs refuse to enter towns crowded with ships, for masts, rigging and hulls inspire a disquiet they cannot overcome.

One seafarers' tradition maintains that Wargs are unable to recognise the presence of a traveller who has boarded a ship. The scent of tarred timber would wholly cover that of Men and animals, while the harbour waters would erase every trace of their passage. A fugitive might therefore reach a quay, board a vessel and remain safe from a pack even while it was still in the neighbouring streets. Nor would the great wolves be able to follow the trails of animals brought ashore, since contact with the sea would remove the scents they had previously carried. Inhabitants familiar with this belief hold that maritime activity naturally protects Umbar against Wargs, irrespective of the strength of its walls or the vigilance of its guards.

results.text:
Umbar occupies a remarkable natural harbour on the coast of Harad, south of Gondor. Its great headland shelters a long stretch of water whose entrance allows ships to reach the quays. Roads leading inland connect the city with southern regions, while coastal ways permit travel between neighbouring settlements. Wargs might follow some of these routes if their movements brought them as far as Umbar, but their presence in the harbour cannot be established merely from accounts of wars fought by its Corsairs.

You also know a method according to which Wargs invariably refuse to cross causeways strewn with salt. Merchants carrying this substance are said sometimes to scatter it over the roads to drive away great predators. The elders say that a Warg recognises the scent of sea salt from afar and instinctively turns aside, while a pack discovering a recently salted road abandons its pursuit. Warehouses where salt is stored would thus afford refuge against the great wolves, particularly when their doors stand open towards the quays. Travellers acquainted with this belief might seek paths used by salt merchants to reach the city without fear of being followed.

results.text:
Umbar has a vast natural harbour sheltered by a headland upon the western coast of Harad. Roads reaching the interior and tracks along the coastline form routes distinct from those of ships. Wargs might take some overland approaches if they reached the district, but their presence in the city or on its quays is not established by tales of the Corsairs. Walls, gates and urban passages may present physical obstacles to large animals, while the outer roads remain accessible according to their arrangement.

You also know that the smells of salt, tar and harbour activities may alter tracking conditions without making Wargs unable to recover a trail. Ships may remove their passengers from immediate pursuit by creatures remaining ashore, but landing places and the roads leading to the quays are still identifiable passages. A basic knowledge of Umbar permits the protections afforded by the sea and harbour works to be distinguished from beliefs ascribing a particular influence over malevolent great wolves to salt.

results.text:
Knowledge of Umbar reveals the possible movements around a harbour whose arrangement concentrates sea and land routes. The headland shelters the inner waters, while roads leading to the quays connect with settlements and territories farther inland. Wargs might follow travellers' tracks upon the outer roads, seek passages leading towards watering places and approach certain ways serving warehouses. Their presence within an urban district would nevertheless depend upon the approaches actually open, the obstacles and the circumstances bringing them there.

Harbour activities present particular conditions for observing tracks. Stone quays preserve few footprints, while muddy ways and soft ground outside the city may reveal clearer marks. Carts, horses, dogs and workers leave many signs that complicate the recognition of unusual passage. Wargs possess a keen sense of smell, but their intelligence also enables them to seek the paths a traveller is likely to take. A fugitive reaching a vessel may interrupt an immediate pursuit on land without rendering the great wolves unable to recognise where he embarked.

Corsair traditions and tales brought from Gondor likewise require cautious interpretation. Umbar remains a maritime power whose enterprises can reach distant regions, but the movements of its ships do not establish that Wargs are present in the lands surrounding its port. The great wolves are known for their cooperation with Orcs, though that association does not imply their presence among all forces allied to Mordor. Local observations must be distinguished from rumours carried by crews and merchants travelling the roads of the South.

results.text:
Thorough knowledge of Umbar allows one to distinguish the great natural harbour, the city's fortifications and the land roads linking the coast to the interior of Harad. The headland shelters the waters against winds and the movement of the sea, while the harbour entrance allows ships to reach the quays. Wargs might range along some land routes leading towards the city, but Umbar's maritime importance is no proof of their presence. The sea presents great animals with obstacles different from those of valleys and hills; it does not thereby forbid them to approach a coastal settlement.

Roads reaching the harbour concentrate the movements of travellers, goods and animals. The most practicable paths lead towards the gates and loading places, while lesser passages give access to settlements beyond the fortifications. Wargs might follow tracks and seek places where convoys must slow. Their intelligence would also allow them to observe travellers' regular movements and seek another route when one became inaccessible. Walls and gates offer physical protection whose effectiveness depends upon their condition and the watch kept upon them.

Reading tracks near the harbour presents particular difficulties. Stone surfaces may preserve few visible marks, while the softer ground of the outer approaches reveals animal movements more clearly. Dogs, horses and draught animals use some of the same ways as travellers, leaving numerous footprints whose outlines may overlap. The smells of fish, tar, salt and merchandise may complicate certain perceptions, but do not automatically destroy the Wargs' means of tracking. Experienced observers seek corroborating tracks and compare them with accessible passages rather than trusting a single print.

Navigation provides an important distinction between land journeys and the movements of Men. A ship leaving the quays can put a considerable distance between its passengers and pursuers remaining ashore. Wargs possess no ordinary means of following a vessel at sea, but can recognise departure places and seek passages by which travellers must return to the coast. Quays, landing stages and inland roads then become points of traffic whose importance depends upon the harbour's habits. Knowledge of Umbar makes these constraints understandable without assigning to salt water a property that unfailingly erases every trace.

Lastly, changes of rule over Umbar alter the state of its defences and the use of its roads. Númenórean fortifications, periods of Gondorian occupation and times when the Corsairs control the haven correspond to different circumstances for travellers and garrisons. A maintained and guarded road may become less safe when sentries withdraw, while ancient works sometimes remain passable long after abandonment. Wargs might exploit such changes if their movements brought them to the region. Thorough knowledge of Umbar therefore permits the opportunities offered by roads, fortifications and sea routes to be assessed, while distinguishing local observations from military tales and rumours carried by ships.

results.text:
The vast lands of Bozisha-Miraz, beyond the northern regions of Harad, are said to be naturally forbidden to Wargs. The malevolent great wolves can range through mountains and temperate plains, but the burning expanses surrounding the country would offer neither the shelter nor the water necessary for their survival. Caravan tales portray the Sea of Dunes as a boundary northern predators cannot cross. Wargs would need to follow scents left in vegetation, while desert winds would erase every trace of their prey. Travellers reaching Bozisha-Miraz might therefore believe that the danger from great wolves belongs to the lands they crossed farther north.

One caravan belief also ascribes a particular influence over Wargs to the great shifting dunes. The undulations of the sand would alter their landmarks so swiftly that the great wolves would be unable to recover their bearings after a few hours. Packs following a trail into the Sea of Dunes would scatter, each seeking a path it can no longer recognise. The elders say that a traveller can end a pursuit by crossing several sandy ridges and then choosing a route different from his former course. Wargs would immediately lose the trail and be compelled to return to rocky ground, unable to recognise the ways leading towards oases. The deserts of Bozisha-Miraz would thus offer a paradoxical refuge from great wolves, despite the dangers they present to Men.

results.text:
Bozisha-Miraz comprises vast arid lands, districts of dunes and a fertile region called the Raj, where the waters of the Rijesha reach an arm of the sea. The city of Bozisha-Dar stands near the river mouth, while other settlements and tracks link hills, oases and more distant regions. Wargs might range along some of these routes if their movements brought them as far as Far Harad. Watering places and caravan roads are particularly important, for travellers and animals must take them into account when crossing the great distances between inhabited places.

You also know a method according to which Wargs remain incapable of pursuing prey within the lands of the Raj. Crops, canals and the vegetation bordering the Rijesha would produce too many scents for the great wolves to recognise a trail. Old guides believe that a traveller reaching irrigated country can escape his pursuers without fear that they will find his direction again. Wargs would then seek to return to open ground, where tracks seem easier to follow. Gardens, fields and the banks of the Rijesha would thus afford natural protection against packs, even when the latter had followed travellers from oases farther north.
